docs.title: 4.4.2. Conclusion
docs.text:
Version 2 is much more flexible than Version 1. If, in another year, the tax calculation algorithm remains the same, only the tax brackets and calculation constants change. All that is needed is to update the file [taxadmindata.json]. With Version 1, you have to go into the code to modify the tax brackets and calculation constants. However, it is likely that the people who need to change the values of the tax brackets and calculation constants do not have access to the algorithm’s code.

Version 2, however, has a flaw: the array [$taxAdminData] must be passed to all functions, and there is no guarantee that it actually contains all the expected keys. A typo in a key in the file JSON would not be detected until the calculation is performed. Version 3 will store this data in an object of class [TaxAdminData], whose properties are declared and typed.

docs.title: 25. Conclusion
docs.text:
This document has presented the PHP 8 language through numerous scripts and a common theme—the calculation of income tax—developed in 13 versions:

  • Versions 1 and 2 implement the calculation using functions and text files or JSON;
  • Version 3 writes it using classes, and Version 4 organizes it into layers [dao] / [métier] / [console], tested with [PHPUnit];
  • versions 5 through 7 retrieve tax data from a database ([MySQL]), then [PostgreSQL], and then from one or the other based on a simple configuration file;
  • versions 8 through 11 convert the calculation into a web service, with a console client: authentication, sessions, logging, sending emails to the administrator, cache [Redis], responses JSON and then XML;
  • Version 12 is a web application (MVC) that can respond in JSON, XML, or HTML, with its console client;
  • Version 13 protects the application files by making only the [public] folder visible from the web.

Along the way, we’ve covered most of what PHP 8 offers compared to PHP 7: strict typing and the types of parameters, results, and attributes; read-only classes and attributes, constructor parameter promotion, enumerations, property brackets, and the asymmetric visibility of PHP 8.4; the [match] expression, the null-safe operator, named arguments, and the pipe operator from PHP 8.5; errors that have become exceptions; the new API, [PDO], and [DOM]. We have also seen, each time, what PHP has dropped: none of the scripts in this document display a [Deprecated] message with PHP 8.5.

The server architecture of version 12 (a main controller, secondary controllers, the [métier] and [dao] layers, responses JSON, XML or HTML) is that of modern web frameworks, such as [Symfony] or [Laravel], some of whose components we have, in fact, used ([HttpFoundation], [HttpClient], [Mailer]). Readers who have completed this course now have the foundation to tackle one of these frameworks.

The JSON web service in version 12 can also have clients other than the console client written in PHP: a JavaScript client running in a browser, a mobile app, etc. This is the client/server architecture presented in the introduction to this document.

Training courses for Serge Tahé are available at https://stahe.github.io.

docs.title: 7. Exceptions and Errors
docs.text:
When a method of a class encounters an unrecoverable error (file does not exist, database not connected, network connection down), it does not display an error on a console (file, database) but throws an exception. Exceptions extend the [\Exception] class. In addition to exceptions, the internal operation of PHP also throws errors whose base class is [\Error]. Both classes implement the PHP and [\Throwable] interfaces.

PHP 8 has fundamentally changed error handling: many situations that produced a simple warning (and often an absurd result) in PHP 7 now throw an error that can be caught. We’ll see this as we go through the examples.

docs.title: 7.1. The Script Directory Structure
docs.text:
The scripts in this chapter are located in the [scripts-console/exceptions] folder:

php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions
├── exceptions-01.php
├── exceptions-02.php
├── ...
├── exceptions-11.php
└── throwables.php

docs.title: 7.2. The [\Throwable] Interface
docs.text:
The [\Throwable] interface is as follows (see documentation):

interface Throwable extends Stringable
{
    public function getMessage(): string;
    public function getCode(): int;
    public function getFile(): string;
    public function getLine(): int;
    public function getTrace(): array;
    public function getTraceAsString(): string;
    public function getPrevious(): ?Throwable;
    public function __toString(): string;
}

The roles of the interface methods are as follows:

MethodPurpose[getMessage]Returns the error message[getCode]returns the error code (an integer)[getFile]returns the name of the file where the object was created[getLine]returns the line number where the object was created[getTrace]returns the function call stack as an array[getTraceAsString]returns the call stack as a string[getPrevious]returns the previous (encapsulated) object [Throwable], or [null][__toString]returns a string representation of the object

Note that the [Throwable] interface extends the [Stringable] interface discussed in the chapter on classes. A class cannot directly implement the [Throwable] interface; it must derive from [\Exception] or [\Error].

docs.title: 7.3. Predefined exceptions and errors in PHP 8
docs.text:
The following [throwables.php] script displays the tree structure of the predefined classes that implement the [Throwable] interface. We use it to obtain an exact list—that of PHP 8.5—rather than copying it from documentation. The reader will not miss anything if they do not try to understand its code, which uses API reflection from PHP (the [ReflectionClass] class allows you to query PHP about a class: its name, its original extension, its interfaces, etc.) and a recursive function:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// displays the tree structure of predefined classes that implement the [Throwable] interface
// We limit ourselves to extensions that are always present in PHP 8.5:
// the Core, the standard library, the SPL library, the jSON library, and Random
$extensions = ["Core", "standard", "SPL", "json", "random"];

// the predefined classes of these extensions that implement [Throwable]
$classes = array_filter(
    get_declared_classes(),
    function (string $classe) use ($extensions): bool {
        $reflexion = new ReflectionClass($classe);
        return $reflexion->isInternal()
            && $reflexion->implementsInterface(Throwable::class)
            && in_array($reflexion->getExtensionName(), $extensions, true);
    }
);
sort($classes);

// recursive display of the child classes of the [$parent] class
function afficher(?string $parent, array $classes, string $indentation): void
{
     // the direct child classes of [$parent]
    $filles = array_values(array_filter(
        $classes,
        fn(string $classe): bool => (get_parent_class($classe) ?: null) === $parent
    ));
    foreach ($filles as $i => $fille) {
        $derniere = $i === count($filles) - 1;
        print $indentation . ($derniere ? "└── " : "├── ") . $fille . "\n";
        afficher($fille, $classes, $indentation . ($derniere ? "    " : "│   "));
    }
}

print "Throwable\n";
afficher(null, $classes, "");

Results:

> php throwables.php
Throwable
├── Error
│   ├── ArithmeticError
│   │   └── DivisionByZeroError
│   ├── AssertionError
│   ├── CompileError
│   │   └── ParseError
│   ├── FiberError
│   ├── Random\RandomError
│   │   └── Random\BrokenRandomEngineError
│   ├── TypeError
│   │   └── ArgumentCountError
│   ├── UnhandledMatchError
│   └── ValueError
└── Exception
    ├── ClosedGeneratorException
    ├── ErrorException
    ├── JsonException
    ├── LogicException
    │   ├── BadFunctionCallException
    │   │   └── BadMethodCallException
    │   ├── DomainException
    │   ├── InvalidArgumentException
    │   ├── LengthException
    │   └── OutOfRangeException
    ├── Random\RandomException
    ├── RequestParseBodyException
    └── RuntimeException
        ├── OutOfBoundsException
        ├── OverflowException
        ├── RangeException
        ├── UnderflowException
        └── UnexpectedValueException

Comments

  • line 13: the function [get_declared_classes] returns a list of all classes known at this point, whether predefined or not;
  • Lines 16–18: Only predefined (internal) classes are retained—those that implement the [Throwable] interface and belong to extensions that are always present in PHP 8.5 (line 9). Other extensions add their own exceptions (for example, [PDOException] for database access, which we will encounter later);
  • lines 24–36: a recursive function that displays the direct child classes of class [$parent], then the children of each of those, and so on. The function [get_parent_class] returns [false] for a class with no parent: the operator [?:] then transforms [false] into [null];
  • line 29: an arrow function (PHP 7.4), a shorthand form of an anonymous function reduced to an expression;
  • line 39: we start with classes without a parent: [Error] and [Exception].

The results show two families:

  • the [Exception] family: these are the exceptions thrown by libraries and application code. It includes:
    • [ErrorException], which converts a warning from PHP into an exception (we’ll use this at the end of the chapter);
    • [JsonException] (PHP 7.3), thrown by [json_encode] and [json_decode] with the [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR] option;
    • [Random\RandomException] (PHP 8.2), initiated by the random number generation functions;
    • exceptions from the SPL library (Standard PHP Library), a collection of classes and interfaces designed to solve problems frequently encountered by developers. They form two subfamilies:
    • [LogicException] and its derivatives: programming errors that can be resolved by correcting the code: invalid argument ([InvalidArgumentException]), value outside the expected range ([DomainException]), nonexistent method ([BadMethodCallException])...;
    • [RuntimeException] and its variants: errors that can only be detected at runtime: index out of bounds ([OutOfBoundsException]), unexpected value ([UnexpectedValueException]), capacity exceeded ([OverflowException])... ;
  • the [Error] family: these are errors thrown by the PHP engine itself. They include:
    • [TypeError]: a value is not of the expected type (function parameter, typed attribute, return value, operand of an operator, etc.). Its derivative, [ArgumentCountError], indicates an insufficient number of arguments;
    • [ValueError] (PHP 8.0): a value is of the correct type but has an invalid value (for example, a negative or zero length);
    • [ArithmeticError] and its derivative [DivisionByZeroError]: errors in arithmetic operations;
    • [UnhandledMatchError] (PHP 8.0): No branch of the expression [match] is suitable;
    • [AssertionError]: [assert] assertion failed;
    • [CompileError] and its derivative [ParseError]: syntax error in a file loaded by [require] or [include];
    • [FiberError] (PHP 8.1) and [Random\RandomError] (PHP 8.2): errors related to fibers and random number generators, which we will not use.

The two families are unrelated: a [catch (\Exception $e)] clause does not intercept a [Error] error. Only the [Throwable] interface links them.

docs.title: 7.4. Example 1
docs.text:
The first example, [exceptions-01.php], shows both a PHP warning and an error:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// display of all errors
error_reporting(E_ALL);
ini_set("display_errors", "1");
// code --------
$var = [];
// unknown key
print $var["abcd"];
// division by zero
$var = 7 / 0;
var_dump($var);
// array with fixed bounds
$array = new \SplFixedArray(5);
$array[1] = 2;
$array[4] = "foo";
// index out of bounds
$array[5] = 8;

Comments

  • Line 7: PHP is instructed to report all errors. The parameter for the [error_reporting] function is the error reporting level. It is a combination of the following constants (the main ones):
ConstantMeaning[E_ERROR]Fatal runtime error: the script is terminated[E_WARNING]Warning: the script continues[E_PARSE]Syntax error detected during compilation[E_NOTICE]Note: Something that might be an error[E_DEPRECATED]Use of a deprecated feature, which will be removed in a future version[E_USER_WARNING], [E_USER_NOTICE], [E_USER_DEPRECATED]The same levels, triggered by the code using the [trigger_error] function[E_ALL]all levels
  • the constant [E_STRICT], which no longer corresponds to any message since PHP 8.0, has been deprecated since PHP 8.4, as is the use of level [E_USER_ERROR] with [trigger_error]: to signal a fatal error, the code throws an exception;
  • line 8: the code is set to display errors on the console. In production, the opposite is done: errors are written to a log file and not displayed;
  • line 12: an attempt is made to access a nonexistent element of the array [$var];
  • line 14: a division by zero occurs;
  • line 17: an instance of the [SplFixedArray] class from the SPL library is created. This class allows you to create a fixed-bound array with integer indices;
  • line 21: an attempt is made to access a non-existent element of the array.

Results:

> php exceptions-01.php

Warning: Undefined array key "abcd" in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions/exceptions-01.php on line 12

Fatal error: Uncaught DivisionByZeroError: Division by zero in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions/exceptions-01.php:14
Stack trace:
#0 {main}
  thrown in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions/exceptions-01.php on line 14

Comments on the results

  • line 3: Accessing a nonexistent key in an array triggers a warning of level [E_WARNING] (this was a simple note [E_NOTICE] in PHP 7). This does not interrupt the script’s execution;
  • Lines 5–8: In PHP 7, dividing a number by zero triggered a [E_WARNING] warning and returned the value [INF] (infinity). In PHP 8, the operator [/] triggers an error of type [DivisionByZeroError]. Since it is not caught, it interrupts the script’s execution: this is a fatal error (Fatal error: Uncaught...). The message displays the call stack (Stack trace) at the time of the error;
  • the code following the division is not executed: the attempt to access a non-existent index in the array [SplFixedArray] does not occur. We’ll see this again in the following examples.

docs.title: 7.5. Handling Exceptions
docs.text:
The script [exceptions-02.php] demonstrates how to handle exceptions:

<?php

// strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// Displays all errors
error_reporting(E_ALL);
ini_set("display_errors", "1");
// wrap the code in a try/catch block
try {
    $var = [];
     // unknown key
    print $var["abcd"];
     // division by zero
    $var = 7 / 0;
    var_dump($var);
     // array with fixed bounds
    $array = new \SplFixedArray(5);
    $array[1] = 2;
    $array[4] = "foo";
     // index out of bounds
    $array[5] = 8;
     // validation
    print "ce message ne sera pas affiché\n";
} catch (\Throwable $ex) {
     // \Throwable is the interface implemented by all errors and exceptions
     // the exception is displayed
    print "erreur, message : " . $ex->getMessage() . ", type : " . $ex::class . "\n";
}

Comments

  • The script is the one presented in the previous paragraph. However, we have now enclosed the code that could cause errors within a [try / catch] structure: if the code in lines 11–24 causes (throws) an exception or an error, it will be handled by the [catch] clause in lines 25–29;
  • Line 25: The parameter of the [catch] clause is the type of exception or error to be handled. By setting the type to [\Throwable], which is an interface, we indicate that we want to handle any class instance that implements the [\Throwable] interface. Since all error and exception classes implement this interface, the [catch] clause handles all errors and exceptions here;
  • line 15: the statement that triggers the error. As soon as an exception occurs, control is transferred to the [catch] clause. The code that follows in [try] is therefore not executed;
  • line 28: the notation [$ex::class] returns the class name of the object [$ex].

Results:

> php exceptions-02.php

Warning: Undefined array key "abcd" in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions/exceptions-02.php on line 13
erreur, message : Division by zero, type : DivisionByZeroError

Comments on the results

  • Line 3: We see the warning at level [E_WARNING]. A warning is not an exception and is therefore not handled by the clause [catch]. We will see at the end of this chapter how to convert warnings into exceptions;
  • Line 4: The error message is written in the [catch] clause. This means an exception derived from [\Exception] or an error derived from [\Error] occurred. Here we see that this is the class [DivisionByZeroError]. The script completed normally.

docs.title: 7.6. Parameters of the [catch] clause
docs.text:
Let’s examine the following [exceptions-03.php] script:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// All errors are displayed
error_reporting(E_ALL);
ini_set("display_errors", "1");

// an array with fixed bounds
$array = new \SplFixedArray(5);
try {
     // Index out of bounds
    $array[5] = 8;
} catch (\Throwable $ex) {
     // Display error message
    print "Erreur 1 : " . $ex->getMessage() . " (" . $ex::class . ")\n";
}

try {
     // index out of bounds
    $array[5] = 8;
} catch (\Exception $ex) {
     // error message display
    print "Erreur 2 : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}

try {
     // index out of range
    $array[5] = 8;
} catch (\RuntimeException $ex) {
     // error message displayed
    print "Erreur 3 : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}

try {
     // index out of range
    $array[5] = 8;
} catch (\OutOfBoundsException $ex) {
     // error message display
    print "Erreur 4 : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}

try {
     // Division by 0
    intdiv(5, 0);
} catch (\Throwable $ex) {
     // error message display
    print "Erreur 5 : " . $ex->getMessage() . " (" . $ex::class . ")\n";
}

try {
     // Division by 0
    intdiv(5, 0);
} catch (\DivisionByZeroError $ex) {
     // error message displayed
    print "Erreur 6 : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}

try {
     // division by 0
    intdiv(5, 0);
} catch (\ArithmeticError $ex) {
     // display error message
    print "Erreur 7 : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}

try {
     // division by 0
    intdiv(5, 0);
} catch (\Error $ex) {
     // display error message
    print "Erreur 8 : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}

try {
     // division by 0
    intdiv(5, 0);
} catch (\Exception $ex) {
     // display error message
    print "Erreur 9 : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}

Comments

  • Lines 11–41: Four different ways to handle the exception generated by using an incorrect index with class [\SplFixedArray]. The execution shows that this error generates an exception of type [OutOfBoundsException] (line 2 of the results). In course PHP 7 (and again in PHP 8.3), it was a [RuntimeException] exception. The change did not break the existing code since the [OutOfBoundsException] class derives from the [RuntimeException] class;
    • line 15: handles an error of type [\Throwable]. This is valid because the type [OutOfBoundsException] derives from the type [\Exception], which implements the interface [\Throwable];
    • line 23: handles an error of type [\Exception]. This is valid because the type [OutOfBoundsException] derives from the type [\Exception];
    • line 31: handles an error of type [\RuntimeException]. This is valid because the type [OutOfBoundsException] derives from the type [\RuntimeException]. This is a good choice: the code works regardless of the version of PHP;
    • line 39: handles the exact type of the exception generated;
  • lines 46–81: 5 different ways to handle the error generated by the function [intdiv] when a divisor equal to 0 is passed to it. The function [intdiv(int $dividend, int $divisor): int] performs the integer division [$dividend / $divisor]. When the divisor is zero, error [\DivisionByZeroError] is thrown;
    • line 47: any error implementing the [\Throwable] interface is caught. This is valid;
    • line 55: the exact type of the error is intercepted; this is the preferred method;
    • line 63: the type [\ArithmeticError] is caught. This is valid since the class [DivisionByZeroError] extends the class [ArithmeticError];
    • Line 71: The type [\Error] is intercepted. This is valid because the class [DivisionByZeroError] derives from the class [Error];
    • Line 79: The type [\Exception] is intercepted. This is invalid because the class [DivisionByZeroError] has no relationship with the class [\Exception].

Results:

> php exceptions-03.php
Erreur 1 : Index invalid or out of range (OutOfBoundsException)
Erreur 2 : Index invalid or out of range
Erreur 3 : Index invalid or out of range
Erreur 4 : Index invalid or out of range
Erreur 5 : Division by zero (DivisionByZeroError)
Erreur 6 : Division by zero
Erreur 7 : Division by zero
Erreur 8 : Division by zero

Fatal error: Uncaught DivisionByZeroError: Division by zero in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions/exceptions-03.php:78
Stack trace:
#0 .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions/exceptions-03.php(78): intdiv(5, 0)
#1 {main}
  thrown in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions/exceptions-03.php on line 78

Lines 11–15 of the results show that the error [DivisionByZeroError] was not caught by the last clause [catch (\Exception $ex)]: this is a fatal error.

docs.title: 7.7. Clause [finally]
docs.text:
The structure [try / catch] may have a third element and become a structure [try / catch / finally]. The code in clause [finally] is executed in the following two cases:

  • the [try] clause does not throw an exception. It is then executed in its entirety, after which execution proceeds to the [finally] clause, which is executed in its entirety;
  • The clause [try] throws an exception. It is then executed up to the statement that throws the exception. Execution then proceeds to clause [catch], which is executed in its entirety. Execution then proceeds to clause [finally], which is executed in its entirety.

Finally, the code in clause [finally] is still executed. This scenario is useful in the following case:

  • In the [try] clause, the code has acquired resources (files, databases, network connections, queues). These resources are generally expensive. They must therefore be released (most often referred to as “closed”) as soon as possible;
  • if the resources were acquired in [try], their release will be handled in [finally]. This ensures that in all cases (whether an error occurs or not), the acquired resources are returned to the system.

The following script, [exceptions-04.php], demonstrates how the [finally] clause works in various situations:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// an exception instance is created
$e = new \Exception("Erreur...");

// first test
try {
    print "Premier test\n";
    throw $e;
} catch (\Exception $ex1) {
    print $ex1->getMessage() . "\n";
} finally {
    print "Terminé\n";
}

// second test
try {
    print "Second test\n";
} catch (\Exception $ex1) {
    print $ex1->getMessage() . "\n";
} finally {
    print "Terminé\n";
}

// third test
try {
    print "Troisième test\n";
    return;
} catch (\Exception $ex1) {
    print $ex1->getMessage() . "\n";
} finally {
    print "Terminé\n";
}

Code Comments

  • Line 7: [$e] is an instance of the predefined class [\Exception]. We will instantiate it in different places;
  • Lines 11–12: The exception [$e] is thrown in [try] by the statement [throw];
  • line 13: the [\Exception] exception is caught, and its error message is written to the console;
  • Lines 15–16: The [finally] clause writes a message. Based on what was mentioned earlier, this message should always be written, regardless of whether there is an error in [try];
  • line 21: there is no error in [try]. Here, too, the program should proceed to [finally];
  • Line 31: There is a [return] statement in the [try] file, and no error. This raises the question of whether the script will proceed to the [finally] clause. Execution shows that it does. When used outside a function, the [return] statement terminates the script.

Results:

> php exceptions-04.php
Premier test
Erreur...
Terminé
Second test
Terminé
Troisième test
Terminé

Let’s examine another case, [exceptions-05.php]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// fourth test
try {
    print "Quatrième test\n";
    exit;
} finally {
    print "Terminé\n";
}

Comments

  • Line 9: The statement [exit] immediately terminates script execution: the clause [finally] is not executed;
  • Lines 7–12: An example of [try / finally] without the [catch] clause. This is possible.

Results:

> php exceptions-05.php
Quatrième test

docs.title: 7.8. Creating Your Own Exception Classes
docs.text:
In a somewhat large project, it’s useful to differentiate between various errors by encapsulating them in different exception classes. In the previous scripts, we saw that any exception could be caught by a [catch (\Throwable $ex)] clause. This is recommended if you have no idea what the intercepted error is and the handling is the same for all errors. This is sometimes the case, but you often need to adapt the handling to the exact type of error. In that case, you need to distinguish between the different errors.

Let’s examine the following [exceptions-06.php] script:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// Defining our own exception family
class Exception1 extends \RuntimeException
{
}

class Exception2 extends \RuntimeException
{
}

// Using our exceptions
$e1 = new Exception1("Erreur1...");
var_dump($e1);
$e2 = new Exception2("Erreur2...", 2);

// first test
print "premier test\n";
try {
     // Throwing an Exception1
    throw $e1;
} catch (Exception1 $ex1) {
    print "Exception 1\n";
    print $ex1->getMessage() . "\n";
} catch (Exception2 $ex2) {
    print "Exception 2\n";
    print $ex2->getMessage() . "\n";
}

// Second test
print "second test\n";
try {
     // Throwing an Exception2
    throw $e2;
} catch (Exception1 $ex1) {
    print "Exception 1\n";
    print $ex1->getMessage() . "\n";
} catch (Exception2 $ex2) {
    print "Exception 2\n";
    print $ex2->getMessage() . "\n";
}

// third test
print "troisième test\n";
try {
     // Throwing an Exception1
    throw $e1;
} catch (Exception1 | Exception2 $ex) {
    print "Exception 1 ou 2\n";
    print $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}

// fourth test
print "quatrième test\n";
try {
     // An Exception2 is thrown
    throw $e2;
} catch (Exception1 | Exception2 $ex) {
    print "Exception 1 ou 2 : " . $ex::class . "\n";
     // Information contained in the exception
    print "message : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
    print "code : " . $ex->getCode() . "\n";
    print "fichier : " . basename($ex->getFile()) . "\n";
    print "ligne : " . $ex->getLine() . "\n";
}

Comments

  • Lines 7–9: We define two classes, *[Exception1] and *[Exception2], both derived from the predefined class ***[\\RuntimeException]***. The body of these classes is empty. In other words, they are used solely for their types: it is because they have different types that we will be able to distinguish between these two exceptions in the [catch] clauses;
  • lines 16–18: We define two variables, [$e1] and [$e2], which have the types [Exception1] and [Exception2], respectively. The constructor used is that of the [Exception] class, whose signature is [__construct(string $message = "", int $code = 0, ?Throwable $previous = null)]. For [$e2], an error code has been specified;
  • lines 21–31: there is a [try / catch / catch] structure. This allows for handling different types of exceptions with different [catch] clauses. The first clause whose type matches is executed; the others are ignored;
  • line 25: intercepts exceptions of type [Exception1];
  • line 28: intercepts exceptions of type [Exception2];
  • line 51: intercepts exceptions of type [Exception1] or ([|]) [Exception2]. This syntax has been available since PHP 7.1;
  • line 62: the class name of the intercepted exception;
  • lines 64–67: the information contained in the exception, obtained via the methods of the [Throwable] interface. The [basename] function returns a filename without the folder path.

  • Lines 2–18: The “content” of an exception, displayed by [var_dump]:
    • lines 3–4: the error message;
    • lines 7–8: the error code;
    • lines 9–10: the name of the file in which the exception was raised. The length indicated (string(76)) is that of the full file path: it depends on the folder in which the script is located;
    • lines 11–12: the line where the exception was raised;
    • lines 13–15: the call stack at the time the exception was raised. It is empty here because the exception was raised in the main script and not within a function;
    • lines 16–17: the previous exception. An exception can encapsulate another exception, thereby defining a stack of exceptions. The [previous] attribute allows this stack to be analyzed;
  • lines 29–33: Note that the file and line number of the exception are those from its creation by [new] (line 18) and not those from its throw by [throw].

docs.title: 7.9. Re-throwing an Exception
docs.text:
An exception can be thrown multiple times, as shown in the following script, [exceptions-07.php]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

try {
    try {
         // An exception is thrown
        throw new \Exception("test");
    } catch (\Exception $ex) {
         // The intercepted exception is rethrown
        throw $ex;
    } finally {
         // the program will indeed enter the `finally` block
        print "finally 1\n";
    }
} catch (\Exception $ex2) {
     // The original exception is successfully retrieved
    print $ex2->getMessage() . " dans try / catch / finally externe\n";
} finally {
     // We will indeed enter the `finally` block
    print "finally 2\n";
}

Comments

  • line 9: an exception is thrown;
  • line 10: the exception is caught;
  • line 12: the exception is rethrown. It is then passed to the [try / catch / finally] structure at the higher level. This scenario is common: code intercepts an exception to perform local processing (write a log, roll back a transaction, etc.) and then rethrows it so that the calling code is also notified;
  • line 17: it is intercepted again;
  • Lines 13–15: The execution shows that even after the [throw] in line 12, the program does indeed proceed to the [finally] clause of the internal [try / catch / finally].

Results:

> php exceptions-07.php
finally 1
test dans try / catch / finally externe
finally 2

docs.title: 7.10. Handling an Exception Stack
docs.text:
An exception can encapsulate another exception, which in turn can encapsulate yet another, ultimately forming an exception stack. Here is an example: [exceptions-08.php]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// We define our own exception family
class Exception1 extends \RuntimeException
{
}

class Exception2 extends \RuntimeException
{
}

class Exception3 extends \RuntimeException
{
}

// We use our exceptions
$e1 = new Exception1("Erreur 1...", 1, new Exception2("Erreur 2...", 2, new Exception3("Erreur 3...")));
var_dump($e1);
// Working with the exception stack
$e = $e1;
do {
     // Error message for the current exception
    print $e::class . " : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
     // We move to the previous exception (null if there isn't one)
    $e = $e->getPrevious();
} while ($e !== null);

Comments

  • Lines 7–15: Define three exception classes derived from the predefined exception [RuntimeException];
  • line 20: an instance of the [Exception3] class is encapsulated within an instance of the [Exception2] class, which is itself encapsulated within an instance of the [Exception1] class. The constructor used here is the constructor for the [Exception] class: [__construct(string $message = "", int $code = 0, ?Throwable $previous = null)]. The third parameter of the constructor allows an exception to be encapsulated. This can be useful in the following scenario:
    • a method M is defined that can throw an exception of type [Exception1]—and only that type—for compatibility reasons, such as with an interface;
    • however, other types of exceptions may occur within method M. To propagate an error back to the code calling method M, these exceptions are then encapsulated into the type [Exception1], which is then thrown. This ensures that the information contained in the encapsulated exception—which was the original cause of the error—is not lost;
  • Lines 24–29: demonstrate how to traverse the stack of exceptions nested within an exception. The method [getPrevious] returns the encapsulated exception or [null] if there is none. The [do ... while] loop executes its body at least once and then continues as long as the condition is true.

docs.title: 7.11. Warnings from PHP 7 that became errors in PHP 8
docs.text:
We have seen that division by zero, which produced a warning in PHP 7, triggers an error in PHP 8. This is not an isolated case: PHP 8 has converted many warnings—which previously continued execution with a false result—into errors. The script [exceptions-09.php] illustrates a few of them:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// displays the type and message of an error
function afficher(int $n, \Throwable $ex): void
{
    print "$n - " . $ex::class . " : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}

// A function with two parameters
function somme(int $a, int $b): int
{
    return $a + $b;
}

// 1 - Undefined variable: a simple warning (Notice in PHP 7, Warning in PHP 8)
print "1 - [" . $inconnue . "]\n";
// 2 - modulo by zero: warning + false result in PHP 7, error in PHP 8
try {
    print 1 % 0;
} catch (\DivisionByZeroError $ex) {
    afficher(2, $ex);
}
// 3 - Arithmetic operation on an array
try {
    print [] + 1;
} catch (\TypeError $ex) {
    afficher(3, $ex);
}
// 4 - Arithmetic operation on a non-numeric string
try {
    print "abc" * 2;
} catch (\TypeError $ex) {
    afficher(4, $ex);
}
// 5 - Incorrect parameter type for a predefined function
try {
    print strlen([1, 2]);
} catch (\TypeError $ex) {
    afficher(5, $ex);
}
// 6 - Parameter is of the correct type but has an invalid value
try {
    print_r(array_chunk([1, 2, 3], 0));
} catch (\ValueError $ex) {
    afficher(6, $ex);
}
// 7 - Insufficient number of arguments
try {
    print somme(1);
} catch (\ArgumentCountError $ex) {
    afficher(7, $ex);
}
// 8 - Expression [match] without a corresponding branch (PHP 8.0)
try {
    $jour = 8;
    print match ($jour) {
        6, 7 => "week-end",
        1, 2, 3, 4, 5 => "semaine",
    };
} catch (\UnhandledMatchError $ex) {
    afficher(8, $ex);
}
// 9 - method called on null
try {
    $objet = null;
    $objet->methode();
} catch (\Error $ex) {
    afficher(9, $ex);
}
// 10 - The null-safe operator ?-> prevents the previous error: the result is null
var_dump($objet?->methode());

Results:

> php exceptions-09.php

Warning: Undefined variable $inconnue in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions/exceptions-09.php on line 19
1 - []
2 - DivisionByZeroError : Modulo by zero
3 - TypeError : Unsupported operand types: array + int
4 - TypeError : Unsupported operand types: string * int
5 - TypeError : strlen(): Argument #1 ($string) must be of type string; array given
6 - ValueError : array_chunk(): Argument #2 ($length) must be greater than 0
7 - ArgumentCountError : Too few arguments to function somme(), 1 passed in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions/exceptions-09.php on line 52 and exactly 2 expected
8 - UnhandledMatchError : Unhandled match case 8
9 - Error : Call to a member function methode() on null
NULL

Comments

  • Line 19: The use of an undefined variable remains a simple warning, but at the [E_WARNING] level (it was a [E_NOTICE] note in PHP 7). The variable is set to [null], and the script continues (lines 2–4 of the results);
  • line 22: division by zero triggers an error [DivisionByZeroError] (line 5). This was already the case in PHP 7: only division by zero in [/] produced a simple warning there;
  • line 28: an arithmetic operation on an array causes a [TypeError] error (line 6);
  • line 34: in PHP 7, an arithmetic operation on a non-numeric string triggered the warning “A non-numeric value encountered,” and the string was 0. In PHP 8, this is an error [TypeError] (line 7). A numeric string (["12" * 2]) is still accepted;
  • line 40: In PHP 7, passing a parameter of the wrong type to a predefined function triggered a warning, and the function returned [null]. In PHP 8, all predefined functions throw an error [TypeError], just like functions written by the developer (line 8). The message identifies the parameter by its number and name;
  • line 46: the parameter has the correct type ([int]) but an invalid value (a length must be positive): this is error [ValueError], new in PHP 8.0 (line 9). In PHP 7, this was a warning;
  • line 52: the [somme] function expects two arguments but receives only one: error [ArgumentCountError] (line 10);
  • Lines 59–62: The expression [match] has no branch for the value 8 and has no branch [default]: error [UnhandledMatchError] (line 11). This is a significant difference from the [switch] statement, which does nothing when no [case] is suitable;
  • line 69: Calling a method on [null] results in an error [Error] (line 12). This was already the case in PHP 7;
  • Line 74: The null-safe operator [?->] (PHP 8.0) returns [null] if the object is [null], instead of calling the method. This avoids having to write a test for [if ($objet !== null)] (line 13).

These changes make PHP 8 programs safer: an error halts processing instead of allowing it to continue with incorrect data. They also require the developer to include the corresponding [catch] clauses.

docs.title: 7.12. Multiple [catch], [catch] without a variable, and [throw] expression
docs.text:
The [exceptions-10.php] script offers three features of PHP 8 and a common use of exception handling:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// [throw] is an expression as of PHP 8.0: it can be used after ?? or in an arrow function
function lireAge(array $data): int
{
    $age = $data["age"] ?? throw new \InvalidArgumentException("L'âge est absent");
    return is_int($age) && $age >= 0 ? $age : throw new \DomainException("Âge [$age] invalide");
}

// an arrow function that simply throws an exception
$interdit = fn(string $operation) => throw new \LogicException("Opération [$operation] interdite");

// test data
$tests = [["age" => 48], [], ["age" => -4]];
foreach ($tests as $i => $data) {
    try {
        print "test $i : âge=" . lireAge($data) . "\n";
    } catch (\InvalidArgumentException | \DomainException $ex) {
         // a single [catch] clause for two types of exceptions
        print "test $i : " . $ex::class . " : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
    }
}

try {
    $interdit("suppression");
} catch (\LogicException) {
     // Starting with PHP 8.0, the variable in the [catch] clause is optional
    print "l'opération a été refusée\n";
}

// Wrap a low-level exception in an application exception
class DaoException extends \RuntimeException
{
}

function lireConfiguration(string $json): array
{
    try {
        return json_decode($json, true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
    } catch (\JsonException $ex) {
         // The original cause is passed as the third parameter: it is not lost
        throw new DaoException("Configuration illisible", 10, $ex);
    }
}

try {
    lireConfiguration('{"dsn": "mysql:host=localhost"');
} catch (DaoException $ex) {
    print $ex::class . " : " . $ex->getMessage() . " (code " . $ex->getCode() . ")\n";
    print "cause : " . $ex->getPrevious()::class . " : " . $ex->getPrevious()->getMessage() . "\n";
}

Results:

> php exceptions-10.php
test 0 : âge=48
test 1 : InvalidArgumentException : L'âge est absent
test 2 : DomainException : Âge [-4] invalide
l'opération a été refusée
DaoException : Configuration illisible (code 10)
cause : JsonException : Syntax error

Comments

  • Line 9: Starting with PHP 8.0, [throw] is an expression and no longer just an instruction. It can therefore be used wherever a value is expected: here, after the [??] operator. If the key [age] does not exist, an exception is thrown; otherwise, [$age] is assigned its value;
  • line 10: [throw] used in a conditional expression [? :];
  • line 14: an arrow function whose body simply throws an exception. Prior to PHP 8.0, this was not possible: an arrow function can contain only one expression;
  • line 21: a single clause [catch] for two types of exceptions (lines 3–4 of the results). Note that [InvalidArgumentException] and [DomainException] both derive from [LogicException]: a [catch (\LogicException $ex)] would have had the same effect;
  • line 29: Starting with PHP 8.0, the variable in the [catch] clause is optional when you do not need the exception itself, only its type (line 5);
  • lines 35–37: an application-specific exception. In the following chapters, we will write data access layers (DAO, Data Access Object) that will throw only this type of exception, regardless of the source of the error (file, jSON, database);
  • lines 39–47: The function [lireConfiguration] decodes a string jSON. The low-level exception [JsonException] is intercepted and wrapped (line 45) in a [DaoException] exception. The original cause is passed as the third parameter to the constructor;
  • line 53: the calling code only knows [DaoException], but it can retrieve the original cause of the error using the [getPrevious] method (lines 6–7 of the results).

docs.title: 7.13. Convert warnings to exceptions: [ErrorException]
docs.text:
Despite the improvements in PHP 8, certain anomalies remain mere warnings: nonexistent array key, undefined variable, file cannot be opened with [fopen]... These warnings cannot be intercepted by a [try / catch]. However, you can install an error handler that converts them into [ErrorException] exceptions. This is what the [exceptions-11.php] script does:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// Error handler: converts PHP warnings into [ErrorException] exceptions
set_error_handler(function (int $niveau, string $message, string $fichier, int $ligne): bool {
    throw new \ErrorException($message, 0, $niveau, $fichier, $ligne);
});

// An unknown key no longer triggers a simple warning but an exception
$personne = ["nom" => "Langevin"];
try {
    print $personne["prenom"] . "\n";
} catch (\ErrorException $ex) {
    print "Erreur : " . $ex->getMessage() . " (ligne " . $ex->getLine() . ")\n";
    print "niveau E_WARNING : " . var_export($ex->getSeverity() === E_WARNING, true) . "\n";
}
// Same applies to attempting to open a nonexistent file
try {
    $flux = fopen(__DIR__ . "/inexistant.txt", "r");
} catch (\ErrorException $ex) {
    print "Erreur : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// We return to the error handler from PHP
restore_error_handler();
print "fin\n";

Results:

> php exceptions-11.php
Erreur : Undefined array key "prenom" (ligne 14)
niveau E_WARNING : true
Erreur : fopen(.../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/exceptions/inexistant.txt): Failed to open stream: No such file or directory
fin

Comments

  • Lines 7–9: The [set_error_handler] function sets up an error handler—a function that PHP will call whenever a warning, note, or deprecation occurs, instead of displaying the message. It receives the error level, the error message, the file, and the line where the error occurred. Here, it throws a [ErrorException] exception that stores this information. The return type [bool] is the one specified in the documentation for [set_error_handler]: the function would return [false] to let PHP handle the error normally. It never returns anything here because it always throws an exception;
  • line 14: the key [prenom] does not exist. Instead of a warning, a [ErrorException] exception is thrown, which is caught (line 2 of the results);
  • line 17: the method [getSeverity], specific to the class [ErrorException], returns the level of the original error (line 3);
  • line 21: Attempting to open a nonexistent file also results in an exception (line 4);
  • line 26: restores the previous error handler, in this case that of PHP.

This technique is used by many PHP frameworks (Symfony, Laravel): during development, any warning becomes an exception, which forces the developer to fix the code. The [PHPUnit] testing tool that we’ll use later works in a similar way: it can cause a test to fail if it produces a warning or a deprecation.

docs.title: 6. Interfaces
docs.text: An interface is a structure that defines method prototypes. A class that implements an interface must implement the code for all of the interface’s methods. An interface is a contract: it specifies what an object can do, without specifying how it does it.

docs.title: 6.1. The script directory structure
docs.text:
The scripts for this chapter are in the [scripts-console/interfaces] folder:

php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/interfaces
├── ICalcul.php
├── IExemple.php
├── IExemple2.php
├── interface-01.php
├── interface-02.php
├── interface-03.php
└── interface-04.php

docs.title: 6.2. A First Interface
docs.text:
We define an interface named [IExemple] in a script named [IExemple.php]. In the same script, we define two classes that implement the [IExemple] interface:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Exemples;

// an interface
interface IExemple
{
     // the interface's methods
    public function ajouter(int $i, int $j): int;

    public function soustraire(int $i, int $j): int;
}

// Implementation 1 of the interface IExemple
class Classe1 implements IExemple
{
    public function ajouter(int $a, int $b): int
    {
        return $a + $b + 10;
    }

    public function soustraire(int $a, int $b): int
    {
        return $a - $b + 20;
    }
}

// Implementation 2 of the interface IExemple
class Classe2 implements IExemple
{
    public function ajouter(int $a, int $b): int
    {
        return $a + $b + 100;
    }

    public function soustraire(int $a, int $b): int
    {
        return $a - $b + 200;
    }
}

Comments

  • Lines 10–15: The [IExemple] interface defines two methods: the [ajouter] function (line 13) and the [soustraire] function (line 15). The interface does not define the code for these methods. The classes that implement the interface will do so. The methods of an interface must be public;
  • line 19: the class [Classe1] implements ([implements]) the interface [IExemple]. It therefore defines code for the methods [ajouter] (line 21) and [soustraire] (line 26). The parameter names may differ from those in the interface ([$a] instead of [$i]), but their types must be compatible. Note, however: with the named arguments of PHP 8, a call to [ajouter(i: 1, j: 2)] would not work with [Classe1]. It is therefore preferable to keep the interface names;
  • Lines 33–44: Same applies to class [Classe2].

We use the [IExemple] interface in the following [interface-01.php] script:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// inclusion and declaration of classes and interfaces used by the script
require_once __DIR__ . "/IExemple.php";
use Exemples\Classe1;
use Exemples\Classe2;
use Exemples\IExemple;

// function
function calculer(int $a, int $b, IExemple $interface): void
{
    print $interface->ajouter($a, $b) . "\n";
    print $interface->soustraire($a, $b) . "\n";
}

// ------------------- main
// creation of 2 objects of type Class1 and Class2
$c1 = new Classe1();
$c2 = new Classe2();
// Calling the `calculate` function
calculer(4, 3, $c1);
calculer(14, 13, $c2);
// An interface cannot be instantiated
try {
    new IExemple();
} catch (\Error $e) {
    print "Erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}

Results:

> php interface-01.php
17
21
127
201
Erreur : Cannot instantiate interface Exemples\IExemple

Comments

  • lines 7–10: inclusion and declaration of the classes and interfaces used by the script. The file [IExemple.php] is included using the statement [require_once]: it will be included only once, even if multiple scripts in the project include it;
  • Lines 13–17: A function is defined;
  • Line 13: Here, we have declared the types of the three parameters. If, at runtime, the actual parameter is not of the expected type, a [TypeError] error is thrown. The third parameter is of type [IExemple]. This means that the actual parameter must be an instance of a class that implements the [IExemple] interface; therefore, in our example, an instance of the classes [Classe1] or [Classe2]. The function [calculer] is not aware of these classes; it only recognizes the interface. We can pass it objects of classes written later, provided they implement the [IExemple] interface;
  • lines 15–16: we use the [ajouter, soustraire] methods of the [IExemple] interface;
  • line 24: the third actual parameter is of type [Classe1], which is compatible with the type [IExemple] of the function’s third formal parameter;
  • line 25: same applies to the class [Classe2];
  • line 28: an interface cannot be instantiated; an error is returned (line 6 of the results).

docs.title: 6.3. Deriving an Interface
docs.text:
Just as a child class can extend a parent class, a child interface can extend a parent interface.

Consider the interface [IExemple2] defined in the file [IExemple2.php]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Exemples;

// inclusion of the definition of the interface IExemple
require_once __DIR__ . "/IExemple.php";

// An interface that derives from IExemple
interface IExemple2 extends IExemple
{
     // the method added by the interface
    public function multiplier(int $i, int $j): int;
}

// Implementation of the IExemple2 interface
class Classe3 extends Classe2 implements IExemple2
{
     // [Override] verifies that the method actually exists in the interface
     #[\Override]
    public function multiplier(int $a, int $b): int
    {
        return $a * $b;
    }
}

Comments

  • line 7: the [IExemple2] interface will be in the same namespace as the [IExemple] interface;
  • line 10: the definition file for the [IExemple] interface is included;
  • Lines 13–17: define the [IExemple2] interface, which extends ([extends]) the [IExemple] interface and adds a new method to it (line 16). An interface can even extend multiple interfaces: [interface I3 extends I1, I2];
  • lines 20–28: The class [Classe3] extends the class [Classe2]. Since the latter implements the [IExemple] interface, the [Classe3] class will also do so. In fact, [Classe3] inherits all the public and protected methods of the [Classe2] class, including the [ajouter] and [soustraire] methods. Furthermore, it is specified that [Classe3] implements the [IExemple2] interface. As such, it must also implement the [multiplier] method, which [Classe2] does not do. This is what lines 24–27 do;
  • line 23: Starting with PHP 8.3, the attribute [#[\Override]], discussed in the previous chapter, also applies to a method that implements an interface method. If the method [multiplier] were to disappear from the interface [IExemple2], PHP would signal this.

The [IExemple2] interface is used by the following [interface-02.php] script:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// inclusion and declaration of the classes and interfaces required by the script
require_once __DIR__ . "/IExemple2.php";
use Exemples\IExemple2;
use Exemples\Classe3;

// function
function calculer(int $a, int $b, IExemple2 $interface): void
{
    print $interface->ajouter($a, $b) . "\n";
    print $interface->soustraire($a, $b) . "\n";
    print $interface->multiplier($a, $b) . "\n";
}

// ------------------- main
// creation of 1 object of type Class3 that implements IExemple2
$c3 = new Classe3();
// call to the `calculate` function
calculer(4, 3, $c3);

Results:

> php interface-02.php
107
201
12

Comments

  • Line 12: The third parameter of the [calculer] function is of type [IExemple2];
  • Lines 14–16: The three methods of the [IExemple2] interface are used: the two inherited from [IExemple] and its own;
  • line 23: the function [calculer] is called with, as its third parameter, an object of type [Classe3] that implements [IExemple2] (line 21).

docs.title: 6.4. Passing an Interface as a Function Parameter
docs.text:
We saw in the previous chapter (in the section “Passing an Object as a Function Parameter”) that when the expected type for a function parameter is a class, the actual parameter can be an object of the expected type or a derived type. The same applies to interfaces, as shown in the following script, [interface-03.php]:

<?php

// strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// Inclusion and declaration of the classes and interfaces required by the script
require_once __DIR__ . "/IExemple.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/IExemple2.php";
use Exemples\IExemple;
use Exemples\IExemple2;
use Exemples\Classe1;
use Exemples\Classe3;

// function
function calculer(int $a, int $b, IExemple $interface): void
{
    print $interface->ajouter($a, $b) . "\n";
    print $interface->soustraire($a, $b) . "\n";
}

// ------------------- main
// creation of 1 object of type Class3 that implements IExemple2 and therefore IExemple
$c3 = new Classe3();
// call to the `calculate` function
calculer(4, 3, $c3);
// The operator [instanceof] checks whether an object implements an interface
foreach ([new Classe1(), $c3] as $objet) {
    print $objet::class . " : IExemple=" . var_export($objet instanceof IExemple, true)
        . ", IExemple2=" . var_export($objet instanceof IExemple2, true) . "\n";
}
// the interfaces implemented by the Class3 class
print_r(class_implements($c3));

Results:

> php interface-03.php
107
201
Exemples\Classe1 : IExemple=true, IExemple2=false
Exemples\Classe3 : IExemple=true, IExemple2=true
Array
(
    [Exemples\IExemple] => Exemples\IExemple
    [Exemples\IExemple2] => Exemples\IExemple2
)

Comments

  • Line 15: The function [calculer] expects a type [IExemple] as its third parameter. This means that the actual parameter can be of type [IExemple] or a derived type;
  • Line 23: An object of type [$c3] is instantiated from the class [Classe3], which implements the interface [IExemple2], which in turn extends the interface [IExemple]. So ultimately, [$c3] implements the [IExemple] interface;
  • Line 25: The function [calculer] is called with the object [$c3] (of type [Classe3]) as its third parameter. Through class inheritance and implementations, we saw that the object [$c3] implements the type [IExemple]. We can therefore use it as the third parameter;
  • lines 27–30: The [instanceof] operator checks whether an object implements an interface. An object of type [Classe1] implements [IExemple] but not [IExemple2] (line 4 of the results). An object of type [Classe3] implements both (line 5);
  • line 32: The [class_implements] function returns the list of interfaces implemented by an object or class, either directly or through inheritance (lines 6–10 of the results).

docs.title: 6.5. Interface constants, multiple interfaces, and intersection types
docs.text:
An interface can also declare constants, and a class can implement multiple interfaces. We define two interfaces, [ICalcul] and [INommable], and two classes that implement them in the file [ICalcul.php]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Exemples;

// An interface can declare constants
interface ICalcul
{
     // typed constant (PHP 8.3)
    public const int PRECISION = 2;

    public function calculer(float $a, float $b): float;
}

// a second interface
interface INommable
{
    public function getNom(): string;
}

// A class can implement multiple interfaces
final class Addition implements ICalcul, INommable
{
     #[\Override]
    public function calculer(float $a, float $b): float
    {
        return round($a + $b, self::PRECISION);
    }

     #[\Override]
    public function getNom(): string
    {
        return "addition";
    }
}

final class Division implements ICalcul, INommable
{
     #[\Override]
    public function calculer(float $a, float $b): float
    {
         // [ICalcul::PRECISION] and [self::PRECISION] refer to the same constant
        return round($a / $b, ICalcul::PRECISION);
    }

     #[\Override]
    public function getNom(): string
    {
        return "division";
    }
}

Comments

  • line 13: The [ICalcul] interface declares a constant. All classes that implement the interface inherit it. Starting with PHP 8.3, a class or interface constant can be typed (here, [int]);
  • Lines 19–22: A second interface, with a single method;
  • line 25: the class [Addition] implements both interfaces: the interface names are separated by commas. It must define the methods of both;
  • line 30: the constant inherited from the interface is accessed by [self::PRECISION]. The function [round] rounds a number to the specified number of decimal places;
  • line 46: The constant can also be referred to by the interface name: [ICalcul::PRECISION].

These interfaces are used by the script [interface-04.php]:

<?php

// strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// inclusion and declaration of the classes and interfaces required by the script
require_once __DIR__ . "/ICalcul.php";
use Exemples\ICalcul;
use Exemples\INommable;
use Exemples\Addition;
use Exemples\Division;

// The parameter [$calcul] has a default value: an object created by [new] (PHP 8.1)
function executer(float $a, float $b, ICalcul $calcul = new Addition()): float
{
    return $calcul->calculer($a, $b);
}

// type intersection (PHP 8.1): [$operation] must implement both interfaces
function afficher(float $a, float $b, ICalcul&INommable $operation): void
{
    print $operation->getNom() . "($a, $b)=" . $operation->calculer($a, $b) . "\n";
}

// ------------------- main
// interface constant
print "précision : " . ICalcul::PRECISION . " décimales\n";
// default value of the third parameter
print "executer(1.234, 2.345)=" . executer(1.234, 2.345) . "\n";
// explicit parameter
print "executer(10, 3, new Division())=" . executer(10, 3, new Division()) . "\n";
// intersection type
afficher(10, 4, new Division());
afficher(10, 4, new Addition());
// classes implement both interfaces
print_r(class_implements(Division::class));

Results:

> php interface-04.php
précision : 2 décimales
executer(1.234, 2.345)=3.58
executer(10, 3, new Division())=3.33
division(10, 4)=2.5
addition(10, 4)=14
Array
(
    [Exemples\ICalcul] => Exemples\ICalcul
    [Exemples\INommable] => Exemples\INommable
)

Comments

  • Line 14: The third parameter of the [executer] function is of type [ICalcul] and has a default value—a [Addition] object created with [new]. Up to PHP 8.0, the default value of a parameter could only be a constant. Starting with PHP 8.1, the expression [new] is accepted in parameter default values (“new in initializers”), as well as in the arguments of PHP attributes ([#[...]]), static variables, and global constants. It remains prohibited in the default value of a class attribute. The object is created on every call that omits the parameter;
  • line 20: the type [ICalcul&INommable] is an intersection type (PHP 8.1): the actual parameter must implement both [ICalcul] and [INommable]. The function can then call methods from both interfaces. This should not be confused with the union type [ICalcul|INommable] (either one);
  • line 27: the constant is accessible from outside via the interface name (line 2 of the results);
  • line 29: the third parameter is omitted; it is a [Addition] object that performs the calculation (line 3);
  • line 31: a [Division] object is explicitly passed (line 4). Note that the integers 10 and 3 are accepted for parameters of type [float] despite the declaration [strict_types=1]: the conversion of a ***[int] to a [float]*** is the only automatic conversion allowed in strict mode;
  • Lines 33–34: Both classes implement both interfaces; they are accepted by the [afficher] function (lines 5–6);
  • line 36: the notation [Division::class] represents the full class name, in this case [Exemples\Division]. The function [class_implements] accepts both a class name and an object.

Interfaces are ubiquitous in PHP itself. We have already encountered two in the previous chapter: [Stringable], automatically implemented by any class with a [__toString] method, and [JsonSerializable], which allows you to control an object’s jSON encoding. In the next chapter, we’ll look at the [Throwable] interface, which is implemented by all errors and exceptions. An enumeration can also implement an interface. Finally, we’ll see later in this course that interfaces form the basis of our applications’ layered architecture: each layer knows only the interface of the adjacent layer.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
The PDF in the document is HERE.

The code in this document is HERE.

This document is a product of Claude from Anthropic. This is a rewrite, for the PHP 8 language, of the course “Introduction to the PHP 7 Language” based on the example written by Serge Tahé in July 2019. It retains the outline, examples, and central theme, while changing the language:

  • the 2019 course used PHP 7.3. Since then, PHP has undergone six major versions: 8.0 (2020), 8.1 (2021), 8.2 (2022), 8.3 (2023), 8.4 (2024), and 8.5 (2025). This document uses PHP 8.5;
  • between these two versions, PHP has changed significantly: many features have been introduced (types, enumerations, read-only classes, [match], named arguments…), and many others have been deprecated: They still work, but PHP displays a warning message each time they are used, to alert users that they will be removed in a future version. The code in this document does not use any deprecated features: all scripts were run with PHP 8.5 configured to display all errors, warnings, and deprecations, and no [Deprecated] messages appear in their results;
  • The tools have also changed: the [VS Code] editor replaces IDE and [NetBeans]; the [PHPUnit] testing framework replaces [Codeception]; the [curl] command replaces the [Postman] tool, the [Symfony Mailer] library replaces [SwiftMailer], which has been deprecated, and the [Mailpit] mail server replaces [hMailServer], which has also been deprecated.

This document provides a list of PHP console scripts in various areas (language structures, classes, access to files, databases, and the Internet). Web programming is addressed through web services. In this document, a web service refers to any web application that produces data (plain text, JSON, XML) rather than HTML pages. These are data servers, not web page servers—a combination of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It covers classic web concepts (the HTTP protocol, JSON or XML responses, session management, and authentication) that are also used in traditional web programming. The final section of the document also builds a HTML web application.

docs.title: 1.1. The Role of PHP in a Client/Server Application
docs.text:
Nowadays, it is common to build web applications in client/server mode:

  • In [1], the web browser displays web pages for a user. These pages contain JavaScript, which implements a client for a [2] data web service, as well as a client for a [3] web page fragment server. Frameworks such as JavaScript, [Vue.js], [React], or [Angular] are designed for this purpose;
  • In [2], the web server is a data server. It can be written in any language, for example, in PHP. It does not generate web pages in the traditional sense (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) except perhaps the first time. However, this first page can be obtained from a traditional web server ([3]). The JavaScript for the initial page will then generate the application’s various web pages by retrieving the [4] data to be displayed from the data server [2]. It can also retrieve web page fragments ([5]) to format this data from the web page server ([3]);
  • In [4], the user initiates an action;
  • in [6, 7], the user receives data formatted with a web page fragment.

In this document, we will write client/server applications in PHP with the following structure:

Here we have a client/server application written entirely in PHP. A [9] console script will query a [4] data server. What you’ll learn here about writing the data service can be reused in a web application: the data service in PHP can be kept, and the client PHP can be replaced by a client JavaScript.

As the central theme of this document, we will build an income tax calculation service in 13 versions. Version 12 will have the following architecture:

The server’s [web] layer will have a MVC architecture (Model–View–Controller). It will be able to respond in JSON, XML, or HTML. The entire course is aimed at building this version, which version 13 secures.

docs.title: 1.3. Tools Used
docs.text:
The examples were written and tested using the following tools (their installation is described in the next chapter):

  • [PHP] 8.5, configured to report all errors, warnings, and deprecations;
  • The [Laragon] 8 package, which combines [Windows] and PHP 8.5, the [Apache] 2.4 web server, SGBD and [MySQL] 8.4, the [Redis] server, and the [Composer] dependency manager; the SGBD and [PostgreSQL] can be added with just a few clicks;
  • the [Visual Studio Code] editor (VS Code) and its extension [PHP Intelephense];
  • the PHP libraries installed with [Composer]: [symfony/http-foundation], [symfony/http-client], [symfony/mailer], [symfony/mime] 8, [predis/predis] 3, [zbateson/mail-mime-parser] 3, and, for testing, [phpunit/phpunit] 12;
  • the test mail server [Mailpit] and, for the IMAP protocol, a server IMAP (an account [Gmail], or a local server);
  • the command-line tool [curl], included with [Windows], which displays raw HTTP exchanges;
  • a browser ([Chrome], [Firefox], [Edge]…).

The scripts in this document are commented, and their console output is reproduced. Additional explanations are sometimes provided. This document requires active reading: to understand a script, you must read its code, its comments, and its execution results. The screenshots of the web pages were taken using a program-controlled browser: these are actual pages from the course applications.
