        "smtp-port": 1025,
        "from": "guest@localhost",
        "to": "guest@localhost",
        "subject": "plantage du serveur de calcul d'impôts",
        "tls": false,
        "attachments": []
    },
    "logsFilename": "Data/logs.txt",
    "redis": {
        "scheme": "tcp",
        "host": "127.0.0.1",
        "port": 6379
    },
    "vues": {
        "vue-authentification.php": [700, 221, 400],
        "vue-calcul-impot.php": [200, 300, 341, 350, 800],
        "vue-liste-simulations.php": [500, 600]
    },
    "vue-erreurs": "vue-erreurs.php"
}

Comments

  • line 2: the file JSON describing the database MySQL [dbimpots-2019], which is for version 8. The path is relative to the folder [version-12];
  • Lines 3–33: the PHP files for the application. These first contain the classes that have already been written:
    • the [ExceptionImpots, TaxAdminData, Database] entities and the [Utilitaires] class from version 5;
    • layers [dao] and [métier] from versions 8 and 9;
    • the utilities [Logger] and [SendAdminMail] from version 9 and [XmlUtilitaires] from version 11;
    • and the classes from version 12, which we will now present. The file PHP 7 also contained the absolute paths to third-party libraries ([C:/myprograms/laragon-lite/www/vendor/autoload.php]): the class loader from [Composer] is now loaded directly by [main.php], using a relative path;
  • lines 34–39: the user authorized to use the application;
  • lines 40–48: the email contact information for the application administrator. The email is sent to the [Mailpit] server, which listens on port 1025 (see version 9);
  • line 49: the path to the log file;
  • lines 50–54: the details of the [Redis] server, which serves as the scope memory for [application] (see version 10);
  • lines 55–59: [vue HTML => tableau des codes d'état menant à cette vue] associations. These are described a little further on;
  • line 60: the [vue-erreurs.php] view is displayed in a HTML session whenever an abnormal error occurs:
    • An application such as JSON or XML is typically queried using a programmed client. The client passes parameters to the server, which may be missing or incorrect. The controllers handle these cases and return error codes to the client. All possible error cases must be handled;
    • with a HTML application, it’s a little different. Under normal use, the web application utilizes only a subset of the possible use cases for the JSON and XML clients. Let’s take an example: the [calculer-impot] action expects three posted parameters (sent by a POST): [marié, enfants, salaire]. With a JSON client that allows you to enter URL manually, you can request the action [calculer-impot] with a GET instead of a POST, or with a POST without any posted parameters when three are required, and so on. The JSON server must handle all these cases. With a web application, the [calculer-impot] action will be requested from a web form where neither of the two previous cases is possible: the [calculer-impot] action will be called with a POST and all three [marié, enfants, salaire] parameters. However, the user can reproduce certain errors by manually entering URL values into the browser. For security reasons, this scenario must be handled;
    • the view [vue-erreurs.php] will be displayed whenever a secondary controller returns a status code that is incompatible with the web application, c.-à-d—a status code not present in the [vues] key of the configuration file. We are opting for this solution for educational purposes. Another possible option would be to re-display the view currently shown in the client’s browser so that the user gets the impression that the server is not responding to their hand-crafted URL requests.

Compared to the configuration file for Course PHP 7, the keys [rootDirectory] (the root directory is now known as [main.php]), [actions] (replaced by the enumeration [Action]), and [types] (replaced by the enumeration [ResponseType] presented below) have been removed.

docs.title: 23.5.1. The [curl] tool
docs.text:
Course PHP 7 used the graphical tool [Postman] to query the various URL components of the web application. We use the command-line tool [curl], introduced in the chapter on web services. It allows us to:

  • use any URL: these are created manually;
  • to query the web server using a GET, POST, PUT, OPTIONS… (options [-X] and [-d]);
  • specify the parameters for GET (in URL) or POST (options [-d] and [--data-urlencode]);
  • set the HTTP headers for the request (option [-H]);
  • to receive a response in the JSON, XML, or HTML format;
  • to have access to the HTTP headers of the response (option [-i]);
  • to handle the session cookie like a browser: the [-c cookies.txt] option saves the cookies sent by the server to the [cookies.txt] file, while the [-b cookies.txt] option sends them back to the server.

Since we manually generate the requested URL files, we’ll be able to test all possible error scenarios and see how the server responds. Remember that in a [PowerShell] terminal, you must type [curl.exe] instead of [curl]. All commands in this chapter are entered in a terminal opened in any working directory, where [curl] creates the file [cookies.txt].

To post a parameter whose name contains accented characters, such as [marié], we’ll use the option [--data-urlencode "marié=oui"], which encodes the parameter’s name and value ([mari%C3%A9=oui]). In URL, we’ll write the encoded name ourselves: [num%C3%A9ro] for [numéro].

docs.title: 23.5.2. The Symfony / Serializer Library
docs.text:
Course PHP 7 used the [Symfony / Serializer] library to serialize server responses into JSON and XML, which may contain [Simulation] objects. It had two advantages: the same API for both JSON and XML; the serialization of objects with private attributes, exposed via getters.

We do not use it in this version, although it is installed in the [vendor] folder for the course:

  • our class [Simulation] is a [readonly] class with public attributes (see the following paragraph). The function [json_encode] directly serializes an object’s public attributes: the JSON serialization no longer requires a library;
  • for XML, we have the [XmlUtilitaires] class from version 11, which produces XML documents in the same format as those from version 11, which XML clients already know how to process. All you need to do is provide it with an array, after converting the [Simulation] objects into associative arrays;
  • the server never has to deserialize JSON or XML into objects, which was the other advantage highlighted by the PHP 7 course.

The [Symfony / Serializer] library would therefore only add one more dependency here. It remains a good choice when you need to deserialize documents into typed objects or handle many different formats.

docs.title: 23.6. Application Entities
docs.text:
The [Entities] folder contains two enumerations, [Action] (already presented) and [ResponseType] (presented along with the server responses), and two classes. The [Simulation] class encapsulates the elements of a tax calculation simulation:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// A tax calculation simulation: an immutable object
final readonly class Simulation
{
     // The attributes are public: they cannot be modified (read-only) but
     // they are read directly, without getters, and serialized by [json_encode]
    public function __construct(
         // the calculation parameters
        public string $marié,
        public int $enfants,
        public int $salaire,
         // the result of the calculation
        public int $impôt,
        public int $surcôte,
        public int $décôte,
        public int $réduction,
        public float $taux,
    ) {
    }
}

Comments

  • line 9: the class is [readonly] (PHP 8.2): all its attributes are read-only. A simulation is an immutable object: once constructed, it does not change;
  • Lines 13–24: The attributes are declared and initialized by passing in the constructor’s parameters (PHP 8.0). They are typed: [string] for marital status, [int] for other parameters and amounts, and [float] for the tax rate;
  • the attributes are public: since they are read-only, it is no longer necessary to protect them with getters. The class PHP 7 [Simulation] derived from the class [BaseEntity], had eight untyped attributes [protected], and eight getters.

The second class, [ControllerResult], represents the result that a secondary controller returns to the main controller:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// the result returned by a secondary controller to the main controller
final readonly class ControllerResult
{
    public function __construct(
         // the status code HTTP of the response
        public int $statusCode,
         // the application state after the action is executed
        public int $état,
         // the response itself: a message, a list of messages, a simulation...
        public mixed $réponse,
         // HTTP headers to be added to the response
        public array $headers = [],
    ) {
    }
}
  • line 13: the status code HTTP of the response to be sent to the client;
  • line 15: the state of the application after the action has been executed;
  • line 17: the response itself. Its type depends on the action: a message, a list of error messages, a simulation, or a list of simulations. The type [mixed] (PHP 8.0) accepts any value;
  • line 19: the HTTP headers to be added to the response. This is an optional parameter.

In course PHP 7, the controllers returned the array [[$statusCode, $état, $content, $headers]]. An object with named and typed attributes is safer: you cannot make a mistake in the order of the elements.

docs.title: 23.7. The app's utilities
docs.text:
The application uses three utilities that have already been described:

  • the [Logger] class from version 9 allows you to log events to a text file;
  • the [SendAdminMail] class from version 9 allows you to send an email to the application administrator;
  • the [XmlUtilitaires] class from version 11 retrieves the XML document from a table.

docs.title: 23.8. The [métier] and [dao] layers
docs.text:
The classes and interfaces of the layers [métier] and [dao] have all been defined and used in previous versions:

ClassRoleExceptionImpotsThe class of exceptions thrown by the [dao] layer. Version 5, folder [Entities]InterfaceServerDaoInterface implemented by the [dao] layer of the server. Version 8, folder [Dao]ServerDaoImplementation of the [InterfaceServerDao] interface: tax data is read from the database. Version 8ServerDaoWithSessionClass derived from [ServerDao]: Tax data can be provided to the manufacturer. Version 9, folder [Dao]InterfaceServerMetierInterface implemented by the [métier] layer of the server. Version 8, folder [Metier]ServerMetierImplementation of the [InterfaceServerMetier] interface: tax calculation. Version 8

The application currently under development therefore makes extensive use of elements that have already been presented and used:

  • the [métier] and [dao] layers;
  • the utilities [Logger], [SendAdminMail], and [XmlUtilitaires];
  • the entities [ExceptionImpots, TaxAdminData, Database].

We will focus on the [web] layer of the application:

docs.title: 23.9.1. Introduction
docs.text:
The main controller [main.php] is configured by the file [Data/config.json]. Let’s review its position in our MVC architecture:

The main controller [main.php] is the first element in the MVC architecture to process the client’s request. It has several roles:

  • First, it performs basic checks:
    • Does its configuration file exist and is it valid?
    • it loads all the project dependencies. This involves loading all components of the MVC architecture;
    • Has the requested action been specified? If so, is it valid?
  • If the requested action is valid, it selects [2a]—the secondary controller that will process it—and passes it the information it needs: the application configuration, the request HTTP, and the session;
  • it retrieves [2c] the response from the secondary controller. Depending on the type (JSON, XML, HTML) of response requested by the client, it selects [3a] the response (JsonResponse, XmlResponse, HtmlResponse) responsible for sending the response to the client and passes it all the information it needs (the request HTTP, the session, the application configuration, and the response from the secondary controller).

docs.title: 23.9.2. [main.php] - 1
docs.text:
The beginning of the primary controller [main.php] is as follows:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of parameters and function return values
declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// Symfony dependencies
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// PHP errors are not sent to the client (they go to the web server log)
ini_set("display_errors", "0");

// the application root directory: paths in the configuration file are relative to this directory
const ROOT_DIRECTORY = __DIR__;
// Configuration file path
const CONFIG_FILENAME = ROOT_DIRECTORY . "/Data/config.json";

// the Composer autoloader (Symfony, Predis)
require_once ROOT_DIRECTORY . "/../../../vendor/autoload.php";

// retrieving the configuration
$fileContents = is_readable(CONFIG_FILENAME) ? file_get_contents(CONFIG_FILENAME) : false;
if ($fileContents === false) {
    sendConfigError(131, "Le fichier de configuration [config.json] n'existe pas");
}
try {
    $config = json_decode($fileContents, true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
} catch (\JsonException) {
    sendConfigError(132, "Le fichier de configuration [config.json] n'a pu être exploité correctement");
}

Comments

  • Lines 10–12: The main controller uses the following classes from the Symfony library [HttpFoundation]:
    • [Request]: the HTTP request currently being processed;
    • [Response]: the HTTP response to the client;
    • [Session]: the web application session;
  • Line 15: Errors detected by PHP are not included in the document sent to the client: they would corrupt the responses JSON or XML. They remain logged in the web server’s error log (Apache’s [error.log] file). During development, this line can be commented out: the PHP errors will then appear in the responses received by [curl] or the browser. This aids in debugging. The PHP 7 script also modified the error reporting level using [error_reporting(E_ALL && !E_WARNING && !E_NOTICE)], an expression that was, incidentally, incorrect (it required the bitwise operators [&] and [~]): on the contrary, we want to ignore no errors;
  • line 18: the application’s root directory, which is that of the [main.php] script. The paths in the configuration file are relative to this directory. The constant is defined in the [Application] namespace: it is therefore visible to classes in that namespace, particularly the controller that will calculate the tax;
  • line 20: the path to the configuration file;
  • line 23: the class loader from [Composer] is loaded, making the Symfony and Predis classes available. It is loaded before the configuration is read: the error response sent if the configuration fails uses the Symfony class [Response]. The PHP 7 script used an absolute path here;
  • lines 26–29: the configuration file is read. If it does not exist or cannot be read, an error response with status [131] is sent to the client via the [sendConfigError] function;
  • lines 30–34: The JSON from the configuration file is decoded. With the [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR] option, the [json_decode] function throws a [JsonException] exception if the JSON is invalid. An error response is then sent with status [132]. Starting with PHP 8.0, the [catch] clause can omit the exception variable when it is not used: [catch (\JsonException)];

Here we have an existing and syntactically correct configuration file. It would also be necessary to verify that the expected keys are actually present in this file. We will consider this to be part of the developer’s normal debugging work.

The function [sendConfigError] is defined at the end of the script:

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
// error in the configuration file: response JSON 500, then the script ends
// The application classes have not yet been loaded: we use [Response] directly
function sendConfigError(int $état, string $message): never
{
    $json = json_encode(["action" => "", "état" => $état, "réponse" => $message], JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE);
    $response = new Response($json, Response::HTTP_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR);
    $response->headers->set("Content-Type", "application/json; charset=utf-8");
    $response->send();
    exit;
}
  • Line 124: The return type [never] (PHP 8.1) indicates that the function never returns control to the caller; it always terminates with [exit] or an exception. A code analyzer such as the [PHP Intelephense] extension of [VS Code] then knows that the code following a call to [sendConfigError] is executed only if the configuration could be read;
  • line 126: all responses generated by the web application will have three keys:
    • [action]: the action requested by the client (unknown here);
    • [état]: the state of the application after executing this action;
    • [réponse]: the web server’s response;
  • line 127: Since the application’s classes have not yet been loaded, a Symfony response is constructed directly, with the status [500 Internal Server Error];
  • line 128: the response is a JSON document encoded in UTF-8;
  • line 129: the response is sent to the client.

docs.title: 23.9.3. [curl] Tests - 1
docs.text:
We will verify the server’s behavior when the configuration file is missing or incorrect. Let’s rename [Data/config.json] to [Data/config2.json], then request the URL from the main controller:

> curl -i "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/impots/version-12/main.php"
HTTP/1.0 500 Internal Server Error
Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:51:52 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.58
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.5.11
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
Connection: close
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"action":"","état":131,"réponse":"Le fichier de configuration [config.json] n'existe pas"}
  • Line 1: The option [-i] instructs [curl] to display the HTTP headers from the response;
  • Line 2: The server returned status code [500 Internal Server Error];
  • line 8: The response is a JSON document;
  • line 10: the JSON document from the response. This is indeed the one we were expecting.

Let's rename the file back to [config.json], then make it syntactically incorrect—for example, by deleting everything after its second line. We no longer display the headers HTTP:

> curl "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/impots/version-12/main.php"
{"action":"","état":132,"réponse":"Le fichier de configuration [config.json] n'a pu être exploité correctement"}

This initial test showed us that we can send any type of request to the server under test and that we receive the complete response: the HTTP headers and the document that follows them. Let’s not forget to restore the contents of the [config.json] file.

docs.title: 23.9.4. [main.php] – 2
docs.text:
We’ll now resume our analysis of the main controller, [main.php]:

// Including the application's dependencies
foreach ($config["dependencies"] as $dependency) {
    require_once ROOT_DIRECTORY . "/$dependency";
}

// the current request
$request = Request::createFromGlobals();
// the session—started after the classes were loaded: it contains objects [Simulation]
$session = new Session();
$session->start();

// log file creation
try {
    $logger = new Logger(ROOT_DIRECTORY . "/" . $config["logsFilename"]);
} catch (ExceptionImpots) {
     // Error 500—response JSON without logs
    $content = [
        "action" => "",
        "état" => 133,
        "réponse" => "Le fichier de logs [{$config["logsFilename"]}] n'a pu être créé",
    ];
    (new JsonResponse())->send($request, $session, $config, Response::HTTP_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, $content);
    exit;
}

Comments

  • lines 37–39: We include all the application’s dependencies. We’ve already encountered this code several times;
  • line 42: All information from the client’s request is encapsulated in the Symfony object [Request];
  • lines 44–45: a new session is started, or the existing session is retrieved if the client has sent a session cookie. The session is started after the application classes have been loaded: it will contain [Simulation] objects, and the [Simulation] class must be defined by the time PHP reconstructs the session objects;
  • Lines 48–59: We attempt to create the [Logger] object, which will allow us to log events to the [Data/logs.txt] file. This creation may fail: the constructor for [Logger] then throws a [ExceptionImpots] exception;
  • lines 52–56: the error response, with status [133]. The message uses the log file name specified in the configuration rather than the full path: the full path would reveal the server’s folder structure to the client;
  • line 57: the response is sent via a [JsonResponse] object, without a log since one could not be created. The application classes are now loaded: they can be used;
  • Line 58: The script is terminated.

All responses sent to the client implement the following [InterfaceResponse] interface, from the [Responses] folder:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// Symfony dependencies
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// the interface implemented by the three response types [JsonResponse, XmlResponse, HtmlResponse]
interface InterfaceResponse
{
     // Sending the response to the client
     // Request $request: the request currently being processed
     // Session $session: the web application session
     // array $config: the application configuration
     // int $statusCode: the response status code HTTP
     // array $content: the server response, the array [action, état, réponse]
     // array $headers: the HTTP headers to be added to the response
     // ?Logger $logger: the application log (null if it could not be created)
    public function send(
        Request $request,
        Session $session,
        array $config,
        int $statusCode,
        array $content,
        array $headers = [],
        ?Logger $logger = null
    ): void;
}
  • Lines 23–31: The [InterfaceResponse] interface has a single method, [send], for sending the response to the client;
  • lines 16–22: the meaning of the various parameters of the [send] method;
  • lines 27–29: The parameters [$statusCode], [$content], and [$headers] contain the result from the secondary controller and the keys [action, état] added by the primary controller. However, the response may require additional information. Therefore, it is provided with the first three parameters, which give it access to all information regarding the request, the session, and the configuration;
  • Line 30: The response requires [Logger] because it will log the response sent to the client. The type [?Logger] indicates that the parameter may be [null]: this is the case when the log could not be created. In the PHP 7 signature, the parameters [Request $request = NULL] and [Logger $logger = NULL] were implicitly nullable: this syntax has been deprecated since PHP 8.4. Additionally, declaring an optional parameter before required parameters has been deprecated since PHP 8.0.

The class [JsonResponse] implements the interface [InterfaceResponse] as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// Symfony dependencies
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// a response JSON
final class JsonResponse extends ParentResponse
{
     #[\Override]
    public function send(
        Request $request,
        Session $session,
        array $config,
        int $statusCode,
        array $content,
        array $headers = [],
        ?Logger $logger = null
    ): void {
         // serialization JSON: [json_encode] also serializes the public attributes of objects [Simulation]
        $json = json_encode($content, self::JSON_OPTIONS);
         // sending the response via the parent class
        $this->sendResponse($statusCode, $json, "application/json", $headers);
         // log
        $logger?->write("réponse=$json");
    }
}

Comments

  • Line 13: The class extends the abstract class [ParentResponse], which implements the interface [InterfaceResponse]. All response types extend this class. It is this parent class that sends the response to the client. Because this code is common to all response types, it has been factored into a parent class. Our [JsonResponse] class is not Symfony’s [JsonResponse] class: it is in the [Application] namespace, and we do not import the Symfony class;
  • Line 15: The attribute [Override] (PHP 8.3) indicates that the method [send] implements a method from a parent class or an interface. If this were not the case (due to a typo in the name, for example), PHP would report an error;
  • Line 26: The response [$content] is serialized to JSON. The options for [json_encode] are defined once and for all in the parent class. The function [json_encode] serializes a [Simulation] object as a JSON object whose keys are the names of its public attributes;
  • line 28: the parent class is asked to send the response to the client, specifying the document type as [application/json];
  • line 30: the response JSON is logged. The null-safe operator [?->] calls the method [write] only if [$logger] is not [null].

The code for the parent class [ParentResponse] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// Symfony dependencies
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;

// the parent class of the three response types: it factors out what they have in common
// It is abstract: the [send] method of the interface is implemented by the child classes
abstract class ParentResponse implements InterfaceResponse
{
     // the [json_encode] options used by all responses
    protected const int JSON_OPTIONS = JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE | JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES
        | JSON_PRESERVE_ZERO_FRACTION | JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR;

     // Actual sending of the response to the client
     // $statusCode: the response status code
     // $body: the response body, which may be a string such as JSON, XML, or HTML
     // $contentType: the type of the sent document (application/json, application/xml, text/html)
     // $headers: the headers HTTP to be added to the response
    protected function sendResponse(int $statusCode, string $body, string $contentType, array $headers): void
    {
         // the Symfony response
        $response = new Response($body, $statusCode, $headers);
         // the type of the sent document, encoded as UTF-8
        $response->headers->set("Content-Type", "$contentType; charset=utf-8");
         // sending the HTTP headers followed by the response body
        $response->send();
    }

     // response log in JSON, regardless of the type of response sent
    protected function log(?Logger $logger, array $content): void
    {
        $logger?->write("réponse=" . json_encode($content, self::JSON_OPTIONS));
    }

     // returns the data [$data] in which the objects (from the simulations) have been replaced
     // with the associative array of their public attributes
    protected static function toArray(mixed $data): mixed
    {
        return match (true) {
            is_object($data) => self::toArray(get_object_vars($data)),
            is_array($data) => array_map(self::toArray(...), $data),
            default => $data,
        };
    }
}

Comments

  • Line 13: The class is abstract; it cannot be instantiated. It implements the [InterfaceResponse] interface without defining the [send] method, which will be defined by the child classes. In course PHP 7, [ParentResponse] was a regular class that the child classes extended while implementing the interface;
  • Line 16: the options of [json_encode] common to all responses. Since PHP 8.3, a class constant can be typed:
    • [JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE]: accented characters are written as-is and not in the form [\u00e9];
    • [JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES]: The character [/] is not encoded as [\/];
    • [JSON_PRESERVE_ZERO_FRACTION]: A real number is always written with a decimal point (a zero rate is written as [0.0]);
    • [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR]: A serialization error throws a [JsonException] exception;
  • line 24: the [sendResponse] method sends the response to the client. Note that the response body [$body] is of type [string] and is therefore ready to be sent;
  • line 27: the Symfony class constructor [Response] receives the response body, status, and headers;
  • line 29: the type of the sent document, encoded as UTF-8;
  • line 31: the response is sent to the client;
  • line 35: the method [log] logs the response as JSON. It will be used by the responses XML and HTML;
  • lines 42–49: the static method [toArray] returns the data [$data], in which the objects have been replaced by the associative array of their public attributes. It will be used by the response XML:
    • the expression [match (true)] selects the first branch whose condition is true;
    • line 45: an object is replaced by the array of its attributes, returned by the function [get_object_vars]. When called from outside the object’s class, it returns only its public attributes. The attributes themselves may be objects; therefore, [toArray] is called;
    • line 46: Each element of an array is transformed by [toArray]. The syntax [self::toArray(...)] (PHP 8.1) creates an anonymous function (a [Closure]) from the method [toArray]: this is the syntax for first-class callables. With a single array, the function [array_map] preserves the array keys;
    • line 47: the other values (strings, numbers) are returned as-is.

docs.title: 23.9.5. [curl] Tests – 2
docs.text:
Let’s modify the file [config.json] as follows: ["logsFilename": "Data"]. The log file is now [Data], which is a folder. Creating the file [Data] should therefore fail:

> curl -i "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/impots/version-12/main.php"
HTTP/1.0 500 Internal Server Error

docs.title: 23.9.6. [main.php] – 3
docs.text:
Let’s continue examining the main controller [main.php]:

// 1st log
$logger->write("---nouvelle requête");

// the requested action
$nomAction = strtolower(trim($request->query->getString("action")));
$logger->write("action [$nomAction] demandée");
// Is the action one of the cases in the enumeration [Action]? (null otherwise)
$action = Action::tryFrom($nomAction);
// Preliminary checks: an error result, or null if the action can be executed
$erreur = match (true) {
    !$request->query->has("action") => [101, "paramètre [action] manquant"],
    $action === null => [102, "action [$nomAction] invalide"],
    $action->exigeTypeSession() && !$session->has("type")
        => [103, "pas de session en cours. Commencer par action [init-session]"],
    $action->exigeAuthentification() && !$session->has("user")
        => [104, "action demandée par utilisateur non authentifié"],
    default => null,
};
if ($erreur !== null) {
     // Prepare the error response without sending it
    [$état, $message] = $erreur;
    $résultat = new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_BAD_REQUEST, $état, [$message]);
} else {
     // Executing the action using its secondary controller
    $controller = match ($action) {
        Action::InitSession => new InitSessionController(),
        Action::AuthentifierUtilisateur => new AuthentifierUtilisateurController(),
        Action::CalculerImpot => new CalculerImpotController(),
        Action::ListerSimulations => new ListerSimulationsController(),
        Action::SupprimerSimulation => new SupprimerSimulationController(),
        Action::FinSession => new FinSessionController(),
        Action::AfficherCalculImpot => new AfficherCalculImpotController(),
    };
    $logger->write("contrôleur : " . $controller::class);
    $résultat = $controller->execute($config, $request, $session);
}

// Response to the client: [action, état], followed by the controller's response
$content = ["action" => $nomAction, "état" => $résultat->état, "réponse" => $résultat->réponse];
// Fatal error: An email is sent to the administrator
if ($résultat->statusCode === Response::HTTP_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR) {
     // [SendAdminMail] catches all exceptions and logs them itself
    (new SendAdminMail($config["adminMail"], $logger))
        ->send(json_encode($content, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE | JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES | JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR));
}
// The response type is in the session—JSON by default if it has not yet been set
$type = ResponseType::tryFrom($session->get("type", "")) ?? ResponseType::Json;
// the object [InterfaceResponse] of the requested type sends the response to the client
$type->response()->send(
    $request,
    $session,
    $config,
    $résultat->statusCode,
    $content,
    $résultat->headers,
    $logger
);
// end
exit;

Comments

  • line 62: We log the fact that we have a new request. We couldn’t do this before because we weren’t sure we had a valid log file;
  • line 65: the parameter [action] must be part of URL in the form [main.php?action=uneAction]. It is therefore part of the [$request->query] parameters of URL. Symfony’s [getString] method returns the parameter’s value as a string, or an empty string if the parameter is missing;
  • line 66: the requested action is logged;
  • line 68: the static method [tryFrom] of a backed enumeration returns the enumeration case whose value is [$nomAction], or [null] if no case has that value. The method [from] would do the same thing but would throw a [ValueError] exception in the second case;
  • lines 70–78: preliminary checks. Their result, [$erreur], is either an array [état, message] describing the first error encountered, or [null] if the action can be executed. The conditions are evaluated in the following order:
    • line 71: the parameter [action] is missing from URL: status [101];
    • line 72: the action is unknown: status [102];
    • line 73: the application provides three response types (JSON, XML, HTML). This type is set by action [init-session], which places it in the session, associated with key [type]. Except for action [init-session], all actions must be performed with a key [type] in the session; otherwise, the status is [103];
    • Line 75: Except for actions [init-session] and [authentifier-utilisateur], all actions must be performed after authentication. Authentication is performed using the [authentifier-utilisateur] action, which, if authentication is successful, sets a [user] key in the session; otherwise, the status is [104];
    • line 77: no error;
  • lines 79–82: if the requested action or its execution context is incorrect, the error response is prepared but not sent: status [400 Bad Request], status, error list (with a single error in this case). The [[$état, $message] = $erreur] destructuring assigns the two elements of the [$erreur] array in a single statement;
  • lines 85–93: this is a valid operation. We instantiate the secondary controller that will process it. Course PHP 7 constructed the controller class name from the configuration ([__NAMESPACE__ . $config["actions"][$action]]) and then instantiated it with [new $controller()]. The expression [match] on the cases of the enumeration [Action] is safer: the code analyzer for [VS Code] checks the class names, and if a case is added to the enumeration without adding it here, [match] will throw a [UnhandledMatchError] exception instead of instantiating a random class;
  • line 94: the name of the secondary controller is logged for verification during development. Starting with PHP 8.0, [$objet::class] returns the full class name of an object;
  • line 95: the secondary controller is executed. It returns a [ControllerResult] object. We’ll come back to secondary controllers a little later;
  • We then reach line 99 either because an error occurred or after a controller was executed. In either case, the object [$résultat] contains everything needed to generate the response to the client;
  • Line 99: The response to the client is a three-key array named [action, état, réponse]. The key [action] will facilitate better tracking of the logs in the file [logs.txt]. The key [état] will serve two purposes:
    • it will allow clients JSON and XML to determine the state into which the executed action has placed the web application;
    • in the case of a HTML response, it will allow the system to select the HTML view to be sent to the client browser;
  • Lines 101–104: Special case of status code [500 Internal Server Error]. If a controller has set this status code, it means the application cannot function. This is the case, for example, with tax calculations if SGBD or the [Redis] server has not been started or is no longer responding. An email is then sent to the application administrator to notify them, using class [SendAdminMail] from version 9;
  • Line 107: The response type [JSON, XML, HTML] is determined. If the action [init-session] was executed successfully, this type is present in the session, associated with the key [type]. If this is not the case, the [get] method of the session returns the default value [""], [tryFrom] returns [null], and the operator [??] selects the type JSON;
  • Lines 109–117: The method [response] of the enumeration [ResponseType], described later, returns the object [JsonResponse], [XmlResponse] or [HtmlResponse], which is appropriate for the session type. Its method [send] sends the response to the client. Since the three classes implement the same [InterfaceResponse] interface, their [send] methods all have the same signature;
  • Line 119: The main controller has completed its work. The script PHP 7 used to close the log file here; our class [Logger] no longer has a method [close].

docs.title: 23.10. Secondary controllers
docs.text:
Each action is executed by one of the controllers in the [Controllers] folder:

In the overall architecture of the application above, the secondary controllers are in [2a]. Each controller implements the following [InterfaceController] interface:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// Symfony dependencies
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// the interface implemented by all secondary controllers
interface InterfaceController
{
     // processing of the requested action
     // array $config: the application configuration
     // Request $request: the request currently being processed
     // Session $session: the web application session, which the controller can modify
     // returns a [ControllerResult] object: HTTP status, application state, response, HTTP headers
    public function execute(array $config, Request $request, Session $session): ControllerResult;
}

Comments

  • Line 20: All secondary controllers are executed via the [execute] method. Information known to the main controller is passed to this method:
    • [array $config]: the application configuration;
    • [Request $request]: the HTTP request currently being processed;
    • [Session $session]: the current web application session;
  • The [execute] method returns a [ControllerResult] object: the response status code HTTP, the state of the application at the end of execution, the response to be sent to the client, and the headers HTTP to be added to the response.

Method PHP 7 had a fourth parameter, [array $infos = NULL], which was included “just in case” but never used: we have removed it. Each secondary controller is called by the following code in the main controller:

     // the action is executed using its secondary controller
    $controller = match ($action) {
        Action::InitSession => new InitSessionController(),
        Action::AuthentifierUtilisateur => new AuthentifierUtilisateurController(),
        Action::CalculerImpot => new CalculerImpotController(),
        Action::ListerSimulations => new ListerSimulationsController(),
        Action::SupprimerSimulation => new SupprimerSimulationController(),
        Action::FinSession => new FinSessionController(),
        Action::AfficherCalculImpot => new AfficherCalculImpotController(),
    };
    $logger->write("contrôleur : " . $controller::class);
    $résultat = $controller->execute($config, $request, $session);

docs.title: 23.11. Actions
docs.text:
We will now review the various possible actions of the web service:

ActionRoleExecution Contextinit-sessionUsed to specify the type (json, xml, html) of the desired responsesRequest GET main.php?action=init-session&type=xCan be issued at any timeauthenticate-userAuthorizes or denies a user’s loginRequest POST main.php?action=authenticate-userThe request must include two POST parameters: [user, password]Can only be issued if the session type (json, xml, html) is knowncalculate-taxPerforms a tax calculation simulationRequest: POST main.php?action=calculate-taxThe request must have three POST parameters: [marié, enfants, salaire]Can only be issued if the session type is known and the user is authenticatedlist-simulationsRequests a list of simulations performed since the start of the sessionRequest GET main.php?action=list-simulationsThe request does not accept any other parametersCan only be issued if the session type is known and the user is authenticateddelete-simulationDeletes a simulation from the list of simulationsRequest GET main.php?action=delete-simulation&number=xThe request does not accept any other parametersCan only be issued if the session type is known and the user is authenticatedend-sessionEnds the simulation sessionRequest GET main.php?action=end-sessionTechnically, the old web session is deleted and a new session is createdCan only be issued if the session type is known and the user is authenticateddisplay-tax-calculationDisplays the tax calculation view (application HTML)Request GET main.php?action=display-tax-calculationCan only be issued if the session type is known and the user is authenticated

All secondary controllers proceed in the same way:

  • they check their parameters. These are found in the [$request->query] object for parameters present in the URL object and in the [$request->request] object for those that are posted (request POST);
  • A controller is similar to a function or method that checks the validity of its parameters. For the controller, however, it’s a bit more complicated:
    • the expected parameters may be missing;
    • the expected parameters are all character strings, whereas a function can specify the type of its parameters. If the expected parameter is a number, then you must verify that the parameter’s string actually represents a number;
    • once it has been verified that the expected parameters are present and syntactically correct, you must verify that they are valid within the current execution context. This context is stored in the session. Authentication is an example of an execution context: certain actions should only be processed once the client has been authenticated. A key in the session indicates whether this authentication has taken place or not;
  • Once the previous checks have been completed, the secondary controller can begin processing. This parameter validation is very important. We cannot allow a client to send us just anything at any point during the application’s lifecycle. We must maintain complete control over the application’s lifecycle;
  • Once its work is done, the secondary controller returns the [ControllerResult] object expected by the primary controller that called it.

We will now review the various controllers—or, in other words, the various actions that drive the web application’s lifecycle.

docs.title: 23.11.1. The [init-session] action
docs.text:
The action [init-session] is handled by the following controller, [InitSessionController]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// Symfony dependencies
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// [init-session] action: sets the type (json, xml, html) of the session responses
final class InitSessionController implements InterfaceController
{
     #[\Override]
    public function execute(array $config, Request $request, Session $session): ControllerResult
    {
         // You must have a GET with only the [action, type] parameters in the URL
        if ($request->getMethod() !== "GET" || $request->query->count() !== 2) {
            $message = "méthode GET exigée avec les paramètres [action, type] dans l'URL";
            return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_BAD_REQUEST, 701, $message);
        }
         // the parameter [type] must be present
        if (!$request->query->has("type")) {
            return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_BAD_REQUEST, 702, "paramètre [type] manquant");
        }
         // and valid: [tryFrom] returns null if the string is not the value of any case in the enumeration
        $type = strtolower(trim($request->query->getString("type")));
        if (ResponseType::tryFrom($type) === null) {
            return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_BAD_REQUEST, 703, "paramètre type [$type] invalide");
        }
         // The session type is set in the session
        $session->set("type", $type);
         // Success
        return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_OK, 700, "session démarrée avec type [$type]");
    }
}

Comments

  • A request for [GET main.php?action=init-session&type=xxx] is expected;
  • Line 14: The class implements the [InterfaceController] interface. It is [final]: it cannot be derived from;
  • Lines 20–23: We verify that the request is a GET request with two parameters in the URL. If this is not the case, an error result is returned to the main controller with the status [701]. The Symfony method [getMethod] returns the name of the method HTTP in uppercase: it is no longer necessary to convert it to lowercase as the script PHP 7 did;
  • lines 25–27: We verify that the parameter [type] is present in URL. If not, we return an error result with status [702];
  • line 29: Record the session type;
  • Lines 30–32: Check that the session type is one of the terms (json, xml, html), c.-à-d. The value must be one of the cases in the enumeration [ResponseType]. If this is not the case, return an error result with status [703];
  • line 34: the session type is set in the web application session;
  • line 36: the controller has finished its work. A success result is returned to the main controller, with status [700].

Every error case results in an immediate [return]. The script PHP 7 used a Boolean variable [$erreur] that was checked at each step: the code is now shorter and more readable. Let’s review what the main controller does with the responses from the secondary controllers: it adds the keys [action] and [état] to the response and sends it by instantiating one of the [JsonResponse, XmlResponse, HtmlResponse] classes depending on the type (json, xml, html) of the current session.

Next, we will perform [curl] tests as part of a [json] simulation session.

docs.title: 23.11.3. The [authentifier-utilisateur] action
docs.text:
The action [authentifier-utilisateur] is executed by the following controller, [AuthentifierUtilisateurController]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// Symfony dependencies
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// [authentifier-utilisateur] action: authenticates the user with the posted parameters [user, password]
final class AuthentifierUtilisateurController implements InterfaceController
{
     #[\Override]
    public function execute(array $config, Request $request, Session $session): ControllerResult
    {
         // You must have a POST with only the parameter [action] in the URL
        if ($request->getMethod() !== "POST" || $request->query->count() !== 1) {
            $message = "méthode POST requise, paramètre [action] dans l'URL, paramètres postés [user, password]";
            return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_BAD_REQUEST, 201, $message);
        }
         // we retrieve the posted parameters
        $erreurs = [];
        $état = 210;
         // user
        if (!$request->request->has("user")) {
            $état += 2;
            $erreurs[] = "paramètre [user] manquant";
        }
         // password
        if (!$request->request->has("password")) {
            $état += 4;
            $erreurs[] = "paramètre [password] manquant";
        }
         // errors?
        if ($erreurs !== []) {
            return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_BAD_REQUEST, $état, $erreurs);
        }
        $user = trim($request->request->getString("user"));
        $password = trim($request->request->getString("password"));
         // Is the user one of the authorized users?
        $trouvé = array_any(
            $config["users"],
            fn(array $u): bool => $u["login"] === $user && hash_equals($u["passwd"], $password)
        );
        if (!$trouvé) {
             // failure: code 401 - the password is never sent back to the client
            return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_UNAUTHORIZED, 221, "Echec de l'authentification [$user]");
        }
         // The authenticated user's ID is recorded in the session
        $session->set("user", $user);
         // Success
        return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_OK, 200, "Authentification réussie [$user]");
    }
}

Comments

  • We are waiting for a [POST main.php?action=authentifier-utilisateur] request with two posted parameters, [user, password];
  • Lines 20–23: The system checks whether there is a POST request with a single parameter in URL. If not, an error result is returned with status [201];
  • line 26: the error status for the posted parameters starts at value 210;
  • lines 28–31: We check for the presence of the parameter [user] in the posted values. If it is not present, we log the error and increment the status by 2;
  • Lines 33–36: We check for the presence of the parameter [password]. If it is not present, we log the error and add 4 to the status. The status is therefore 212 if only [user] is missing, 214 if only [password] is missing, and 216 if both are missing;
  • lines 38–40: if any of the posted values is missing, an error result is returned, with the response being the list of errors;
  • lines 41–42: the posted identifiers;
  • lines 44–47: verify that the pair [[$user, $password]] is present in the [$config["users"]] array in the configuration file. The function [array_any] (PHP 8.4) returns [true] if at least one element of the array satisfies the condition expressed by the arrowed function. The password is compared using the function [hash_equals], whose execution time does not depend on the position of the first differing character: an attacker cannot guess the password character by character by measuring response times. The script PHP 7 used a loop [while];
  • lines 48–51: if the user is not found, an error result is returned with status HTTP [401 Unauthorized] and status [221]. Message PHP 7 contained the entered password: a password must never be sent back to the client or written to the logs;
  • line 53: authentication was successful. This is recorded in the session by adding the key [user], with the user ID as its value. The presence of this key indicates successful authentication;
  • Line 55: A success result is returned to the main controller, with the status [200].

  • Lines 1–2: Before any authentication, a tax calculation is requested. The option [-d] converts the request to POST. The main controller rejects the action: status [104];
  • lines 4–5: the action [authentifier-utilisateur] uses a GET when a POST is required: status [201];
  • lines 7–8: a POST (option [-X POST]) with no posted parameters: status [216];
  • lines 10–11: a POST with only the [password] parameter: status [212]. With the [-d] option, parameters are submitted just as they would be in a HTML form: the request body is the string [password=x], and the header [Content-Type] is set to [application/x-www-form-urlencoded];

docs.title: 23.11.5. Action [calculer-impot]
docs.text:
The [calculer-impot] action is processed by the following [CalculerImpotController] controller:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// Symfony dependencies
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;
// Predis dependencies
use Predis\Client as RedisClient;
use Predis\PredisException;
// class alias: the [dao] layer from version 9 is used with Redis
use Application\ServerDaoWithSession as ServerDaoWithRedis;

// [calculer-impot] action: tax calculation using posted parameters [marié, enfants, salaire]
final class CalculerImpotController implements InterfaceController
{
     #[\Override]
    public function execute(array $config, Request $request, Session $session): ControllerResult
    {
         // You must have a POST with only the parameter [action] in the URL
        if ($request->getMethod() !== "POST" || $request->query->count() !== 1) {
            $message = "il faut utiliser la méthode [post] avec [action] dans l'URL"
                . " et les paramètres postés [marié, enfants, salaire]";
            return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_BAD_REQUEST, 301, $message);
        }
         // We verify the posted parameters
         // Each error adds a different value to the status: the final status indicates which errors occurred
        $erreurs = [];
        $état = 310;
         // marital status
        if (!$request->request->has("marié")) {
            $état += 2;
            $erreurs[] = "paramètre [marié] manquant";
        } else {
            $marié = strtolower(trim($request->request->getString("marié")));
            if (!in_array($marié, ["oui", "non"], true)) {
                $état += 4;
                $erreurs[] = "valeur [$marié] invalide pour le paramètre [marié]";
            }
        }
         // number of children and annual income: integers >= 0
        $valeurs = [];
        foreach (["enfants" => [8, 9], "salaire" => [16, 17]] as $paramètre => [$manquant, $invalide]) {
            if (!$request->request->has($paramètre)) {
                $état += $manquant;
                $erreurs[] = "paramètre [$paramètre] manquant";
                continue;
            }
            $valeur = trim($request->request->getString($paramètre));
            if (preg_match('/^\d+$/', $valeur) !== 1) {
                $état += $invalide;
                $erreurs[] = "valeur [$valeur] invalide pour le paramètre [$paramètre]";
            } else {
                $valeurs[$paramètre] = (int) $valeur;
            }
        }
         // Errors?
        if ($erreurs !== []) {
            return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_BAD_REQUEST, $état, $erreurs);
        }
        [$enfants, $salaire] = [$valeurs["enfants"], $valeurs["salaire"]];

         // We have valid parameters—the scope memory [application]: a Redis server
        try {
            $redis = new RedisClient($config["redis"]);
             // We connect to the server immediately to check if it's available
            $redis->connect();
        } catch (PredisException $ex) {
             // Error 500
            return new ControllerResult(
                Response::HTTP_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR,
                350,
                "[redis], " . self::utf8($ex->getMessage())
            );
        }
         // Creating the layer [dao]
        try {
            $json = $redis->get("taxAdminData");
            if ($json === null) {
                 // Tax data is retrieved from the database and stored in Redis
                $dao = new ServerDaoWithRedis(ROOT_DIRECTORY . "/" . $config["databaseFilename"]);
                $redis->set("taxAdminData", (string) $dao->getTaxAdminData());
            } else {
                 // Tax data is retrieved from Redis
                $taxAdminData = TaxAdminData::fromArray(json_decode($json, true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR));
                $dao = new ServerDaoWithRedis($taxAdminData);
            }
        } catch (ExceptionImpots $ex) {
             // Error 500
            return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, 341, self::utf8($ex->getMessage()));
        } finally {
             // The Redis server is no longer needed
            $redis->disconnect();
        }
         // Creation of the [métier] layer and tax calculation
        $résultat = (new ServerMetier($dao))->calculerImpot($marié, $enfants, $salaire);
         // Simulation: The keys in the [$résultat] array become named arguments
        $simulation = new Simulation($marié, $enfants, $salaire, ...$résultat);
         // It is added to the session’s list of simulations
        $session->set("simulations", [...$session->get("simulations", []), $simulation]);
         // Success
        return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_OK, 300, $simulation);
    }

     // An error message from a SGBD driver or Redis may not be encoded in UTF-8
     // (Windows-1252 on Windows): it could not then be included in a string JSON
    private static function utf8(string $message): string
    {
        return mb_check_encoding($message, "UTF-8") ? $message : mb_convert_encoding($message, "UTF-8", "Windows-1252");
    }
}

Comments

  • The expected request is [POST main.php?action=calculer-impot] with three posted parameters [marié, enfants, salaire]:
    • [marié] must have its value in [oui, non];
    • [enfants, salaire] must be positive integers or zero;
  • Lines 13–16: As in version 10, we use the [Predis] library and the [dao] layer from version 9, under the alias [ServerDaoWithRedis];
  • lines 25–29: We verify that there is indeed a POST with a single parameter in the URL. If this is not the case, an error result is returned to the main controller, with status [301];
  • lines 32–33: error messages are accumulated in the array [$erreurs]. The count starts at 310, and each error increments it by one;
  • lines 35–44: We check for the presence of parameter [marié] (+2 if missing), then verify that its value is in [oui, non] (+4 otherwise);
  • lines 47–60: The parameters [enfants] and [salaire] are checked by the same loop. The array being iterated through associates each parameter with the pair of values added to the state when the parameter is missing or invalid: (8, 9) for [enfants], (16, 17) for [salaire]. The unpacking of [[$manquant, $invalide]] is performed directly within the [foreach] statement. The PHP script 7 wrote the same code twice;
    • lines 48–52: the parameter is missing; the [continue] statement moves on to the next parameter;
    • lines 54–59: the value must be a sequence of at least one digit. If so, it is converted to an integer and stored in the array [$valeurs];
  • lines 62–64: If there were any errors, a result is returned containing a list of the errors;
  • line 65: the parameters are valid. The tax can be calculated. To do this, the layers [dao] and [métier] must be created, which are capable of performing this calculation;
  • lines 68–79: A client named [Redis] is created, and a connection to the server is established immediately. If we were unable to connect to the server [Redis], we return a result with status [500 Internal Server Error] and condition [350];
  • lines 81–98: construction of the [dao] layer:
    • Line 82: Check whether the server [Redis] has the key [taxAdminData]. This key represents the tax administration data. The method [get] of [Predis] returns [null] if the key does not exist;
    • line 85: the key does not exist; the tax data must be retrieved from the database. The path to the database description file is relative to the application’s root directory, which is determined by the constant [ROOT_DIRECTORY] defined by [main.php];
    • line 86: the data retrieved from the database is stored in memory [Redis] with the key [taxAdminData], in the form of its string JSON;
    • lines 89–90: if the key [taxAdminData] exists in memory [Redis], the tax data is passed directly to the layer builder [dao];
  • lines 92–94: if the database query failed, a result is returned with status [500 Internal Server Error], report [341], and the exception message thrown by layer [dao]. The listing for course PHP 7 showed status 340 here, whereas its source code, its configuration (which associates status 341 with the tax calculation view), and its text all used 341. We chose 341: status 340 is already the status for a request with three invalid posted parameters (310 + 4 + 9 + 17);
  • lines 95–98: the [finally] clause is executed in all cases, regardless of whether an exception occurred, and even if the [catch] block ends with a [return]. Here, the connection to the [Redis] server is closed;
  • line 100: the [métier] layer is created and calculates the tax. The result is the [impôt, surcôte, décôte, réduction, taux] array;
  • Line 102: Based on the result of the calculation, an object [Simulation] is created. The first three arguments are positional. The operator [...] then decomposes the associative array [$résultat]: Starting with PHP 8.1, its keys become named arguments—in this case, [impôt, surcôte, décôte, réduction, taux]—which are the names of the last parameters of the constructor;
  • line 104: the simulation that has just been constructed is added to the list of simulations already calculated, which is located in the session. The second parameter of the session’s [get] method is the value returned if the key is absent: an empty list if no simulations have been performed yet. The new list is constructed by decomposing the old list, followed by the new simulation, and then returned to the session;
  • line 106: the simulation is returned to the main controller, with the status [300];
  • line 111: An error message from a driver of type SGBD may not be encoded as UTF-8 (see version 8). In that case, it could not be placed in a JSON string. The PHP 7 script used the [utf8_encode] function, which has been deprecated since PHP 8.2; we now use [mb_convert_encoding].

docs.title: 23.11.9. Action [supprimer-simulation]
docs.text:
Action [supprimer-simulation] is processed by the following secondary controller, [SupprimerSimulationController]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// Symfony dependencies
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// action [supprimer-simulation]: removes simulation # [numéro] from the list of simulations
final class SupprimerSimulationController implements InterfaceController
{
     #[\Override]
    public function execute(array $config, Request $request, Session $session): ControllerResult
    {
         // there must be a GET with only the parameters [action, numéro] in the URL
        if ($request->getMethod() !== "GET" || $request->query->count() !== 2) {
            return self::erreur(602, "GET requis, avec les paramètres [action, numéro]");
        }
         // The parameter [numéro] must exist
        if (!$request->query->has("numéro")) {
            return self::erreur(604, "paramètre [numéro] manquant");
        }
         // The parameter [numéro] must be an integer >= 0
        $numéro = trim($request->query->getString("numéro"));
        if (preg_match('/^\d+$/', $numéro) !== 1) {
            return self::erreur(612, "paramètre [$numéro] invalide");
        }
         // Simulation No. [numéro] must exist: [numéro] within the range [0, n-1]
        $numéro = (int) $numéro;
        $simulations = $session->get("simulations", []);
        if ($numéro >= count($simulations)) {
            return self::erreur(628, "la simulation n° [$numéro] n'existe pas");
        }
         // The simulation is deleted: [array_splice] renumbers the following items in the list
        array_splice($simulations, $numéro, 1);
         // restores the simulations to the session
        $session->set("simulations", $simulations);
         // returns the new list of simulations
        return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_OK, 600, $simulations);
    }

     // an error result
    private static function erreur(int $état, string $message): ControllerResult
    {
        return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_BAD_REQUEST, $état, $message);
    }
}

Comments

  • request [GET main.php?action=supprimer-simulation&numéro=x];
  • lines 20–22: Check that there is a request GET with two parameters. Otherwise, the status is [602];
  • lines 24–26: Check that the parameter [numéro] exists among the parameters of URL. Otherwise, the status is [604];
  • lines 28–31: Check that the value of parameter [numéro] is syntactically correct: a positive integer or zero. Otherwise, the status is [612];
  • lines 33–37: Verify that simulation No. [numéro] actually exists: the number must be in the range [0, n-1], where n is the number of simulations in the session. Otherwise, the status is [628]. Since the number cannot be negative, it is sufficient to verify that it is less than n. If the session contains no simulations, n is 0;
  • line 39: simulation No. [numéro] is deleted by function [array_splice], which deletes an element starting at position [$numéro] and renumbers the subsequent elements. The script PHP 7 used [unset], which does not change the keys of the other elements, and then [array_values] to obtain a list with keys [0, n-2];
  • line 41: the new simulation table is returned to the session;
  • line 43: the new list of simulations is returned to the main controller, with the status [600];
  • line 47: a utility method that constructs an error result. The error statuses are those from script PHP 7, which calculated them by adding 2, 4, 8, and then 16 to status 600 as the checks progressed.

docs.title: 23.11.11. Action [fin-session]
docs.text:
Action [fin-session] is processed by the following secondary controller, [FinSessionController]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// Symfony dependencies
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// action [fin-session]: ends the simulation session
final class FinSessionController implements InterfaceController
{
     #[\Override]
    public function execute(array $config, Request $request, Session $session): ControllerResult
    {
         // There must be a GET with only the parameter [action] in the URL
        if ($request->getMethod() !== "GET" || $request->query->count() !== 1) {
            $message = "GET requis avec le seul paramètre [action] dans l'URL";
            return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_BAD_REQUEST, 401, $message);
        }
         // The session type is stored
        $type = $session->get("type");
         // The current session is invalidated: its data is deleted and a new session begins
        $session->invalidate();
         // the type is restored in the new session
        $session->set("type", $type);
         // Success
        return new ControllerResult(Response::HTTP_OK, 400, "session supprimée");
    }
}

Comments

  • request [GET main.php?action=fin-session];
  • lines 20–23: Verify that the action is a GET with the single parameter [action]. Otherwise, the status is [401];
  • line 25: Before the session ends, the session type ([json, xml, html]) is stored;
  • line 27: the current session is invalidated. This deletes the data stored in it, and a new session is started with a new identifier;
  • Line 29: The type from the previous session is restored in the new session. Finally, we start over with a new session having the unique key [type]: the user will need to authenticate again;
  • Line 31: The result is returned to the main controller, with the status [400].

{"action":"lister-simulations","état":104,"réponse":["action demandée par utilisateur non authentifié"]}
  • Lines 1–2: We request session termination with a POST instead of the expected GET: status [401];
  • Lines 4–16: A valid [fin-session] action: status [400];
  • lines 10–11: the server sends two [Set-Cookie] headers. The first instructs the client to delete the old session cookie (its expiration date has passed). The second provides the client with the new session cookie: a new web session begins. We saw that, within the same session, the server no longer sends the session cookie after the first response;
  • lines 18–19: In the new session, the user is no longer authenticated: status [104].

docs.title: 23.12.1. Introduction
docs.text:
Let’s review the application’s overall architecture:

We will now present the possible response types [3a]. These are located in the [Responses] folder of the project. We have already introduced the [InterfaceResponse] interface, the parent class [ParentResponse], and the [JsonResponse] class. The response type for a session is set by the action [init-session], which places it in the session. It is represented by the enumeration [ResponseType] in the folder [Entities]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// The response types the client can request with the action [init-session]
enum ResponseType: string
{
    case Json = "json";
    case Xml = "xml";
    case Html = "html";

     // the object responsible for sending a response of this type
    public function response(): InterfaceResponse
    {
        return match ($this) {
            self::Json => new JsonResponse(),
            self::Xml => new XmlResponse(),
            self::Html => new HtmlResponse(),
        };
    }
}

Comments

  • lines 11–13: the three response types. The value for each case is the expected value for the [type] parameter of action [init-session];
  • Lines 16–23: The [response] method returns the object responsible for sending a response of this type. The return type is the [InterfaceResponse] interface: the calling code is only aware of the [send] method of the interface. The PHP 7 course associated each type in the configuration file with a class name (key [types]) and instantiated it using [new $response()].

Let’s review the code from the main controller that requests that the response be sent to the client:

// the response type is in the session—JSON by default if it has not yet been set
$type = ResponseType::tryFrom($session->get("type", "")) ?? ResponseType::Json;
// the object [InterfaceResponse] of the requested type sends the response to the client
$type->response()->send(
    $request,
    $session,
    $config,
    $résultat->statusCode,
    $content,
    $résultat->headers,
    $logger
);
  • Line 107: The response type is determined;
  • line 109: the appropriate response class is instantiated, and the response is sent to the client using its method [send($request, $session, $config, $statusCode, $content, $headers, $logger)].

docs.title: 23.12.2. The [JsonResponse] class
docs.text:
has already been introduced. However, we are including its code again to better highlight the consistency among the three response classes:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// Symfony dependencies
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// a response JSON
final class JsonResponse extends ParentResponse
{
     #[\Override]
    public function send(
        Request $request,
        Session $session,
        array $config,
        int $statusCode,
        array $content,
        array $headers = [],
        ?Logger $logger = null
    ): void {
         // serialization JSON: [json_encode] also serializes the public attributes of objects [Simulation]
        $json = json_encode($content, self::JSON_OPTIONS);
         // sending the response via the parent class
        $this->sendResponse($statusCode, $json, "application/json", $headers);
         // log
        $logger?->write("réponse=$json");
    }
}

docs.title: 23.12.3. The [XmlResponse] class
docs.text:
The [XmlResponse] class is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Application;

// Symfony dependencies
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// a response XML
final class XmlResponse extends ParentResponse
{
     #[\Override]
    public function send(
        Request $request,
        Session $session,
        array $config,
        int $statusCode,
        array $content,
        array $headers = [],
        ?Logger $logger = null
    ): void {
         // serialization of XML using the [XmlUtilitaires] class from version 11
         // The objects [Simulation] are first converted into associative arrays
        $xml = XmlUtilitaires::arrayToXml(self::toArray($content), "root");
         // Response sent by the parent class
        $this->sendResponse($statusCode, $xml, "application/xml", $headers);
         // log in JSON, more concise than XML
        $this->log($logger, $content);
    }
}

Comments

  • Line 27: The response [$content] is serialized to XML by the method [arrayToXml] of the class [XmlUtilitaires] in version 11. This method expects an array whose values are either arrays or simple values: the [toArray] method of the parent class first replaces the [Simulation] objects with the array of their attributes. The root element of the document is named [root], as in course PHP 7;
  • line 29: the parent class sends the response to the client, with the type [application/xml];
  • line 31: the response is logged as JSON, which is more concise than XML.

The PHP 7 course used the XML encoder from the [Symfony / Serializer] library, and a second encoder, JSON, for the logs.

docs.title: 23.12.4. [curl] Tests
docs.text:

  • lines 9–15: a successful authentication;
  • lines 17–32: a tax calculation. The element [réponse] contains the simulation attributes as child elements;
