personne : charline martin (F)
  • Lines 2–38: the document XML in the form of a [SimpleXMLElement] object. Note that the text [ceci est un commentaire] does not appear: [print_r] shows only the elements and attributes;
  • lines 39–42: an attribute is also a [SimpleXMLElement] object;
  • lines 43–48: the values read from the document;
  • lines 49–50: the XPath traversal of the two people.

docs.title: 21.3. Processing with the new API DOM from PHP 8.4
docs.text:
Starting with PHP 8.4, the [Dom] namespace offers a new API and DOM: the [Dom\XMLDocument] class for XML documents and the [Dom\HTMLDocument] class for HTML5 documents. It is a better replacement for the old [DOMDocument] class (which is still available): it complies with the current DOM standard and provides the [querySelector] and [querySelectorAll] methods familiar to JavaScript developers. These methods allow you to search for elements using CSS selectors.

The [dom-01.php] script uses the same document:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// the same document processed using the new API DOM from PHP 8.4

use Dom\XMLDocument;

// the XML file to be processed
const FILE_NAME = "data.xml";

try {
     // Loading the XML document
    $document = XMLDocument::createFromFile(FILE_NAME);
} catch (Throwable $ex) {
    print "Le fichier [" . FILE_NAME . "] n'a pu être exploité : {$ex->getMessage()}\n";
    exit(1);
}
// the root element
print "racine=" . $document->documentElement->tagName . "\n";
// the first teacher, found using the selector CSS
$personne = $document->querySelector('enseignant > personne');
print "nom=" . $personne->querySelector('nom')->textContent . "\n";
print "sexe=" . $personne->getAttribute('sexe') . "\n";
print "formation=" . $document->querySelector('etudiant > formation')->textContent . "\n";
// a missing element: querySelector returns null
print "xx existe=" . var_export($personne->querySelector('xx') !== null, true) . "\n";
// all people in the document
foreach ($document->querySelectorAll('personne') as $personne) {
     // the null-safe operator ?-> protects against a missing element
    $prénom = $personne->querySelector('prenom')?->textContent ?? '?';
    $nom = $personne->querySelector('nom')?->textContent ?? '?';
    print "personne : $prénom $nom ({$personne->getAttribute('sexe')})\n";
}
// document modification: the content of the <section> element for the teacher is changed
$section = $document->querySelector('enseignant > section');
$section->textContent = "26";
// the modified document, as text XML
print $document->saveXml($document->querySelector('enseignant')) . "\n";

Comments

  • line 7: the [XMLDocument] class in the [Dom] namespace;
  • Line 14: The static method [createFromFile] loads the document. Unlike [simplexml_load_file], it throws an exception if an error occurs;
  • line 20: the property [documentElement] is the root element; [tagName] is its name;
  • line 22: the selector CSS [enseignant > personne] refers to an element [personne] that is a direct child of an element [enseignant]. [querySelector] returns the first matching element, or [null] if there are none;
  • line 23: the [textContent] property is the text contained in the element;
  • line 24: the value of an attribute;
  • line 27: a missing element returns [null];
  • line 29: all [personne] elements in the document;
  • Line 31: If the element [prenom] were missing, [querySelector('prenom')] would result in [null]. The null-safe operator [?->] (PHP 8.0) then returns [null] instead of causing an error, and the operator [??] replaces this [null] with ['?'];
  • line 37: the API DOM also allows the document to be modified: here, the text of the [section] element is changed;
  • line 39: [saveXml] returns the text XML from the document, or from one of its elements if it is passed as a parameter.

Console output

> php dom-01.php
racine=tribu
nom=dupont
sexe=M
formation=dess IAIE
xx existe=false
personne : jean dupont (M)
personne : charline martin (F)
<enseignant>
        <personne sexe="M">
            <nom>dupont</nom>
            <prenom>jean</prenom>
            <age>28</age>
            ceci est un commentaire
        </personne>
        <section>26</section>
    </enseignant>
  • line 16: the modification made by the script.

These two examples do not show all the capabilities of [SimpleXML] and [DOM], but they are sufficient for us to write a new version of the application exercise. The documentation for PHP describes them in detail: SimpleXML and DOM.

docs.title: 2. Setting Up a Development Environment
docs.text:
The scripts were written and tested in the following environment:

  • a [Apache] / SGBD [MySQL] / [PHP] 8.5 web server environment called [Laragon];
  • the [Visual Studio Code] editor and its extension [PHP Intelephense];
  • the dependency manager [Composer], provided with [Laragon], which installs the PHP libraries used by the course.

Other tools (the mail server [Mailpit], SGBD, [PostgreSQL], and the server [Redis]) are only relevant to certain chapters: their installation is described in the relevant chapters.

docs.title: 2.1. Installing Laragon
docs.text:
[Laragon] is a package for [Windows] that combines several software components:

  • a web server ([Apache]). We will use it to write web scripts in PHP;
  • SGBD and [MySQL] ([PostgreSQL] can be added to this, see the chapter on version 6);
  • the PHP scripting language, in several versions, including version 8.5;
  • a [Redis] server that implements a cache for web applications;
  • the [Composer] tool;
  • a command-line terminal in which all these tools can be used directly.

[Laragon] can be downloaded from https://laragon.org/download/. It is free to use with all its features; a prompt occasionally appears asking you to purchase a license to support its development, which is optional. Installation is straightforward: simply accept the default settings. [Laragon] is then installed in the [C:\laragon] folder, which we will refer to as <laragon> from here on:

C:\laragon
├── bin\        les logiciels : apache, mysql, php, redis, composer…
├── data\       les données des SGBD
├── etc\        des fichiers de configuration
├── tmp\
└── www\        la racine du serveur web Apache : http://localhost

Launching [Laragon] displays its main window:

  • The [Démarrer tout] (Start All) button starts the [Apache] web server, as well as SGBD and [MySQL]. The window then indicates, for each of them, that it is active and on which port it is listening: 80 for [Apache], 3306 for [MySQL];
  • the [Web] button displays the [http://localhost] page, which corresponds to the [<laragon>/www] folder;
  • the [Base de données] (Database) button launches a database administration tool ([HeidiSQL], included with [Laragon]);
  • The [Terminal] button opens a command terminal in which [php], [composer], [mysql]… can be used directly;
  • The [Racine] (Root) button opens the [Windows] file explorer to the [<laragon>/www] folder. This is where you should place all web applications managed by the [Apache] server from [Laragon];
  • Right-clicking in the window (or on the [Laragon] icon in the taskbar) opens the [Laragon] menu, which provides access to the configuration settings for each application.

docs.title: 2.1.1. Select PHP 8.5
docs.text:
[Laragon] may contain multiple versions of PHP. The version to use is selected from its menu under the [PHP > Version] section. Select version 8.5 (the most recent in the 8.5 series). It will then be used by both the [Apache] server and the [php] terminal command.

In order for the [php] command to also be usable in [VS Code] terminals, the PHP folder must be located within the PATH folder of [Windows]. [Laragon] handles this: [Outils > Path > Ajouter Laragon au Path] menu (Tools > Path > Add Laragon to Path). Then open a new terminal (terminals that are already open will not see the change) and type:

> php -v

The command should display the version of PHP, 8.5.x.

docs.title: 2.1.2. Configure PHP for training
docs.text:
PHP is configured via a text file named [php.ini], accessible through the [Laragon] menu under the [PHP > php.ini] section. During training, PHP must report all errors, warnings, and deprecations. Verify that the file contains the following lines (or modify them):

error_reporting = E_ALL
display_errors = On
display_startup_errors = On
log_errors = On
error_log = C:/laragon/tmp/php_errors.log
date.timezone = Europe/Paris
  • [error_reporting = E_ALL]: PHP reports everything, including the [Deprecated] messages that announce deprecated features. A production configuration often uses [E_ALL & ~E_DEPRECATED], which hides them: that’s not what we want here;
  • [display_errors = On]: Messages are displayed in the script’s output (the terminal or the web page);
  • [log_errors = On]: Messages are also written to the error log;
  • [error_log]: the log file. Without this line, a console script writes its log to the terminal itself, and each message would appear there twice (once preceded by [PHP], once without it);
  • [date.timezone]: the time zone used by date functions.

The course also uses several extensions of PHP. They are enabled in the [Laragon] menu, under the [PHP > Extensions] section, or in the [php.ini] file using lines of the form [extension=nom]. The extensions used are: [curl], [mbstring], [openssl], [pdo_mysql], [pdo_pgsql], [fileinfo], and [zip] (the latter is used by [Composer] to decompress the libraries it downloads). After modifying the [php.ini] file, you must restart [Apache] (the [Recharger] button in [Laragon]); the console scripts, on the other hand, re-read the [php.ini] file each time they run.

You can verify the configuration in a terminal using the command [php --ini] (the [php.ini] file used) and [php -m] (the list of loaded extensions). The first script in the next chapter, [phpinfo.php], displays the entire configuration.

docs.title: 2.2. Installing VS Code
docs.text:
[Visual Studio Code] is a free editor from Microsoft, available for download at https://code.visualstudio.com/. Here, it replaces the IDE and [NetBeans] used in Course PHP 7.

Once [VS Code] is installed, add support for the PHP language: in the [Extensions] panel (Ctrl+Shift+X), search for and install the [PHP Intelephense] extension. It provides:

  • code completion: PHP functions, classes, their methods, and their attributes are suggested as you type;
  • display of documentation for a function or method when you hover over its name;
  • error detection as you type (undefined variables, incorrect types, nonexistent methods, etc.), which are underlined in the code and listed in the [Problèmes] panel;
  • code navigation: pressing Ctrl+click on a class or function name opens its definition, including those in the libraries within the [vendor] folder.

[Intelephense] must know the version of PHP being used to identify its new features: in the [VS Code] settings (Ctrl+comma), search for “intelephense php version” and enter 8.5.

Next, open the course code folder in [VS Code] ([Fichier > Ouvrir le dossier] menu). A terminal opens via the [Terminal > Nouveau terminal] menu: it is set to the open folder, and you type the commands [php], [composer], [curl]… To run a console script, navigate to its folder (command [cd]) and type [php nom-du-script.php].

docs.title: 2.3. Installing the Course Code
docs.text:
The course code files are contained in a folder named [php8-oct-2026], which can be downloaded at the beginning of this document. Place it in the [<laragon>/www] folder:

C:\laragon\www
└── php8-oct-2026
    ├── composer.json
    ├── phpunit.xml
    ├── scripts-console
    └── scripts-web

Its web scripts are then accessible at URL and [http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/...]. For example, once [Apache] is launched, URL and [http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/composer.json] should display the file [composer.json].

docs.title: 2.4. Installing Libraries with Composer
docs.text:
Like most programming languages, PHP has a dependency manager, [Composer], which downloads the libraries a project needs from the [packagist.org] repository. The libraries used by the course are declared in the [composer.json] file in the [php8-oct-2026] folder:

{
    "name": "stahe/php8-oct-2026",
    "description": "Codes du cours « Introduction au langage PHP 8 par l'exemple » (octobre 2026)",
    "type": "project",
    "license": "MIT",
    "require": {
        "php": ">=8.5",
        "symfony/http-foundation": "^8.0",
        "symfony/http-client": "^8.0",
        "symfony/mailer": "^8.0",
        "symfony/mime": "^8.0",
        "predis/predis": "^3.0",
        "zbateson/mail-mime-parser": "^3.0"
    },
    "require-dev": {
        "phpunit/phpunit": "^12.0"
    },
    "config": {
        "sort-packages": true
    }
}
  • Line 6: the libraries required to run the scripts. Each is identified by a name in the form [éditeur/bibliothèque] and a version constraint: [^8.0] means “any version of 8.x starting with 8.0.” Their roles are described in the chapters that use them;
  • line 7: the project requires PHP 8.5 or later;
  • line 15: libraries used solely for development, in this case the [PHPUnit] testing framework.

To install these libraries, open a terminal in the [php8-oct-2026] folder (the [Laragon] terminal, or the [VS Code] terminal) and type:

> composer install

[Composer] then creates a folder named [vendor] containing the libraries and their dependencies, as well as a file named [vendor/autoload.php]. A script that wants to use these libraries simply needs to include this file, which automatically loads their classes the first time they are used. The scripts in this course do this using a path relative to their own folder, for example:

require_once __DIR__ . '/../../vendor/autoload.php';

The constant [__DIR__] refers to the folder of the script that uses it: therefore, the path does not depend on the folder in which the script is run, nor on where the [php8-oct-2026] folder is located.

Verify the installation by displaying the version of [PHPUnit]:

> php vendor/bin/phpunit --version
PHPUnit 12.5.37 by Sebastian Bergmann and contributors.

Now that the working environment has been installed, we can cover the basics of PHP.

docs.title: 3.1. The Script Directory Structure
docs.text:
The scripts for this chapter are located in two folders within the [scripts-console] folder of the course code:

php8-oct-2026
└── scripts-console
    ├── bases
    │   ├── phpinfo.php
    │   ├── bases-01.php
    │   ├── bases-02.php
    │   ├── ...
    │   ├── bases-17.php
    │   └── infos.txt
    └── json
        ├── famille.json
        ├── json-01.php
        ├── json-02.php
        └── json-03.php

These are “console” scripts: they run in a terminal using the [php nom-du-script.php] command and output their results to that same terminal. Web scripts, which are executed by the [Apache] server running on [Laragon] and displayed by a browser, will be covered later.

docs.title: 3.2. Configuring PHP
docs.text:
PHP comes preconfigured via a text file named [php.ini]. All of these settings can be changed programmatically. The configuration of PHP greatly influences script execution. It is therefore important to understand it. The following script, [phpinfo.php], allows you to do this:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// displays the configuration of PHP
phpinfo();

Comments:

  • line 3: This line will appear at the beginning of all scripts in this course. We will explain it in the section on type conversions;
  • Line 6: The function [phpinfo] displays the configuration of PHP.

Let’s open a terminal in the [scripts-console/bases] folder and run the script. Here is an excerpt:

> php phpinfo.php
phpinfo()
PHP Version => 8.5.11
…
Server API => Command Line Interface
…
PHP API => 20250925
PHP Extension => 20250925
Zend Extension => 420250925
PHP Integer Size => 64 bits
Debug Build => no
Zend Memory Manager => enabled
IPv6 Support => enabled
…
display_errors => STDOUT => STDOUT
error_reporting => 30719 => 30719
memory_limit => 512M => 512M
max_execution_time => 0 => 0
…

The [phpinfo] function displays nearly 1,500 configuration lines here. We won’t comment on them because most pertain to advanced usage of PHP. Let’s highlight a few:

  • [PHP Version]: the version of PHP being used—in this case, 8.5;
  • [Server API]: how PHP was launched. [Command Line Interface] (CLI) refers to the interpreter running in a terminal. When PHP is executed by the [Apache] server, this line changes, and the configuration may be different;
  • [display_errors] and [error_reporting]: PHP displays all errors, warnings, and deprecation notices. The value 30719 corresponds to the constant [E_ALL] as of PHP 8.4. This is the configuration required during training: a warning almost always indicates a programming error.

An important line in the full output is line [Loaded Configuration File]: it indicates which [php.ini] file was used to configure the PHP that runs your scripts. With [Laragon], this is a file like [C:\laragon\bin\php\php-8.5.x-Win32-vs17-x64\php.ini]. You can also obtain it directly using the command [php --ini]. If you want to modify the execution configuration of PHP, this is the file you need to edit ([Laragon] provides access to it via its menu, under the [PHP > php.ini] section). There are numerous comments in this file explaining the purpose of the various configurations.

docs.title: 3.3.1. The code
docs.text:
Below is a [bases-01.php] program that demonstrates the basic features of PHP:

<?php

// strict type checking of function parameters and return values
declare(strict_types=1);

// this is a comment
// variable used without being declared
$nom = "dupont";
// a screen display
print "nom=$nom\n";
// an array with elements of different types
$tableau = ["un", "deux", 3, 4];
// its number of elements
$n = count($tableau);
// a loop
for ($i = 0; $i < $n; $i++) {
    print "tableau[$i]=$tableau[$i]\n";
}
// initializing two variables with the contents of an array
[$chaine1, $chaine2] = ["chaine1", "chaine2"];
// concatenation of the two strings
$chaine3 = $chaine1 . $chaine2;
// displaying the result
print "[$chaine1,$chaine2,$chaine3]\n";
// using a function
affiche($chaine1);
// The type of a variable can be known
afficheType("n", $n);
afficheType("chaine1", $chaine1);
afficheType("tableau", $tableau);
// A variable's type can change during execution
$n = "a changé";
afficheType("n", $n);
// A function can return a result
$res1 = f1(4);
print "res1=$res1\n";
// A function can return an array of values
[$res1, $res2, $res3] = f2();
print "(res1,res2,res3)=[$res1,$res2,$res3]\n";
// These values could have been retrieved in an array
$t = f2();
for ($i = 0; $i < count($t); $i++) {
    print "t[$i]=$t[$i]\n";
}
// tests
for ($i = 0; $i < count($t); $i++) {
     // displays only strings
    if (gettype($t[$i]) === "string") {
        print "t[$i]=$t[$i]\n";
    }
}
// comparison operators == and ===
if ("2" == 2) {
    print "avec l'opérateur ==, la chaîne 2 est égale à l'entier 2\n";
} else {
    print "avec l'opérateur ==, la chaîne 2 n'est pas égale à l'entier 2\n";
}
if ("2" === 2) {
    print "avec l'opérateur ===, la chaîne 2 est égale à l'entier 2\n";
} else {
    print "avec l'opérateur ===, la chaîne 2 n'est pas égale à l'entier 2\n";
}
// a comparison whose result changed with PHP 8
if (0 == "abc") {
    print "avec l'opérateur ==, l'entier 0 est égal à la chaîne abc\n";
} else {
    print "avec l'opérateur ==, l'entier 0 n'est pas égal à la chaîne abc\n";
}
// other tests
for ($i = 0; $i < count($t); $i++) {
     // displays only integers > 10
    if (is_int($t[$i]) && $t[$i] > 10) {
        print "t[$i]=$t[$i]\n";
    }
}
// a while loop
$t = [8, 5, 0, -2, 3, 4];
$i = 0;
$somme = 0;
while ($i < count($t) && $t[$i] > 0) {
    print "t[$i]=$t[$i]\n";
    $somme += $t[$i];   // $somme = $somme + $t[$i]
    $i++;               // $i = $i + 1
}
print "somme=$somme\n";

// end of program
exit;

//----------------------------------
function affiche(string $chaine): void
{
     // displays $chaine
    print "chaine=$chaine\n";
}

//----------------------------------
function afficheType(string $name, mixed $variable): void
{
     // displays the type of $variable
    print "type[variable $" . $name . "]=" . gettype($variable) . "\n";
}

//----------------------------------
function f1(int $param): int
{
     // adds 10 to $param
    return $param + 10;
}

//----------------------------------
function f2(): array
{
     // returns 3 values
    return ["un", 0, 100];
}

The results:

> php bases-01.php
nom=dupont
tableau[0]=un
tableau[1]=deux
tableau[2]=3
tableau[3]=4
[chaine1,chaine2,chaine1chaine2]
chaine=chaine1
type[variable $n]=integer
type[variable $chaine1]=string
type[variable $tableau]=array
type[variable $n]=string
res1=14
(res1,res2,res3)=[un,0,100]
t[0]=un
t[1]=0
t[2]=100
t[0]=un
avec l'opérateur ==, la chaîne 2 est égale à l'entier 2
avec l'opérateur ===, la chaîne 2 n'est pas égale à l'entier 2
avec l'opérateur ==, l'entier 0 n'est pas égal à la chaîne abc
t[2]=100
t[0]=8
t[1]=5
somme=13

Comments:

  • line 4: instructs PHP to strictly check the declared types of the parameters and function returns. We’ll return to this in the section on type changes. For now, note that all the scripts in this course begin this way;
  • line 8: In PHP, variables are not declared. They have a dynamic type that can change over time. [$nom] represents the variable with identifier [nom];
  • line 10: To write to the screen, you can use the statement [print] or the statement [echo];
  • Line 12: The notation [[...]] is used to define an array. The notation [$tableau[$i]] represents element No. [$i] of the array [$tableau], where the first element is numbered 0. The older notation [array("un", "deux", 3, 4)] is still accepted, but we will not use it;
  • line 14: the function [count($tableau)] returns the number of elements in the array [$tableau];
  • lines 16–18: a loop. Since this loop contains only one statement, curly braces are optional. In the rest of this document, we will always use curly braces regardless of the number of statements;
  • line 17: strings are enclosed in double quotes " or single quotes '. Inside double quotes, the variables [$variable] are evaluated (also called “interpolated”), but not inside single quotes;
  • line 20: You can assign the elements of an array to multiple variables in a single operation. Here, [$chaine1="chaine1"] and [$chaine2="chaine2"]. This syntax, called destructuring, replaces the [list] function from older versions of PHP: [list($chaine1, $chaine2) = ...] is still accepted;
  • line 22: the . (period) operator is the string concatenation operator;
  • Lines 91–95: The keyword [function] defines a function. A function can be defined anywhere in the script, even after it has been used. Here, [string $chaine] indicates that the parameter [$chaine] must be a string, and [: void] indicates that the function returns no result. These type declarations are optional in PHP, but we will use them consistently: they document the code and allow PHP (and the editor) to detect errors;
  • line 98: the type [mixed] (PHP 8.0) means “any type.” The parameter [$variable] can accept an integer, a string, an array, etc.;
  • line 101: the predefined function [gettype($variable)] returns a string representing the type of [$variable]. The results show that this type can change over time: [$n] is first an integer and then a string;
  • line 105: a function returns a result using the statement [return]. The type of this result is declared after the parentheses: [: int]. The calling code can ignore or retrieve the results of a function;
  • line 112: a function can return multiple values by grouping them into an array;
  • lines 53–62: The [===] operator performs a strict comparison of two elements: they must have the same type and the same value to be equal. The [] operator is less strict: two elements can be equal without being of the same type. In this case, the comparison is performed after both elements have been converted to the same type. It is quite easy to “overlook” these implicit conversions and thus end up with unexpected results, such as discovering that a condition is true when you expected it to be false. To avoid this pitfall, we will consistently use the comparison operator [=] (and its negation, [!==]);
  • lines 64–68: an example of these implicit conversions. In PHP 7, the string “abc” was converted to the number 0, and the expression [0 == "abc"] was true! Since PHP 8.0, when comparing a number to a string that does not represent a number, the number is converted to a string, and the expression is false. The behavior of [] has therefore changed from one version to the next: all the more reason to prefer [=];
  • Line 72: The function [is_int] returns [true] if its parameter is an integer. Similarly, there are [is_string], [is_float], [is_bool], [is_array]… The operator [&&] is the logical inverse of ET. You can also use the logical operators [||] (OU) and [!] (NON). PHP also supports the keywords [and] and [or], but their lower priority compared to assignment can lead to unexpected results: we will not use them;
  • line 80: a loop [while]. It stops as soon as the condition is false—in this case, as soon as the array is traversed or a negative or zero element is encountered;
  • Line 88: The [exit] statement stops the script from executing. The functions that follow are not executed at this point, but they are recognized by the entire script.

Note that the script does not end with the [?>] closing tag for the PHP code. It is not essential. Furthermore, in a web context, it can cause problems if it is followed by spaces or line breaks, which are difficult to detect because they are not visible in a text editor. The [PSR-12] recommendation, in fact, specifies that it should be omitted in files containing only PHP. Therefore, in the remainder of this document, we will systematically omit it.

Note: In this document, we will use the keyword [print] to display text on the console. Another way to do the same thing is to use the keyword [echo]. There are subtle differences between these two keywords, but in the context of this document, there will be none. So if you prefer to use [echo], then go ahead.

docs.title: 3.3.2. Using VS Code
docs.text:
To work on the course scripts, open the [php8-oct-2026] folder within [VS Code] ([Fichier > Ouvrir le dossier] menu). The file tree appears in the explorer on the left side of the window. To run a script:

  • open an integrated terminal ([Terminal > Nouveau terminal] menu). It opens in the [php8-oct-2026] folder;
  • navigate to the script’s folder: [cd scripts-console/bases];
  • run the script: [php bases-01.php]. The results are displayed in the terminal. Alternatively, in the file explorer, you can right-click the [bases] folder and select [Ouvrir dans le terminal intégré].

If the command [php] is not recognized, it means that the PHP folder is not located in the Windows PATH directory: [Laragon] adds it there when you check the corresponding option in its [Outils > Path] menu. The [php -v] command should display version 8.5.

The [PHP Intelephense] extension analyzes the code as you type and flags problems with a wavy line under the incorrect code. Hovering the mouse over this line displays the message. All issues in the file are listed in the [Problèmes] panel ([Affichage > Problèmes] menu). Among the useful warnings:

  • [Undefined variable]: a variable is being used without having been initialized. This is often a typo in the variable name;
  • [Undefined function]: A function that does not exist is being called; again, this is often a typo;
  • [Expected type 'int'. Found 'string'.]: An actual parameter does not have the type declared by the function. This is one of the major benefits of type declarations: the error is reported even before execution;
  • [Expected 2 arguments. Found 1.]: The number of actual parameters does not match the function’s definition.

Hovering over a function name displays its signature (parameters, types, return value) and its documentation, including for the predefined functions of PHP. To ensure that [Intelephense] is aware of recent language updates, check the settings for [VS Code] ([Fichier > Préférences > Paramètres] menu, search for “intelephense php version”) to ensure that the specified version of PHP is 8.5. While learning the language, it is advisable to correct all reported warnings. This is a great way to learn.

[Intelephense] can also format a file (right-click, [Mettre en forme le document]) according to the coding recommendations in [PSR-12]. The PSR (PHP Standard Recommendations) are guidelines for producing standard code, thereby facilitating interoperability and the maintenance of code written by different people. They are published by the [PHP-FIG] on the www.php-fig.org website. The [PSR-1] and [PSR-12] recommendations establish the rules for writing code. Here are the rules from [PSR-1]:

ElementRuleClass constantsClass constants DOIVENT must be written in uppercase letters with the _ character as a separator.Ex: [const TAUX_TVA]MethodsMethod names such as DOIVENT should be written as camelCase.Example: [public function executeBatchImpots()]PropertiesProperty names such as DEVRAIENT should be written consistently within a single codebase, as StudlyCaps, camelCase, or under_score.Examples: [$SalaireAnnuel], [$salaireAnnuel], [$salaire_annuel]Side EffectsA DEVRAIT file can either declare new symbols (classes, functions, constants, etc.) without any side effects, or execute code with side effects, but NE, DEVRAIT, and PAS do both.TypesType names (classes, interfaces, etc.) DOIVENT must be written in StudlyCaps. Each type is in its own file and in a namespace with at least one level.Example: [class EtudiantBoursier]

The side-effects rule states that a file must contain:

  • either declarations of types (classes, interfaces), functions, or constants;
  • or executable code without declarations of new types.

For simplicity, the examples in this chapter do not follow this rule: each script is a single file that defines its functions and uses them. Splitting the code across multiple files would be too cumbersome for basic examples. For the application presented as the central theme of this document, we will strive to follow these recommendations as closely as possible once it is written using classes.

docs.title: 3.4.1. Example 1
docs.text:
The script [bases-02.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// variable scope

function f1(): void
{
     // the global variable $i is used
    global $i;
    $i++;
    $j = 10;
    print "f1[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";
}

function f2(): void
{
     // the global variable $i is used
    global $i;
    $i++;
    $j = 20;
    print "f2[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";
}

function f3(): void
{
     // a local variable $i is used
    $i = 4;
    $j = 30;
    print "f3[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";
}

// tests
$i = 0;
$j = 0;  // these two variables are not known to a function f
// unless the function explicitly declares them using the `global` statement
// that it intends to use them
f1();
f2();
f3();
print "test[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";

The results:

> php bases-02.php
f1[i,j]=[1,10]
f2[i,j]=[2,20]
f3[i,j]=[4,30]
test[i,j]=[2,0]

Comments:

  • Lines 34–35: Define two variables, [$i] and [$j], in the main program. These variables are not recognized within the functions. Thus, on line 12, the variable [$j] in the function [f1] is a local variable of the function [f1] and is different from the variable [$j] in the main program;
  • line 10: a function can access a variable named [$variable] from the main program via the keyword [global]. Here, the statement refers to the global variable [$i] in the main program;
  • line 28: the function [f3] has not declared [$i] as global; its variable [$i] is a local variable, unrelated to the one in the main program.

The use of [global] is not recommended: a function that modifies global variables is difficult to understand and test. It is preferable for a function to receive its data via its parameters and return its results via [return]. This is what we will do in the following example.

docs.title: 3.4.2. Example 2
docs.text:
The [bases-03.php] script is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// a variable’s scope is global to code blocks
$i = 0;
{
    $i = 4;
    $i++;
}
print "i=$i\n";

The results:

> php bases-03.php
i=5

Comments:

In some languages, a variable defined within curly braces has a scope limited to those braces: it is not accessible outside of them. The results above show that this is not the case in PHP. The variable [$i] used on line 8 inside the curly braces is the same as the one used on lines 6 and 11 outside of them.

docs.title: 3.5. Type Changes
docs.text:
Variables in PHP do not have a fixed type. The type may change at runtime depending on the value assigned to the variable. In operations involving data of various types, the PHP interpreter performs implicit conversions to bring the operands into a common type. These implicit conversions, if unknown to the developer, can be a source of errors that are difficult to detect. Below is a [bases-04.php] script demonstrating implicit and explicit conversions. Let’s start with the first part:

<?php

// Strict typing in parameter passing
declare(strict_types=1);

// implicit type conversions
// type --> bool
print "Conversion vers un booléen------------------------------\n";
showBool("abcd", "abcd");
showBool("", "");
showBool("[1, 2, 3]", [1, 2, 3]);
showBool("[]", []);
showBool("null", null);
showBool("0.0", 0.0);
showBool("0", 0);
showBool("4.6", 4.6);
showBool("\"0\"", "0");

function showBool(string $prefixe, mixed $var): void
{
    print "(bool) $prefixe : ";
     // The conversion of $var to a boolean is performed automatically in the following test
    if ($var) {
        print "true";
    } else {
        print "false";
    }
    print "\n";
}

Comments:

  • line 4: Requests strict type checking of a function’s parameters when the type is specified (and of the type of its return value). We’ll explain this instruction a bit later;
  • line 19: The purpose of the function [showBool] is to demonstrate the implicit (automatic) conversion performed by the PHP interpreter when a value of any type must be converted to a Boolean (line 23);
  • line 19: the parameter [$prefixe] must be of type [string]. The parameter [$var] is of type [mixed]: the actual parameter can therefore be of any type. The function [showBool] returns no value ([void]);
  • Line 23: In the [if ($var)] statement, the value of [$var] must be converted to a Boolean so that [if] can be evaluated. Surprisingly, the PHP interpreter returns a result for any type of value provided to it;
  • lines 9–17: the value of the function parameter for [showBool] will be, in succession:
    • line 9: a non-empty string: result [true] (case is not significant, TRUE=true);
    • line 10: an empty string: result [false];
    • line 11: a non-empty array: result [true];
    • line 12: an empty array: result [false];
    • line 13: the value [null] (no value): result [false];
    • line 14: the real number 0: result [false];
    • line 15: the integer 0: result [false];
    • line 16: a real number (or integer) other than 0: result [true];
    • line 17: a trap: the string "0" is converted to [false], while any other non-empty string is converted to [true].

This is shown by the resulting screen outputs:

Conversion vers un booléen------------------------------
(bool) abcd : true
(bool)  : false
(bool) [1, 2, 3] : true
(bool) [] : false
(bool) null : false
(bool) 0.0 : false
(bool) 0 : false
(bool) 4.6 : true
(bool) "0" : false

Let’s continue with the script code:

// Implicit conversions from string to a numeric type
// string --> number
print "Conversion chaîne vers nombre------------------------------\n";
showNumber("12");
showNumber("45.67");
showNumber("12abcd");
try {
    showNumber("abcd");
} catch (TypeError $erreur) {
    print "(abcd): erreur [" . $erreur->getMessage() . "]\n";
}

function showNumber(string $var): void
{
    $nombre = $var + 1;
    var_dump($nombre);
    print "($var): $nombre\n";
}

Comments:

  • line 43: the function [showNumber] accepts a parameter of type [string] and does not return a result ([void]);
  • line 45: this parameter is used in an arithmetic operation, which will force the PHP interpreter to attempt to convert [$var] into a number:
    • line 34: will convert the string "12" to the integer 12;
    • line 35: will convert the string "45.67" to the real number 45.67;
    • line 36: the string "12abcd" begins with a number. PHP uses this number, 12, but issues a warning;
    • line 38: the string "abcd" contains no numbers. In PHP 7, it was converted to 0 with a simple warning. Since PHP 8.0, this operation is no longer possible: PHP throws a [TypeError]-type error, which, if not intercepted, would terminate the script;
  • lines 37–41: the [try { ... } catch (TypeError $erreur) { ... }] structure allows this error to be caught and execution to continue. [$erreur->getMessage()] is the error message. Exceptions will be covered in a later chapter; for now, it is sufficient to know that the code in the [catch] block is executed when the code in the [try] block causes a [TypeError] error.

Here are the results of the execution:

Conversion chaîne vers nombre------------------------------
int(13)
(12): 13
float(46.67)
(45.67): 46.67

Warning: A non-numeric value encountered in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/bases/bases-04.php on line 45
int(13)
(12abcd): 13
(abcd): erreur [Unsupported operand types: string + int]

The function [var_dump] displays the type and value of its parameter: int(13) is the integer 13, and float(46.67) is the floating-point number 46.67.

Note that the [declare(strict_types=1)] statement did not prevent the string "12" from being converted to a number. This is an important point: strict mode applies only to the passing of parameters to functions and the results they return. It does not affect conversions performed by operators (+, ., ==…) or by the [if]. Here’s what it does change:

  • without [declare(strict_types=1)] (so-called “coercive” mode), if a function expects a [int] and is passed the string “12,” PHP converts the string to the integer 12;
  • with [declare(strict_types=1)] (strict mode), the same call results in a [TypeError] error. The actual parameter must be exactly of the expected type. There is one exception: a [int] is accepted where a [float] is expected.

This statement must be the first in the file and applies only to function calls made within that file. We will use it in all scripts: it transforms silent conversions—which are sources of errors—into reported errors. We will see an example in the section on passing parameters.

Let’s continue the script code with explicit type conversions:

// Explicit type conversions
// to int
print "Conversion explicite vers int------------------------------\n";
showInt("12.45");
showInt(67.8);
showInt(true);
showInt(null);

function showInt(mixed $var): void
{
    print "paramètre : ";
    var_dump($var);
    print "résultat de la conversion : ";
    var_dump((int) $var);
}

Comments:

  • Line 58: The function [showInt] accepts a parameter of any type ([mixed]) and does not return a result. It converts the parameter [$var] to an integer (line 63). In general, to convert a variable of type [$var] to type T, write [(T) $var], where T can be: int, bool, float, string, array, or object. The notations (integer), (boolean), (double), and (binary) from older versions of PHP are obsolete: PHP 8.5 flags them as deprecated. The (real) syntax, on the other hand, was removed as of PHP 8.0;
  • line 53: converts the string "12.45" to the integer 12;
  • line 54: converts the floating-point number 67.8 to the integer 67 (the decimal part is lost);
  • line 55: converts the Boolean [true] to the integer 1 (the Boolean [false] to the integer 0);
  • line 56: converts the value [null] to the integer 0.

This is what the screen displays show:

Conversion explicite vers int------------------------------
paramètre : string(5) "12.45"
résultat de la conversion : int(12)
paramètre : float(67.8)
résultat de la conversion : int(67)
paramètre : bool(true)
résultat de la conversion : int(1)
paramètre : NULL
résultat de la conversion : int(0)

We continue our analysis of the script with the explicit conversion of values to the [float] type:

// to float
print "Conversion explicite vers float------------------------------\n";
showFloat("12.45");
showFloat(67);
showFloat(true);
showFloat(null);

function showFloat(mixed $var): void
{
    print "paramètre : ";
    var_dump($var);
    print "résultat de la conversion : ";
    var_dump((float) $var);
}

Comments:

  • line 73: the function [showFloat] takes a parameter of any type and does not return a result;
  • line 78: the value of this parameter is explicitly converted to [float];
  • line 68: the string "12.45" is converted to the real number 12.45;
  • line 69: the integer 67 is converted to the real number 67;
  • line 70: the Boolean value [true] is converted to the real number 1 (the value [false] is converted to the number 0);
  • line 71: the value [null] is converted to the real number 0.

This is shown by the screen output:

Conversion explicite vers float------------------------------
paramètre : string(5) "12.45"
résultat de la conversion : float(12.45)
paramètre : int(67)
résultat de la conversion : float(67)
paramètre : bool(true)
résultat de la conversion : float(1)
paramètre : NULL
résultat de la conversion : float(0)

We conclude the presentation of the script by examining conversions to the type [string]:

// to string
print "Conversion explicite vers string------------------------------\n";
showString(5);
showString(6.7);
showString(false);
showString(null);

function showString(mixed $var): void
{
    print "paramètre : ";
    var_dump($var);
    print "résultat de la conversion : ";
    var_dump((string) $var);
}

Comments:

  • line 88: the function [showString] takes a parameter of any type and does not return a result;
  • line 93: the parameter value is converted to type [string];
  • line 83: the integer 5 will be converted to the string "5";
  • line 84: the floating-point number 6.7 will be converted to the string "6.7";
  • line 85: the boolean [false] will be converted to an empty string;
  • line 86: the value [null] will be converted to an empty string.

docs.title: 3.6.1. Standard one-dimensional arrays
docs.text:
There are two notations for arrays in PHP:

$tableau = ["un", 2, "trois"];
$contraires = ["petit" => "grand", "beau" => "laid", "cher" => "bon marché"];

Array 1 is called an array (or list), and array 2 is called a dictionary or associative array, where elements are denoted as key => value. The notation [$contraires["beau"]] refers to the value associated with the key "beautiful." In this case, it is the string "ugly." Array 1 is simply a variant of the dictionary and could be written as:

$tableau = [0 => "un", 1 => 2, 2 => "trois"];

This gives us [$tableau[2]="trois"]. Ultimately, there are only dictionaries. In the case of a classic array of n elements, the keys are the integers in the range [0,n-1].

The script [bases-05.php] demonstrates operations for manipulating an array of values:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// classic arrays
// initialization
$tab1 = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
// iteration - 1
print "tab1 a " . count($tab1) . " éléments\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab1); $i++) {
    print "tab1[$i]=$tab1[$i]\n";
}
// iteration - 2
print "tab1 a " . count($tab1) . " éléments\n";
foreach ($tab1 as $clé => $valeur) {
    print "tab1[$clé]=$valeur\n";
}
// adding elements
$tab1[] = $i++;
$tab1[] = $i++;
// iteration - 3
print "tab1 a " . count($tab1) . " éléments\n";
$i = 0;
foreach ($tab1 as $élément) {
    print "tab1[$i]=$élément\n";
    $i++;
}
// Delete Last Element
array_pop($tab1);
// iteration - 4
print "tab1 a " . count($tab1) . " éléments\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab1); $i++) {
    print "tab1[$i]=$tab1[$i]\n";
}
// Remove first element
array_shift($tab1);
// iteration - 5
print "tab1 a " . count($tab1) . " éléments\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab1); $i++) {
    print "tab1[$i]=$tab1[$i]\n";
}
// add to end of array
array_push($tab1, -2);
// iteration - 6
print "tab1 a " . count($tab1) . " éléments\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab1); $i++) {
    print "tab1[$i]=$tab1[$i]\n";
}
// add to beginning of array
array_unshift($tab1, -1);
// iteration - 7
print "tab1 a " . count($tab1) . " éléments\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab1); $i++) {
    print "tab1[$i]=$tab1[$i]\n";
}
// first and last elements (PHP 8.5)
print "premier élément : " . array_first($tab1) . ", dernier élément : " . array_last($tab1) . "\n";

Comments:

  • Line 15: The array is iterated over using a [foreach]. This syntax element allows you to iterate over a dictionary—and therefore an array—using two different syntaxes: [foreach ($dictionnaire as $clé => $valeur)] and [foreach ($tableau as $valeur)]. The first syntax returns a (key, value) pair on each iteration, while the second returns only the value. Course PHP 7 used the function [each] here, which was already obsolete at the time: it was removed in PHP 8.0. [foreach] is the standard way to iterate through an array;
  • Line 19: The notation [$tableau[] = valeur] adds the element [valeur] as the last element of [$tableau]. Here, [$i] is equal to 6 after the first loop for [for]: 6 is added, then 7;
  • line 24: an iteration using the second syntax of [foreach]. Note that variable names may contain accented characters;
  • line 29: the function [array_pop($tableau)] removes the last element from [$tableau];
  • line 36: the function [array_shift($tableau)] removes the first element from [$tableau]. The remaining elements are renumbered starting from 0;
  • line 43: The function [array_push($tableau, valeur)] adds [valeur] as the last element of [$tableau];
  • line 50: The function [array_unshift($tableau, valeur)] adds [valeur] as the first element of [$tableau];
  • line 57: the functions [array_first] and [array_last], introduced with PHP 8.5, return the first and last elements of an array (or [null] if the array is empty).

docs.title: 3.6.2. The dictionary or associative array
docs.text:
The script [bases-06.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// dictionaries
$conjoints = ["Pierre" => "Gisèle", "Paul" => "Virginie", "Jacques" => "Lucette", "Jean" => ""];
// iteration - 1
print "Nombre d'éléments du dictionnaire : " . count($conjoints) . "\n";
foreach ($conjoints as $clé => $valeur) {
    print "conjoints[$clé]=$valeur\n";
}
// sorting the dictionary by key
ksort($conjoints);
// iteration - 2
foreach ($conjoints as $clé => $valeur) {
    print "conjoints[$clé]=$valeur\n";
}
// list of dictionary keys
$clés = array_keys($conjoints);
for ($i = 0; $i < count($clés); $i++) {
    print "clés[$i]=$clés[$i]\n";
}
// List of dictionary values
$valeurs = array_values($conjoints);
for ($i = 0; $i < count($valeurs); $i++) {
    print "valeurs[$i]=$valeurs[$i]\n";
}
// Is a standard array a list? And a dictionary?
print "valeurs est une liste : " . var_export(array_is_list($valeurs), true) . "\n";
print "conjoints est une liste : " . var_export(array_is_list($conjoints), true) . "\n";
// Searching for a key
existe($conjoints, "Jacques");
existe($conjoints, "Lucette");
existe($conjoints, "Jean");
// default value if the key does not exist: operator??
print "conjoint de Lucette : " . ($conjoints["Lucette"] ?? "inconnu") . "\n";
// Deleting a key-value pair
unset($conjoints["Jean"]);
print "Nombre d'éléments du dictionnaire : " . count($conjoints) . "\n";
foreach ($conjoints as $clé => $valeur) {
    print "conjoints[$clé]=$valeur\n";
}
// end
exit;

function existe(array $conjoints, string $mari): void
{
     // checks whether the key $mari exists in the dictionary $conjoints
    if (isset($conjoints[$mari])) {
        print "La clé [$mari] existe associée à la valeur [$conjoints[$mari]]\n";
    } else {
        print "La clé [$mari] n'existe pas\n";
    }
}

The results:

> php bases-06.php
Nombre d'éléments du dictionnaire : 4
conjoints[Pierre]=Gisèle
conjoints[Paul]=Virginie
conjoints[Jacques]=Lucette
conjoints[Jean]=
conjoints[Jacques]=Lucette
conjoints[Jean]=
conjoints[Paul]=Virginie
conjoints[Pierre]=Gisèle
clés[0]=Jacques
clés[1]=Jean
clés[2]=Paul
clés[3]=Pierre
valeurs[0]=Lucette
valeurs[1]=
valeurs[2]=Virginie
valeurs[3]=Gisèle
valeurs est une liste : true
conjoints est une liste : false
La clé [Jacques] existe associée à la valeur [Lucette]
La clé [Lucette] n'existe pas
La clé [Jean] existe associée à la valeur []
conjoint de Lucette : inconnu
Nombre d'éléments du dictionnaire : 3
conjoints[Jacques]=Lucette
conjoints[Paul]=Virginie
conjoints[Pierre]=Gisèle

Comments:

The code above applies to a dictionary what we previously saw for a simple array. We’ll only comment on the new features:

  • line 13: the function [ksort] (key sort) sorts a dictionary in natural key order;
  • line 19: the function [array_keys($dictionnaire)] returns the list of dictionary keys as an array;
  • line 24: the [array_values($dictionnaire)] function returns the list of dictionary values as a table;
  • line 29: the function [array_is_list] (PHP 8.1) returns [true] if the array keys are 0, 1, 2… in that order, that is, if the array is a list. The function [var_export] returns the representation PHP of a value (“true” or “false”);
  • line 46: the function [existe] takes an array ([array]) and a string ([string]);
  • line 49: the function [isset($variable)] returns [true] if the variable [$variable] exists and does not have the value [null]; otherwise, it returns [false]. When applied to an array element, it determines whether a key exists. The function [array_key_exists($clé, $tableau)] does the same thing, but returns [true] even if the value associated with the key is [null];
  • line 36: the [??] operator (“null coalescent”) returns its left operand if it exists and is not [null], and its right operand otherwise. This is a concise way to obtain a default value for a missing key, without a warning;
  • line 38: the function [unset($variable)] deletes the variable [$variable], which is an element of the dictionary here.

docs.title: 3.6.3. Multidimensional Arrays
docs.text:
The script [bases-07.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// classic multidimensional tables
// initialization
$multi = [[0, 1, 2], [10, 11, 12, 13], [20, 21, 22, 23, 24]];
// iteration
for ($i1 = 0; $i1 < count($multi); $i1++) {
    for ($i2 = 0; $i2 < count($multi[$i1]); $i2++) {
        print "multi[$i1][$i2]=" . $multi[$i1][$i2] . "\n";
    }
}
// multidimensional dictionaries
// initialization
$multi = ["zéro" => [0, 1, 2], "un" => [10, 11, 12, 13], "deux" => [20, 21, 22, 23, 24]];
// iteration
foreach ($multi as $clé => $valeur) {
    for ($i2 = 0; $i2 < count($valeur); $i2++) {
        print "multi[$clé][$i2]={$multi[$clé][$i2]}\n";
    }
}

Results:

> php bases-07.php
multi[0][0]=0
multi[0][1]=1
multi[0][2]=2
multi[1][0]=10
multi[1][1]=11
multi[1][2]=12
multi[1][3]=13
multi[2][0]=20
multi[2][1]=21
multi[2][2]=22
multi[2][3]=23
multi[2][4]=24
multi[zéro][0]=0
multi[zéro][1]=1
multi[zéro][2]=2
multi[un][0]=10
multi[un][1]=11
multi[un][2]=12
multi[un][3]=13
multi[deux][0]=20
multi[deux][1]=21
multi[deux][2]=22
multi[deux][3]=23
multi[deux][4]=24

Comments:

  • Line 7: The elements of the array [$multi] are themselves arrays;
  • line 11: Inside a string enclosed in quotation marks, simple interpolation of [$multi[$i1][$i2]] does not work: PHP would evaluate to only [$multi[$i1]]. So we remove the expression from the string and use concatenation;
  • line 16: the array [$multi] becomes a dictionary (key, value) where each value is an array;
  • line 20: another solution: within a string enclosed in quotes, the notation [{$expression}] allows a complex expression to be evaluated. We’ll revisit this in the next section.

docs.title: 3.7.1. Notation
docs.text:
The script [bases-08.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// string notation
$chaine1 = "un";
$chaine2 = 'un';
print "[$chaine1,$chaine2]\n";
// Variables enclosed in single quotes are not evaluated
print '[$chaine1,$chaine2]' . "\n";
// the {$...} notation delimits the expression to be evaluated
$personne = ["nom" => "dupont", "âge" => 34];
print "{$personne['nom']} a {$personne['âge']} ans\n";
// a multi-line string (heredoc)
$texte = <<<FIN
    nom : $chaine1
    âge : {$personne['âge']}
    FIN;
print "$texte\n";

Results:

> php bases-08.php
[un,un]
[$chaine1,$chaine2]
dupont a 34 ans
nom : un
âge : 34

Comments:

  • Lines 6–7: A string can be enclosed in quotation marks or single quotes;
  • line 8: when enclosed in quotation marks, variables are evaluated;
  • line 10: within single quotes, they are not evaluated: the string is displayed as-is. Similarly, [\n] does not denote a line break here, hence the concatenation of ["\n"];
  • line 13: the notation [{$...}] allows for the evaluation of expressions more complex than a simple variable within a string—in this case, elements of a dictionary. The [${variable}] notation from older versions of PHP has been deprecated since PHP 8.2: it should not be used;
  • Lines 15–18: The [heredoc] syntax allows a string to span multiple lines. The string begins after [<<<FIN] and ends with the marker [FIN] (the name is arbitrary). Variables within it are evaluated as if they were enclosed in quotes. Starting with PHP 7.3, the end marker can be indented: this indentation is then removed from all lines of the string.

docs.title: 3.7.2. Comparison
docs.text:
The script [bases-09.php] is as follows:

<?php

// Strict adherence to function parameter types
declare(strict_types=1);

// comparison function
function compareChaines(string $chaine1, string $chaine2): void
{
     // compares string1 and string2
    if ($chaine1 === $chaine2) {
        print "[$chaine1] est égal à [$chaine2]\n";
    } else {
        print "[$chaine1] est différent de [$chaine2]\n";
    }
}

// string comparison tests
compareChaines("abcd", "abcd");
compareChaines("", "");
compareChaines("1", "");

// search for a substring (PHP 8)
$fichier = "taxpayersdata.txt";
print "[$fichier] contient [data] : " . var_export(str_contains($fichier, "data"), true) . "\n";
print "[$fichier] commence par [tax] : " . var_export(str_starts_with($fichier, "tax"), true) . "\n";
print "[$fichier] se termine par [.json] : " . var_export(str_ends_with($fichier, ".json"), true) . "\n";
// position of a substring
print "position de [data] dans [$fichier] : " . strpos($fichier, "data") . "\n";
// length, uppercase
print "longueur de [$fichier] : " . strlen($fichier) . ", en majuscules : " . strtoupper($fichier) . "\n";
// Note: `strlen` counts bytes, while `mb_strlen` counts characters
print "strlen(\"été\")=" . strlen("été") . ", mb_strlen(\"été\")=" . mb_strlen("été") . "\n";

Results:

> php bases-09.php
[abcd] est égal à [abcd]
[] est égal à []
[1] est différent de []
[taxpayersdata.txt] contient [data] : true
[taxpayersdata.txt] commence par [tax] : true
[taxpayersdata.txt] se termine par [.json] : false
position de [data] dans [taxpayersdata.txt] : 9
longueur de [taxpayersdata.txt] : 17, en majuscules : TAXPAYERSDATA.TXT
strlen("été")=5, mb_strlen("été")=3

Comments:

  • Line 10: We could have used the comparator [] instead of [=]. The latter operator is more restrictive in that it requires both operands to be of the same type. Note that here, it could have been replaced by the operator [] since the type of both parameters is set to [string]* in the function signature. However, we will continue to use *[=];
  • line 24: the function [str_contains($chaîne, $sousChaîne)] (PHP 8.0) returns [true] if [$sousChaîne] is present in [$chaîne];
  • line 25: the function [str_starts_with] (PHP 8.0) checks for the start of a string;
  • line 26: the function [str_ends_with] (PHP 8.0) checks for the end of a string;
  • line 28: the function [strpos($chaîne, $sousChaîne)] returns the position of [$sousChaîne] in [$chaîne], where the first character has position 0, and [false] if the substring is absent. Before PHP 8, the presence of a substring was checked using [strpos(...) !== false], which was a misleading notation since position 0 is converted to [false]: [str_contains] is much more readable;
  • line 30: the function [strlen] returns the length of a string, and [strtoupper] converts it to uppercase;
  • line 32: [strlen] counts bytes, not characters. The course files are encoded in UTF-8, where an accented character takes up two bytes: “été” has 3 characters but 5 bytes. The functions of the [mbstring] extension (mb_strlen, mb_substr, mb_strtoupper…) operate on characters.

docs.title: 3.7.3. Relationships Between Strings and Arrays
docs.text:
The script [bases-10.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// convert string to array
$chaine = "1:2:3:4";
$tab = explode(":", $chaine);
// iterate through array
print "tab a " . count($tab) . " éléments\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab); $i++) {
    print "tab[$i]=$tab[$i]\n";
}
// array to string
$chaine2 = implode(":", $tab);
print "chaine2=$chaine2\n";
// Let's add an empty field
$chaine .= ":";
print "chaîne=$chaine\n";
$tab = explode(":", $chaine);
// iterate through array
print "tab a " . count($tab) . " éléments\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab); $i++) {
    print "tab[$i]=$tab[$i]\n";
} // We now have 5 elements, the last one being empty
// Let's add another empty field
$chaine .= ":";
print "chaîne=$chaine\n";
$tab = explode(":", $chaine);
// Iterate through the array
print "tab a " . count($tab) . " éléments\n";
for ($i = 0; $i < count($tab); $i++) {
    print "tab[$i]=$tab[$i]\n";
} // We now have 6 elements, the last two of which are empty

Results:

> php bases-10.php
tab a 4 éléments
tab[0]=1
tab[1]=2
tab[2]=3
tab[3]=4
chaine2=1:2:3:4
chaîne=1:2:3:4:
tab a 5 éléments
tab[0]=1
tab[1]=2
tab[2]=3
tab[3]=4
tab[4]=
chaîne=1:2:3:4::
tab a 6 éléments
tab[0]=1
tab[1]=2
tab[2]=3
tab[3]=4
tab[4]=
tab[5]=

Comments:

  • Line 7: The [explode($séparateur, $chaine)] function retrieves the fields from [$chaine] separated by [$séparateur]. Thus, [explode(":", $chaine)] retrieves the elements of [$chaine]—which are separated by the string ":"—in array form;
  • Line 14: The function [implode($séparateur, $tableau)] performs the inverse operation of the function [explode]. It returns a string consisting of the elements of [$tableau] separated by [$séparateur];
  • line 17: The operator [.=] appends one string to the end of another. The results show that an empty field at the end of a string results in an empty element in the array returned by [explode].

docs.title: 3.7.4. Regular Expressions
docs.text:
The script [bases-11.php] is as follows:

<?php

// strict typing for function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// regular expressions in PHP
// extracting the various fields from a string
// The pattern: a sequence of digits surrounded by any characters
// We only want to extract the sequence of digits
$modèle = "/(\d+)/";
// We compare the string to the pattern
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "xyz1234abcd");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "12 34");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "abcd");

// The pattern: a sequence of digits surrounded by any characters
// We want the sequence of digits as well as the fields that come before and after it
$modèle = "/^(.*?)(\d+)(.*?)$/";
// We match the string against the pattern
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "xyz1234abcd");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "12 34");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "abcd");

// the pattern: a date in dd/mm/yy format
$modèle = "/^\s*(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\s*$/";
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "10/05/97");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "  04/04/01  ");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "5/1/01");

// the pattern—a decimal number
$modèle = "/^\s*([+-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*/";
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "187.8");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "-0.6");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "4");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, ".6");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, "4.");
compareModele2Chaine($modèle, " + 4");

// end
exit;

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
function compareModele2Chaine(string $modèle, string $chaîne): void
{
     // compares the string $chaîne to the pattern $modèle
     // the string is compared to the pattern
    $champs = [];
    $correspond = preg_match($modèle, $chaîne, $champs);
     // display results
    print "\nRésultats($modèle,$chaîne)\n";
    if ($correspond === 1) {
        for ($i = 0; $i < count($champs); $i++) {
            print "champs[$i]=$champs[$i]\n";
        }
    } else {
        print "La chaîne [$chaîne] ne correspond pas au modèle [$modèle]\n";
    }
}
