champs[1]=
champs[2]=.6

Résultats(/^\s*([+-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*/,4.)
champs[0]=4.
champs[1]=
champs[2]=4.

Résultats(/^\s*([+-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*/, + 4)
champs[0]= + 4
champs[1]=+
champs[2]=4

Comments:

Here, we use regular expressions to extract the various fields from a string. Regular expressions allow us to overcome the limitations of the [explode] function. The principle is to compare a string to another string called a pattern using the [preg_match] function: [$correspond = preg_match($modèle, $chaîne, $champs)] (line 48). The function [preg_match] returns the integer 1 if the pattern can be found in the string, and 0 otherwise. If so, [$champs[0]] represents the substring corresponding to the pattern. Furthermore, if the pattern contains subpatterns enclosed in parentheses, [$champs[1]] is the portion of [$chaîne] corresponding to the first subpattern, [$champs[2]] is the portion of [$chaîne] corresponding to the second subpattern, and so on. Let’s return to the script:

  • line 10: The pattern matches a sequence of one or more (+) digits (\d) appearing anywhere in a string. Additionally, the pattern defines a subpattern enclosed in parentheses;
  • line 12: the pattern /(\d+)/ is matched against the string "xyz1234abcd." We see that the substring 1234 matches the pattern. Therefore, [$champs[0]] equals "1234." Furthermore, the pattern has a subpattern enclosed in parentheses. We will get [$champs[1]="1234"];
  • line 13: the pattern /(\d+)/ is compared to the string "12 34". We see that the substrings 12 and 34 match the pattern. The comparison stops at the first substring that matches the pattern. Therefore, we will have [$champs[0]=12] and [$champs[1]=12];
  • Line 14: The pattern /(\d+)/ is compared to the string "abcd". No match is found;
  • line 51: [preg_match] returns an integer (and [false] if there is an error in the pattern): it is strictly compared to 1.

Let’s explain the patterns used in the rest of the code:

$modèle = "/^(.*?)(\d+)(.*?)$/";

matches the start of the string (^), followed by zero or more (*) arbitrary characters (.), followed by one or more (+) digits, followed by zero or more (*) arbitrary characters (.). The pattern (.*) matches zero or more any characters. Such a pattern will match any string. Thus, in the pattern /^(.*)(\d+)(.*)$/, the first subpattern (.*) would match all digits except the last one, which is the only one left for the subpattern (\d+). The pattern (.*?)(\d+) matches 0 or more any characters up to the next subpattern (?), which in this case is \d+. Therefore, the digits are no longer captured by the (.*) pattern. The pattern above thus matches [début de chaîne (^), une suite de caractères quelconques (.*?), une suite d'un ou plusieurs chiffres (\d+), une suite de caractères quelconques (.*?), la fin de la chaîne ($)].

$modèle = "/^\s*(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\s*$/";

matches [début de chaîne (^), une suite de 0 ou plusieurs espaces (\s*), 2 chiffres (\d\d), le caractère / (\/), 2 chiffres, /, 2 chiffres, une suite de 0 ou plusieurs espaces (\s*), la fin de chaîne ($)].

$modèle = "/^\s*([+-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*/";

matches [début de chaîne (^), 0 ou plusieurs espaces (\s*), un signe + ou - ([+-]) présent 0 ou 1 fois (?), une suite de 0 ou plusieurs espaces (\s*), 1 ou plusieurs chiffres suivis d'un point décimal suivi de zéro ou plusieurs chiffres (\d+\.\d*) ou (|) un point décimal (\.) suivi d'un ou plusieurs chiffres (\d+) ou (|) un ou plusieurs chiffres (\d+), une suite de 0 ou plusieurs espaces (\s*)]. The course PHP was written as [+|-]: within square brackets, the | character has no special meaning, and this pattern also accepted the | symbol before a number. [+-] is the correct notation.

Note: The term [espace] in regular expressions refers to a set of characters: whitespace, newline \n, tab \t, carriage return \r, form feed \f…

docs.title: 3.8.1. Parameter Passing Method
docs.text:
The [bases-12.php] script is as follows:

<?php

// How to Pass Parameters to a Function
// Strict adherence to parameter types
declare(strict_types=1);

function f(int &$i, int $j): void
{
     // $i will be passed by reference
     // $j will be passed by value
    $i++;
    $j++;
    print "f[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";
}

// Tests
$i = 0;
$j = 0;
// $i and $j are passed to function f
f($i, $j);
print "test[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";

Results:

> php bases-12.php
f[i,j]=[1,1]
test[i,j]=[1,0]

Comments:

The code above demonstrates the two ways to pass parameters to a function. Consider the following example:

function f(int &$a, int $b): void
{
    …
}

// main program
$i = 10;
$j = 20;
f($i, $j);
  • Line 1: Defines the formal parameters [$a] and [$b] for the function [f]. This function processes these two formal parameters;
  • Line 9: Calls the function [f] with two actual parameters, [$i] and [$j]. The relationships between the formal parameters ([$a], [$b]) and the actual parameters ([$i], [$j]) are defined by lines 1 and 9:
    • [&$a]: The & symbol indicates that the formal parameter [$a] will take on the value of the address of the actual parameter [$i]. In other words, [$a] and [$i] are two references to the same memory location. Manipulating the formal parameter [$a] is equivalent to manipulating the actual parameter [$i]. This is demonstrated by the code execution. This passing mode is suitable for output parameters. This passing mode is called “pass-by-reference”;
    • [$b]: The formal parameter [$b] will take on the value of the actual parameter [$j]. This is passing by value. The formal and actual parameters are two different variables. Manipulating the formal parameter [$b] has no effect on the actual parameter [$j]. This is demonstrated by the code execution. This passing mode is suitable for input parameters.

Consider the function [échange], which accepts two formal parameters: [$a] and [$b]. The function swaps the values of these two parameters. Thus, when [échange($i, $j)] is called, the calling code expects the values of the two actual parameters to be swapped. These are therefore output parameters (they are modified). We will therefore write:

function échange(mixed &$a, mixed &$b): void
{
    [$a, $b] = [$b, $a];
}

Note: One might think that passing by reference is also suitable for large data sets, arrays, and dictionaries, to avoid copying them. This is unnecessary: PHP actually copies an array passed by value only if the function modifies it. Therefore, passing by reference should be reserved for output parameters.

The following script, [bases-13.php], shows additional examples:

<?php

// parameter passing mode
// No `declare(strict_types=1)` in this script: we are in “coercive” mode

function f(&$i, $j)
{
     // $i will be passed by reference
     // $j will be passed by value
    $i++;
    $j++;
    print "f[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";
}

function g(int &$i, int $j): void
{
     // $i will be passed by reference
     // $j will be obtained by value
    $i++;
    $j++;
    print "g[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";
}

// tests
$i = 0;
$j = 0;
// $i and $j are passed to function f
f($i, $j);
print "test[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";
// $i and $j are passed to function g
g($i, $j);
print "test[i,j]=[$i,$j]\n";
// float-type parameters are passed to f
$a = 5.0;
$b = 6.2;
f($a, $b);
print "test[a,b]=[$a,$b]\n";
// float-type parameters are passed to g
$a = 5.0;
$b = 6.0;
g($a, $b);
print "test[a,b]=[$a,$b]\n";

Comments:

  • line 4: Unlike all the other scripts in this course, this script does not include the [declare(strict_types=1)] statement: PHP operates in “coercive” mode;
  • Lines 6–13: The [f] function discussed in the previous paragraph, but the parameters are not typed;
  • lines 15–22: the function [g] does the same thing as the function [f], but the types of the expected parameters are specified. It expects two parameters of type [int]. We want to see what happens when the actual parameter passed to the function does not have the type expected by the function;
  • lines 25–26: [$i] and [$j] are two integers;
  • line 28: call to the function [f] with parameters of the expected type;
  • line 31: call to the function [g] with parameters of the expected type;
  • lines 34–35: the variables [$a] and [$b] are of type [float];
  • line 36: call to the function [f] with parameters of type [float];
  • Lines 39–41: Call to the function [g] with parameters of type [float], which is not the expected type.

Results:

> php bases-13.php
f[i,j]=[1,1]
test[i,j]=[1,0]
g[i,j]=[2,1]
test[i,j]=[2,0]
f[i,j]=[6,7.2]
test[a,b]=[6,6.2]
g[i,j]=[6,7]
test[a,b]=[6,6]
  • The function [f], whose parameters are untyped, accepted both parameters of type [float] and processed them as follows: [$i] is 6.0 (displayed as 6), and [$j] is 7.2;
  • the function [g] accepted both parameters of type [float] but converted them to type [int]. This can be seen in the variable [$a], passed by reference, which has become the integer 6.

The floating-point numbers 5.0 and 6.0 have no decimal part: converting them to integers does not result in any loss of information. What would happen with the floating-point number 5.3? In PHP 7, it was silently converted to the integer 5. Since PHP 8.1, this conversion—which loses information—has been marked as deprecated: it will become an error in a future version of PHP.

Now let’s do the same thing in strict mode. The script [bases-13b.php] is identical to the script [bases-13.php] except that it begins with the statement:

declare(strict_types=1);

This instruction specifies that the types of the formal parameters must be respected. If they are not, an error is reported. The results of the execution are then:

> php bases-13b.php
f[i,j]=[1,1]
test[i,j]=[1,0]
g[i,j]=[2,1]
test[i,j]=[2,0]
f[i,j]=[6,7.2]
test[a,b]=[6,6.2]

Fatal error: Uncaught TypeError: g(): Argument #1 ($i) must be of type int; a float was passed; called in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/bases/bases-13b.php on line 42 and defined in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/bases/bases-13b.php:16
Stack trace:
#0 .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/bases/bases-13b.php(42): g(5.0, 6.0)
#1 {main}
  thrown in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/bases/bases-13b.php on line 16

The PHP interpreter raised a [TypeError] error to indicate that the first parameter passed to the [g] function was of the wrong type: g(): Argument #1 ($i) must be of type int; float was provided. The message indicates the line number of the faulty call (42) and that of the function definition (16). Since this error is not caught (there is no [try / catch]), the script terminates. It is recommended to be strict about parameter types whenever possible to detect function call errors: this is why all scripts in the course begin with [declare(strict_types=1)].

docs.title: 3.8.2. Function parameters in PHP 8
docs.text:
PHP 8 has greatly enhanced function declaration and calling. The script [bases-14.php] demonstrates these new features:

<?php

// function parameters in PHP 8
declare(strict_types=1);

// 1 - parameters with default values
function salutation(string $nom, string $formule = "Bonjour", bool $majuscules = false): string
{
    $message = "$formule $nom";
    return $majuscules ? strtoupper($message) : $message;
}

print salutation("Pierre") . "\n";
print salutation("Pierre", "Bonsoir") . "\n";
// 2 - named arguments (PHP 8.0): you can skip a parameter and provide them in any order
print salutation("Pierre", majuscules: true) . "\n";
print salutation(majuscules: true, formule: "Salut", nom: "Paul") . "\n";
// Predefined functions also accept named arguments
print str_pad(string: "7", length: 3, pad_string: "0", pad_type: STR_PAD_LEFT) . "\n";

// 3 - Union type (PHP 8.0): The parameter can be of any of the listed types
function double(int|float $nombre): int|float
{
    return 2 * $nombre;
}

var_dump(double(4));
var_dump(double(4.5));

// 4 - nullable type: ?string is equivalent to string|null
function longueur(?string $chaîne): int
{
     // The ?? operator evaluates to the right operand if the left operand is null
    return strlen($chaîne ?? "");
}

print "longueur(\"abc\")=" . longueur("abc") . ", longueur(null)=" . longueur(null) . "\n";

// 5 - mixed type (PHP 8.0) and match expression (PHP 8.0)
function décrire(mixed $valeur): string
{
     // The `match` operator compares using `===` and returns a value
    return match (true) {
        is_int($valeur), is_float($valeur) => "le nombre $valeur",
        is_string($valeur) => "la chaîne [$valeur]",
        is_bool($valeur) => "le booléen " . ($valeur ? "true" : "false"),
        is_array($valeur) => "un tableau de " . count($valeur) . " élément(s)",
        default => "une valeur de type " . get_debug_type($valeur),
    };
}

foreach ([12, 3.5, "abc", false, [1, 2], null] as $valeur) {
    print décrire($valeur) . "\n";
}

// match on a value
$enfants = 3;
$parts = match ($enfants) {
    0 => 0.0,
    1, 2 => $enfants * 0.5,
    default => 1 + ($enfants - 2) * 1.0,
};
print "$enfants enfant(s) apportent $parts part(s)\n";

// 6 - variable number of parameters (variadic) and the ... operator (spread)
function somme(int|float ...$nombres): int|float
{
     // $nombres is an array
    return array_sum($nombres);
}

print "somme()=" . somme() . "\n";
print "somme(1, 2, 3)=" . somme(1, 2, 3) . "\n";
$valeurs = [10, 20, 30.5];
// the array is “spread” into actual parameters
print "somme(...\$valeurs)=" . somme(...$valeurs) . "\n";
// The ... operator can also be used to merge arrays
$tous = [0, ...$valeurs, 40];
print "tous=[" . implode(",", $tous) . "]\n";

Results:

> php bases-14.php
Bonjour Pierre
Bonsoir Pierre
BONJOUR PIERRE
SALUT PAUL
007
int(8)
float(9)
longueur("abc")=3, longueur(null)=0
le nombre 12
le nombre 3.5
la chaîne [abc]
le booléen false
un tableau de 2 élément(s)
une valeur de type null
3 enfant(s) apportent 2 part(s)
somme()=0
somme(1, 2, 3)=6
somme(...$valeurs)=60.5
tous=[0,10,20,30.5,40]

Comments:

  • line 7: The parameters [$formule] and [$majuscules] have default values. They can be omitted when calling the function (line 13), in which case they take their default values;
  • line 10: the ternary operator [condition ? valeur1 : valeur2] returns [valeur1] if the condition is true, and [valeur2] otherwise;
  • line 16: named arguments (PHP 8.0). The actual parameter is preceded by the name of the formal parameter followed by a colon (:). This allows you to assign a value to the third parameter without specifying the second, which retains its default value;
  • line 17: With named arguments, the order of the parameters no longer matters. This improves code readability: [majuscules: true] is more descriptive than a standalone [true];
  • line 19: The predefined functions of PHP also accept named arguments. Their names are those listed in the php.net documentation;
  • line 22: The union type [int|float] (PHP 8.0) indicates that the parameter can be a [int] or a [float]. The same applies to the result;
  • line 31: the type [?string] is a nullable type: the parameter is a string or the value [null]. This is a shorthand notation for [string|null]. Note: In PHP 7, people often wrote [string $chaîne = null] to achieve the same effect. This notation (“implicit nullable”) has been deprecated since PHP 8.4: you must write [?string $chaîne = null];
  • Line 34: the [??] operator, which we’ve already encountered: if [$chaîne] equals [null], the empty string is used. In fact, since PHP 8.1, passing [null] to a non-nullable parameter of a predefined function—such as [strlen(null)] here—is deprecated;
  • line 40: the parameter of type [mixed] accepts any value, including [null];
  • Lines 43–49: The expression [match] (PHP 8.0). It compares the value in parentheses to the values to the left of the => arrows and returns the value to the right of the first arrow for which the comparison is true. With [match (true)], conditions are written on the left: the first true condition takes precedence. Multiple values can be separated by commas (line 44). [default] covers all other cases;
  • line 48: the function [get_debug_type] (PHP 8.0) returns the type name of a value as written in the code: int, float, string, null, or the class name of an object. [gettype], on the other hand, returned historical names such as integer or double;
  • lines 58–62: [match] applied to a value. Here, the variable [$enfants] is compared to the values 0, then 1, and then 2; otherwise, the case for [default] applies. Unlike the [switch] instruction—which [match] effectively replaces—the comparison is performed using [===], [match] is an expression that returns a value, and there is no [break] instruction to worry about. If no branch is suitable and there is no *[default]*, *[match] throws a *[UnhandledMatchError] error;
  • line 66: [int|float ...$nombres] is a variadic parameter: the function accepts any number of actual parameters (even none), which PHP collects in the array [$nombres]. A variadic parameter is always the last one;
  • line 76: the [...] (spread) operator placed before an array in a call “spreads” the array: its elements become the actual parameters of the function. [somme(...$valeurs)] is equivalent to [somme(10, 20, 30.5)];
  • line 78: the same operator allows the elements of one array to be inserted into another array.

docs.title: 3.8.3. Results returned by a function
docs.text:
The script [bases-15.php] is as follows:

<?php

// types in strict mode
declare(strict_types=1);

// results returned by a function
// A function can return multiple values in an array
[$res1, $res2, $res3] = f1(10);
print "[$res1,$res2,$res3]\n";
$res = f1(10);
for ($i = 0; $i < count($res); $i++) {
    print "f1 : res[$i]=$res[$i]\n";
}
// an associative array can also be “destructured”
["min" => $min, "max" => $max] = minMax([4, -2, 17, 8]);
print "minMax : [min=$min,max=$max]\n";

// A function can return an object
$res = f2(10);
print "f2 : [$res->res1,$res->res2,$res->res3]\n";
// What kind of object?
print "nature de l'objet : ";
var_dump($res);

// We do the same thing with the function f3
$res = f3(10);
print "f3 : [$res->res1,$res->res2,$res->res3]\n";
// What kind of object?
print "nature de l'objet : ";
var_dump($res);

// A function can return an object or null
$res = f4(10);
// The null-safe operator ?-> returns null instead of causing an error if $res is null
print "f4(10) : res1=" . ($res?->res1 ?? "aucun") . "\n";
$res = f4(-10);
print "f4(-10) : res1=" . ($res?->res1 ?? "aucun") . "\n";

// end
exit;

// function f1
function f1(int $valeur): array
{
     // returns an array ($valeur+1, $valeur+2, $valeur+3)
    return [$valeur + 1, $valeur + 2, $valeur + 3];
}

// function minMax
function minMax(array $nombres): array
{
     // returns an associative array
    return ["min" => min($nombres), "max" => max($nombres)];
}

// function f2
function f2(int $valeur): object
{
     // returns an object ($valeur+1,$valeur+2,$valeur+3)
     // obtained by converting an associative array into an object
    return (object) ["res1" => $valeur + 1, "res2" => $valeur + 2, "res3" => $valeur + 3];
}

// function f3—does the same thing as function f2
function f3(int $valeur): object
{
     // returns an object ($valeur+1,$valeur+2,$valeur+3)
    $res = new stdClass();
    $res->res1 = $valeur + 1;
    $res->res2 = $valeur + 2;
    $res->res3 = $valeur + 3;
     // returns the object
    return $res;
}

// function f4—returns an object if $valeur is positive, null otherwise
function f4(int $valeur): ?object
{
    return $valeur >= 0 ? f3($valeur) : null;
}

Results:

> php bases-15.php
[11,12,13]
f1 : res[0]=11
f1 : res[1]=12
f1 : res[2]=13
minMax : [min=-2,max=17]
f2 : [11,12,13]
nature de l'objet : object(stdClass)#1 (3) {
  ["res1"]=>
  int(11)
  ["res2"]=>
  int(12)
  ["res3"]=>
  int(13)
}
f3 : [11,12,13]
nature de l'objet : object(stdClass)#2 (3) {
  ["res1"]=>
  int(11)
  ["res2"]=>
  int(12)
  ["res3"]=>
  int(13)
}
f4(10) : res1=11
f4(-10) : res1=aucun

Comments:

  • The previous program shows that a PHP function can return a set of results rather than a single one, in the form of an array or an object. The concept of an object is explained in a later chapter;
  • lines 43–47: The function [f1] returns multiple values in the form of an array ([array]);
  • line 8: the returned array is unpacked into three variables;
  • line 15: destructuring also works with an associative array: for each variable, the key of the value to be retrieved is specified. The function [minMax] returns a dictionary (line 53). The predefined functions [min] and [max] return the smallest and largest elements of an array;
  • lines 57–62: The function [f2] returns multiple values in the form of an object ([object]). It does this by converting an associative array into an object using the operator [(object)]: each key in the array becomes a property of the object;
  • Lines 65–74: The function [f3] does the same thing as the function [f2], but it explicitly creates an object of type [stdClass] (line 68) and then adds properties to it. The attribute A of an object O is denoted by [$O->A];
  • line 23: the function [var_dump] provides access to the object’s type and its content. In the results, we see that the object is of type [stdClass], that its property [res1] is of type integer and has the value 11, etc. The number #1 or #2 following the type is an internal object number;
  • line 77: the result type [?object] indicates that the function [f4] returns an object of type [null];
  • Lines 35–37: The null-safe operator [?->] (PHP 8.0). If [$res] equals [null], the expression [$res?->res1] equals [null] instead of causing an error; the operator [??] then replaces [null] with “none.” Here, the operator [??] would suffice on its own, since it does not signal the absence of the property. The operator [?->] will prove particularly useful with objects and their methods: [$client?->getAdresse()?->getVille()].

Note: Course PHP 7 featured a function that wrote [$res->res1 = ...] without having created the object [$res]. PHP 7 would then create a [stdClass] object by default with a simple warning. Starting with PHP 8.0, this is a fatal error (Attempt to assign property on null): an object must always be created before it is used.

docs.title: 3.8.4. Functions are also values
docs.text:
In PHP, a function can be stored in a variable, passed as a parameter to another function, or returned as a result. The [bases-17.php] script demonstrates the different ways to write and use these functions:

<?php

// Functions are also values
declare(strict_types=1);

$nombres = [4, -2, 17, 8, -5];

// 1 - an anonymous function assigned to a variable
$carré = function (int $x): int {
    return $x * $x;
};
print "carré(5)=" . $carré(5) . "\n";

// 2 - an anonymous function passed as an argument to a predefined function
// array_map applies the function to each element of the array
$carrés = array_map($carré, $nombres);
print "carrés=[" . implode(",", $carrés) . "]\n";

// 3 - an anonymous function using an external variable: the `use` keyword
$seuil = 5;
$grands = array_filter($nombres, function (int $x) use ($seuil): bool {
    return $x > $seuil;
});
print "nombres > $seuil : [" . implode(",", $grands) . "]\n";

// 4 - the arrow function (PHP 7.4): a single expression, outer variables automatically captured
$positifs = array_filter($nombres, fn(int $x): bool => $x >= 0);
print "positifs=[" . implode(",", $positifs) . "]\n";
// sorting with a comparison function: the <=> operator returns -1, 0, or 1
$triés = $nombres;
usort($triés, fn(int $a, int $b): int => $b <=> $a);
print "tri décroissant=[" . implode(",", $triés) . "]\n";

// 5 - searching in an array (PHP 8.4)
print "premier négatif : " . array_find($nombres, fn(int $x): bool => $x < 0) . "\n";
print "au moins un > 10 : " . var_export(array_any($nombres, fn(int $x): bool => $x > 10), true) . "\n";
print "tous > -10 : " . var_export(array_all($nombres, fn(int $x): bool => $x > -10), true) . "\n";

// 6 - first-class callable syntax (PHP 8.1): nomFonction(...)
$majuscules = strtoupper(...);
print $majuscules("bonjour") . "\n";
$noms = ["dupont", "durand", "martin"];
print "noms=[" . implode(",", array_map(ucfirst(...), $noms)) . "]\n";

// 7 - the pipe operator |> (PHP 8.5): the result on the left is passed to the function on the right
$résultat = "  Bonjour tout le monde  "
    |> trim(...)
    |> strtolower(...)
    |> (fn(string $s): string => str_replace(" ", "-", $s));
print "résultat=[$résultat]\n";
// equivalent without the pipe operator
$résultat = str_replace(" ", "-", strtolower(trim("  Bonjour tout le monde  ")));
print "résultat=[$résultat]\n";

Results:

> php bases-17.php
carré(5)=25
carrés=[16,4,289,64,25]
nombres > 5 : [17,8]
positifs=[4,17,8]
tri décroissant=[17,8,4,-2,-5]
premier négatif : -2
au moins un > 10 : true
tous > -10 : true
BONJOUR
noms=[Dupont,Durand,Martin]
résultat=[bonjour-tout-le-monde]
résultat=[bonjour-tout-le-monde]

Comments:

  • lines 9–11: An anonymous (unnamed) function is assigned to the variable [$carré]. Note the semicolon at the end: this is an assignment;
  • line 12: the function is called via the variable;
  • line 16: the predefined function [array_map] applies the function passed as the first parameter to each element of the array passed as the second parameter, and returns the array of results;
  • lines 21–23: the predefined function [array_filter] returns the array elements for which the function passed as the second parameter returns [true]. An anonymous function is not aware of the variables in the surrounding code: the keyword [use ($seuil)] gives it access to the variable [$seuil]. Note that [array_filter] retains the keys of the selected elements; this has no effect here because [implode] uses only the values;
  • Line 27: an arrow function (PHP 7.4): [fn(paramètres) => expression]. It contains only one expression, whose value is the result of the function. It automatically has read access to the variables in the surrounding code: no need for [use]. This is the most concise way to write small functions passed as parameters;
  • Line 31: The function [usort] sorts an array using a comparison function that takes two elements, [$a] and [$b], and returns a negative number, zero, or a positive number, depending on whether [$a] should be placed before, at the same rank as, or after [$b]. The operator [<=>] (“spaceship”) returns exactly -1, 0, or 1. By writing [$b <=> $a] instead of [$a <=> $b], we obtain a descending sort. Note that [usort] modifies the array passed to it (pass-by-reference): we have therefore sorted a copy ([$triés]) of the array [$nombres];
  • Line 35: The functions [array_find], [array_any], and [array_all] were introduced with PHP 8.4. [array_find] returns the first element for which the function returns [true] (or [null] if there are none), [array_any] returns [true] if at least one element satisfies the condition, and [array_all] if all of them do;
  • line 40: first-class callable syntax (PHP 8.1): [nomFonction(...)], with three dots between the parentheses, does not call the function but returns the function itself as a [Closure] object. It can then be used as an anonymous function;
  • Line 43: The predefined function [ucfirst] (first letter capitalized) has been changed to [array_map];
  • Lines 46–49: the pipe operator [|>] (PHP 8.5). The expression [valeur |> fonction] calls the function with the value as its only parameter. The calls are chained from left to right, in the order in which they are read: leading and trailing spaces are removed with [trim], the text is converted to lowercase with [strtolower], and then spaces are replaced with hyphens. An arrow function used with [|>] must be enclosed in parentheses;
  • line 52: the same thing without the pipe operator. Functions are nested and read from the inside out, in the reverse order of execution.

docs.title: 3.9. Text files
docs.text:
The script [bases-16.php] is as follows:

<?php

// strict adherence to function parameter types
declare(strict_types=1);

// sequential processing of a text file
// this is a set of lines in the form login:pwd:uid:gid:infos:dir:shell
// Each line is stored in a dictionary in the form login => [uid, gid, infos, dir, shell]
// Set the file name
$INFOS = "infos.txt";
// Open it for creation
$fic = fopen($INFOS, "w");
if ($fic === false) {
    print "Erreur d'ouverture du fichier $INFOS en écriture\n";
    exit;
}
// Generates arbitrary content
for ($i = 0; $i < 100; $i++) {
    fputs($fic, "login$i:pwd$i:uid$i:gid$i:infos$i:dir$i:shell$i\n");
}
// the file is closed
fclose($fic);

// Exploit—`fgets` preserves the end-of-line marker
// this prevents an empty string from being read when encountering a blank line
// Open the file for reading
$fic = fopen($INFOS, "r");
if ($fic === false) {
    print "Erreur d'ouverture du fichier $INFOS en lecture\n";
    exit;
}

// the information dictionary
$dico = [];
// the lines are less than 1,000 characters long
// Reading the line stops at the end-of-line character
// or the end-of-file marker
while (($ligne = fgets($fic, 1000)) !== false) {
     // The end-of-line marker is removed if it exists
    $ligne = cutNewLineChar($ligne);
     // The line is added to an array
    $infos = explode(":", $ligne);
     // retrieve the login
    $login = array_shift($infos);
     // ignore the password
    array_shift($infos);
     // Create an entry in the dictionary
    $dico[$login] = $infos;
}
// close it
fclose($fic);

// using the dictionary
afficheInfos($dico, "login10");
afficheInfos($dico, "X");

// Another way to read a text file: the `file` function
$lignes = file($INFOS, FILE_IGNORE_NEW_LINES);
print "le fichier $INFOS a " . count($lignes) . " lignes, la dernière est [" . array_last($lignes) . "]\n";

// end
exit;

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
function afficheInfos(array $dico, string $clé): void
{
     // displays the value associated with the key in the dictionary $dico if it exists
    if (isset($dico[$clé])) {
         // value exists—is it an array?
        $valeur = $dico[$clé];
        if (is_array($valeur)) {
            print "[$clé," . implode(":", $valeur) . "]\n";
        } else {
             // $valeur is not an array
            print "[$clé,$valeur]\n";
        }
    } else {
         // $clé is not a key in the dictionary $dico
        print "la clé [$clé] n'existe pas\n";
    }
}

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
function cutNewLineChar(string $ligne): string
{
     // The line-end character in $ligne is removed if it exists
     // (\n on Unix, \r\n on Windows)
    return rtrim($ligne, "\r\n");
}

The [infos.txt] file created by the script:

login0:pwd0:uid0:gid0:infos0:dir0:shell0
login1:pwd1:uid1:gid1:infos1:dir1:shell1
login2:pwd2:uid2:gid2:infos2:dir2:shell2
…
login98:pwd98:uid98:gid98:infos98:dir98:shell98
login99:pwd99:uid99:gid99:infos99:dir99:shell99

The results:

> php bases-16.php
[login10,uid10:gid10:infos10:dir10:shell10]
la clé [X] n'existe pas
le fichier infos.txt a 100 lignes, la dernière est [login99:pwd99:uid99:gid99:infos99:dir99:shell99]

Comments:

  • Line 12: [fopen(nom_fichier, "w")] opens the file [nom_fichier] in write mode (w=write). If the file does not exist, it is created. If it exists, it is cleared. The file is created in the current directory, the one from which the script was run. If creation fails, [fopen] issues a warning and returns the value [false];
  • line 13: the result of [fopen] is tested by strictly comparing it to [false];
  • line 19: [fputs($fic, $chaîne)] writes [$chaîne] to the file [$fic]. Here, the string ends with the end-of-line marker [\n];
  • line 22: [fclose($fic)] closes the file [$fic];
  • line 27: [fopen(nom_fichier, "r")] opens the file [nom_fichier] in read mode (r=read). If opening the file fails (for example, if the file does not exist), [fopen] returns the value [false];
  • line 34: the dictionary is initialized as empty before being populated. PHP would create the array on the first assignment of [$dico[$login] = ...], but if the file were empty, the variable would not exist and its use would trigger a warning;
  • line 38: [fgets($fic, 1000)] reads the next line of the file, limited to 1,000 characters. The [while (($ligne = fgets($fic, 1000)) !== false) {...}] operation consists of two successive operations: 1) [$ligne = fgets(...)] and 2) [while ($ligne !== false)]. After the last character of the file has been read, the function [fgets] returns the value [false], and the loop [while] stops. Here, the function [fgets] attempts to read up to 1,000 characters but stops as soon as it encounters a line-end character. Since all lines here have fewer than 1,000 characters, [fgets] reads one line of text, including the line-end character. The PHP 7 course wrote [while ($ligne = fgets($fic, 1000))]: the loop would have stopped prematurely on a final line reduced to "0," without a line-end character, because the string "0" is converted to [false]. The strict comparison [!== false] avoids this pitfall;
  • line 40: the function [cutNewLineChar] removes any line-end characters;
  • line 44: the function [array_shift($tableau)] removes the first element of [$tableau] and returns it as the result;
  • line 46: here, we ignore the result returned by [array_shift];
  • Line 58: Another way to read a text file. The [file] function returns an array containing all the lines in the file. With the [FILE_IGNORE_NEW_LINES] option, line-end characters are removed. This is simpler than the [fgets] loop, but the entire file is loaded into memory: for a very large file, reading line by line is still preferable;
  • line 71: the function [is_array($variable)] returns [true] if [$variable] is an array, and [false] otherwise;
  • line 84: The end-of-line character is the string "\r\n" on Windows systems and "\n" on Unix systems. The function [rtrim($chaîne, $caractères)] removes all characters present in [$caractères]—in this case, \r and \n—from the end of [$chaîne]. Without a second parameter, [rtrim] removes all “spaces” (whitespace, tabs, line breaks, etc.); the function [trim] does the same at both ends of the string.

docs.title: 3.10. Encoding/Decoding JSON
docs.text:
The [scripts-console/json] folder contains the scripts for this section:

json
├── famille.json
├── json-01.php
├── json-02.php
└── json-03.php

The JSON encoding/decoding (JavaScript Object Notation) is something we will use extensively in the exercise that serves as the central theme of this document. The [json-01.php, json-02.php, json-03.php] scripts explain what you need to know for the rest of the document.

The [json-01.php] script is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

$array1 = ["nom" => "séléné", "prénom" => "bénédicte", "âge" => 34];
// encode the array1 array using JSON with escaped Unicode characters
print "encodage JSON du tableau array1 avec caractères Unicode échappés\n";
$json1 = json_encode($array1);
print "json1=$json1\n";
// JSON encoding of the array1 array with unescaped Unicode characters
print "encodage JSON du tableau array1 avec caractères Unicode non échappés\n";
$json2 = json_encode($array1, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE);
print "json2=$json2\n";
// JSON decoding into an associative array
print "décodage JSON de json2 dans tableau associatif\n";
$array2 = json_decode($json2, true);
var_dump($array2);
foreach ($array2 as $key => $value) {
    print "$key:$value\n";
}
// Decoding JSON into an object
print "décodage JSON de json2 dans objet stdClass\n";
$objet2 = json_decode($json2);
var_dump($objet2);
print "prénom=$objet2->prénom\n";
print "nom=$objet2->nom\n";
print "âge=$objet2->âge\n";

Results:

> php json-01.php
encodage JSON du tableau array1 avec caractères Unicode échappés
json1={"nom":"s\u00e9l\u00e9n\u00e9","pr\u00e9nom":"b\u00e9n\u00e9dicte","\u00e2ge":34}
encodage JSON du tableau array1 avec caractères Unicode non échappés
json2={"nom":"séléné","prénom":"bénédicte","âge":34}
décodage JSON de json2 dans tableau associatif
array(3) {
  ["nom"]=>
  string(9) "séléné"
  ["prénom"]=>
  string(11) "bénédicte"
  ["âge"]=>
  int(34)
}
nom:séléné
prénom:bénédicte
âge:34
décodage JSON de json2 dans objet stdClass
object(stdClass)#1 (3) {
  ["nom"]=>
  string(9) "séléné"
  ["prénom"]=>
  string(11) "bénédicte"
  ["âge"]=>
  int(34)
}
prénom=bénédicte
nom=séléné
âge=34

Comments:

  • line 8: the [json_encode] function converts its parameter into the string JSON. In the resulting string, the accented characters é and â have been replaced by their Unicode codes, which begin with \u;
  • line 12: We repeat the same process, this time specifying that the Unicode characters should be preserved as-is. The resulting string JSON is much more readable;
  • Lines 16–20: We perform the reverse operation. We convert the string JSON into an associative array: this is the role of the second parameter, [true], of [json_decode]. The results show that we have indeed obtained an associative array;
  • Lines 23–27: Without the parameter [true], [json_decode] converts the string JSON into an object of type [stdClass]. Attribute A of an object O is denoted as [$O->A].

Multi-level arrays can be encoded as JSON, as shown in the following script [json-02.php]:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

$array = [
    "nom" => "séléné", "prénom" => "bénédicte", "âge" => 34,
    "mari" => ["nom" => "icariù", "prénom" => "ignacio", "âge" => 35],
    "enfants" => [
        ["prénom" => "angèle", "age" => 8],
        ["prénom" => "andré", "age" => 2],
    ],
];
// encoding of JSON from a multi-level array
print "encodage JSON d'un tableau à plusieurs niveaux\n";
$json = json_encode($array, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE);
print "json=$json\n";
// the same encoding, presented in a human-readable format
print "encodage JSON avec l'option JSON_PRETTY_PRINT\n";
print json_encode($array["mari"], JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE | JSON_PRETTY_PRINT) . "\n";

Results:

> php json-02.php
encodage JSON d'un tableau à plusieurs niveaux
json={"nom":"séléné","prénom":"bénédicte","âge":34,"mari":{"nom":"icariù","prénom":"ignacio","âge":35},"enfants":[{"prénom":"angèle","age":8},{"prénom":"andré","age":2}]}
encodage JSON avec l'option JSON_PRETTY_PRINT
{
    "nom": "icariù",
    "prénom": "ignacio",
    "âge": 35
}

Comments:

In the string JSON:

  • non-associative arrays (lists) are enclosed in square brackets [] ;
  • associative arrays are enclosed in curly braces {} .

Line 19: The options for [json_encode] are combined using the | operator (binary OU). The [JSON_PRETTY_PRINT] option produces a JSON string that is indented across multiple lines, making it more readable.

The script [json-03.php] demonstrates how to process the following JSON and [famille.json] files:

{
    "épouse": {
        "nom": "séléné",
        "prénom": "bénédicte",
        "âge": 34
    },
    "mari": {
        "nom": "icariù",
        "prénom": "ignacio",
        "âge": 35
    },
    "enfants": [
        {
            "prénom": "angèle",
            "age": 8
        },
        {
            "prénom": "andré",
            "age": 2
        }
    ]
}

The [json-03.php] script is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// Reading the JSON file
$json = file_get_contents("famille.json");
// Is the read content valid JSON? (PHP 8.3)
if ($json === false || !json_validate($json)) {
    print "Le fichier [famille.json] est absent ou ne contient pas du JSON valide\n";
    exit;
}
// Decoding JSON into an object
$famille1 = json_decode($json);
print "----famille1\n";
var_dump($famille1);
// Decoding JSON into an associative array
print "----famille2\n";
$famille2 = json_decode($json, true);
var_dump($famille2);

Comments:

  • line 6: The [file_get_contents] function reads the contents of the file named [famille.json] and stores them in the variable [$json]. It returns [false] if the read operation fails;
  • Line 8: The function [json_validate] (PHP 8.3) returns [true] if the string passed as a parameter is a valid JSON. Previously, it was necessary to decode the string and then call the function [json_last_error];
  • lines 13–19: the string is then decoded into an object and then into an associative array.

Results:

> php json-03.php
----famille1
object(stdClass)#2 (3) {
  ["épouse"]=>
  object(stdClass)#1 (3) {
    ["nom"]=>
    string(9) "séléné"
    ["prénom"]=>
    string(11) "bénédicte"
    ["âge"]=>
    int(34)
  }
  ["mari"]=>
  object(stdClass)#3 (3) {
    ["nom"]=>
    string(7) "icariù"
    ["prénom"]=>
    string(7) "ignacio"
    ["âge"]=>
    int(35)
  }
  ["enfants"]=>
  array(2) {
    [0]=>
    object(stdClass)#4 (2) {
      ["prénom"]=>
      string(7) "angèle"
      ["age"]=>
      int(8)
    }
    [1]=>
    object(stdClass)#5 (2) {
      ["prénom"]=>
      string(6) "andré"
      ["age"]=>
      int(2)
    }
  }
}
----famille2
array(3) {
  ["épouse"]=>
  array(3) {
    ["nom"]=>
    string(9) "séléné"
    ["prénom"]=>
    string(11) "bénédicte"
    ["âge"]=>
    int(34)
  }
  ["mari"]=>
  array(3) {
    ["nom"]=>
    string(7) "icariù"
    ["prénom"]=>
    string(7) "ignacio"
    ["âge"]=>
    int(35)
  }
  ["enfants"]=>
  array(2) {
    [0]=>
    array(2) {
      ["prénom"]=>
      string(7) "angèle"
      ["age"]=>
      int(8)
    }
    [1]=>
    array(2) {
      ["prénom"]=>
      string(6) "andré"
      ["age"]=>
      int(2)
    }
  }
}
  • The first part of the results shows the object resulting from the decoding of the file JSON [famille.json]: The JSON objects have become [stdClass] objects, and the JSON list of children has become a PHP array;
  • the second part shows the associative array resulting from the same decoding: all JSON objects have become associative arrays.

docs.title: 5. The classes
docs.text:
Vocabulary: A class (keyword [class]) is a type PHP. A variable of this type is called an object. An object is an instance (an instance) of a class.

It is in this chapter that the evolution of PHP between versions 7 and 8 is most evident. PHP 8 introduced a series of new features that make writing classes more concise and safer: typed attributes, constructor parameter promotion, read-only attributes ([readonly]), enumerations ([enum]), property hooks and asymmetric visibility (PHP 8.4), cloning with modification (PHP 8.5)... We introduce these concepts through the examples, following the progression of Course PHP 7: we start with the most basic class and work our way up to a class written according to current best practices.

docs.title: 5.1. The script directory structure
docs.text:
The scripts for this chapter are located in the [scripts-console/classes] folder:

php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes
├── json
│   ├── json-01.php
│   ├── json-02.php
│   ├── json-03.php
│   ├── json-04.php
│   ├── Personne.php
│   ├── Personne2.php
│   ├── Personne3.php
│   └── Personne4.php
├── classes-01.php
├── classes-02.php
├── ...
├── classes-26.php

├── Etudiant.php

As in previous chapters, a console script is run in a [VS Code] terminal opened in the script’s folder, using the [php nom-du-script.php] command.

docs.title: 5.2. Can any variable become an object with attributes?
docs.text:
In PHP 7, it was possible to write [$obj1->attr1 = "un";] to a nonexistent variable [$obj1]: PHP would then silently (with a simple warning) create a [stdClass]-type object with the [attr1] attribute. This is no longer possible in PHP 8. The [classes-01.php] script is as follows:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// In PHP 8, a nonexistent variable is no longer magically converted into an object
try {
    $obj0->attr1 = "un";
} catch (\Error $e) {
    print "Erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// A generic object must be created explicitly
$obj1 = new \stdClass();
// A [stdClass] object can accept dynamically created attributes
$obj1->attr1 = "un";
$obj1->attr2 = 100;
// displays the object
print "objet1=[$obj1->attr1,$obj1->attr2]\n";
// modifies the object
$obj1->attr2 += 100;
// displays the object
print "objet1=[$obj1->attr1,$obj1->attr2]\n";
// copies the value of object1 (the address of the object it points to) into object2
// The two variables are now different but point to the same object
$obj2 = $obj1;
// modifies obj2
$obj2->attr2 = 0;
// displays both objects
print "objet1=[$obj1->attr1,$obj1->attr2]\n";
print "objet2=[$obj2->attr1,$obj2->attr2]\n";
// changes the object pointed to by obj1
$obj1 = new \stdClass();
print "obj1 :\n";
print_r($obj1);
print "obj2 :\n";
print_r($obj2);
// assigns the reference (address) of object2 to object3
// $obj2 and $obj3 are then one and the same variable
$obj3 = &$obj2;
print "obj2 :\n";
print_r($obj2);
print "obj3 :\n";
print_r($obj3);
// modifies obj3
$obj3->attr2 = 10;
// displays both objects
print "objet2=[$obj2->attr1,$obj2->attr2]\n";
print "objet3=[$obj3->attr1,$obj3->attr2]\n";
// changes the object pointed to by obj2
$obj2 = new \stdClass();
$obj2->attr3 = "deux";
$obj2->attr4 = 20;
// displays the two objects $obj2 and $obj3
print "obj2 :\n";
print_r($obj2);
print "obj3 :\n";
print_r($obj3);

// Is an object a dictionary?
try {
    print count($obj3) . "\n";
} catch (\TypeError $e) {
    print "Erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// The number of attributes can be obtained using [get_object_vars]
print "nombre d'attributs : " . count(get_object_vars($obj3)) . "\n";
// An object can be iterated over using [foreach]
foreach ($obj3 as $attribut => $valeur) {
    print "obj3[$attribut]=$valeur\n";
}
// An associative array can be converted to an object using [stdClass], and vice versa
$obj4 = (object) ["nom" => "Langevin", "age" => 48];
print "obj4=[$obj4->nom,$obj4->age]\n";
print_r((array) $obj4);
// end
exit;

Results:

> php classes-01.php
Erreur : Attempt to assign property "attr1" on null
objet1=[un,100]
objet1=[un,200]
objet1=[un,0]
objet2=[un,0]
obj1 :
stdClass Object
(
)
obj2 :
stdClass Object
(
    [attr1] => un
    [attr2] => 0
)
obj2 :
stdClass Object
(
    [attr1] => un
    [attr2] => 0
)
obj3 :
stdClass Object
(
    [attr1] => un
    [attr2] => 0
)
objet2=[un,10]
objet3=[un,10]
obj2 :
stdClass Object
(
    [attr3] => deux
    [attr4] => 20
)
obj3 :
stdClass Object
(
    [attr3] => deux
    [attr4] => 20
)
Erreur : count(): Argument #1 ($value) must be of type Countable|array, given stdClass
nombre d'attributs : 2
obj3[attr3]=deux
obj3[attr4]=20
obj4=[Langevin,48]
Array
(
    [nom] => Langevin
    [age] => 48
)

Comments

  • Lines 7–9: In PHP 8, the variable [$obj0] does not exist, and the operation [$obj0->attr1 = "un"] throws an error of type [\Error] (line 2 of the results) instead of creating an object. We will examine the [try / catch] structure in the chapter on exceptions. For now, just note that it allows you to catch the error and continue executing the script;
  • line 13: a generic object must be explicitly created using the [new] operator. The predefined class [stdClass] is an empty class;
  • Lines 15–16: The notation [$obj->attr] refers to the attribute [attr] of the object [$obj]. If it does not exist, it is created; this is called a dynamic attribute. The class [stdClass] is designed for this purpose: you can add as many attributes to it as you want;
  • Line 25: The expression [$obj2 = $obj1], when [$obj1] is an object, is a copy of references: [$obj2] and [$obj1] are references (addresses) to the same object. The object itself can be modified by either reference;
  • Lines 27–30: are intended to show that [$obj1] and [$obj2] are two different variables that point to the same object. [$obj2 = $obj1] copied the value of [$obj1] into the variable [$obj2] (operation 1 below). The value of [$obj1] is the address of an object. Thus, [$obj1] and [$obj2] point to the same object. When a variable [$obj] that points to an object is manipulated, PHP manipulates the object being pointed to. As shown in the diagram below, we can modify the referenced object either via [$obj1] or via [$obj2]. This is illustrated in lines 5 and 6 of the results;

  • line 39: the expression [$obj3 = &$obj2] causes [$obj2] and [$obj3] to be at the same address as [1 ci-dessous]. One could say that the two variables are aliases for the same memory location. They both point to an object, Object A below: [2];
  • Line 50: The operation [$obj2 = new \stdClass()] creates a new object, Object B [3 ci-dessous], and the address of this new object is assigned to the variable [$obj2] [4]. Since [$obj2] and [$obj3] are two aliases for the same memory location, [$obj3] also points to the new Object B. This is shown in lines 31–42 of the results;

  • Line 61: Is an object a dictionary? In PHP 7, the function [count] accepted an object (with a warning) and returned 1, which made no sense. In PHP 8, it throws an error [TypeError]: [count] accepts only arrays or objects that implement the [Countable] interface (line 43 of the results);
  • line 66: the function [get_object_vars] returns an object’s attributes as an associative array. The number of elements in the array is equal to the number of attributes of the object;
  • Lines 68–69: An object can be iterated over using [foreach], just like a dictionary. The keys are the names of the attributes, and the values are the values of those same attributes. Thus, an object shares similarities with a dictionary but is not one. In PHP 7, this iteration was performed using the [each] function, which has since been removed;
  • lines 72–74: the conversion operator [(object)] converts an associative array into a [stdClass] object, and the operator [(array)] performs the reverse operation.

docs.title: 5.3. A Person class with no declared attributes
docs.text:
In PHP 7, a class could use attributes it had not declared: it was sufficient to write [$p->prenom = "Paul";] to create the attribute [prenom] in the object [$p], just as one does with [stdClass]. These dynamic attributes on objects of an ordinary class have been deprecated since PHP 8.2: each time such an attribute is created, the message “Deprecated: Creation of dynamic property Personne::$prenom is deprecated” is displayed. They will be removed in a future version of PHP. The reason is simple: a typo in an attribute name ([$p->prenon = "Paul"]) would silently create a new attribute instead of reporting the error.

There are three exceptions to this rule:

  • the [stdClass] class, which we just used, still accepts dynamic attributes;
  • a class preceded by the attribute [#[\AllowDynamicProperties]] also accepts them. This attribute was designed to facilitate the migration of legacy code. We will not use it in this course;
  • a class that defines the magic methods [__get] and [__set] decides for itself what to do with an undeclared attribute.

It is this third solution that the script [classes-02.php] presents:

<?php

// strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

class Personne
{
     // Attributes are not declared one by one:
     // they are stored in a private array
    private array $attributs = [];

     // called when writing an undeclared attribute: $p->x = value
    public function __set(string $nom, mixed $valeur): void
    {
        $this->attributs[$nom] = $valeur;
    }

     // called when reading an undeclared attribute: $p->x
    public function __get(string $nom): mixed
    {
        return $this->attributs[$nom] ?? null;
    }

     // called by isset($p->x)
    public function __isset(string $nom): bool
    {
        return isset($this->attributs[$nom]);
    }

     // method
    public function identite(): string
    {
         // uses attributes that have not been declared
        return "[$this->prenom,$this->nom,$this->age]";
    }
}

// test
// attributes are created by the magic method [__set]
$p = new Personne();
$p->prenom = "Paul";
$p->nom = "Langevin";
$p->age = 48;
// method call
print "personne=" . $p->identite() . "\n";
// isset
print "isset(\$p->age) : " . var_export(isset($p->age), true) . "\n";
print "isset(\$p->adresse) : " . var_export(isset($p->adresse), true) . "\n";
// end
exit;

Results:

> php classes-02.php
personne=[Paul,Langevin,48]
isset($p->age) : true
isset($p->adresse) : false

Comments

  • Lines 6–38: define a class named [Personne]. A class is a template used to create objects. It consists of attributes and functions called methods;
  • line 10: The only attribute declared for the class is a private array (we’ll soon see the meaning of the keyword [private]). This array will store the “undeclared” attributes;
  • lines 13–16: The magic method [__set] is automatically called by PHP when writing to an attribute that does not exist (or is not accessible). It receives the attribute’s name and the value to be assigned to it. Here, it stores this value in the array [$attributs]. Methods whose names begin with two underscores are called magic methods: they are not called explicitly; instead, PHP calls them;
  • lines 19–22: The magic method [__get] is called when reading an attribute that does not exist. It returns the stored value or [null]. The operator [??] returns its left operand if it exists and is not [null]; otherwise, it returns its right operand;
  • line 25: the magic method [__isset] is called by the function [isset];
  • Line 31: The method [identite] uses three attributes that are not declared in the class. The keyword [$this] refers to the object to which the method is applied. Each call to [$this->prenom] triggers a call to [__get];
  • Line 40: A [$p] object of type [Personne] is created. The keyword [new] is used to create a new object. The operation returns a reference to the created object (i.e., an address). Various notations are possible: [new Personne()], [new Personne], [new personne]. The class name is case-insensitive;
  • lines 41–43: The three attributes required by the [identite] method are created in the [$p] object by the [__set] method;
  • line 45: the [identite] method of the [Personne] class is applied to the [$p] object. In the code for the [identite] method, [$this] references the same object as [$p].

This technique has its uses (configuration objects, encapsulation of data read from a file), but it is not the standard way to write a class. In a regular class, you declare its attributes.

docs.title: 5.4. The Person class with declared attributes
docs.text:
The script [classes-03.php] is as follows:

<?php

// strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

class Personne
{
     // class attributes, public and typed
    public string $prenom;
    public string $nom;
    public int $age;

     // method
    public function identite(): string
    {
        return "[$this->prenom,$this->nom,$this->age]";
    }
}

// test
// Attributes are public
$p = new Personne();
$p->prenom = "Paul";
$p->nom = "Langevin";
$p->age = 48;
// method call
print "personne=" . $p->identite() . "\n";
// A typed attribute accepts only values of its type
try {
    $p->age = "quarante-huit";
} catch (\TypeError $e) {
    print "Erreur 1 : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// An uninitialized typed attribute cannot be read
$p2 = new Personne();
try {
    print "personne=" . $p2->identite() . "\n";
} catch (\Error $e) {
    print "Erreur 2 : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// end
exit;

Results:

> php classes-03.php
personne=[Paul,Langevin,48]
Erreur 1 : Cannot assign string to property Personne::$age of type int
Erreur 2 : Typed property Personne::$prenom must not be accessed before initialization

Comments

  • Lines 9–11: The class attributes are explicitly declared. The keyword [public] means that they are accessible from outside the class. In PHP 7, the course used the keyword [var], inherited from PHP 4, which is a synonym for [public] and is no longer used today;
  • Each attribute is preceded by its type: [string] for first name and last name, [int] for age. These are typed attributes, which were introduced with PHP 7.4. The possible types are those of function parameters: [int], [float], [string], [bool], [array], a class or interface name, a nullable type [?string], a union type [int|float]...;
  • line 30: a typed attribute accepts only values of its type. Any other value causes an error [TypeError] (line 3 of the results);
  • lines 35–37: A typed attribute without a default value is in the “uninitialized” state until a value is assigned to it. Reading it causes an error (line 4 of the results). Untyped attributes, on the other hand, have a default value of [null]. This is one reason to initialize all of an object’s attributes as soon as it is created: that is the role of the constructor.

docs.title: 5.5. The Person class with a constructor
docs.text:
The previous examples showed exotic classes such as those found in PHP 4. It is not recommended to follow these examples. We now present a [Personne] [classes-04.php] class that follows standard best practices, as found in all object-oriented languages (Java, C#, etc.):

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

class Personne
{
     // Class attributes
    private string $prenom;
    private string $nom;
    private int $age;

     // getters and setters
    public function getPrenom(): string
    {
        return $this->prenom;
    }

    public function getNom(): string
    {
        return $this->nom;
    }

    public function getAge(): int
    {
        return $this->age;
    }

    public function setPrenom(string $prenom): void
    {
        $this->prenom = $prenom;
    }

    public function setNom(string $nom): void
    {
        $this->nom = $nom;
    }

    public function setAge(int $age): void
    {
        $this->age = $age;
    }

     // constructor
    public function __construct(string $prenom, string $nom, int $age)
    {
         // We use the set methods
        $this->setPrenom($prenom);
        $this->setNom($nom);
        $this->setAge($age);
    }

     // toString method
    public function __toString(): string
    {
        return "[$this->prenom,$this->nom,$this->age]";
    }
}

// test
// creating a Person object
$p = new Personne("Paul", "Langevin", 48);
// identity of this person
print "personne=$p\n";
// changing the age
$p->setAge(14);
// person's identity
print "personne=$p\n";
// A class with a method [__toString] implements the interface [Stringable]
print "Stringable : " . var_export($p instanceof \Stringable, true) . "\n";
// A private attribute is not accessible from outside the class
try {
    print $p->nom;
} catch (\Error $e) {
    print "Erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// end
exit;

Results:

> php classes-04.php
personne=[Paul,Langevin,48]
personne=[Paul,Langevin,14]
Stringable : true
Erreur : Cannot access private property Personne::$nom

Comments

  • Line 4: We specify that the declared types of the function parameters must be strictly adhered to. Without this declaration, PHP would attempt to convert a value of the wrong type (for example, the string ["48"] to an integer [48]);
  • Lines 6–60: the class [Personne];
  • Lines 9–11: the class’s private attributes ([private]). These attributes are visible only within the class. Other keywords that can be used are:
    • [public]: makes the attribute a public attribute visible from outside the class;
    • [protected]: makes the attribute a protected attribute visible from within the class and its derived classes;
  • Because the attributes are private, they cannot be accessed from outside the class. Therefore, we cannot write [$p->nom = "Landru"]: we are outside the class [Personne], and the attribute [nom] is private. Lines 72–74 verify this: attempting to read [$p->nom] results in an error (line 5 of the results). To initialize the private attributes of the [$p] object, there are two ways:
    • use the public methods [set] and [get] (the names of these methods can be anything) in lines 14–39. In this case, we write: [$p->setNom("Landru")];
    • use the constructor in lines 45–50. You would then write: [$p = new Personne("Michel", "Landru", 44)]. This syntax automatically calls the method of the [Personne] class named [__construct];
  • line 64: This line displays the person [$p] as a string. To do this, the method of the [Personne] class called [__toString] (line 54) is used;
  • line 70: Starting with PHP 8.0, any class that defines a method named [__toString] automatically implements the predefined interface [Stringable] (we will cover interfaces in the next chapter). The [instanceof] operator checks whether an object is of a given type. A function can thus declare a parameter of type [string|Stringable]: it then accepts a string or any object that can be converted to a string;
  • all methods of the class have been prefixed with the keyword [public], which indicates that the method is visible outside the class. The other keywords that can be used are, as with attributes and with the same meaning, [private] and [protected]. Without an explicit visibility keyword, the method is implicitly [public]. The PSR-12 style guidelines, which the scripts in this course follow, require that visibility always be specified explicitly.

docs.title: 5.6. Promotion of Constructor Parameters
docs.text:
The previous class is verbose: each attribute is named four times (declaration, constructor parameter, assignment in the constructor, getter). Since PHP 8.0, constructor parameter promotion allows you to declare and initialize an attribute directly in the list of constructor parameters. The script [classes-22.php] demonstrates this:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

class Personne
{
     // constructor with parameter promotion:
     // Each parameter preceded by a visibility modifier becomes a class attribute
    public function __construct(
        private string $prenom,
        private string $nom,
        private int $age = 0,
    ) {
         // nothing else to do: the attributes are already initialized
    }

     // getters
    public function getPrenom(): string
    {
        return $this->prenom;
    }

    public function getNom(): string
    {
        return $this->nom;
    }

    public function getAge(): int
    {
        return $this->age;
    }

     // setter
    public function setAge(int $age): void
    {
        $this->age = $age;
    }

     // method toString
    public function __toString(): string
    {
        return "[$this->prenom,$this->nom,$this->age]";
    }
}

// test
// standard call: arguments are passed in the order of the parameters
$p1 = new Personne("Paul", "Langevin", 48);
print "p1=$p1\n";
// named arguments: the order no longer matters
$p2 = new Personne(nom: "Lefur", age: 70, prenom: "Sylvie");
print "p2=$p2\n";
// The parameter [age] has a default value: it can be omitted
$p3 = new Personne(prenom: "Steve", nom: "Boer");
print "p3=$p3\n";
// promoted attributes are true attributes
var_dump($p3);
// end
exit;

Results:

> php classes-22.php
p1=[Paul,Langevin,48]
p2=[Sylvie,Lefur,70]
p3=[Steve,Boer,0]
object(Personne)#3 (3) {
  ["prenom":"Personne":private]=>
  string(5) "Steve"
  ["nom":"Personne":private]=>
  string(4) "Boer"
  ["age":"Personne":private]=>
  int(0)
}

Comments

  • Lines 10–14: Each constructor parameter preceded by a visibility keyword ([private], [protected], [public]) is “promoted”: PHP declares an attribute with the same name and type and assigns it the value of the parameter. These three lines replace the attribute declarations and assignments from the previous class;
  • line 13: A promoted parameter can have a default value. The comma after the last parameter has been allowed since PHP 8.0; it makes it easier to add a parameter later;
  • line 15: The body of the constructor can contain code (such as validations). Here, there is nothing to do;
  • line 52: Named arguments (PHP 8.0) allow arguments to be passed in any order by referring to them by the parameter name. This makes the code more readable, especially when a function has many parameters;
  • line 55: the parameter [age] is omitted; it takes its default value;
  • line 58: the function [var_dump] shows that the promoted attributes are true private attributes of the class (lines 5–12 of the results).

docs.title: 5.7. The Person Class with Validity Checks in the Constructor
docs.text:
A class’s constructor is the appropriate place to verify that the object’s initialization values are correct. However, an object can also be initialized using its [set] methods or equivalents. To avoid duplicating the same checks in two different places, these checks can be placed in the [set] methods. If an object’s initialization value turns out to be incorrect, an exception will be thrown. Here is an example.

First, move the definition of the [Personne] class to its own file, [Personne.php]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Exemples;

// Person class
class Personne
{
     // Class attributes
    private string $prenom;
    private string $nom;
    private int $age;

     // getters and setters
    public function getPrenom(): string
    {
        return $this->prenom;
    }

    public function getNom(): string
    {
        return $this->nom;
    }

    public function getAge(): int
    {
        return $this->age;
    }

    public function setPrenom(string $prénom): void
    {
         // The first name must not be empty
        $prénom = trim($prénom);
        if ($prénom === "") {
            throw new \Exception("Le prénom doit être non vide");
        }
        $this->prenom = $prénom;
    }

    public function setNom(string $nom): void
    {
         // The last name must not be empty
        $nom = trim($nom);
        if ($nom === "") {
            throw new \Exception("Le nom doit être non vide");
        }
        $this->nom = $nom;
    }

    public function setAge(int $âge): void
    {
         // The age must be valid
        if ($âge < 0) {
            throw new \Exception("L'âge doit être un entier positif ou nul");
        }
        $this->age = $âge;
    }

     // constructor
    public function __construct(string $prenom, string $nom, int $age)
    {
         // We use the set methods
        $this->setPrenom($prenom);
        $this->setNom($nom);
        $this->setAge($age);
    }

     // method acting as a second constructor
    public function initWithPersonne(Personne $p): void
    {
         // initializes the current object with a person named $p
        $this->__construct($p->prenom, $p->nom, $p->age);
    }

     // static construction method (named constructor)
    public static function fromPersonne(Personne $p): self
    {
         // creates a new person as a copy of the person $p
        return new self($p->prenom, $p->nom, $p->age);
    }

     // method toString
    public function __toString(): string
    {
        return "[$this->prenom,$this->nom,$this->age]";
    }
}

Comments

  • Line 4: Specifies that the types of function parameters must be respected as declared;
  • Line 7: Defines a namespace. The full (or qualified) name of the class [Personne] is therefore [\Exemples\Personne]. Note the character [\] at the beginning of the qualified name: this results in an absolute qualified name. If this character is absent, the name is a relative qualified name (relative to the current namespace). Thus, if two classes, A and B, belong to the same namespace E, in the code for class A, class B can be accessed using the relative notation B. If class A is part of the namespace E1 and class B is part of the namespace E2, then in class A’s code, class B can be accessed using the absolute notation [\E2\B]. Defining a class within a namespace is not mandatory but is considered best practice: two libraries can then each define a class named [Personne] without conflict;
  • namespaces often correspond to the file directory structure. Thus, class A in the namespace E1 is often located in a file named [E1/A.php]. This is the PSR-4 convention used by the [Composer] tool to automatically load classes, which we will use in later chapters. The [PHP Intelephense] extension of [VS Code] does not require this. Do not confuse the file tree with a namespace: the fully qualified name of a class uses a namespace and has nothing to do with the file tree of the PHP file containing the class. Here, the class [\Exemples\Personne] is in the file [scripts-console/classes/Personne.php];
  • lines 13–15: the class’s three private attributes;
  • lines 33–41: initialization of the [prenom] attribute and verification of the initialization value;
  • line 36: the function [trim($chaine)] removes the spaces at the beginning and end of [$chaine]. Thus, [trim(" abcd ")] is the string ["abcd"], and [trim(" ")] is the empty string. Note that a variable name may contain accented characters;
  • line 37: if the first name is empty, then an exception is thrown (line 38); otherwise, the first name is stored (line 40). To throw an exception, the predefined class [Exception] is used here. Here, we are required to use its absolute name, [\Exception]. If we use its relative name, [Exception], then this class will be searched for in the current namespace, c.-à-d, and in the namespace [Exemples] of the class [Personne]. Thus, the PHP interpreter will search for a class with the absolute name [\Exemples\Exception], which does not exist;
  • lines 63–69: the constructor uses the methods [set] to initialize the attributes: the validations are written only once;
  • The methods on lines 72 and 79 are described in the following paragraph.

The class [Personne] is used by the following script, [classes-05.php]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// includes the definition of the Person class
require_once __DIR__ . "/Personne.php";
// for demonstration purposes
print __DIR__ . "/Personne.php\n";

// qualified name of the Person class
use Exemples\Personne;

// test
// creation of a Person object
$p = new Personne("Paul", "Langevin", 48);
// identity of this person
print "Exemple1, personne=$p\n";
// creation of an incorrect Person object
try {
    $p = new Personne("xx", "yy", "zz");
} catch (\Exception $e1) {
    print "Exemple2, erreur : " . $e1->getMessage() . "\n";
} catch (\TypeError $e2) {
    print "Exemple2, erreur : " . $e2->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// creation of an incorrect Person object
try {
    $p = new Personne("", "yy", 10);
} catch (\Exception $e1) {
    print "Exemple3, erreur : " . $e1->getMessage() . "\n";
} catch (\TypeError $e2) {
    print "Exemple3, erreur : " . $e2->getMessage() . "\n";
}

// end
exit;

Results:

> php classes-05.php
.../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/Personne.php
Exemple1, personne=[Paul,Langevin,48]
Exemple2, erreur : Exemples\Personne::__construct(): Argument #3 ($age) must be of type int; a string was provided, called in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-05.php on line 21
Exemple3, erreur : Le prénom doit être non vide

Comments

  • Line 7: The script will use the [Personne] class. You must therefore tell the PHP interpreter where to find the definition of this class. This is the purpose of the [include fichier] and [require fichier] statements. The difference between the two statements is as follows: if the [include fichier] statement encounters errors while loading [fichier], a [E_WARNING]-level error is issued, butexecution continues, whereas [require], in the same situation, generates a fatal error and stops the script from running. Each of these two instructions has a variant: [include_once] and [require_once]. These two variants allow for handling cases where the same file is included multiple times. Consider, for example, a project consisting of several PHP scripts, some of which reference the [Personne] class. Executing these scripts would then cause the file [Personne.php] to be included multiple times, resulting in an error because a class cannot be defined twice. The solution is to use the [_once] variants, which ensure that the file is included only once in the project’s global script;
  • The constant [__DIR__] is a constant PHP that refers to the full name of the folder containing the script with the constant [__DIR__]. Line 9 displays it (line 2 of the results). On the reader’s machine, the result will be something like [C:\laragon\www\php8-oct-2026\scripts-console\classes/Personne.php]. In a file path, you can use either [/] or [\] interchangeably on Windows. Using [__DIR__] makes the script independent of the current folder at the time of execution;
  • Line 12: The script [classes-05.php] has no namespace. When the code uses the relative name [Personne], it is searched for in the root namespace [\] and will therefore not be found. There are two solutions to this problem:
    • use the full class name [\Exemples\Personne];
    • use the statement [use], which specifies that, in the code that follows, the name [Personne] refers to the class [\Exemples\Personne]. In a [use] statement, the name is always absolute: the initial [\] is unnecessary (this is the recommended notation). The statement is equivalent to [use Exemples\Personne as Personne;], which specifies that the alias [Personne] refers to the class [\Exemples\Personne];
  • the instruction [use] tells the interpreter that the class [Personne] is actually the class [\Exemples\Personne]. That said, where will the interpreter find the code for this class? The instruction [require_once] tells it. The two instructions have very different roles: [use] works on names, [require_once] loads a file;
  • line 16: a [Personne] object is created. The [__construct] method of the [Personne] class will be implicitly executed here;
  • line 18: displays the person [$p]. To be displayed, the value of the variable [$p] must be converted to a string. Implicitly, the method [Personne::__toString] is then executed. This method must therefore return a string;
  • we have seen that the constructor of the [Personne] class can throw a [\Exception] exception. This exception must therefore be handled. Consequently, the creation of a person should always be enclosed within a ***[try / catch] structure, as shown in lines 20–34. Here, we intentionally trigger an error by passing an age that is not an integer. In this specific case, the error is thrown by the PHP interpreter and not by the code in the [Personne] class. This is because the signature of the [Personne::__construct]* method is [__construct(string $prenom, string $nom, int $age)]. Therefore, the [age] parameter passed to the constructor must be of type integer. If this is not the case, the PHP interpreter throws an error of type [TypeError]. Furthermore, the methods [set] of the class [Personne]* throw an exception of type [\Exception]. Since the constructor that calls them does not have a [try / catch] structure, the exception is propagated up one level to the code that called the constructor, c.-à-d. the code in the [classes-05.php] script. Finally, the script [classes-05.php]* can receive two types of errors: [\Exception] or [\TypeError]. For this reason, the [try] structure has two [catch] clauses to handle the two types of errors separately. When the developer is certain that certain errors cannot occur, they will not use the corresponding [catch]** clauses. Here, they are used systematically solely for demonstration purposes;
  • Line 22: You can write either [Exception] or [\Exception]. The first version uses the relative class name, relative to the script’s namespace. Since the script has no namespace, its namespace is the root of the namespaces: [\]. Therefore, writing [Exception] here is equivalent to writing [\Exception]. It is preferable to use the absolute names of the predefined classes, such as PHP, in a script that does not have its own namespace. Thus, if you decide to assign a namespace to this script, using the absolute class names remains valid, whereas in the other case, changing the namespace will cause errors with the relative class names;
  • Line 23: When an exception occurs, the [Exception::getMessage] method retrieves the error message for the exception. The same applies to an error of type [TypeError]. In the [Personne::setPrenom] method, [throw new \Exception("Le prénom doit être non vide")] was written. This is the message retrieved by the [getMessage] method in Example 3 (line 5 of the results);
  • line 4 of the results: the error message for [TypeError]. Starting with PHP 8.0, it identifies the problematic parameter by its number and name: “Argument #3 ($age) must be of type int; string was provided.” The error messages in PHP 8 are more specific than those in PHP 7.

docs.title: 5.8. Adding a method that acts as a second constructor
docs.text:
In PHP, it is not possible to have multiple constructors with different parameters that would allow an object to be constructed in various ways. Therefore, methods can be used to act as constructors. The [Personne] class has two such methods:

    public function initWithPersonne(Personne $p): void
    {
         // initializes the current object with a person $p
        $this->__construct($p->prenom, $p->nom, $p->age);
    }

     // static constructor (named constructor)
    public static function fromPersonne(Personne $p): self
    {
         // creates a new person as a copy of the person $p
        return new self($p->prenom, $p->nom, $p->age);
    }

Comments

  • Lines 72–76: The [initWithPersonne] method allows the values of the attributes of another [Personne] object to be assigned to the current object. Here, it calls the constructor [__construct], but this is not required. It could initialize the attributes of the class [Personne] on its own. Note that a method of the [Personne] class has access to the private attributes of all [Personne] objects, not just those of [$this];
  • lines 79–83: The [fromPersonne] method is another way of doing this, which is more common today. It is a static method (keyword [static]): it does not apply to an object but to the class. It is called using the notation [Personne::fromPersonne($p)]. It creates a new object using [new self(...)]: the keyword [self] refers to the class in which the code is written, in this case [Personne]. The return type [self] indicates that the method returns an object of this class. Such a method is called a named constructor or factory method. We’ll come back to static methods a little later.

The new class [Personne] is used by the following script, [classes-06.php]:

<?php

// strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// inclusion of the Person class definition
require_once __DIR__ . "/Personne.php";
// Declaration of the qualified name of the Person class
use Exemples\Personne;

// test
// Creation of a Person object
try {
    $p = new Personne("Paul", "Langevin", 48);
} catch (\Exception $e) {
    print "erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
    exit;
}
// identity of this person
print "personne=$p\n";
// creation of a second Person
try {
    $p2 = new Personne("Laure", "Adeline", 67);
} catch (\Exception $e) {
    print "erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
    exit;
}
// initializing the first person with the values of the second
try {
    $p->initWithPersonne($p2);
} catch (\Exception $e) {
    print "erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
    exit;
}
// Verification
print "personne=$p\n";

// creation of a third person using the constructor named
$p3 = Personne::fromPersonne($p2);
print "personne=$p3\n";
// $p3 and $p2 are two different objects with the same values
print "même objet : " . var_export($p3 === $p2, true) . "\n";
print "mêmes valeurs : " . var_export($p3 == $p2, true) . "\n";
// end
exit;

Results:
