> php classes-06.php
personne=[Paul,Langevin,48]
personne=[Laure,Adeline,67]
personne=[Laure,Adeline,67]
même objet : false
mêmes valeurs : true

Comments

  • Line 17, line 26, line 33: It is common that, after an exception, you must stop the execution of a console script if the error encountered is unrecoverable. This is not the case in a web script: you do not stop the script’s execution but instead display an error page. If you are inside a function, the [exit] statement will not be used; instead, [return] will be used: the script’s execution is not halted ([exit]), but the function is exited ([return]) after an error has been set;
  • line 39: call to the named constructor;
  • line 42: the [===] operator applied to two objects evaluates to true if they are the same object (same address). [$p3] and [$p2] are two distinct objects (line 5 of the results);
  • line 43: the operator [==], when applied to two objects of the same class, evaluates to true if their attributes have the same values (line 6 of the results). The function [var_export] returns a PHP representation of its parameter, in this case [true] or [false].

docs.title: 5.9. Validity checks using property brackets (PHP 8.4)
docs.text:
The previous class, [Personne], protects its attributes by making them private and requiring external code to use the [get] and [set] methods. PHP 8.4 offers another solution: property hooks. A public attribute can be accompanied by a [set] hook—the code executed each time the attribute is written—and a [get] hook—the code executed each time the attribute is read. This preserves the simplicity of writing [$p->age = 49] while maintaining control over the values. This is demonstrated by the script [classes-23.php]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

class Personne
{
     // public attribute with a bracket [set]: validation occurs on every write
    public string $prenom {
        set(string $value) {
            $value = trim($value);
            if ($value === "") {
                throw new \InvalidArgumentException("Le prénom doit être non vide");
            }
            $this->prenom = $value;
        }
    }

    public string $nom {
        set(string $value) {
            $value = trim($value);
            if ($value === "") {
                throw new \InvalidArgumentException("Le nom doit être non vide");
            }
            $this->nom = $value;
        }
    }

     // Without an explicit parameter, the received value is called [$value]
    public int $age {
        set {
            if ($value < 0) {
                throw new \InvalidArgumentException("L'âge doit être un entier positif ou nul");
            }
            $this->age = $value;
        }
    }

     // virtual attribute: it has only one bracket [get] and occupies no space in the object
    public string $identite {
        get => "[$this->prenom,$this->nom,$this->age]";
    }

     // constructor: assignments are made via the brackets [set]
    public function __construct(string $prenom, string $nom, int $age)
    {
        $this->prenom = $prenom;
        $this->nom = $nom;
        $this->age = $age;
    }
}

// test
$p = new Personne(" Paul ", "Langevin", 48);
print "personne=$p->identite\n";
// The attributes are public: they are read and written directly
$p->age = 49;
print "âge=$p->age\n";
// but writing always goes through the bracket [set]
foreach (["prenom" => "  ", "age" => -4] as $attribut => $valeur) {
    try {
        $p->$attribut = $valeur;
    } catch (\InvalidArgumentException $e) {
        print "Erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
    }
}
// A virtual attribute without a bracket ([set]) cannot be written
try {
    $p->identite = "?";
} catch (\Error $e) {
    print "Erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// the object remains valid
print "personne=$p->identite\n";
var_dump($p);

Results:

> php classes-23.php
personne=[Paul,Langevin,48]
âge=49
Erreur : Le prénom doit être non vide
Erreur : L'âge doit être un entier positif ou nul
Erreur : Property Personne::$identite is read-only
personne=[Paul,Langevin,49]
object(Personne)#1 (3) {
  ["prenom"]=>
  string(4) "Paul"
  ["nom"]=>
  string(8) "Langevin"
  ["age"]=>
  int(49)
}

Comments

  • lines 9–17: The public attribute [prenom] is followed by a block enclosed in curly braces that contains its square brackets. Here, there is only one square bracket, [set];
  • line 10: The bracket [set] receives the value to be assigned to the attribute. It validates it using [trim], checks it, and throws an exception if it is incorrect;
  • line 15: Inside its brackets, [$this->prenom] specifies the memory location of the attribute: the value is stored there. Everywhere else, [$this->prenom] is passed through the brackets;
  • line 13: an exception of type [\InvalidArgumentException] is thrown; this is a predefined class derived from [\Exception] and more specific than it, signaling an invalid argument. We will cover the predefined exceptions of type PHP in the chapter on exceptions;
  • line 31: when the bracket [set] does not declare a parameter, the received value is available in the implicit variable [$value], and its type is that of the attribute;
  • Lines 40–42: An attribute that has only one hook, [get], and never references its own memory location is a virtual attribute: it is calculated on each read and occupies no space in the object. The notation [get => expression] is a shorthand for a bracket [get] that evaluates to the value of the expression;
  • lines 45–50: the constructor assigns the attributes; these assignments are performed via the brackets [set]. Validation is therefore performed during construction as well as during any subsequent modification, without using the methods [set];
  • line 54: the first name [" Paul "] is cleared by the hook [set];
  • line 57: the attribute [age] is modified directly, but via its hook [set];
  • Lines 60–66: An attempt is made to assign invalid values. The notation [$p->$attribut] uses the contents of the variable [$attribut] as the attribute name. The [set] hooks throw their exceptions (lines 4–5 of the results);
  • line 69: the virtual attribute [identite] does not have a hook [set]: it is read-only (line 6 of the results);
  • line 75: the object retained valid values. [var_dump] shows only three attributes: the virtual attribute [identite] does not exist in memory.

Property hooks have long existed in other languages (C#, Kotlin, Swift). They eliminate the need to write getters and setters “just in case”: you start with a simple public attribute and add a hook when validation becomes necessary, without changing the code that uses the class.

docs.title: 5.10. Asymmetric Visibility (PHP 8.4)
docs.text:
It’s often the case that a property needs to be readable by everyone but modifiable only by the class itself. In the past, we would have written a private property and a public getter. PHP 8.4 allows you to set different visibility levels for reading and writing a property: this is called asymmetric visibility. The script [classes-24.php] demonstrates this using a bank account:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

class CompteBancaire
{
     // Asymmetric visibility: public read, private write
    public private(set) float $solde = 0.0;

     // Parameter promotion also supports asymmetric visibility
    public function __construct(public private(set) string $titulaire)
    {
    }

     // Only methods of the class can modify the balance
    public function deposer(float $montant): void
    {
        if ($montant <= 0) {
            throw new \InvalidArgumentException("Le montant doit être positif");
        }
        $this->solde += $montant;
    }

    public function retirer(float $montant): void
    {
        if ($montant <= 0 || $montant > $this->solde) {
            throw new \InvalidArgumentException("Retrait de $montant impossible");
        }
        $this->solde -= $montant;
    }
}

// test
$compte = new CompteBancaire("Paul Langevin");
$compte->deposer(100);
$compte->retirer(30);
// Direct reading of attributes, without getters
print "{$compte->titulaire} : {$compte->solde} euros\n";
// Writing from outside the class is prohibited
try {
    $compte->solde = 1_000_000;
} catch (\Error $e) {
    print "Erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// the class maintains control over the validity of the balance
try {
    $compte->retirer(500);
} catch (\InvalidArgumentException $e) {
    print "Erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
print "{$compte->titulaire} : {$compte->solde} euros\n";

Results:

> php classes-24.php
Paul Langevin : 70 euros
Erreur : Cannot modify private(set) property CompteBancaire::$solde from global scope
Erreur : Retrait de 500 impossible
Paul Langevin : 70 euros

Comments

  • Line 9: The attribute [solde] is public for reading ([public]) and private for writing ([private(set)]). External code can read [$compte->solde], but only the class’s methods can modify it. You can also write [protected(set)]: in this case, derived classes can modify the attribute;
  • line 12: asymmetric visibility is also possible for a promoted parameter;
  • lines 17–25: The methods [deposer] and [retirer] are the only ways to modify the balance. They verify the validity of the operations;
  • line 39: attributes are read directly, without getters. The notation [{$expression}] inside a string enclosed in quotation marks allows for the insertion of an expression more complex than a simple variable;
  • line 42: Writing to the balance from outside the class causes an error (line 3 of the results). The character [_] can be used as a thousands separator in a literal number (PHP 7.4);
  • Line 48: The withdrawal is rejected by the [retirer] method (line 4 of the results). The balance has not changed (line 5).

docs.title: 5.11. Read-Only Attributes and Classes ([readonly])
docs.text:
An object whose state cannot change after it is created is called immutable. Immutable objects greatly simplify programming: they can be shared among multiple parts of the code without fear that any of those parts will modify them. PHP 8.1 introduced read-only attributes (keyword [readonly]): such an attribute can be initialized only once, from within the class. PHP 8.2 introduced read-only classes: all their attributes are then [readonly]. The script [classes-25.php] presents an immutable class [Personne]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// read-only class: all its attributes are [readonly]
final readonly class Personne
{
    public function __construct(
        public string $prenom,
        public string $nom,
        public int $age,
    ) {
        if ($age < 0) {
            throw new \InvalidArgumentException("L'âge doit être un entier positif ou nul");
        }
    }

     // "Modifying" an immutable object = creating a modified copy
    public function avecAge(int $age): static
    {
         // Clone with attribute modification (PHP 8.5)
        return clone($this, ["age" => $age]);
    }

    public function __toString(): string
    {
        return "[$this->prenom,$this->nom,$this->age]";
    }
}

// test
$p1 = new Personne("Paul", "Langevin", 48);
print "p1=$p1\n";
// An attribute [readonly] is initialized once and for all
try {
    $p1->age = 49;
} catch (\Error $e) {
    print "Erreur 1 : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// You also cannot add attributes to a [readonly] class
try {
    $p1->adresse = "Paris";
} catch (\Error $e) {
    print "Erreur 2 : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// A new person, a copy of the first one with a different age
$p2 = $p1->avecAge(49);
print "p1=$p1\n";
print "p2=$p2\n";

Results:

> php classes-25.php
p1=[Paul,Langevin,48]
Erreur 1 : Cannot modify readonly property Personne::$age
Erreur 2 : Cannot create dynamic property Personne::$adresse
p1=[Paul,Langevin,48]
p2=[Paul,Langevin,49]

Comments

  • line 7: the class is declared as [readonly]: its three promoted attributes are read-only. The keyword [final], which we will examine shortly, prevents the class from being subclassed;
  • Lines 10–12: The attributes are public: they can be read directly, without getters. They cannot be modified: a getter would serve no purpose;
  • line 14: The constructor checks the validity of the age. An immutable object must be valid upon construction since it will never change;
  • lines 20–24: “Modifying” an immutable object involves creating a modified copy of that object. This is what the [avecAge] method does. Its return type, [static] (PHP 8.0), means “an object of the class on which the method was called.” The difference from [self] only becomes apparent with derived classes: if a derived class inherits the method, the type [static] refers to the derived class;
  • Line 23: The [clone] operator creates a copy of the [$this] object. Starting with PHP 8.5, [clone] can be used as a function and accept, as its second parameter, an array of attributes to be modified in the copy (clone with). Prior to PHP 8.5, you had to use the "magic" method [__clone] or rebuild the object with [new];
  • line 37: Modifying a [readonly] attribute causes an error (line 3 of the results);
  • Line 43: A class [readonly] also does not accept dynamic attributes: this is an error, not a simple deprecation warning (line 4 of the results);
  • line 48: [$p2] is a new person; [$p1] has not changed (lines 5–6 of the results).

In the following chapters, we will often use [readonly] classes to represent data (tax data from the government, the results of a tax calculation, etc.).

docs.title: 5.12. An array of [Personne] objects
docs.text:
The following example, [classes-07.php], shows that arrays of objects are possible:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

require_once __DIR__ . "/Personne.php";
use Exemples\Personne;

// test
// creation of an array of Person objects
// To make the code easier to understand, we do not handle any potential exceptions
$groupe = [new Personne("Paul", "Langevin", 48), new Personne("Sylvie", "Lefur", 70)];

// identity of these people
for ($i = 0; $i < count($groupe); $i++) {
    print "groupe[$i]=$groupe[$i]\n";
}

// end
exit;

Results:

> php classes-07.php
groupe[0]=[Paul,Langevin,48]
groupe[1]=[Sylvie,Lefur,70]

Comments

  • line 12: creation of an array of 2 people;
  • line 15: iterating through the array;
  • Line 16: [$groupe[$i]] is an object of type [Personne]. The [Personne::__toString] method is used to display it.

docs.title: 5.13. Creating a class derived from the Person class
docs.text:
Create the following class, [Enseignant], in a file named [Enseignant.php]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Exemples;

// a class derived from Person
class Enseignant extends Personne
{
     // attribute: subject taught
    private string $discipline;

     // getters and setters
    public function getDiscipline(): string
    {
        return $this->discipline;
    }

    public function setDiscipline(string $discipline): void
    {
        $this->discipline = $discipline;
    }

     // manufacturer
    public function __construct(string $prénom, string $nom, int $âge, string $discipline)
    {
         // parent attributes
        parent::__construct($prénom, $nom, $âge);
         // other attributes
        $this->setDiscipline($discipline);
    }

     // override of the __toString method of the parent class
     #[\Override]
    public function __toString(): string
    {
        return "[" . parent::__toString() . ",$this->discipline]";
    }
}

Comments

  • line 7: The class [Enseignant] is also part of the [Exemples] namespace;
  • Line 10: The class [Enseignant] is derived ([extends]) from the class [Personne]. The derived class [Enseignant] inherits the attributes and methods of its parent class;
  • Line 13: The class [Enseignant] adds a new attribute, [discipline], that is unique to it;
  • line 27: the constructor of the [Enseignant] class takes 4 parameters:
    • 3 to initialize its parent class (first name, last name, age), line 30;
    • 1 for its own initialization (subject), line 32;
  • line 30: The derived class has access to the methods and constructors of its parent class via the keyword [parent::]. Here, the parameters (first name, last name, age) are passed to the parent class’s constructor;
  • line 36: [#[\Override]] is an attribute of PHP (PHP 8.3). An attribute, written as [#[] et []], is information associated with a class, a method, a parameter, etc., that PHP or other tools can use. This attribute declares that the following method overrides a method of the parent class. If this is not the case (e.g., a typo in the method name or a method that has been removed from the parent class), PHP reports a fatal error. We’ll see an example of this a little later;
  • lines 37–40: The [__toString] method of the derived class uses the [__toString] method of the parent class.

The class [Enseignant] is used by the following script, [classes-08.php]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// Inclusion of the definitions of both classes
require_once __DIR__ . "/Personne.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/Enseignant.php";
// Declaration of the two classes used
use Exemples\Personne;
use Exemples\Enseignant;

// test
// Creation of an array of Person objects and derived classes
// For the sake of simplicity in this example, exceptions are not handled
$groupe = [new Enseignant("Paul", "Langevin", 48, "anglais"), new Personne("Sylvie", "Lefur", 70)];

// identities of these people
for ($i = 0; $i < count($groupe); $i++) {
    print "groupe[$i]=$groupe[$i]\n";
}
// end
exit;

Results:

> php classes-08.php
groupe[0]=[[Paul,Langevin,48],anglais]
groupe[1]=[Sylvie,Lefur,70]

Comments

  • Lines 7–8: We need to tell the PHP interpreter where the two [Enseignant, Personne] classes are located. The order is important: the parent class [Personne] must be defined before the class [Enseignant] is defined;
  • lines 10–11: declaration of the full names of the two classes. This will allow us to refer to them in the code simply by their names, without the namespace prefix;
  • line 16: we create an array containing an object of type [Enseignant] and an object of type [Personne];
  • lines 19–21: display the elements of the array;
  • line 20: The [__toString] method of each [$groupe[$i]] element will be called. The [Personne] class has a [__toString] method. The [Enseignant] class has two: the one from its parent class and its own. One might wonder which one will be called. The execution shows that the one from the [Enseignant] class was called. This is always the case: when a method is called on an object, it is searched for in the following order: in the object’s class, in its parent class if it has one, then in the parent class of the parent class, and so on. The search stops as soon as the method is found.

docs.title: 5.14. Creating a Second Class Derived from the Person Class
docs.text:
The following example creates a class named [Etudiant] derived from the class [Personne], in the file [Etudiant.php]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Exemples;

// a second class derived from Person
class Etudiant extends Personne
{
     // attribute: education completed
    private string $formation;

     // getters and setters
    public function getFormation(): string
    {
        return $this->formation;
    }

    public function setFormation(string $formation): void
    {
        $this->formation = $formation;
    }

     // constructor
    public function __construct(string $prénom, string $nom, int $âge, string $formation)
    {
         // parent attributes
        parent::__construct($prénom, $nom, $âge);
         // other attributes
        $this->setFormation($formation);
    }

     // override of the __toString method of the parent class
     #[\Override]
    public function __toString(): string
    {
        return "[" . parent::__toString() . ",$this->formation]";
    }
}

This class is used by the following script, [classes-09.php]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// Inclusion and declaration of classes used by the script
require_once __DIR__ . "/Personne.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/Enseignant.php";
require_once __DIR__ . "/Etudiant.php";
use Exemples\{Personne, Enseignant, Etudiant};

// test
// Creating an array of Person objects and derived classes
// To make the example easier to understand, exceptions are not handled
$groupe = [
    new Enseignant("Paul", "Langevin", 48, "anglais"),
    new Personne("Sylvie", "Lefur", 70),
    new Etudiant("Steve", "Boer", 23, "iup2 qualité"),
];

// identities of these people
foreach ($groupe as $i => $personne) {
    print "groupe[$i]=$personne (" . $personne::class . ")\n";
}
// end
exit;

Results:

> php classes-09.php
groupe[0]=[[Paul,Langevin,48],anglais] (Exemples\Enseignant)
groupe[1]=[Sylvie,Lefur,70] (Exemples\Personne)
groupe[2]=[[Steve,Boer,23],iup2 qualité] (Exemples\Etudiant)

Comments

  • Line 10: A single [use] statement can declare multiple classes from the same namespace by enclosing them in curly braces;
  • Line 22: The array is iterated over using [foreach], which returns both the index [$i] and the element [$personne];
  • line 23: the notation [$objet::class] (PHP 8.0) returns the full name of the object’s class. It replaces the [get_class] function, which has been deprecated when used without parameters since PHP 8.3.

docs.title: 5.15. Relationship Between the Constructor of a Derived Class and That of the Parent Class
docs.text:
In some object-oriented languages, the constructor of a derived class automatically calls that of its parent class. The following code [classes-16.php] shows that with PHP this is not the case:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

class Classe1
{
     // constructor
    public function __construct()
    {
        print "constructeur de la classe Classe1\n";
    }
}

class Classe2 extends Classe1
{
     // constructor
    public function __construct()
    {
         // the parent class's constructor is not implicitly called
        print "constructeur de la classe Classe2\n";
    }
}

class Classe3 extends Classe1
{
     // constructor
    public function __construct()
    {
         // Explicit call to the parent class constructor
        parent::__construct();
         // Code specific to Class3
        print "constructeur de la classe Classe3\n";
    }
}

class Classe4 extends Classe1
{
     // No constructor: the parent class's constructor is used
}

// tests
print "test1---------\n";
new Classe2();
print "test2---------\n";
new Classe3();
print "test3---------\n";
new Classe4();

Results:

> php classes-16.php
test1---------
constructeur de la classe Classe2
test2---------
constructeur de la classe Classe1
constructeur de la classe Classe3
test3---------
constructeur de la classe Classe1

Comments

  • lines 15–23: The constructor of [Classe2] does not call that of its parent class; the parent class’s constructor is not executed (line 3 of the results);
  • line 31: the constructor of [Classe3] explicitly calls that of its parent class (lines 5–6 of the results);
  • lines 37–40: The class [Classe4] has no constructor. It therefore inherits the constructor from its parent class, which is executed (line 8 of the results).

docs.title: 5.16. Overriding a Method from the Parent Class
docs.text:
We have already seen that a method of the parent class can be overridden in a child class. Thus, the method [__toString] of the class [Personne] has been overridden in the child classes [Enseignant] and [Etudiant]. The script [classes-13.php] illustrates this concept once again:

<?php

// strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// main class
class Classe1
{
    public function f(): int
    {
        return 1;
    }

    public function g(): int
    {
        return 2;
    }
}

// derived class
class Classe2 extends Classe1
{
     // redefining the function f from the parent class
     #[\Override]
    public function f(): int
    {
        return parent::f() + 10;
    }
}

// code
$c2 = new Classe2();
print $c2->f() . "\n";
print $c2->g() . "\n";
$c1 = new Classe1();
print $c1->f() . "\n";

Results:

> php classes-13.php
11
2
1

Comments

  • lines 7–18: The class [Classe1] defines two methods, f and g;
  • lines 21–29: The class [Classe2] extends the class [Classe1] and redefines its method f. The attribute [#[\Override]] documents this redefinition;
  • line 32: creates a [$c2] object of type [Classe2];
  • line 33: calls the f method of the [$c2] object. Since this method exists in the [Classe2] class, it is executed. It, in turn, calls the f method of the parent class using the notation [parent::f()];
  • line 34: calls the g method of the [$c2] object. Since this method does not exist in the [Classe2] class, it is looked up in the parent class, where it is found and executed;
  • line 35: creates a [$c1] object of type [Classe1];
  • line 36: calls the f method of the [$c1] object. It is the f method of the [Classe1] class that is executed.

Now let’s look at the purpose of the [#[\Override]] attribute. In the [classes-10.php] script, the developer intended to redefine the f method but used the wrong name:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// main class
class Classe1
{
    public function f(): int
    {
        return 1;
    }
}

// derived class
class Classe2 extends Classe1
{
     // We think we’re redefining the f method of the parent class
     // but the name is incorrect: the attribute [Override] detects this
     #[\Override]
    public function F2(): int
    {
        return parent::f() + 10;
    }
}

// code
$c2 = new Classe2();
print $c2->f() . "\n";

Results:

> php classes-10.php

Fatal error: Classe2::F2() has #[\Override] attribute, but no matching parent method exists in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-10.php on line 21
Stack trace:
#0 {main}

Without the [#[\Override]] attribute, the [F2] method would simply be a new method of [Classe2], and the script would display [1] without flagging any anomalies: the error would go unnoticed. With the attribute, PHP rejects the class as soon as it is loaded (line 3 of the results). In the rest of this course, we will consistently use [#[\Override]] on redefined methods.

docs.title: 5.17. Passing an object as a function parameter
docs.text:
Let's consider the following [classes-14.php] script:

<?php

// strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// main class
class Classe1
{
    public function f(): int
    {
        return 1;
    }

    public function g(): int
    {
        return 2;
    }
}

// derived class
class Classe2 extends Classe1
{
     // The function f of the parent class is redefined
     #[\Override]
    public function f(): int
    {
        return parent::f() + 10;
    }
}

// The function parameter is of type Class1 or a derived class
function doSomething(Classe1 $c1): void
{
    print $c1->f() + $c1->g() . "\n";
}

// code
// an object of type Class2, derived from Class1, is created
$c2 = new Classe2();
// doSomething is called with an object of type Class2
doSomething($c2);
// An object of a different type is rejected
try {
    doSomething(new \stdClass());
} catch (\TypeError $e) {
    print "Erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}

Results:

> php classes-14.php
13
Erreur : doSomething(): Argument #1 ($c1) must be of type Class1; stdClass was provided and called in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-14.php on line 44

Comments

  • lines 7–18: the class [Classe1];
  • lines 21–29: a class [Classe2] derived from [Classe1];
  • line 32: a function that expects a parameter of type [Classe1]. When the expected type is a class, the actual parameter can be an object of the expected type or a derived type;
  • line 41: the function [doSomething] is called with a parameter of type [Classe2], even though the expected type is [Classe1]. This is accepted because [Classe2] is derived from [Classe1] (line 2 of the results);
  • line 44: an object of type [stdClass] is not of type [Classe1]: the call causes an error of type [TypeError] (line 3 of the results).

docs.title: 5.18. Abstract Classes
docs.text:
An abstract class is an incomplete class that cannot be instantiated. It must be derived from in order to be usable.

What is the purpose of an abstract class? Sometimes we have classes that share one or more methods but differ in other methods or attributes. In such cases, it is desirable to group everything they have in common into a parent class. For now, we don’t need an abstract class. But suppose the child classes differ only in one method, M: the method’s signature would be the same in all child classes, but its implementation would differ. To require the child classes to implement method M:

  • we will declare the signature of method M in the parent class. Since the parent class does not know how to implement it, we prefix the method with the keyword [abstract]: this means that the implementation of method M is deferred to the child classes;
  • because the parent class is not fully implemented, it is also declared abstract using the same keyword [abstract]. This means the class can no longer be instantiated. A child class must be created to define the implementation of method M so that the body of the parent class can be used.

Here is an example [classes-15.php]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// abstract base class
abstract class Classe1
{
     // Method known to all derived classes
    public function f(): int
    {
        return 1;
    }

     // abstract method g—to be defined by derived classes
    abstract public function g(): int;
}

// derived class
class Classe2 extends Classe1
{
     // The `g` method of the parent class must be defined
     #[\Override]
    public function g(): int
    {
        return parent::f() + 10;
    }
}

// derived class
class Classe3 extends Classe1
{
     // The g method of the parent class must be defined
     #[\Override]
    public function g(): int
    {
        return parent::f() + 20;
    }

     // The f method of the parent class can be redefined
     #[\Override]
    public function f(): int
    {
        return 2;
    }
}

// code
$c2 = new Classe2();
print $c2->f() . "\n";
print $c2->g() . "\n";
$c3 = new Classe3();
print $c3->f() . "\n";
print $c3->g() . "\n";
// An abstract class cannot be instantiated
try {
    new Classe1();
} catch (\Error $e) {
    print "Erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}

Results:

> php classes-15.php
1
11
2
21
Erreur : Cannot instantiate abstract class Classe1

Comments

  • lines 7–17: The class [Classe1] is abstract because it does not implement the g method on line 16. It must therefore be derived from another class to be usable;
  • lines 20–28: The class [Classe2] extends the class [Classe1] and defines the g method of its parent class. The attribute [#[\Override]] also applies to the implementation of an abstract method;
  • lines 31–46: The class [Classe3] extends the class [Classe1] and defines the method g of its parent class;
  • lines 40–44: The class [Classe3] also redefines the method f of its parent class;
  • lines 49–54: two objects of types [Classe2] and [Classe3] are created, and their methods f and g are called;
  • line 57: An abstract class cannot be instantiated; an error occurs (line 6 of the results).

docs.title: 5.19. Final Classes
docs.text:
A final class is a class that cannot be derived from. Consider the following script, [classes-11.php]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Exemples;

// non-derivable class
final class Classe1
{
}

// derived class - causes an error
class Classe2 extends Classe1
{
}

// code
new Classe2();

Results:

> php classes-11.php

Fatal error: Class Exemples\Classe2 cannot extend final class Exemples\Classe1 in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-11.php on line 15
Stack trace:
#0 {main}

Comments

  • line 10: the keyword [final] makes the class [Classe1] a final class that cannot be derived from;
  • line 15: the class [Classe2] extends the final class [Classe1], which is an error;
  • The error is reported as soon as the PHP interpreter loads the definition of the [Classe2] class: this is a fatal error that cannot be intercepted by a [try / catch]. The script is not executed.

Declaring a class as [final] is a best practice when it was not designed to be derived from; this prevents other developers from relying on the class's internal details.

docs.title: 5.20. Final Methods
docs.text:
A final method is a method that cannot be overridden by a subclass. Here is an example, [classes-12.php]:

<?php

// strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Exemples;

// main class
class Classe1
{
     // This method cannot be overridden in a derived class
    final public function f(): int
    {
        return 1;
    }
}

// derived class
class Classe2 extends Classe1
{
     // Redefinition prohibited—causes an error
    public function f(): int
    {
        return 2;
    }
}

// code
new Classe2();

Results:

> php classes-12.php

Fatal error: Cannot override final method Exemples\Classe1::f() in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-12.php on line 23
Stack trace:
#0 {main}

Comments

  • line 13: The method f of the class *[Classe1] is declared final using the keyword ***[final]**;
  • line 20: the class [Classe2] extends the class [Classe1];
  • line 23: The method f of the parent class *[Classe1]* is redefined. This causes a fatal error, which is reported as soon as the class *[Classe2]* is loaded.

docs.title: 5.21. Static Methods and Attributes
docs.text:
A static method is a method associated with the class in which it is defined, rather than with the class’s instance objects. Thus, if class C declares a static method M, to use it from outside the class, one would write:

  • [C::M] if you are outside the class;
  • [self::M] if you are inside the class.

Here is an example: [classes-17.php]:

<?php

// strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

class Classe1
{
     // static method
    public static function say(string $message): void
    {
        print "$message\n";
    }

     // static method using another static method of the class
    public static function sayTwice(string $message): void
    {
        self::say($message);
        self::say($message);
    }
}

// test -------------------
Classe1::say("hello");
Classe1::sayTwice("bonjour");
// syntax for first-class callables: [Classe1::say(...)] is a function
$dire = Classe1::say(...);
$dire("salut");
// that can be passed to another function
array_map($dire, ["un", "deux"]);

Results:

> php classes-17.php
hello
bonjour
bonjour
salut
un
deux

Comments

  • line 9: the method [say] is declared static using the keyword [static];
  • line 17: Inside the class, the static method [say] is called using the notation [self::say];
  • line 23: the static method [say] is called using the notation [Classe1::say];
  • line 26: first-class callable syntax (PHP 8.1): writing [(...)] in place of the arguments of a call does not make the call but returns the function itself, in the form of a [Closure] object. The variable [$dire] then contains a function that is called just like an ordinary function (line 27). The same syntax applies to functions ([strlen(...)]) and to object methods ([$p->identite(...)]);
  • line 29: such a function can be passed as an argument to another function. The function [array_map] applies the function [$dire] to each element of the array (lines 6–7 of the results).

Now let’s consider the following code, [classes-18.php]:

<?php

// strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

class Classe1
{
     // static attribute
    private static int $nbObjects = 0;

    public function __construct()
    {
        print "constructeur Classe1\n";
        self::$nbObjects++;
    }

     // static method
    public static function say(): void
    {
        print self::$nbObjects . " objets de type [Classe1] ont été construits\n";
    }
}

// test -------------------
new Classe1();
new Classe1();
Classe1::say();

Results:

> php classes-18.php
constructeur Classe1
constructeur Classe1
2 objets de type [Classe1] ont été construits

Comments

  • Line 9: A static attribute is declared to count the number of instances of the [Classe1] class that have been created. This is not an attribute that can belong to an instance of the class. In fact, if two objects, O1 and O2, are created, neither is aware of the other. Having a counter in the instance doesn’t make sense: when a new object is created, in which instance would the counter be incremented? A static attribute is a class attribute, not an instance attribute of the class;
  • lines 11–15: the constructor is where we count the created objects, since the creation of each new object triggers the execution of the constructor;
  • line 14: Note the notation [self::$nbObjects], which indicates that we are referring to a static attribute of the class in which the executed code resides;
  • lines 18–21: The static method [say] is responsible for displaying the number of objects created;
  • Lines 25–27: Two objects are created, and the object counter is displayed.

docs.title: 5.22. Visibility Between Parent and Child Classes
docs.text:
Let’s examine the following script, [classes-19.php]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

class SomeParent
{
     // attribute
    private int $attributeOfParent = 4;

     // method
    public function doTest(): void
    {
         // Who calls it?
        print "parent :\n";
        var_dump($this);
         // parent view
        print "parent : attributeOfParent={$this->attributeOfParent}\n";
        print "parent : attributeOfChild={$this->attributeOfChild}\n";
    }
}

class SomeChild extends SomeParent
{
     // attribute
    private int $attributeOfChild = 14;

     // method
     #[\Override]
    public function doTest(): void
    {
         // child view
        print "child : attributeOfParent={$this->attributeOfParent}\n";
        print "child : attributeOfChild={$this->attributeOfChild}\n";
         // parent
        parent::doTest();
    }
}

// main script
print "---------------------------test1\n";
(new SomeParent())->doTest();
print "---------------------------test2\n";
(new SomeChild())->doTest();

Comments

  • Lines 6–21: the class [SomeParent];
  • Lines 23–38: the child class [SomeChild]. We can see that it extends the class [SomeParent];
  • line 9: the class [SomeParent] has only one attribute;
  • Lines 12–20: The [SomeParent::doTest] method is designed to display two attributes:
    • [$attributeOfParent], which belongs to the class [SomeParent];
    • [$attributeOfChild], which belongs to the class [SomeChild];
  • Lines 15–16: The caller’s identity is displayed; the method will be called in two different ways:
    • from the parent class [SomeParent];
    • from the child class [SomeChild];
  • lines 18–19: display the two attributes;
  • line 26: the class [SomeChild] has only one attribute;
  • line 30: the [SomeChild::doTest] method is designed to display two attributes:
    • [$attributeOfParent], which belongs to the class [SomeParent];
    • [$attributeOfChild], which belongs to the class [SomeChild];
  • Lines 33–34: display of the two attributes;
  • line 36: calls the [doTest] method of the parent class, which in turn displays both attributes;
  • line 42: the method [SomeParent::doTest] is called;
  • line 44: the [SomeChild::doTest] method is called.

In the first test, the visibility of both attributes is [private]. We can therefore expect that the child class will not see the attribute of its parent class. That attribute would need to have at least the visibility [protected]. But what about the child class’s attribute? Is it visible in the parent class?

Here are the results of this first test:

> php classes-19.php
---------------------------test1
parent :
object(SomeParent)#1 (1) {
  ["attributeOfParent":"SomeParent":private]=>
  int(4)
}
parent : attributeOfParent=4

Warning: Undefined property: SomeParent::$attributeOfChild in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-19.php on line 19
parent : attributeOfChild=
---------------------------test2

Warning: Undefined property: SomeChild::$attributeOfParent in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-19.php on line 33
child : attributeOfParent=
child : attributeOfChild=14
parent :
object(SomeChild)#1 (2) {
  ["attributeOfParent":"SomeParent":private]=>
  int(4)
  ["attributeOfChild":"SomeChild":private]=>
  int(14)
}
parent : attributeOfParent=4

Fatal error: Uncaught Error: Cannot access private property SomeChild::$attributeOfChild in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-19.php:19
Stack trace:
#0 .../php8-Oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-19.php(36): SomeParent->doTest()
#1 .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-19.php(44): SomeChild->doTest()
#2 {main}
  thrown in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-19.php on line 19

Comments

  • lines 2–11: results of the first test where the [SomeParent::doTest] method is called;
  • lines 3–7: we can see that the object calling the method is of type [SomeParent];
  • line 8: the [$attributeOfParent] attribute is displayed;
  • lines 10–11: We can see that the attribute [SomeParent::$attributeOfChild] does not exist. Therefore, it is not displayed. In PHP 8, reading a nonexistent attribute triggers a [Warning]-level warning (it was a simple [Notice] in PHP 7);
  • lines 12–31: results of the second test, in which the [SomeChild::doTest] method is called;
  • lines 14–15: We can see that the attribute [SomeChild::$attributeOfParent] does not exist. Therefore, it is not displayed. This is normal: the attribute [SomeParent::$attributeOfParent] is [private] and is therefore not recognized in the child class;
  • line 16: the attribute [$attributeOfChild] is displayed;
  • Lines 17–31: We are in the [SomeParent::doTest] method called by the child class;
  • lines 18–23: we see that [$this] is of type [SomeChild] with two private attributes;
  • line 24: Surprisingly, [$this]—which is of type [SomeChild]—can see the private attribute of its parent, [$attributeOfParent];
  • Lines 26–31: Equally surprising, [$this], which is of type [SomeChild], cannot access its attribute [$attributeOfChild]: attempting to access it causes a fatal error.

This result is very surprising: although lines 18–23 indicate that [$this] is of type [SomeChild], this [$this] inside the [SomeParent::doTest] method behaves as if it were an instance of the [SomeParent] class rather than the [SomeChild] class. In fact, visibility is checked relative to the class in which the code is written (here, [SomeParent]) and not relative to the object’s class.

Let’s run a new test with the script [classes-20.php]. The attribute [$attributeOfParent] now has visibility [protected]:

<?php

// strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

class SomeParent
{
     // attribute
    protected int $attributeOfParent = 4;

     // method
    public function doTest(): void
    {
         // Who calls it?
        print "parent :\n";
        var_dump($this);
         // parent view
        print "parent : attributeOfParent={$this->attributeOfParent}\n";
        print "parent : attributeOfChild={$this->attributeOfChild}\n";
    }
}

class SomeChild extends SomeParent
{
     // attribute
    private int $attributeOfChild = 14;

     // method
     #[\Override]
    public function doTest(): void
    {
         // child view
        print "child : attributeOfParent={$this->attributeOfParent}\n";
        print "child : attributeOfChild={$this->attributeOfChild}\n";
         // parent
        parent::doTest();
    }
}

// main script
print "---------------------------test1\n";
(new SomeParent())->doTest();
print "---------------------------test2\n";
(new SomeChild())->doTest();

Results:

> php classes-20.php
---------------------------test1
parent :
object(SomeParent)#1 (1) {
  ["attributeOfParent":protected]=>
  int(4)
}
parent : attributeOfParent=4

Warning: Undefined property: SomeParent::$attributeOfChild in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-20.php on line 19
parent : attributeOfChild=
---------------------------test2
child : attributeOfParent=4
child : attributeOfChild=14
parent :
object(SomeChild)#1 (2) {
  ["attributeOfParent":protected]=>
  int(4)
  ["attributeOfChild":"SomeChild":private]=>
  int(14)
}
parent : attributeOfParent=4

Fatal error: Uncaught Error: Cannot access private property SomeChild::$attributeOfChild in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-20.php:19
Stack trace:
#0 .../php8-Oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-20.php(36): SomeParent->doTest()
#1 .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-20.php(44): SomeChild->doTest()
#2 {main}
  thrown in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-20.php on line 19

Comments

  • Line 13: The class [SomeChild] can now see the attribute of its parent, [$attributeOfParent]. This is normal since the parent now has a scope of [protected];
  • In the [SomeParent::doTest] method, the [$this] object is of type [SomeChild] (lines 16–21). It can see the attribute of its parent, [$attributeOfParent] (line 22), but still cannot see its own private attribute, [$attributeOfChild] (lines 24–29).

In the third attempt, [classes-21.php], the attribute [$attributeOfChild] also has a scope of [protected]:

<?php

// strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

class SomeParent
{
     // attribute
    protected int $attributeOfParent = 4;

     // method
    public function doTest(): void
    {
         // Who calls it?
        print "parent :\n";
        var_dump($this);
         // parent view
        print "parent : attributeOfParent={$this->attributeOfParent}\n";
        print "parent : attributeOfChild={$this->attributeOfChild}\n";
    }
}

class SomeChild extends SomeParent
{
     // attribute
    protected int $attributeOfChild = 14;

     // method
     #[\Override]
    public function doTest(): void
    {
         // child view
        print "child : attributeOfParent={$this->attributeOfParent}\n";
        print "child : attributeOfChild={$this->attributeOfChild}\n";
         // parent
        parent::doTest();
    }
}

// main script
print "---------------------------test1\n";
(new SomeParent())->doTest();
print "---------------------------test2\n";
(new SomeChild())->doTest();

The results of the execution are as follows:

> php classes-21.php
---------------------------test1
parent :
object(SomeParent)#1 (1) {
  ["attributeOfParent":protected]=>
  int(4)
}
parent : attributeOfParent=4

Warning: Undefined property: SomeParent::$attributeOfChild in .../php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-21.php on line 19
parent : attributeOfChild=
---------------------------test2
child : attributeOfParent=4
child : attributeOfChild=14
parent :
object(SomeChild)#1 (2) {
  ["attributeOfParent":protected]=>
  int(4)
  ["attributeOfChild":protected]=>
  int(14)
}
parent : attributeOfParent=4
parent : attributeOfChild=14
  • Line 23: This time, inside the parent, [$this], which is of type [SomeChild] (lines 16–21), sees the protected attribute [$attributeOfChild] of its own class, [SomeChild].

What can we learn from these tests?

  • That the [$this] instance of a parent class, used in a method of the parent class, can see:
    • the attributes and methods of the parent class, regardless of their visibility;
    • does not see any of the attributes or methods of its child classes;
  • this is the expected behavior;
  • that the [$this] instance of a child class, used in a method of the child class, sees:
    • the attributes and methods of the parent class if they have at least [protected] visibility. Those with [private] visibility are not visible;
    • the attributes and methods of the child class, regardless of their visibility;
  • this is the expected behavior;
  • the [$this] instance of a child class, used in a method of the parent class, sees:
    • the attributes and methods of the parent class, regardless of their visibility;
    • the attributes and methods of its own class only if they have at least visibility [protected]. Those with visibility [private] are not visible;
  • This is unexpected behavior, which can be explained by the rule stated above: visibility depends on the class in which the code is written.

docs.title: 5.23. Enumerations (PHP 8.1)
docs.text:
A person has a gender: female or male. How can this information be represented? In PHP 7, a string (["F"], ["H"]) or class constants were used. At that time, there was nothing to prevent passing an incorrect value (["X"], ["femme"]...). PHP 8.1 introduced enumerations (keyword [enum]): an enumeration is a type that has only a finite number of possible values, called cases. We define the enumeration [Genre] in the file [Genre.php]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// namespace
namespace Exemples;

// a string-backed enumeration (backed enum)
enum Genre: string
{
    case Femme = "F";
    case Homme = "H";

     // An enumeration can have methods
    public function libelle(): string
    {
        return match ($this) {
            Genre::Femme => "Madame",
            Genre::Homme => "Monsieur",
        };
    }
}

Comments

  • Line 10: the enumeration [Genre]. The type [string] following its name makes it a “backed” enumeration: each case is associated with a scalar value, in this case a string. This value is useful for storing the case in a file or database. Without this type, it is a pure enumeration whose cases have no associated values;
  • lines 12–13: the two cases of the enumeration and their values;
  • lines 16–22: An enumeration can have methods (as well as constants and static methods). Within a method, ***[$this]*** refers to the case on which the method is called;
  • lines 18–21: the expression [match] (PHP 8.0) compares its parameter to the values of each branch using the operator [===] and returns the value of the first matching branch. If no branch matches, a [UnhandledMatchError] error is thrown. Here, all branches are defined.

The enumeration is used by the script [classes-26.php]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

require_once __DIR__ . "/Genre.php";
use Exemples\Genre;

// a person with a gender
final readonly class Personne
{
    public function __construct(
        public string $prenom,
        public string $nom,
        public Genre $genre,
    ) {
    }

    public function __toString(): string
    {
        return "{$this->genre->libelle()} $this->prenom $this->nom";
    }
}

// test
$p1 = new Personne("Paul", "Langevin", Genre::Homme);
$p2 = new Personne("Sylvie", "Lefur", Genre::Femme);
print "$p1\n$p2\n";
// An enumeration case has a name and a value
print "nom={$p2->genre->name}, valeur={$p2->genre->value}\n";
// Cases are unique objects: they are compared using ===
print "p1 est un homme : " . var_export($p1->genre === Genre::Homme, true) . "\n";
// the list of cases
foreach (Genre::cases() as $genre) {
    print "$genre->name ($genre->value) : {$genre->libelle()}\n";
}
// from a value (read from a file, a database, etc.) to a case
print "from('F') : " . Genre::from("F")->name . "\n";
print "tryFrom('X') : " . var_export(Genre::tryFrom("X"), true) . "\n";
try {
    Genre::from("X");
} catch (\ValueError $e) {
    print "Erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// The type [Genre] accepts only cases from the enumeration
try {
    new Personne("Steve", "Boer", "H");
} catch (\TypeError $e) {
    print "Erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}

Results:

> php classes-26.php
Monsieur Paul Langevin
Madame Sylvie Lefur
nom=Femme, valeur=F
p1 est un homme : true
Femme (F) : Madame
Homme (H) : Monsieur
from('F') : Femme
tryFrom('X') : NULL
Erreur : "X" is not a valid backing value for enum Exemples\Genre
Erreur : Personne::__construct(): Argument #3 ($genre) must be of type Examples\Genre, string given, called in .../php8-Oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/classes-26.php on line 47

Comments

  • line 15: the attribute [genre] of class [Personne] is of type [Genre];
  • line 21: call to the [libelle] method of the instance stored in the [genre] attribute;
  • line 26: a case is denoted by the notation [Genre::Homme];
  • line 30: each case has an attribute [name], its name, and for a backed enumeration, an attribute [value], its value (line 4 of the results);
  • line 32: each case is a unique object: cases are compared using the operator [===];
  • line 34: the static method [cases] returns the list of cases in the enumeration (lines 6–7 of the results);
  • line 38: the static method [from] returns the case associated with a value. This is the reverse process of [value]: ["F"] is read from a database, and the case [Genre::Femme] is obtained;
  • line 39: the method [tryFrom] returns [null] if the value does not match any case;
  • line 41: the method [from], on the other hand, throws an error [ValueError] (line 10 of the results);
  • line 47: the type [Genre] accepts only the enum cases, not their values: ["H"] is rejected (line 11 of the results). This is the whole point of enumerations: an incorrect value is detected immediately.

docs.title: 5.24. jSON Encoding of a Class
docs.text:
In a class, the [__toString] method is often present: it is supposed to return a string representing the object that calls it. It may be tempting to make this string a jSON string. We’ll explore this approach now. The scripts are in the [scripts-console/classes/json] folder:

php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/classes/json
├── json-01.php
├── json-02.php
├── json-03.php
├── json-04.php
├── Personne.php
├── Personne2.php
├── Personne3.php
└── Personne4.php

We will use the following [Personne] class:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

class Personne
{
     // attributes
    private ?string $nom = null;
    private ?string $prénom = null;
    private ?int $âge = null;
    private ?array $enfants = null;

     // global setter
    public function setFromArray(array $arrayOfAttributes): static
    {
         // initialization of certain class attributes
        foreach ($arrayOfAttributes as $attribute => $value) {
             // Undeclared class attributes are rejected
            if (!property_exists($this, $attribute)) {
                throw new \InvalidArgumentException("Attribut [$attribute] inconnu");
            }
            $this->$attribute = $value;
        }
         // returns the object
        return $this;
    }

     // getters
    public function getNom(): ?string
    {
        return $this->nom;
    }

    public function getPrénom(): ?string
    {
        return $this->prénom;
    }

    public function getÂge(): ?int
    {
        return $this->âge;
    }

    public function getEnfants(): ?array
    {
        return $this->enfants;
    }


     // __toString
    public function __toString(): string
    {
         // the object is identified
        var_dump($this);
         // retrieve its attributes
        $attributes = \get_object_vars($this);
        var_dump($attributes);
         // return the string jSON containing the attributes
        return \json_encode($attributes, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE);
    }
}

Comments

  • lines 9–12: the four attributes of the class. They are nullable types ([?string] means either [string] or [null]) and are initially set to [null];
  • lines 30–45: the getters that allow you to retrieve the values of these attributes;
  • lines 15–27: a global setter that initializes the attributes from an associative array ***[$arrayOfAttributes],*** whose keys match the names of the class’s attributes;
  • line 20: the function [property_exists] verifies that the attribute is declared in the class. Without this verification, an unknown key would create a dynamic attribute, which has been deprecated since PHP 8.2;
  • Line 23: The notation [$this->$attribute] refers to the attribute whose name is the value of the variable [$attribute];
  • line 15: The method returns the current object [$this]. Its return type is [static]: “an object of the class on which the method was called.” This allows for chained calls: [(new Personne())->setFromArray([...])];
  • Lines 52–61: the [__toString] method of the class;
  • line 57: the function PHP [get_object_vars] retrieves the values of the object’s attributes in the form of an associative array [['nom'=>'nom1', 'prénom'=>'prénom1', 'âge'=>âge1, 'enfants'=>[...]]]. When called from within the class, it also returns the private attributes;
  • line 60: the string jSON from this array of attributes is returned. The option [JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE] specifies that accented characters should not be converted to sequences [\u00e9].

Let’s examine the script [json-01.php], which uses the class [Personne]:

<?php

// strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// Person class
require_once __DIR__ . "/Personne.php";

// instantiation of the parent
$père = new Personne();
// initialization of the parent
$père->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Dieudonné",
    "âge" => 58,
]);
// instantiation and initialization of child1
$enfant1 = (new Personne())->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Sylvain",
    "âge" => 17,
]);
// instantiation and initialization of child2
$enfant2 = (new Personne())->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Géraldine",
    "âge" => 12,
]);
// initialization of the parent's children
$père->setFromArray([
    "enfants" => [$enfant1, $enfant2],
]);

// displaying the parent's elements
$enfant1 = $père->getEnfants()[0];
$enfant2 = $père->getEnfants()[1];
print "------------------------enfant1\n";
print "enfant1=$enfant1\n";
print "------------------------enfant2\n";
print "enfant2=$enfant2\n";
print "------------------------père\n";
print "père=$père\n";

Comments

  • lines 10–16: an object of type [Personne] [$père] is initialized using the [Personne::setFromArray] method;
  • lines 18–22: an object [Personne] [$enfant1] is initialized in the same way;
  • lines 24–28: initialize a [Personne] [$enfant2] object;
  • line 31: the parent’s [enfants] attribute is initialized with an array containing the two children;
  • lines 35–36: retrieve the parent’s two children;
  • line 38: the [print] operation attempts to convert the [$enfant1] object into a string. To do this, it uses the [__toString] method of the object. We therefore expect to see the object’s string jSON;
  • line 42: we do the same with the parent.

The results are as follows:

> php json-01.php
------------------------enfant1
object(Personne)#2 (4) {
  ["nom":"Personne":private]=>
  string(11) "Bertholomé"
  ["prénom":"Personne":private]=>
  string(7) "Sylvain"
  ["âge":"Personne":private]=>
  int(17)
  ["enfants":"Personne":private]=>
  NULL
}
array(4) {
  ["nom"]=>
  string(11) "Bertholomé"
  ["prénom"]=>
  string(7) "Sylvain"
  ["âge"]=>
  int(17)
  ["enfants"]=>
  NULL
}
enfant1={"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Sylvain","âge":17,"enfants":null}
------------------------enfant2
object(Personne)#3 (4) {
  ["nom":"Personne":private]=>
  string(11) "Bertholomé"
  ["prénom":"Personne":private]=>
  string(10) "Géraldine"
  ["âge":"Personne":private]=>
  int(12)
  ["enfants":"Personne":private]=>
  NULL
}
array(4) {
  ["nom"]=>
  string(11) "Bertholomé"
  ["prénom"]=>
  string(10) "Géraldine"
  ["âge"]=>
  int(12)
  ["enfants"]=>
  NULL
}
enfant2={"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Géraldine","âge":12,"enfants":null}
------------------------père
object(Personne)#1 (4) {
  ["nom":"Personne":private]=>
  string(11) "Bertholomé"
  ["prénom":"Personne":private]=>
  string(10) "Dieudonné"
  ["âge":"Personne":private]=>
  int(58)
  ["enfants":"Personne":private]=>
  array(2) {
    [0]=>
    object(Personne)#2 (4) {
      ["nom":"Personne":private]=>
      string(11) "Bertholomé"
      ["prénom":"Personne":private]=>
      string(7) "Sylvain"
      ["âge":"Personne":private]=>
      int(17)
      ["enfants":"Personne":private]=>
      NULL
    }
    [1]=>
    object(Personne)#3 (4) {
      ["nom":"Personne":private]=>
      string(11) "Bertholomé"
      ["prénom":"Personne":private]=>
      string(10) "Géraldine"
      ["âge":"Personne":private]=>
      int(12)
      ["enfants":"Personne":private]=>
      NULL
    }
  }
}
array(4) {
  ["nom"]=>
  string(11) "Bertholomé"
  ["prénom"]=>
  string(10) "Dieudonné"
  ["âge"]=>
  int(58)
  ["enfants"]=>
  array(2) {
    [0]=>
    object(Personne)#2 (4) {
      ["nom":"Personne":private]=>
      string(11) "Bertholomé"
      ["prénom":"Personne":private]=>
      string(7) "Sylvain"
      ["âge":"Personne":private]=>
      int(17)
      ["enfants":"Personne":private]=>
      NULL
    }
    [1]=>
    object(Personne)#3 (4) {
      ["nom":"Personne":private]=>
      string(11) "Bertholomé"
      ["prénom":"Personne":private]=>
      string(10) "Géraldine"
      ["âge":"Personne":private]=>
      int(12)
      ["enfants":"Personne":private]=>
      NULL
    }
  }
}
père={"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Dieudonné","âge":58,"enfants":[{},{}]}

Comments

  • lines 3–12: the object [$enfant1];
  • Lines 13–22: the attribute array for the object [$enfant1]. We have them all;
  • line 23: we have the string jSON from the object [$enfant1];
  • lines 24–45: same for the object [$enfant2];
  • lines 46–113: for the parent, it’s a little different since its attribute [enfants] is not [null], as it was for the children;
  • line 113: we see that in the father’s string jSON, the children are empty objects [{}];
  • Lines 80–112: We see that in the father’s attribute table, child 1 has remained an object, as has child 2. In short, the expression [\get_object_vars($this)]—where [$this] represents the father—is not recursive: if an attribute of the class [Personne] is itself an object, the expression [\get_object_vars($this)] does not attempt to retrieve its attribute array. However, the function [json_encode] encodes only the public attributes of an object: the children, all of whose attributes are private, become empty jSON objects.

We can improve this. We modify the [Personne] class to the following [Personne2] class:

     // __toString
    public function __toString(): string
    {
         // retrieve the object's attributes
        $attributes = $this->getAttributes();
        $enfants = $attributes["enfants"];
        if ($enfants !== null) {
            $attributes["enfants"] = [$enfants[0]->getAttributes(), $enfants[1]->getAttributes()];
        }
         // Return the string jSON containing the attributes
        return \json_encode($attributes, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE);
    }

    public function getAttributes(): array
    {
        return \get_object_vars($this);
    }
}

Comments

  • lines 64–67: The [getAttributes] method returns the attribute array of the object that calls it;
  • lines 52–62: the [__toString] method;
  • Line 55: We retrieve the object's attributes from the array [$attributes];
  • line 56: Based on the previous example, we know that [$attributes["enfants"]] is an array of two objects of type [Personne2];
  • Lines 57–59: The two objects are replaced by their array of attributes;
  • line 61: all that remains is to encode the constructed array of attributes as jSON.

The [json-02.php] script uses the [Personne2] class as follows:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// Person2 class
require_once __DIR__ . "/Personne2.php";

// instantiation of the parent
$père = new Personne2();
// initialization of the parent
$père->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Dieudonné",
    "âge" => 58,
]);
// instantiation and initialization of child1
$enfant1 = (new Personne2())->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Sylvain",
    "âge" => 17,
]);
// instantiation and initialization of child2
$enfant2 = (new Personne2())->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Géraldine",
    "âge" => 12,
]);
// initialization of the parent's children
$père->setFromArray([
    "enfants" => [$enfant1, $enfant2],
]);

// displaying the parent
print "------------------------père\n";
print "père=$père\n";

The script [json-02.php] is identical to the script [json-01.php], except that the class [Personne2] has replaced the class [Personne] and only the parent is displayed. The results of the execution are as follows:

> php json-02.php
------------------------père
père={"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Dieudonné","âge":58,"enfants":[{"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Sylvain","âge":17,"enfants":null},{"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Géraldine","âge":12,"enfants":null}]}

This time, the children are correctly displayed along with the parent.

The previous solution is unsatisfactory because the children may have children of their own. This brings us back to the previous problem. The class [Personne3] resolves this problem as follows:

     // __toString
    public function __toString(): string
    {
         // Generate the attribute string jSON
        $attributes = [];
        $this->getRecursiveAttributes($attributes, $this, []);
         // string jSON of attributes
        return \json_encode($attributes, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE);
    }

    public function getAttributes(): array
    {
        return \get_object_vars($this);
    }

    private function getRecursiveAttributes(array &$attributes, mixed $value, array $keys): void
    {
         // analysis of the value [$value]
         // $keys is an array [key1, key2, .., keyn]
         // $value=$attributesQZXW2HTMLBW2tleTFdZQXQZXW2HTMLBW2tleTJdZQX...[keyn]
         // If [$value] is an object, we use its method [getAttributes]
        if (\is_object($value)) {
             // attributes of the object [$value]
            $objectAttributes = $value->getAttributes();
             // Are there any keys?
            if ($keys) {
                 // In [$attributes], we will replace $value with the array of its attributes
                 // we need to construct the element $attributesQZXW2HTMLBW2tleTFdZQXQZXW2HTMLBW2tleTJdZQX...[keyn]
                 // where $keys is the array [key1, key2, .., keyn]
                 // we take the reference to the array [$attributes]
                $attribute = &$attributes;
                 // we scan the key table
                foreach ($keys as $key) {
                     // Get the reference for the attribute
                    $attribute = &$attribute[$key];
                }
                 // Here, $attribute and $attributesQZXW2HTMLBW2tleTFdZQXQZXW2HTMLBW2tleTJdZQX...[keyn] are identical
                 //—they share the same memory location
                 // the object [$value] is replaced by its attribute array:
                 // you must write $attributesQZXW2HTMLBW2tleTFdZQXQZXW2HTMLBW2tleTJdZQX...[keyn]=$objectAttributes
                 // which is equivalent to $attribute = $objectAttributes
                $attribute = $objectAttributes;
            } else {
                 // no keys—we are at the beginning of exploring the object
                 // $objectAttributes represents the first-level attributes of the class
                $attributes += $objectAttributes;
            }
             // perhaps there are still objects in [$objectAttributes]
             // we explore the attributes of [$objectAttributes]
            $this->getRecursiveAttributes($attributes, $objectAttributes, $keys);
        } elseif (\is_array($value)) {
             // We have an array—we analyze each of its elements
            foreach ($value as $key => $élément) {
                 // we add the current key to the array $keys
                $keys[] = $key;
                 // we parse $élément
                $this->getRecursiveAttributes($attributes, $élément, $keys);
                 // we remove the key that was just parsed from the array $keys
                \array_pop($keys);
            }
        }
    }
}

Comments

  • line 56: this time, the method [__toString] retrieves the attributes of its class and requires that this be done recursively: if an attribute is an object or an array of objects, then each object must be replaced by its array of attributes in the class’s final array of attributes;
  • Lines 66–112: The [getRecursiveAttributes] method performs this task. We have commented out its code. Writing a recursive function is often complex. That is the case here. The reader will not miss anything if they do not understand it: we will see shortly that PHP offers a much simpler solution. The recursive call occurs at lines 100 and 107;
  • the advantage of this code is that it wasn’t written solely for the [Personne3] class. It applies to any class with attributes whose values are objects of different types, as long as the classes used by the main class also have, like the main class itself, the [getAttributes] method found on lines 61–64.

The script [json-03.php] uses the class [Personne3] as follows:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// Person3 class
require_once __DIR__ . "/Personne3.php";

// instantiation of the father
$père = new Personne3();
// Initialization of the parent
$père->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Dieudonné",
    "âge" => 58,
]);
// instantiation and initialization of child1
$enfant1 = (new Personne3())->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Sylvain",
    "âge" => 27,
]);
// instantiation and initialization of child2
$enfant2 = (new Personne3())->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Géraldine",
    "âge" => 12,
]);
// initialization of the parent's children
$père->setFromArray([
    "enfants" => [$enfant1, $enfant2],
]);
// instantiation and initialization of child11
$enfant11 = (new Personne3())->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Gaëtan",
    "âge" => 2,
]);
// instantiation and initialization of child12
$enfant12 = (new Personne3())->setFromArray([
    "nom" => "Bertholomé",
    "prénom" => "Mathilde",
    "âge" => 1,
]);
// initialization of child1's children
$enfant1->setFromArray([
    "enfants" => [$enfant11, $enfant12],
]);
// displaying the parent
print "------------------------père\n";
print "père=$père\n";
  • lines 34–47: [$enfant1] is given two children.

The results of the execution are as follows:

> php json-03.php
------------------------père
père={"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Dieudonné","âge":58,"enfants":[{"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Sylvain","âge":27,"enfants":[{"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Gaëtan","âge":2,"enfants":null},{"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Mathilde","âge":1,"enfants":null}]},{"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Géraldine","âge":12,"enfants":null}]}

The strings jSON have been successfully retrieved from all [Personne3] objects that make up the parent.

docs.title: 5.24.1. The [JsonSerializable] interface
docs.text:
There is a much simpler solution, provided by PHP: the predefined interface [JsonSerializable]. We will examine interfaces in the next chapter. For now, let’s just note that a class that “implements” the [JsonSerializable] interface must define a [jsonSerialize(): mixed] method. When the function [json_encode] encounters an object of this class, it calls its method [jsonSerialize] and encodes the returned value in place of the object. It does this at every level of the data tree. The class [Personne4] uses this interface:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// The class implements the predefined interface [JsonSerializable]
class Personne4 implements \JsonSerializable
{
     // constructor with parameter promotion
    public function __construct(
        private string $nom,
        private string $prénom,
        private int $âge,
         // array of objects [Personne4]
        private array $enfants = [],
    ) {
    }

     // adds a child and makes the object the current one to chain calls
    public function ajouterEnfant(Personne4 $enfant): static
    {
        $this->enfants[] = $enfant;
        return $this;
    }

     // method of the [JsonSerializable] interface:
     // returns the value that [json_encode] must encode in place of the object
     #[\Override]
    public function jsonSerialize(): mixed
    {
        return \get_object_vars($this);
    }

     // __toString: the string jSON from the object
    public function __toString(): string
    {
        return \json_encode($this, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE | JSON_PRETTY_PRINT | JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
    }
}

Comments

  • line 7: the class implements the [JsonSerializable] interface;
  • lines 10–16: A constructor with parameter promotion replaces the global setter. The array of children is empty by default;
  • lines 20–24: Adds a child and returns the current object (return type [static]) to allow for chained calls;
  • line 29: the method required by the interface. Its return type is [mixed] (PHP in version 8.0), which means “any type.” Here, it returns the object’s attribute array. The children remain [Personne4] objects: [json_encode] will call their own method, [jsonSerialize]. The recursion is handled by PHP;
  • line 28: the attribute [#[\Override]] also applies to a method imposed by an interface;
  • line 37: [json_encode] is called directly on the object. Three options are combined with the [|] operator:
    • [JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE]: accented characters are written as-is;
    • [JSON_PRETTY_PRINT]: The string jSON is formatted across multiple lines, with indentation;
    • [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR] (PHP 7.3): in the event of an error, [json_encode] throws a [JsonException] exception instead of returning [false]. This is important here: the [__toString] method must return a string and cannot return [false].

The script [json-04.php] uses the class [Personne4]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters
declare(strict_types=1);

// Person4 class
require_once __DIR__ . "/Personne4.php";

// the father, his children, and his grandchildren
$enfant1 = (new Personne4("Bertholomé", "Sylvain", 27))
    ->ajouterEnfant(new Personne4("Bertholomé", "Gaëtan", 2))
    ->ajouterEnfant(new Personne4("Bertholomé", "Mathilde", 1));
$père = (new Personne4("Bertholomé", "Dieudonné", 58))
    ->ajouterEnfant($enfant1)
    ->ajouterEnfant(new Personne4("Bertholomé", "Géraldine", 12));

// display of the father: [json_encode] calls [jsonSerialize] on each object encountered
print "------------------------père\n";
print "père=$père\n";
// a compact jSON string, without escaping accented characters
print "------------------------json_encode\n";
print json_encode($enfant1, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE | JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR) . "\n";
// Decoding: this returns an associative array (second parameter set to true), not a [Personne4] object
print "------------------------json_decode\n";
$data = json_decode((string) $père, true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
print "prénom du 1er petit-enfant : {$data['enfants'][0]['enfants'][0]['prénom']}\n";
// An invalid jSON string causes an exception: [JsonException]
print "------------------------erreur\n";
try {
    json_decode('{"nom": "Bertholomé"', flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
} catch (\JsonException $e) {
    print "Erreur : " . $e->getMessage() . "\n";
}
// Without [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR], the error occurs silently
var_dump(json_decode('{"nom": "Bertholomé"'));
print "json_last_error_msg : " . json_last_error_msg() . "\n";

Results:

> php json-04.php
------------------------père
père={
    "nom": "Bertholomé",
    "prénom": "Dieudonné",
    "âge": 58,
    "enfants": [
        {
            "nom": "Bertholomé",
            "prénom": "Sylvain",
            "âge": 27,
            "enfants": [
                {
                    "nom": "Bertholomé",
                    "prénom": "Gaëtan",
                    "âge": 2,
                    "enfants": []
                },
                {
                    "nom": "Bertholomé",
                    "prénom": "Mathilde",
                    "âge": 1,
                    "enfants": []
                }
            ]
        },
        {
            "nom": "Bertholomé",
            "prénom": "Géraldine",
            "âge": 12,
            "enfants": []
        }
    ]
}
------------------------json_encode
{"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Sylvain","âge":27,"enfants":[{"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Gaëtan","âge":2,"enfants":[]},{"nom":"Bertholomé","prénom":"Mathilde","âge":1,"enfants":[]}]}
------------------------json_decode
prénom du 1er petit-enfant : Gaëtan
------------------------erreur
Erreur : Syntax error
NULL
json_last_error_msg : Syntax error

Comments

  • lines 10–12: construction of [$enfant1] and its two children through chained calls;
  • line 19: the parent’s [__toString] method produces a formatted string jSON that contains all descendants (lines 3–34 of the results). We did not write any recursive code;
  • line 22: without [JSON_PRETTY_PRINT], the string jSON is compact (line 36 of the results);
  • line 25: the function [json_decode] performs the inverse operation: it transforms a string jSON into the value PHP. With a second parameter set to [true], the jSON objects become associative arrays. Note that this returns arrays rather than [Personne4] objects: reconstructing objects from a jSON string requires additional code (or a library such as Symfony’s [Serializer] component). The named argument [flags:] eliminates the need to pass the third parameter [depth];
  • line 30: the string jSON is incorrect (missing closing curly brace). With [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR], a [JsonException] exception is thrown (line 40 of the results);
  • line 35: without [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR], [json_decode] returns [null] without reporting any errors (line 41). You should then check the [json_last_error_msg] function to see if an error occurred. That is why we will consistently use the [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR] option for the remainder of this course.

docs.title: 9. Traits
docs.text:
Traits are structures analogous to classes. However, they cannot be instantiated: they are intended to be included in classes. Including a trait in a class has the same effect as if the trait’s code had been copied into the class. Code that can be reused in multiple classes is placed in a trait.

Traits have been available since PHP 5.4. PHP 8 introduced several new features, which we will discuss at the end of this chapter: signature checking for abstract methods (PHP 8.0), trait constants (PHP 8.2), the [#[\Override]] attribute usable in a trait (PHP 8.3).
