docs.title: 12.6.1. Example 1
docs.text:
Let’s examine the following script: [mysql-05.php]:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of function parameters and return values
declare(strict_types=1);

// database name
const DSN = "mysql:host=localhost;dbname=dbpersonnes;charset=utf8mb4";
// user credentials
const ID = "admpersonnes";
const PWD = "nobody";

try {
     // connection to the database MySQL
    $connexion = PDO::connect(DSN, ID, PWD);
     // Clear the people table
    $connexion->exec("delete from personnes");
     // a list of people
    $personnes = [
        ["nom" => "Langevin", "prenom" => "Paul", "age" => 47],
        ["nom" => "Lefur", "prenom" => "Sylvie", "age" => 28],
    ];
     // We will insert these people into the database using a prepared query SQL
    $statement = $connexion->prepare("insert into personnes (nom, prenom, age) values (:nom, :prenom, :age)");
    foreach ($personnes as $personne) {
         // The values for the parameters :last_name, :first_name, and :age are retrieved from the associative array
        $statement->execute($personne);
        print "{$statement->rowCount()} ligne insérée : {$personne["prenom"]} {$personne["nom"]}\n";
    }
     // a third person, using the method [bindValue]
    $statement->bindValue("nom", "Nicazou");
    $statement->bindValue("prenom", "Pierre");
    $statement->bindValue("age", 35, PDO::PARAM_INT);
    $statement->execute();
    print "{$statement->rowCount()} ligne insérée : Pierre Nicazou\n";
} catch (PDOException $ex) {
     // error message
    print "Erreur : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
} finally {
     // Closing the connection
    $connexion = null;
}
// it's over
print "Terminé\n";

Comments

Here, we are interested in the lines that insert people into the people table of the [dbpersonnes] database.

  • Line 16: The command SQL [delete] without the [where] clause deletes all rows from the table;
  • Line 23: A parameterized SQL command is “prepared.” The parameters are preceded by a colon: [:nom], [:prenom], [:age]. To “prepare” a SQL command, use the [PDO::prepare] method. The result is an object of type [PDOStatement]. “Preparation” is not an execution: nothing is modified in the database;
  • Line 26: Execution of the prepared order using the [PDOStatement::execute] method. To do this, you must assign values to the parameters [:nom], [:prenom], and [:age]. There are several ways to do this. Here, we use an associative array whose keys are the names of the prepared statement’s parameters, which we pass to the [PDOStatement::execute] method;
  • line 27: the method [PDOStatement::rowCount] returns the number of rows modified by the last execution of the prepared statement. In the string enclosed in quotation marks, the method call is enclosed in curly braces [{...}] so that PHP can evaluate it. The same applies to the array element [{$personne["prenom"]}];
  • lines 30–33: Another way to do this is to assign a value to the parameters using the [PDOStatement::bindValue] method before calling [execute] without any arguments. The third optional parameter of [bindValue] specifies the value type SQL ([PDO::PARAM_INT] for an integer, [PDO::PARAM_STR]—the default—for a string). The drawback is that one statement is required per parameter. The associative array method is often more convenient.

The method used here to perform the inserts:

  • one prepared statement;
  • n executions of the prepared statement;

is more efficient in terms of execution time than executing n different SQL statements. Above all, it has another decisive advantage: the parameter values are passed to the SGBD separately from the text of the SQL statement. Therefore, they cannot alter the command’s meaning. If the command SQL were constructed by concatenation—for example, ["insert into personnes values ('$prenom', '$nom', $age)"], where a first name containing an apostrophe (“ Jean-Michel d'Ormesson”) would cause a syntax error, and a malicious user could slip in a value of their choice from the SQL commands: this is known as a SQL injection attack. Prepared queries should therefore be used whenever a query contains values sourced from outside the script. They can be used for the commands SQL, [select], [update], [delete], and [insert]. In the case of the command SQL [select], after it is executed with [PDOStatement::execute], the result rows are retrieved using the methods [PDOStatement::fetch] or [PDOStatement::fetchAll].

Results:

> php mysql-05.php
1 ligne insérée : Paul Langevin
1 ligne insérée : Sylvie Lefur
1 ligne insérée : Pierre Nicazou
Terminé

docs.title: 12.6.2. Example 2
docs.text:
The following script, [mysql-06.php], demonstrates the use of a prepared statement for the operation SQL [select], as well as various ways to retrieve the rows returned by this operation:

<?php

// Strict adherence to the declared types of parameters and function return values
declare(strict_types=1);

// database identity
const DSN = "mysql:host=localhost;dbname=dbpersonnes;charset=utf8mb4";
// user credentials
const ID = "admpersonnes";
const PWD = "nobody";

// a class whose attributes have the same names as the columns in the table [personnes]
class Person
{
    private string $nom;
    private string $prenom;
    private int $age;

    public function __toString(): string
    {
        return "Personne[$this->nom,$this->prenom,$this->age]";
    }
}

// an immutable class constructed from a row in the table [personnes]
final readonly class Personne
{
    public function __construct(
        public string $nom,
        public string $prenom,
        public int $age,
    ) {
    }
}

try {
     // connection to the database MySQL—by default, the rows read will be associative arrays
    $connexion = PDO::connect(DSN, ID, PWD, [PDO::ATTR_DEFAULT_FETCH_MODE => PDO::FETCH_ASSOC]);
     // clear the people table
    $connexion->exec("delete from personnes");
     // Add 10 people to the database
    $statement = $connexion->prepare("insert into personnes (nom, prenom, age) values (:nom, :prenom, :age)");
    for ($i = 0; $i < 10; $i++) {
        $statement->execute(["nom" => "nom$i", "prenom" => "prenom$i", "age" => $i * 10]);
    }
     // Query the database
    $statement = $connexion->prepare("select nom, prenom, age from personnes order by nom");
    $statement->execute();
     // 1st row: default connection mode (associative array)
    $ligne = $statement->fetch();
    var_dump($ligne);
     // 2nd line: table indexed by both column names and column numbers
    $ligne = $statement->fetch(PDO::FETCH_BOTH);
    var_dump($ligne);
     // 3rd line: object [stdClass]
    $ligne = $statement->fetch(PDO::FETCH_OBJ);
    var_dump($ligne);
     // 4th line: [Person] object
    $statement->setFetchMode(PDO::FETCH_CLASS, Person::class);
    $ligne = $statement->fetch();
    var_dump($ligne);
     // sequential reading of the remaining rows
    while ($personne = $statement->fetch()) {
        print "$personne\n";
    }
     // all lines at once, each converted to an object [Personne]
    $statement = $connexion->prepare("select nom, prenom, age from personnes where age >= :age order by nom");
    $statement->execute(["age" => 70]);
    $personnes = array_map(fn(array $ligne): Personne => new Personne(...$ligne), $statement->fetchAll());
    var_dump($personnes);
} catch (PDOException $ex) {
     // display error
    print "Erreur : " . $ex->getMessage() . "\n";
} finally {
     // Close connection
    $connexion = null;
}
// Done
print "Terminé\n";

Comments

  • lines 13–23: a class named [Person] whose typed private attributes have the names of the columns in table [personnes];
  • Lines 26–34: an immutable class [Personne] whose constructor has parameters named after the columns in table [personnes];
  • line 38: the fourth parameter of [PDO::connect] is an array of connection options. The option [PDO::ATTR_DEFAULT_FETCH_MODE] determines how the read rows will be rendered by default: in this case, [PDO::FETCH_ASSOC], which uses associative arrays indexed by column names. Without this option, the default mode is [PDO::FETCH_BOTH] (see below);
  • lines 43–45: 10 rows are inserted into the table [personnes] using a prepared query. The array of values is constructed directly within the call to [execute];
  • lines 47–48: A SQL [select] order is “prepared” and then executed;
  • line 50: the [PDOStatement::fetch] method is used to retrieve the next line from the result of the executed SQL [select] operation—in this case, the first line. The [fetch] method can return rows in various ways. The script demonstrates a few of them. Without any parameters, it uses the connection’s default mode, which in this case is an associative array. Note that age is rendered as an integer ([int(0)]). This is a new feature in PHP 8.1: previously, the MySQL driver rendered all values as character strings ([string(1) "0"] in version PHP 7). The result displayed by [var_dump] is as follows:
array(3) {
  ["nom"]=>
  string(4) "nom0"
  ["prenom"]=>
  string(7) "prenom0"
  ["age"]=>
  int(0)
}
  • Line 53: The parameter [PDO::FETCH_BOTH] causes the returned row to be an array indexed by both column names and column numbers:
array(6) {
  ["nom"]=>
  string(4) "nom1"
  [0]=>
  string(4) "nom1"
  ["prenom"]=>
  string(7) "prenom1"
  [1]=>
  string(7) "prenom1"
  ["age"]=>
  int(10)
  [2]=>
  int(10)
}
  • line 56: the parameter [PDO::FETCH_OBJ] causes the returned row to be an object of type [stdClass], whose attributes are the names of the table’s columns:
object(stdClass)#2 (3) {
  ["nom"]=>
  string(4) "nom2"
  ["prenom"]=>
  string(7) "prenom2"
  ["age"]=>
  int(20)
}
  • Line 59: The read mode of the [fetch] method is set using the [PDOStatement::setFetchMode] method. This mode then becomes the default mode for the [$statement] command until it is changed—either by another [setFetchMode] operation or by passing a mode as a parameter to the [fetch] method, as was done previously. The operation [setFetchMode(PDO::FETCH_CLASS, Person::class)] specifies that the read line must be placed in an object of type [Person]. [Person::class] is the string "Person," the full name of the class. PDO creates the object and then assigns the values from the columns of the same name to its attributes, even if those attributes are private. The following line displays the result:
object(Person)#4 (3) {
  ["nom":"Person":private]=>
  string(4) "nom3"
  ["prenom":"Person":private]=>
  string(7) "prenom3"
  ["age":"Person":private]=>
  int(30)
}
  • Lines 63–65: Show how to process the remaining rows of [select] sequentially. The method [fetch] returns [false] when there are no more rows, which terminates the loop. The display of [$personne] uses the [__toString] method from the [Person] class:
Personne[nom4,prenom4,40]
Personne[nom5,prenom5,50]
Personne[nom6,prenom6,60]
Personne[nom7,prenom7,70]
Personne[nom8,prenom8,80]
Personne[nom9,prenom9,90]
  • lines 67–68: a configured [select]: we only want people who are at least 70 years old;
  • Line 69: The [PDOStatement::fetchAll] method returns all rows of the result at once, in this case as associative arrays (the connection’s default mode). The [array_map] function converts each of them into a [Personne] object. The expression [new Personne(...$ligne)] uses the decomposition operator [...] on an associative array: each key becomes a named argument (PHP 8.1). Thus, the line [["nom" => "nom7", "prenom" => "prenom7", "age" => 70]] results in the call [new Personne(nom: "nom7", prenom: "prenom7", age: 70)]. This technique is suitable for an immutable class whose attributes are initialized by the constructor, whereas the [PDO::FETCH_CLASS] mode—which assigns values directly to the attributes—fails with a class such as [Personne], whose constructor requires arguments. It also has the advantage of having PHP verify the type of each value. The displayed result is as follows:
array(3) {
  [0]=>
  object(Personne)#2 (3) {
    ["nom"]=>
    string(4) "nom7"
    ["prenom"]=>
    string(7) "prenom7"
    ["age"]=>
    int(70)
  }
  [1]=>
  object(Personne)#6 (3) {
    ["nom"]=>
    string(4) "nom8"
    ["prenom"]=>
    string(7) "prenom8"
    ["age"]=>
    int(80)
  }
  [2]=>
  object(Personne)#7 (3) {
    ["nom"]=>
    string(4) "nom9"
    ["prenom"]=>
    string(7) "prenom9"
    ["age"]=>
    int(90)
  }
}

The following table summarizes the read modes encountered:

ModeA line is rendered in the form[PDO::FETCH_ASSOC]an associative array [colonne => valeur][PDO::FETCH_NUM]an array indexed by the column numbers 0, 1, 2…[PDO::FETCH_BOTH]an array indexed by both column names and numbers (default mode for PDO)[PDO::FETCH_OBJ]an object [stdClass] whose attributes are the column names[PDO::FETCH_CLASS]of an object of the specified class whose attributes have the column names

Each driver also has its own options, grouped within its class starting with PHP 8.4. For example, the option that executes a command SQL each time a connection is made to MySQL is written as [Pdo\Mysql::ATTR_INIT_COMMAND]. The old constants [PDO::MYSQL_ATTR_INIT_COMMAND], which are found in many documents, have been deprecated since PHP 8.5.

docs.title: 12.7. Using Transactions
docs.text:
A transaction allows you to group a sequence of SQL commands into a single unit of execution: either all commands succeed, or one of them fails, in which case all preceding SQL commands are rolled back. In other words, when you use a transaction to execute SQL commands, after the transaction completes, the database is in a stable state:

  • either in a new state created by the successful execution of all SQL commands in the transaction;
  • or in the state it was in before the transaction began to be executed.

Let’s revisit the example of executing the SQL commands contained in a text file discussed in the section “Executing Any SQL Commands.” We will include this execution in a transaction. The SQL commands will be contained in the following [sql2.txt] file:

select * from personnes
select nom,prenom from personnes order by nom asc, prenom desc
select * from personnes where age between 20 and 40 order by age desc, nom asc, prenom asc
insert into personnes values('Josette','Bruneau',46)
update personnes set age=47 where nom='Bruneau'
select * from personnes where nom='Bruneau'
delete from personnes where nom='Bruneau'
select * from personnes where nom='Bruneau'
insert into personnes values('Josette','Bruneau',46)
select * from personnes where nom='Bruneau'
xselect * from personnes where nom='Bruneau'

The erroneous command on line 11 will cause the entire transaction to fail. The database should therefore revert to its state prior to the transaction. In the example above, the row inserted by line 9 should not appear in the table. The script differs very little from the [mysql-04.php] script. The name of the SQL command file becomes [__DIR__ . "/sql2.txt"], and the [exécuterCommandes] function loses its fourth parameter:

// executing the command file SQL
$erreurs = exécuterCommandes($connexion, SQL_COMMANDS_FILENAME, suivi: true);

This is because, since the SQL commands run within a transaction, any error will cause the transaction to terminate. The [exécuterCommandes] function becomes the following:

function exécuterCommandes(PDO $connexion, string $sqlFileName, bool $suivi = false): array
{
     // uses the connection $connexion
     // executes the commands SQL contained in the text file $sqlFileName
     // this file is a command file containing SQL commands, one per line
     // if $suivi is true, each execution of a SQL command is followed by a message indicating whether it succeeded or failed
     // The SQL commands are executed within a transaction: if any of them fails, the transaction is rolled back
     // and the database is restored to the state it was in before the transaction
     // the function returns the error message array (empty if no errors occurred)

     // The lines from the file are placed in an array, without line breaks or empty lines
    $requêtes = is_readable($sqlFileName)
        ? file($sqlFileName, FILE_IGNORE_NEW_LINES | FILE_SKIP_EMPTY_LINES)
        : false;
     // Error?
    if ($requêtes === false) {
        return ["Le fichier [$sqlFileName] n'existe pas ou n'a pu être lu"];
    }
     // The queries will be executed within a transaction
    $connexion->beginTransaction();
     // The queries are executed one by one—no errors initially
    $erreurs = [];
    foreach ($requêtes as $requête) {
         // removing leading and trailing spaces
        $requête = trim($requête);
         // Empty query?
        if ($requête === "") {
             // Move on to the next query
            continue;
        }
         // The command name SQL: the first word of the query, in lowercase
        $commande = strtolower(explode(" ", $requête, 2)[0]);
        try {
             // query execution—an exception is thrown if an error occurs
             // A command SELECT returns rows; other commands return the number of modified rows
            $résultat = $commande === "select"
                ? $connexion->query($requête, PDO::FETCH_NUM)
                : $connexion->exec($requête);
             // display output on screen or not?
            if ($suivi) {
                print "[$requête] : Exécution réussie\n";
            }
             // Display the execution result
            afficherInfos($commande, $résultat);
        } catch (PDOException $ex) {
             // An error occurred
            addError($erreurs, $requête, $ex->getMessage(), $suivi);
             // Stop at the first error
            break;
        }
    }
     // End of transaction
    if ($erreurs === []) {
         // No errors occurred: the transaction is committed
        $connexion->commit();
    } else {
         // An error occurred: the transaction is canceled
        $connexion->rollBack();
         // Added an error
        addError($erreurs, "", "Transaction annulée", $suivi);
    }
     // result
    return $erreurs;
}

Comments

  • Lines 41–42: Reminder of the role of a transaction;
  • line 54: a transaction is started using the [PDO::beginTransaction] method. From this point on, any SQL command executed within the [foreach] loop is executed within this transaction;
  • lines 82–83: Upon the first error, the loop is exited: there is no point in executing the subsequent commands since the transaction will be rolled back;
  • lines 87–95: The array [$erreurs] is empty if no error occurred. The transaction is then committed using the method [PDO::commit]: the changes made by the commands SQL become permanent. Otherwise, the transaction is rolled back using method [PDO::rollBack]: the changes made by the SQL commands in the transaction are undone. The transaction error is then added to the error list.

If we check the database status, we find it in the same state as before the script was run. In particular, we do not see the [Josette, Bruneau, 46] row from line 52 of the results above:

> mysql -u admpersonnes -pnobody dbpersonnes -e "select count(*) from personnes where nom='Bruneau'"

Summary:

  • A transaction begins with method [PDO::beginTransaction];
  • it is successfully completed using the [PDO::commit] method;
  • it is terminated upon failure using the [PDO::rollBack] method;
  • the [PDO::inTransaction] method indicates whether a transaction is in progress.

When working with a database, it is good practice to place any SQL operation within a transaction to isolate it from other database users (this is also one of its purposes). A transaction should be as short as possible. Therefore, be sure to end it with a [commit] or a [rollBack], as appropriate. Finally, please note: with MySQL, commands that modify the database structure ([create table], [drop table], etc.) cannot be rolled back. They implicitly commit the current transaction. This is why the [sql2.txt] file contains only [select], [insert], [update], and [delete] commands.

docs.title: 17. Web Services
docs.text: Note: By “web service,” we mean here any web application that delivers raw data consumed by a client—in the examples that follow, a console script. We are not concerned with any particular technology—such as REST (REpresentational State Transfer) or SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol), for example—which deliver data in a well-defined format: JSON most often for REST, and XML for SOAP. Each of these technologies precisely describes how the client must query the server and the format the server’s response must take. In this course, we will be much more flexible regarding the nature of the client’s request and the server’s response. However, the scripts written and the tools used are similar to those of the REST technology.

docs.title: 17.1. Introduction
docs.text:
Since PHP programs can be executed by a web server, such a program becomes a server program capable of serving multiple clients. From the client’s perspective, calling a web service is equivalent to requesting the URL of that service. The client can be written in any language, including PHP. We also need to know how to “communicate” with a web service—that is, understand the HTTP communication protocol between a web server and its clients. That was the purpose of the previous chapter, which introduced us to part of this protocol.

In their simplest form, client/server exchanges proceed as follows:

  • the client opens a connection to port 80 on the web server;
  • the client sends a request for a document;
  • the web server sends the requested document and closes the connection;
  • the client then closes the connection.

The document can be of various types: text in HTML format, an image, a video, etc. It can be an existing document (static document) or a document generated on the fly by a script (dynamic document). In the latter case, this is referred to as web programming. The script for dynamically generating documents can be written in various languages: PHP, Python, Java, JavaScript, C#, Ruby…

In the following, we will use PHP scripts to dynamically generate text documents.

  • In [1], the client establishes a connection with the server, requests a PHP script, and may or may not send parameters to that script;
  • In [2], the web server has the PHP script executed by the PHP interpreter. The script generates a document that is sent to the client [3];
  • The server closes the connection. The client does the same.

The web server can handle multiple clients at the same time.

With [Laragon], the web server is [Apache], an open-source server from the Apache Foundation (https://httpd.apache.org). In the following applications, [Laragon] must be launched and its services started (the [Start All] button in the [Laragon] window). This launches the [Apache] web server as well as SGBD and [MySQL]. The [Apache] server of [Laragon] executes the PHP scripts using the [mod_php] module from the PHP version selected in [Laragon], in this case PHP 8.5.

So far, we have written PHP scripts that run in a console context:

The user uses the console (the VS Code terminal) to request the execution of a PHP script and receive its results.

In the client/server applications described below:

  • the client script is executed in a console context;
  • the server script is executed in a web context.

The server script PHP cannot be located just anywhere in the file system. This is because the web server searches for the static and dynamic documents it is requested to serve in locations specified by configuration. The default configuration for [Laragon] causes documents to be searched for in the [<laragon>/www] folder, where [<laragon>] is the installation folder for [Laragon] (for example, [C:\laragon]). Thus, if a web client requests document D using the URL or [http://localhost/D] path, the web server will serve document D from the [<laragon>/www/D] path.

The code folder for this course, [php8-oct-2026], has been placed in the [<laragon>/www] folder (see the chapter on installation). The server scripts for this chapter are in the [php8-oct-2026/scripts-web] folder. If a server script is named [S.php], the web server will be queried with URL and [http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/S.php]. The document [<laragon>/www/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/S.php] will then be served.

Client scripts are located in the [php8-oct-2026/scripts-console/clients-web] folder. Here is the structure of the two folders (each numbered folder corresponds to a paragraph in this chapter):

php8-oct-2026
├── scripts-console
│   └── clients-web
│       ├── 02      client date / heure
│       ├── 03      client JSON
│       ├── 04      client de l'environnement du serveur
│       ├── 05      clients GET / POST
│       ├── 06      client avec session (exemples 1 et 2)
│       └── 08      client avec authentification
├── scripts-web
│   ├── 01          pages statiques et dynamiques
│   ├── 02          serveur date / heure
│   ├── 03          serveur JSON
│   ├── 04          environnement du serveur
│   ├── 05          serveur GET / POST
│   ├── 06          sessions - exemple 1
│   ├── 07          sessions - exemple 2
│   └── 08          authentification
└── vendor          bibliothèques installées par Composer

In VS Code, open the [php8-oct-2026] folder ([File / Open Folder] menu). All web script and console script files are then accessible in the VS Code explorer, and the [PHP Intelephense] extension analyzes the code in both. There is no “web project” to create: for the [Apache] server, a web script is simply a [.php] file located in the [<laragon>/www] folder.

The HTTP clients used in this chapter are:

  • a web browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, etc.);
  • the [curl] command-line tool, available in Windows 11 (and in the [Laragon] terminal). In a [PowerShell] terminal, you must type [curl.exe] instead of [curl], because in Windows PowerShell, [curl] is an alias for the command [Invoke-WebRequest], which does not have the same options. In a [Invite de commandes] (cmd) terminal or in the [Laragon] terminal, [curl] is sufficient;
  • PHP console scripts using the Symfony [HttpClient] library.

We will use [curl] with a few options:

optionrole[-i]displays the HTTP response headers before the document[-v]verbose mode: also displays the HTTP headers sent by [curl][-d nom=valeur]sends the parameter via a request POST[--data-urlencode "nom=valeur"]same as above, URL-encoding the value[-u login:mot_de_passe]authentication [Basic][-c fichier] / [-b fichier]Saves / returns cookies received from the server

docs.title: 17.2. Writing a static page
docs.text:
Note: For the rest of this process, [Laragon] must be running.

We will show how to create a static page in HTML (HyperText Markup Language). In VS Code, we create the folder [scripts-web/01] and then, within that folder, the file [exemple-01.html]. In an empty HTML file, VS Code provides a page template: simply type [!] and then press the [Tab] key (the [Emmet] function from VS Code). We complete this template as follows:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="fr">
    <head>
        <meta charset="UTF-8">
        <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
        <title>PHP 8 par l'exemple</title>
    </head>
    <body>
        <div><b>Ceci est un exemple de page statique</b></div>
    </body>
</html>
  • Line 6: the page title;
  • line 9: its content.

Now let’s have the HTML page displayed by the [Apache] server from [Laragon]. In a browser, we request the URL [http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/01/exemple-01.html]:

  • At the top, the tab displays the page title and the address bar shows the requested URL;
  • below that, the page content.

The page displayed is a static page: you can reload it as many times as you like in the browser (F5), and the same content is always displayed.

Most browsers provide access to the data exchanged between the client and the server, as described in the previous chapter: type F12 to open the developer tools, then select the [Réseau] (Network) tab and reload the page (F5). By clicking on the loaded document, you can see the command sent to the server, the headers of the browser’s request, the headers of the server’s response, and then the received document.

The [curl] tool allows you to view the same information in a terminal. With the [-i] option, it displays the HTTP headers of the server response, followed by the received document:

> curl -i http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/01/exemple-01.html
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:31:46 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
Last-Modified: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 14:29:23 GMT
ETag: "12f-65cc83df75105"
Accept-Ranges: bytes
Content-Length: 303
Vary: Accept-Encoding
Content-Type: text/html

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="fr">
    <head>
        <meta charset="UTF-8">
        <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
        <title>PHP 8 par l'exemple</title>
    </head>
    <body>
        <div><b>Ceci est un exemple de page statique</b></div>
    </body>
</html>
  • Line 2: the response status line: HTTP protocol version, [200] status code, and its description [OK];
  • Next come the response headers HTTP. These include, in particular, the response date [Date], the server signature [Server], the date the document was last modified [Last-Modified], its size in bytes [Content-Length], and its type [Content-Type];
  • followed by a blank line, which separates the headers from the document;
  • and finally, the document HTML that we created. A browser interprets this code to display the page shown above.

docs.title: 17.3. Creating a Dynamic Page in PHP
docs.text:
We will now write a dynamic page in PHP. In the [scripts-web/01] folder, we create the following file, [exemple-01.php]:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="fr">
    <head>
        <meta charset="UTF-8">
        <title>Exemple de page dynamique</title>
    </head>
    <body>
        <?php
         // time(): number of seconds elapsed since 01/01/1970 00:00:00 UTC
         // date and time display format
         // d: day (2 digits)
         // m: 2-digit month
         // y: 2-digit year
         // H: hour (00–23)
         // i: minutes
         // s: seconds
        print "<b>Date et heure du jour : </b>" . date("d/m/y H:i:s", time());
        ?>
    </body>
</html>

Comments

  • line 5: the page title;
  • line 8: the code PHP is placed between the tags [<?php] and [?>]. Everything outside these tags is HTML;
  • line 17: writes the current date and time. The [time] function returns the number of seconds that have elapsed since January 1, 1970, at 0:00 UTC. The function [date] formats this number according to the format specified by its first parameter, in this case day/month/year hours:minutes:seconds.

Basically, the PHP script above writes the current time to the console. However, when executed by a web server, the output stream from the [print] statement—which is usually directed to the script’s execution console—is redirected to the connection between the server and its client. Therefore, in a web context, the script above sends the current time as text to the client—in this case, a browser.

Let’s try URL and [http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/01/exemple-01.php]:

This is a dynamic page because if you reload the page several times in the browser (F5), its content changes (the time changes).

The browser has received a HTML feed. To view it, you can display the page’s source code in the browser (right-click on the page, select the [Afficher le code source de la page] option, or press Ctrl-U), or use [curl]:

> curl -i http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/01/exemple-01.php
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:31:46 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.5.11
Vary: Accept-Encoding
Content-Length: 223
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="fr">
    <head>
        <meta charset="UTF-8">
        <title>Exemple de page dynamique</title>
    </head>
    <body>
        <b>Date et heure du jour : </b>01/10/26 17:31:46    </body>
</html>
  • after the blank line, the received code HTML. The code PHP has disappeared: it has been replaced by the text it generated, along with the date and time;
  • among the headers, the header [X-Powered-By] was not present when the static page was requested. It indicates that the server’s response was generated by a script PHP. The headers [Last-Modified] and [ETag], on the other hand, have disappeared: the document does not exist on the disk; it is generated at the time of the request. The [Content-Length] header is still present: since the document is short, [Apache] was able to receive it in its entirety before sending the headers, and thus calculate its size.

It is therefore important to remember that a PHP script intended to be executed by a web server for a browser must produce a HTML stream. We will see that the script can also generate the headers HTTP and virtually all elements of the server’s response.

docs.title: 17.4. Basics of the HTML Language
docs.text:
This chapter will not delve into web programming in PHP. A MVC web application is developed later in this course. Instead, this chapter focuses on web services: PHP pages that deliver data to other PHP clients via a web server. Nevertheless, we thought it would be useful to provide the reader with some basics of HTML.

A web browser can display various documents, the most common being the HTML document (HyperText Markup Language). This is formatted text containing tags of the form [<balise>texte</balise>]. For example, the text [<b>important</b>] will display important text in bold. There are standalone tags, such as the [<hr>] tag, which displays a horizontal line. We will not go over all the tags that can be found in a HTML text. A good reference is the Mozilla documentation site: https://developer.mozilla.org/fr/docs/Web/HTML. Knowledge of the HTML language is essential, since dynamic web applications must generate the HTML code themselves to send to web clients.

In short, you don't need to know the entire HTML language to get started with web programming. One way to discover the intricacies of the HTML language is to browse the web and view the source code of pages that feature interesting characteristics you're not yet familiar with.

Consider the following [balises.html] example, which includes some elements commonly found in a web document, such as:

  • a table;
  • an image;
  • a link.

A HTML document generally has the following format:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
    <head>
        <title>Un titre</title>
        ...
    </head>
    <body attributs>
        ...
    </body>
</html>

The entire document is enclosed by the [<html>…</html>] tags. It consists of two parts:

  • [<head>…</head>]: This is the non-displayable part of the document. It provides information to the browser that will display the document. It often contains the [<title>…</title>] tag, which specifies the text that will appear in the browser tab. Other tags may also be present, including tags that define the document’s keywords—keywords that are subsequently used by search engines. This section may also contain scripts, written in JavaScript, which will be executed by the browser;
  • [<body attributs>…</body>]: This is the section that will be displayed by the browser. The HTML tags contained in this section tell the browser the “desired” visual layout for the document.

The HTML code for our example document is as follows:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="fr">
    <head>
        <meta charset="UTF-8">
        <title>Quelques balises HTML</title>
    </head>

    <body style="background-image: url(images/standard.jpg)">
        <h1 style="text-align: left">Quelques balises HTML</h1>
        <hr>

        <table border="1">
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Colonne 1</th>
                    <th>Colonne 2</th>
                    <th>Colonne 3</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td>cellule(1,1)</td>
                    <td style="text-align: center;">cellule(1,2)</td>
                    <td>cellule(1,3)</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>cellule(2,1)</td>
                    <td>cellule(2,2)</td>
                    <td>cellule(2,3)</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>
        <br><br>
        <table border="0">
            <tr>
                <td>Une image</td>
                <td><img src="images/cerisier.jpg" alt="un cerisier"></td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Le site du langage PHP</td>
                <td><a href="https://www.php.net/">ici</a></td>
            </tr>
        </table>
    </body>
</html>
elementHTML tags and examples document title[<title>Quelques balises HTML</title>] (line 5): The text [Quelques balises HTML] will appear in the browser tab displaying the document horizontal bar[<hr>]: displays a horizontal line (line 10) table[<table attributs>….</table>]: to define the table (line 12);[<thead>…</thead>]: to define the column headers ({{L:<thead></thead>}});[<tbody>…</tbody>]: to define the table content ({{L:<tbody></tbody>}});[<tr attributs>…</tr>]: to define a row (line 21);[<td attributs>…</td>]: to define a cell (row 22);examples:[<table border="1">…</table>]: the attribute [border] defines the thickness of the table border;[<td style="text-align: center;">cellule(1,2)</td>] (row 23): defines a cell whose content will be [cellule(1,2)]. This content will be horizontally centered ([text-align: center])image[<img src="images/cerisier.jpg" alt="un cerisier">] (line 37): defines an image whose source file is [images/cerisier.jpg] on the web server. The attribute [alt] provides alternative text, which is displayed if the image cannot be displayed. This tag appears in a web document generated using the URL [http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/01/balises.html]. Therefore, the browser will request the URL [http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/01/images/cerisier.jpg] to retrieve the image referenced here link[<a href="https://www.php.net/">ici</a>] (line 41): causes the text [ici] to serve as a link to URL [https://www.php.net/] page background[<body style="background-image: url(images/standard.jpg)">] (line 8): indicates that the image to be used as the page background is located at URL [images/standard.jpg] on the web server. In the context of our example, the browser will request the URL [http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/01/images/standard.jpg] to retrieve this background image

This simple example shows that to build the entire document, the browser must make three requests to the server:

  • [http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/01/balises.html] to retrieve the source HTML of the document;
  • [http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/01/images/cerisier.jpg] to retrieve the image [cerisier.jpg];
  • [http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/01/images/standard.jpg] to retrieve the background image [standard.jpg].

This is what the [Réseau] tab in the browser’s developer tools (F12) shows: it displays the three requests made by the browser.

Note: On Windows, filenames are not case-sensitive: [Cerisier.jpg] and [cerisier.jpg] refer to the same file. This is not the case on a Linux server, where most websites are hosted. You should therefore get into the habit of writing file names exactly as they appear on the disk, such as URL.

docs.title: 17.5. Making a Static Page Dynamic
docs.text:
Let’s show how we can make the page HTML [exemple-01.html] dynamic. Let’s copy its content into a file named [page-00.php]. This script, PHP, does not contain any PHP—only HTML. Let’s request it from the server:

> curl http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/01/page-00.php
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="fr">
    <head>
        <meta charset="UTF-8">
        <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
        <title>PHP 8 par l'exemple</title>
    </head>
    <body>
        <div><b>Ceci est un exemple de page statique</b></div>
    </body>
</html>

The PHP interpreter processed the [page-00.php] script and produced the same HTML output as the static page [exemple-01.html]. This teaches us one thing: when the PHP interpreter finds HTML within a PHP script, it leaves it untouched and sends it to the client as-is.

Now let’s add a few PHP instructions to the following [page-01.php] script so that the PHP interpreter has something to do:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="fr">
    <head>
        <title><?= $page->title ?></title>
        <meta charset="UTF-8">
        <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    </head>
    <body>
        <div><b><?= $page->contents ?></b></div>
    </body>
</html>
  • Lines 4 and 9: We’ve added PHP code to dynamically generate the page’s title and content. Here, we’re assuming that the variable [$page] is an object containing the data to be displayed. The [<?= expression ?>] tag is a shortcut for [<?php print expression ?>]. It is designed for this type of page: HTML with a few values calculated by PHP.

If we call this script directly, we get the following result:

> curl http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/web-scripts/01/page-01.php
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="fr">
    <head>
        <title><br />
<b>Warning</b>:  Undefined variable $page in <b>.../php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/01/page-01.php</b> on line <b>4</b><br />
<br />
<b>Warning</b>:  Attempt to read property "title" on null in <b>.../php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/01/page-01.php</b> on line <b>4</b><br />
</title>
        <meta charset="UTF-8">
        <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    </head>
    <body>
        <div><b><br />
<b>Warning</b>:  Undefined variable $page in <b>.../php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/01/page-01.php</b> on line <b>9</b><br />
<br />
<b>Warning</b>:  Attempt to read property "contents" on null in <b>.../php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/01/page-01.php</b> on line <b>9</b><br />
</b></div>
    </body>
</html>
  • Lines 5–8: The page title could not be calculated because the variable [$page] was not defined. PHP inserted two warning messages into the HTML stream: the variable [$page] does not exist, and the property [title] of [null] cannot be read;
  • Lines 14–17: same issue with the content.

Note: Starting with PHP 8.0, using an undefined variable and reading a property on [null] triggers a [Warning] warning rather than a simple [Notice] as in PHP 7. The messages are displayed on the page because the configuration of PHP for [Laragon] is a development configuration ([display_errors=On]). On a production server, we use [display_errors=Off], and errors are written to a log file.

Now, let’s write the following [exemple-02.php] web script:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// we define the page elements to be displayed
$page = new stdClass();
$page->title = "Un nouveau titre";
$page->contents = "Un nouveau contenu généré dynamiquement";
// we display [page-01.php]
require_once __DIR__ . "/page-01.php";
  • Line 3: Like all PHP scripts in this course, this script requires strict type checking;
  • Lines 6–8: We define the [$page] object. The predefined class [stdClass] is the only class (along with classes marked by the [#[\AllowDynamicProperties]] attribute) to which undeclared properties can still be added without a warning: Starting with PHP 8.2, creating dynamic properties on objects of other classes is deprecated;
  • Line 10: The script [page-01.php] is included. The code in this script will then be interpreted:
    • The variable [$page] is now defined, and the PHP interpreter will use it;
    • the code HTML from [page-01.php] will be sent as-is to the client;
    • the results of the expressions in [<?= … ?>] will be included in the text stream sent to the client.

Now, if we request the web script [exemple-02.php], we get the following in the browser:

And here is the text received by the browser:

> curl http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/01/exemple-02.php
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="fr">
    <head>
        <title>Un nouveau titre</title>
        <meta charset="UTF-8">
        <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    </head>
    <body>
        <div><b>Un nouveau contenu généré dynamiquement</b></div>
    </body>
</html>
  • Lines 5 and 10: the codes PHP and [page-01.php] have been replaced by the values of the expressions [$page->title] and [$page->contents].

From this example, we can take away two key points:

  • The HTML pages intended for the browser can be isolated into PHP scripts containing only this HTML code and a few dynamic parts generated by PHP code. There should be as little PHP as possible in these pages;
  • all logic that generates the dynamic data included in the HTML pages must be isolated into pure PHP scripts, containing no page presentation code (HTML, CSS, JavaScript…).

This allows for a separation of tasks:

  • the task of generating the web pages to be displayed (HTML, CSS, JavaScript…);
  • the task of implementing the logic for the web application being built. This logic can be implemented using a layered architecture, exactly as we did with the console scripts.

Note: A value inserted into a HTML page should normally be protected by the [htmlspecialchars] function, which replaces the special characters in the HTML ([<], [>], [&], ["]) with their HTML codes. Otherwise, a value provided by a user that contains, for example, a tag such as [<script>] would be executed by the browser (XSS vulnerability). We’ll come back to this when we write HTML pages.

Next, we’ll build specific web scripts:

  • they will send only data to the client and no formatting (HTML, CSS, JavaScript). They will therefore be data servers rather than web pages;
  • the clients for these web scripts will be console scripts that will retrieve the data sent by the server and process it.

docs.title: 17.6. Client/server application for date and time
docs.text:
We are now looking at the following configuration:

We will write:

  • a web script, [1], which sends the current date and time to its client;
  • a console script [2] that will act as the client for the web script: it will retrieve the date and time sent by the web script and display them on the console.
php8-oct-2026
├── scripts-console
│   └── clients-web
│       └── 02
│           ├── config-date-time-client-2.json
│           ├── config-date-time-client.json
│           ├── config-espion.json
│           ├── date-time-client.php
│           └── spy-server.php
└── scripts-web
    └── 02
        ├── date-time-server-2.php
        └── date-time-server.php

docs.title: 17.6.1. The server-side script
docs.text:
We have already written a web script that generates the current date and time: the [exemple-01.php] script from the previous paragraph. We mentioned that we would be writing data servers: raw data without formatting (HTML). The server script [date-time-server.php] will therefore be as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// time zone used by date functions
date_default_timezone_set('Europe/Paris');
// Set the header HTTP [Content-Type]
header('Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8');
//
// sends the date and time
// time(): number of seconds elapsed since 01/01/1970 00:00:00 UTC
// date and time display format
// d: 2-digit day
// m: 2-digit month
// y: 2-digit year
// H: hour (00–23)
// i: minutes
// s: seconds
print date("d/m/y H:i:s", time());
  • Line 6: The date functions use the time zone set by the [date.timezone] directive in the [php.ini] file. To avoid depending on the server configuration, the script sets the time zone itself—in this case, Paris;
  • Line 8: The [header] function adds a HTTP header to the response. Here, the HTTP and [Content-Type] headers are set, which inform the client of the nature of the document it will receive. For the [exemple-01.php] page, the [Content-Type] was [text/html; charset=UTF-8]. Here, we inform the client that the document is plain text (HTML). This is not important for our console client, which will not attempt to use this header. It is more important for web browsers, which do use this header. The HTTP headers precede the document in the server’s response: the [header] function must therefore be called before the script has written anything;
  • Line 19: the document sent to the client: the date and time, without the HTML tag.

Let’s request this script using a browser:

The browser displays the received plain text. With [curl], we see the header HTTP [Content-Type] set by the script and, after the blank line, the received text document:

> curl -i http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/02/date-time-server.php
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:31:46 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.5.11
Content-Length: 17
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8

01/10/26 17:31:46

docs.title: 17.6.2. The client-side script
docs.text:
In the previous chapter, we wrote several HTTP clients. We could use them to retrieve the text document sent by the [date-time-server.php] server script. We won’t do that, however. As we did for the SMTP and IMAP protocols, we will use a third-party library, specifically the [HttpClient] component from the Symfony framework, whose documentation can be found at URL https://symfony.com/doc/current/http_client.html.

Like the previous libraries, the [HttpClient] component is installed using the [Composer] tool. In a terminal window opened in the [php8-oct-2026] folder, the command would be:

composer require symfony/http-client

This isn’t necessary here: the file [composer.json] in the [php8-oct-2026] folder already declares this dependency (in version 8) as well as that of the [HttpFoundation] component, which we’ll be using soon. The [composer install] command run during the installation of the course codes installed them in the [php8-oct-2026/vendor] folder.

The console script [date-time-client.php] will process the following JSON and [config-date-time-client.json] files:

{
    "url": "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/02/date-time-server.php"
}
  • Line 2: the URL server script.

The client-side script [date-time-client.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// date/time service client

// dependencies
require_once __DIR__ . '/../../../vendor/autoload.php';

use Symfony\Component\HttpClient\HttpClient;
use Symfony\Contracts\HttpClient\Exception\ExceptionInterface;

// the configuration file: first command-line argument, if it exists
$configFileName = $argv[1] ?? "config-date-time-client.json";

// retrieve the configuration
if (!file_exists($configFileName)) {
    print "Le fichier de configuration [$configFileName] n'existe pas\n";
    exit(1);
}
try {
    $config = json_decode(file_get_contents($configFileName), true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
} catch (JsonException $ex) {
    print "Erreur lors de l'exploitation du fichier de configuration JSON [$configFileName] : {$ex->getMessage()}\n";
    exit(1);
}

// create a client HTTP
$httpClient = HttpClient::create();

try {
     // Send the request
    $response = $httpClient->request('GET', $config['url']);
     // response status
    $statusCode = $response->getStatusCode();
    print "---Réponse avec statut : $statusCode\n";
     // retrieve the headers
    print "---Entêtes de la réponse\n";
    foreach ($response->getHeaders() as $name => $values) {
        print "$name: $values[0]\n";
    }
     // retrieve the response body
    $content = $response->getContent();
     // displaying it
    print "---Réponse du serveur : [$content]\n";
} catch (ExceptionInterface $ex) {
     // Displaying the error
    print "Erreur de communication avec le serveur : {$ex->getMessage()}\n";
    exit(2);
}

Comments

  • Line 8: As we did for the previous libraries, we load the file [vendor/autoload.php] generated by [Composer]. Its path is calculated based on the constant [__DIR__], which is the script’s folder: the script works regardless of the location of the [php8-oct-2026] folder;
  • Line 10: We declare the [HttpClient] class that we will use;
  • line 11: the [ExceptionInterface] interface is implemented by all exceptions that the Symfony client HTTP may throw;
  • line 14: The name of the configuration file can be passed as an argument to the script: [php date-time-client.php autre-config.json]. Otherwise, the file [config-date-time-client.json] is used. The array [$argv] contains the command-line arguments, where [$argv[0]] is the name of the script. The operator [??] returns its left operand if it exists and is not [null]; otherwise, it returns its right operand;
  • lines 17–25: the script’s configuration is retrieved into the array [$config]. The parameter named [flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR] instructs [json_decode] to throw a [JsonException] exception if JSON is incorrect, instead of letting [null] run silently;
  • Line 29: A HTTP client is created. The static method [create] selects the most appropriate implementation: in this case, the class [CurlHttpClient], which uses the extension [curl] of PHP;
  • line 33: the URL from the server script is requested using a GET command: [GET URL HTTP/1.1]. This operation is asynchronous: execution continues to the next line without waiting for the response;
  • line 35: The response status code is retrieved. This is found in the first line of the server’s response. Thus, if this line is [HTTP/1.1 200 OK], the response status is 200. This operation is blocking: execution does not resume until the client has received the headers from the server’s response;
  • line 39: We retrieve the response headers HTTP. We obtain an associative array whose keys are the header names (in lowercase), and the array values: a single header may indeed appear multiple times in a response. Here, we display the first value of each header;
  • line 43: We retrieve the document returned by the server; we know that this document is text;
  • line 46: if an error occurs, the error message is displayed. The script PHP 7 used to catch the exceptions [TypeError | RuntimeException]; it is more precise to catch the client exceptions HTTP, all of which implement [ExceptionInterface]. Note that [getHeaders] and [getContent] throw an exception when the response status code indicates an error (codes 300 through 599). We will discuss this in the section on authentication.

The client runs in a terminal with the directory open ([Laragon] must be running for the server script to be accessible):

> php date-time-client.php
---Réponse avec statut : 200
---Entêtes de la réponse
date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:55:26 GMT
server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
x-powered-by: PHP/8.5.11
content-length: 17
content-type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8
---Réponse du serveur : [01/10/26 18:55:26]

The current date and time are correctly retrieved on the last line. The headers displayed are the same as those we saw with [curl], with the names in lowercase.

You might be curious to know what the client script sent to the server. In the previous chapter, we used a generic TCP server for this purpose, which displays the lines of text it receives. Here, we’ll write a small “spy” server, TCP, that monitors [spy-server.php]—it does the same thing—and then sends a minimal response, HTTP, back to the client:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// A “spy” server (TCP): it displays whatever a client (HTTP) sends it
// then sends back a minimal HTTP response
// Usage: PHP spy-server.php [port]

$port = (int) ($argv[1] ?? 100);
// the listening service
$server = stream_socket_server("tcp://127.0.0.1:$port", $errorCode, $errorMessage);
if ($server === false) {
    print "Impossible de créer le service sur le port $port : $errorMessage\n";
    exit(1);
}
print "Serveur espion en attente d'un client sur le port $port\n";
// waiting for a client (5 minutes maximum)
$client = stream_socket_accept($server, 300, $clientName);
if ($client === false) {
    print "Aucun client ne s'est présenté\n";
    exit(1);
}
print "Client connecté : $clientName\n";
print "--- lignes reçues\n";
// Reading the headers HTTP up to the blank line
$contentLength = 0;
while (($line = fgets($client)) !== false) {
    $line = rtrim($line, "\r\n");
    print "$line\n";
    if ($line === "") {
         // end of headers
        break;
    }
     // size of the document following the headers
    if (preg_match('/^content-length:\s*(\d+)$/i', $line, $fields)) {
        $contentLength = (int) $fields[1];
    }
}
// read any document
if ($contentLength > 0) {
    print stream_get_contents($client, $contentLength) . "\n";
}
// minimum HTTP response: status line, headers, blank line, document
$document = "réponse du serveur espion";
fwrite($client, "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n"
    . "Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8\r\n"
    . "Content-Length: " . strlen($document) . "\r\n"
    . "Connection: close\r\n"
    . "\r\n"
    . $document);
// end of communication
fclose($client);
fclose($server);
print "--- fin de la communication\n";
  • line 9: the listening port is passed as an argument; the default is 100;
  • line 11: creates a service TCP on port [port] of the local machine;
  • line 18: waiting for a client;
  • line 27: reads and displays the received lines up to the empty line that ends the HTTP headers. Along the way, it notes the value of the [Content-Length] header, which specifies the size of the document that may follow the headers;
  • lines 40–41: read and display this document;
  • lines 45–50: Send a minimal HTTP response: status line, headers, empty line, document;
  • line 52: close the connection with the client so that it detects that it has received the entire response.

We launch the spy server in the first terminal:

php spy-server.php 100

The configuration file [config-espion.json] specifies port 100 on the local machine:

{
    "url": "http://localhost:100/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/02/date-time-server.php"
}

This time, the client contacts the server [localhost] on port 100. Therefore, our spy server will be the one to handle the request. In a second terminal, we run the client with this configuration:

> php date-time-client.php config-espion.json
---Réponse avec statut : 200
---Entêtes de la réponse
content-type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8
content-length: 26
connection: close
---Réponse du serveur : [réponse du serveur espion]
  • Line 7: The client successfully received the document sent by the spy server.

In the first terminal, the spy server displayed what it received:

> php spy-server.php 100
Serveur espion en attente d'un client sur le port 100
Client connecté : 127.0.0.1:49512
--- lignes reçues
GET /php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/02/date-time-server.php HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:100
Accept: */*
User-Agent: Symfony HttpClient (Curl)
Accept-Encoding: gzip

--- fin de la communication
  • Line 5: The command HTTP GET generated by the client script;
  • Line 6: The header [Host] specifies the target machine and port;
  • line 8: the Symfony client signature [HttpClient];
  • line 9: the client indicates that it accepts a compressed response in the [gzip] format;
  • line 10: the empty line that ends the headers. A GET request has no document.

docs.title: 17.6.3. The Server Script – Version 2
docs.text:
By default, the functions for writing a web script are not object-oriented. On the server side, this means you end up mixing classes with traditional PHP functions. To achieve a more consistent coding style, we’ll use the [HttpFoundation] library from the Symfony framework. It encapsulates all the standard PHP functions of a web script within a system of classes and interfaces: the [Request] class represents the client request, and the [Response] class represents the server response. The library’s documentation is available at https://symfony.com/doc/current/components/http_foundation.html.

Like [HttpClient], the [HttpFoundation] library (version 8) is already installed in the [vendor] folder. It was likely installed using the following command:

composer require symfony/http-foundation

The second version of the [date-time-server-2.php] server is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// Use of the Symfony library [HttpFoundation]

// dependencies
require_once __DIR__ . '/../../vendor/autoload.php';

use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;

// time zone used by date functions
date_default_timezone_set('Europe/Paris');

// The response: content, status code, headers HTTP
$response = new Response(
    content: date("d/m/y H:i:s", time()),
    status: Response::HTTP_OK,
    headers: ['Content-Type' => 'text/plain'],
);
// The text sent is encoded in UTF-8
$response->setCharset('UTF-8');

// the response is sent
$response->send();

Comments

  • Line 8: Loading the libraries installed by [Composer]. The script is in the [scripts-web/02] folder: the [vendor] folder is two levels above;
  • Line 10: The [Response] class in the [HttpFoundation] library handles the entire response to the web service clients;
  • Lines 16–20: Creation of the response. The constructor of the [Response] class has three parameters: the document sent to the client (here, the date and time), the response status code (here, the constant [Response::HTTP_OK], which is 200), and an array of headers HTTP. We use the named arguments of PHP 8.0 ([content:], [status:], [headers:]): they make the call more readable and eliminate the need to follow the parameter order;
  • line 22: the response is text UTF-8. [HttpFoundation] will add [charset=UTF-8] to the header [Content-Type];
  • line 25: The response is sent to the client: the status line, the headers, and then the document. The method [send] uses the functions [http_response_code], [header], and [print], which we would have used ourselves.

With [curl]:

> curl -i http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/02/date-time-server-2.php
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:31:46 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.5.11
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
Vary: Accept-Encoding
Connection: close
Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8

01/10/26 17:31:46
  • line 2: response code 200;
  • the header [Cache-Control] was added by [HttpFoundation]. It indicates that the response must not be cached by an intermediary (a proxy);
  • the header [Content-type] is the one set by the script, supplemented by the character set;
  • The last line is the document.

docs.title: 17.6.4. The client script – version 2
docs.text:
The client script remains unchanged. It is simply given a different configuration file, [config-date-time-client-2.json]:

{
    "url": "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/02/date-time-server-2.php"
}

The results are the same as in Version 1:

> php date-time-client.php config-date-time-client-2.json
---Réponse avec statut : 200
---Entêtes de la réponse
date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:55:26 GMT
server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
x-powered-by: PHP/8.5.11
cache-control: no-cache, private
vary: Accept-Encoding
content-encoding: gzip
connection: close
content-type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8
---Réponse du serveur : [01/10/26 18:55:26]

docs.title: 17.7. A JSON data server
docs.text:
A web script’s response may consist of multiple data elements that can be organized into arrays and objects. The script can then send these various elements within a string JSON, which the client will decode.

php8-oct-2026
├── scripts-console
│   └── clients-web
│       └── 03
│           ├── config-json-client.json
│           ├── json-client.php
│           └── Personne.php
└── scripts-web
    └── 03
        ├── json-server.php
        └── Personne.php

docs.title: 17.7.1. The server-side script
docs.text:
The [json-server.php] script uses the following [Personne] class:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace Modèles;

class Personne implements \JsonSerializable
{
     // constructor with property promotion
     // Properties are readable from anywhere but can only be modified within the class
    public function __construct(
        public private(set) string $nom = "",
        public private(set) string $prénom = "",
        public private(set) int $âge = 0,
    ) {
    }

     // conversion of an associative array to an object [Personne]
    public static function fromArray(array $assoc): static
    {
         // The array keys become named arguments of the constructor
        return new static(...$assoc);
    }

     // setter for age
    public function setÂge(int $âge): static
    {
        $this->âge = $âge;
        return $this;
    }

     // toString
    public function __toString(): string
    {
        return "Personne [$this->prénom, $this->nom, $this->âge]";
    }

     // implements the interface JsonSerializable
    public function jsonSerialize(): array
    {
         // Returns an associative array with the object’s properties as keys
         // This array can then be encoded as JSON
        return get_object_vars($this);
    }

     // conversion of a string JSON to an object [Personne]
    public static function jsonUnserialize(string $json): static
    {
        return static::fromArray(json_decode($json, true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR));
    }
}

Comments

  • line 5: The class belongs to the [Modèles] namespace. PHP allows accented characters in identifiers;
  • line 7: The class implements the PHP [JsonSerializable] interface. This requires it to implement the [jsonSerialize] method (lines 39–43). The method must return a value that will be serialized in JSON, in this case an associative array. When the expression [json_encode($personne)] is used, the function [json_encode] checks whether the class [Personne] implements the interface [JsonSerializable]. If so, the expression becomes [json_encode($personne->jsonSerialize())];
  • lines 11–15: the constructor uses property promotion from PHP 8.0: each parameter preceded by a visibility specifier declares a property and initializes it. All three parameters have a default value;
  • line 12: asymmetric visibility, introduced with PHP 8.4: the property is readable from anywhere ([public]) but can only be modified within the class ([private(set)]). We can therefore write [$personne->nom] for reading, without a getter, but not [$personne->nom = "x"] outside the class. The PHP 7 from 2019 required us to declare private properties and write a getter for each one;
  • lines 19–22: a constructor (also called a factory) for a [Personne] object based on an associative array. The expression [new static(...$assoc)] passes the elements of the array to the constructor. Since PHP 8.1, the [...] operator accepts arrays with string keys: each key becomes a named argument. Thus, [Personne::fromArray(["nom" => "x", "âge" => 3])] is equivalent to [new Personne(nom: "x", âge: 3)]. A key that is not a constructor parameter causes an error. Version PHP 7 of the class copied the array elements into properties with arbitrary names, which could create dynamic properties—a feature that has been deprecated since PHP 8.2;
  • lines 26–29: the class’s only setter. It returns the object itself (return type [static]), which allows for chained calls;
  • line 43: the function [get_object_vars] returns the object’s associative array [propriété => valeur];
  • line 47: the static function [jsonUnserialize] allows you to create a [Personne] object from its string JSON.

The script [json-server.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// dependencies
require_once __DIR__ . '/../../vendor/autoload.php';
require_once __DIR__ . '/Personne.php';

use Modèles\Personne;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;

// creating a Person object
$personne = new Personne(nom: "de la Hûche", prénom: "jean-paul", âge: 27);
// an associative array
$assoc = [
    "attr1" => "value1",
    "attr2" => [
        "prenom" => "Jean-Paul",
        "nom" => "de la Hûche",
    ],
];
// the response is the string JSON from an array
$response = new Response(
    content: json_encode([$personne, $assoc], JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR),
    headers: ['Content-Type' => 'application/json'],
);
$response->setCharset('UTF-8');

// sending the response
$response->send();

Comments

  • lines 7 and 9: the [Personne] class is imported;
  • Line 13: A [Personne] object is created with named arguments;
  • Lines 15–21: A two-level associative array is created;
  • Line 24: The document sent to the client is the string JSON from an array:
    • the element [$personne] will be serialized to JSON using its method [jsonSerialize];
    • the element [$assoc] will be natively serialized to JSON;
    • the option [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR] causes [json_encode] to throw an exception in the event of an error (for example, a string that is not in the UTF-8 format) instead of returning [false];
  • Line 25: It specifies that the document is of type [application/json]. Upon receiving this header, browsers render the string JSON.

If you request this script using a browser (Chrome in this case), you get the following response:

Note the encoding of accented characters: by default, [json_encode] replaces any character that is not ASCII with its Unicode sequence [\uXXXX] ([û] becomes [\u00fb]). The [Pretty-print] field in Chrome displays the indented JSON. With [curl]:

> curl -i http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/03/json-server.php
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:31:46 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.5.11
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
Connection: close
Content-Type: application/json

[{"nom":"de la H\u00fbche","pr\u00e9nom":"jean-paul","\u00e2ge":27},{"attr1":"value1","attr2":{"prenom":"Jean-Paul","nom":"de la H\u00fbche"}}]
  • the header [Content-Type] specifies the document type as [application/json];
  • the last line is the received string JSON.

docs.title: 17.7.2. The client
docs.text:
The client [json-client.php] is configured by the following file: JSON [config-json-client.json]:

{
    "url": "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/03/json-server.php"
}

It uses a copy of the [Personne] class from the server, located in its folder. The [json-client.php] script is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// client of a service JSON

// dependencies
require_once __DIR__ . '/../../../vendor/autoload.php';
require_once __DIR__ . '/Personne.php';

use Modèles\Personne;
use Symfony\Component\HttpClient\HttpClient;
use Symfony\Contracts\HttpClient\Exception\ExceptionInterface;

// client configuration
const CONFIG_FILE_NAME = "config-json-client.json";

// retrieve the configuration
if (!file_exists(CONFIG_FILE_NAME)) {
    print "Le fichier de configuration [" . CONFIG_FILE_NAME . "] n'existe pas\n";
    exit(1);
}
try {
    $config = json_decode(file_get_contents(CONFIG_FILE_NAME), true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
} catch (JsonException $ex) {
    print "Erreur lors de l'exploitation du fichier de configuration JSON [" . CONFIG_FILE_NAME . "] : {$ex->getMessage()}\n";
    exit(1);
}

// creating a client HTTP
$httpClient = HttpClient::create();

try {
     // sending the request
    $response = $httpClient->request('GET', $config['url']);
     // response status
    $statusCode = $response->getStatusCode();
    print "---Réponse avec statut : $statusCode\n";
     // retrieve the headers
    print "---Entêtes de la réponse\n";
    foreach ($response->getHeaders() as $name => $values) {
        print "$name: $values[0]\n";
    }
     // retrieve the response body JSON in the form of an array PHP
    [$personne, $assoc] = $response->toArray();
     // an object is instantiated from the array of its properties
    $personne = Personne::fromArray($personne);
     // display the server's response
    print "---Réponse du serveur\n";
    print "$personne\n";
    print "tableau=" . json_encode($assoc, JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR | JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE) . "\n";
} catch (ExceptionInterface $ex) {
     // We display the error
    print "Erreur de communication avec le serveur : {$ex->getMessage()}\n";
    exit(2);
}

Comments

  • lines 9 and 11: import of the [Personne] class;
  • Line 16: This client always uses the same configuration file, whose name is a constant;
  • line 31: creation of the HTTP client;
  • Line 45: The [toArray] method in the response decodes the received JSON document and returns the corresponding PHP array. It throws an exception if the document is not of type JSON. We know that what was encoded is an array with two elements. The [[$personne, $assoc] = …] assignment by decomposition (also known as destructuring) assigns these two elements to two variables. It replaces the old syntax [list($personne, $assoc) = …];
  • line 47: an object [Personne] is created from the array of its properties, to be displayed later (line 50). The object is converted to a string using its method [__toString];
  • line 51: the second associative array is displayed. The [print] instruction cannot display arrays. Therefore, this array is converted to a string using JSON. To preserve accented characters as-is, the option [JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE] must be added. We have seen that without this option, accented characters are encoded in the string JSON.

Running the client-side script yields the following results:

> php json-client.php
---Réponse avec statut : 200
---Entêtes de la réponse
date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:55:26 GMT
server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
x-powered-by: PHP/8.5.11
cache-control: no-cache, private
connection: close
content-type: application/json
---Réponse du serveur
Personne [jean-paul, de la Hûche, 27]
tableau={"attr1":"value1","attr2":{"prenom":"Jean-Paul","nom":"de la Hûche"}}

In the last two lines, the accented characters were correctly retrieved.

docs.title: 17.8. Retrieving Environment Variables from the Web Service
docs.text:
A server-side script runs in a web environment that it can access. This environment is stored in the array [$_SERVER], a global variable of PHP. If we use the [HttpFoundation] library, this environment is found in the [server] property of the [Request] object, which represents the HTTP request processed by the web script.

php8-oct-2026
├── scripts-console
│   └── clients-web
│       └── 04
│           ├── config-env-client.json
│           └── env-client.php
└── scripts-web
    └── 04
        └── env-server.php

docs.title: 17.8.1. The server-side script
docs.text:
We are writing a server application that sends its execution environment to its clients. The web script [env-server.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// dependencies
require_once __DIR__ . '/../../vendor/autoload.php';

use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;

// retrieve the request
$request = Request::createFromGlobals();
// the response is the string JSON from the script's environment
$response = new Response(
    content: json_encode($request->server->all(), JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR | JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES),
    headers: ['Content-Type' => 'application/json'],
);
$response->setCharset('UTF-8');
// sending the response
$response->send();
  • Line 12: We create an object of type [Request] that encapsulates all available information about the HTTP request received by the web script, as well as its execution environment. The static method [createFromGlobals] constructs this object from the global variables of PHP: [$_GET], [$_POST], [$_COOKIE], [$_FILES], and [$_SERVER];
  • Line 15: The information sent to the client is the string JSON from the object [$request->server], which represents the web script's runtime environment. It is an object of type [ServerBag], a kind of dictionary. [$request->server->all()], on the other hand, is a true associative array—the contents of [ServerBag]. Without [HttpFoundation], we would have written [json_encode($_SERVER)]. The [JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES] option prevents the [/] characters in the paths from being encoded as [\/];
  • Line 20: The response is sent.

If you request this script using a browser, it displays the JSON dictionary of environment variables.

docs.title: 17.8.2. The client script
docs.text:
The client script [env-client.php] is configured by the following file: JSON [config-env-client.json]:

{
    "url": "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/04/env-server.php",
    "display": [
        "HTTP_HOST", "HTTP_USER_AGENT", "HTTP_ACCEPT_ENCODING",
        "SERVER_SOFTWARE", "SERVER_NAME", "SERVER_ADDR", "SERVER_PORT",
        "REMOTE_ADDR", "REMOTE_PORT", "REQUEST_SCHEME", "SERVER_ADMIN",
        "SCRIPT_FILENAME", "SERVER_PROTOCOL", "REQUEST_METHOD", "QUERY_STRING",
        "REQUEST_URI", "SCRIPT_NAME", "PHP_SELF", "REQUEST_TIME_FLOAT"
    ]
}
  • Line 2: the URL of the server script;
  • lines 3–9: the names of the environment variables that the client will display. Without this key, it displays all of them.

The client script [env-client.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// server script environment

// dependencies
require_once __DIR__ . '/../../../vendor/autoload.php';

use Symfony\Component\HttpClient\HttpClient;
use Symfony\Contracts\HttpClient\Exception\ExceptionInterface;

// client configuration
const CONFIG_FILE_NAME = "config-env-client.json";

// retrieving the configuration
if (!file_exists(CONFIG_FILE_NAME)) {
    print "Le fichier de configuration [" . CONFIG_FILE_NAME . "] n'existe pas\n";
    exit(1);
}
try {
    $config = json_decode(file_get_contents(CONFIG_FILE_NAME), true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
} catch (JsonException $ex) {
    print "Erreur lors de l'exploitation du fichier de configuration JSON [" . CONFIG_FILE_NAME . "] : {$ex->getMessage()}\n";
    exit(1);
}

// creating a client HTTP
$httpClient = HttpClient::create();
try {
     // sending the request to the server
    $response = $httpClient->request('GET', $config['url']);
     // response status
    $statusCode = $response->getStatusCode();
    print "---Réponse avec statut : $statusCode\n";
     // retrieve the headers
    print "---Entêtes de la réponse\n";
    foreach ($response->getHeaders() as $name => $values) {
        print "$name: $values[0]\n";
    }
     // Display the server's response
    print "---Réponse du serveur\n";
    $env = $response->toArray();
     // only the variables listed in the configuration are retained (all of them if there is no list)
    if (isset($config['display'])) {
        $env = array_filter($env, fn(string $key): bool => in_array($key, $config['display'], true), ARRAY_FILTER_USE_KEY);
    }
    foreach ($env as $key => $value) {
        print "[$key]=>$value\n";
    }
} catch (ExceptionInterface $ex) {
     // display the error
    print "Erreur de communication avec le serveur : {$ex->getMessage()}\n";
    exit(2);
}

Comments

  • line 43: the server’s response JSON is decoded. This yields an associative array;
  • Lines 45–46: The environment is long. If the configuration file contains a list of variable names ([display]), only those names are retained. The function [array_filter] retains the elements of an associative array for which the function passed as a parameter returns [true]. With the option [ARRAY_FILTER_USE_KEY], this function receives the element’s key rather than its value;
  • lines 48–49: all values of this associative array are displayed.

The following console output is obtained (the path to the [php8-oct-2026] folder is abbreviated to [.../php8-oct-2026]):

> php env-client.php

connection: close

---Réponse du serveur
[HTTP_HOST]=>localhost
[HTTP_USER_AGENT]=>Symfony HttpClient (Curl)
[HTTP_ACCEPT_ENCODING]=>gzip
[SERVER_SOFTWARE]=>Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
[SERVER_NAME]=>localhost

[SERVER_PORT]=>80
[REMOTE_ADDR]=>127.0.0.1
[REQUEST_SCHEME]=>http

Here is the meaning of these variables, and a few others that the server also sends:
