In this case, the client was on the same machine as the serverREMOTE_PORTthe port from which the client made its requestDOCUMENT_ROOTthe root of the directory tree for documents served by the web server, [<laragon>/www] along with [Laragon]REQUEST_SCHEMEthe protocol of the requested URL: [http] or [https]SERVER_ADMINthe web server administrator's email addressSCRIPT_FILENAMEThe full path to the server scriptSERVER_PROTOCOLthe version of the HTTP protocol used by the web serverREQUEST_METHODThe HTTP method used by the client: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE…QUERY_STRINGParameters sent in URL: GET /url?parametersREQUEST_URIthe URL requested by the client. If the client requests the URL [http://machine:port/uri], we have REQUEST_URI=/uriSCRIPT_NAMEthe path to the script from the server root: [$_SERVER['SCRIPT_FILENAME']] = [$_SERVER['DOCUMENT_ROOT'] . $_SERVER['SCRIPT_NAME']]REQUEST_TIME_FLOATthe time of the request, in seconds since January 1, 1970, with microsecond precision

docs.title: 17.9. Server retrieval of parameters sent by a client
17.9.1. Introduction
docs.text:
In the HTTP protocol, a client has two methods for passing parameters to the web server:

  • it requests the URL service in the form
GET url?param1=val1&param2=val2&param3=val3… HTTP/1.1

where the [vali] values must first be encoded so that certain reserved characters are replaced by their hexadecimal values;

  • it requests the service’s URL in the form
POST url HTTP/1.1

then, among the HTTP headers sent to the server, includes the following header:

Content-Length: N

The rest of the headers sent by the client end with a blank line. The client can then send its data in the form

param1=val1&param2=val2&param3=val3…

where the values [vali] must, as with the GET method, be encoded beforehand. The number of bytes sent to the server must be N, where N is the value declared in the [Content-Length] header.

The PHP script of the web service that retrieves the [parami] parameters sent by the client obtains their values from the arrays:

  • [$_GET['parami']] for the parameters of URL;
  • [$_POST['parami']] for the parameters sent in a POST order document;

This applies to the basic functions of PHP. If the [HttpFoundation] library is used, these parameters are found in:

  • [$request->query->get('parami')] for the parameters of URL;
  • [$request->request->get('parami')] for the parameters of the document associated with a POST command;

where [$request] is the [Request] object that represents all the information about the request received by the web script.

php8-oct-2026
├── scripts-console
│   └── clients-web
│       └── 05
│           ├── config-espion.json
│           ├── config-parameters-client.json
│           ├── parameters-get-client-2.php
│           ├── parameters-get-client.php
│           ├── parameters-mixte-get-client.php
│           ├── parameters-mixte-post-client.php
│           └── parameters-post-client.php
└── scripts-web
    └── 05
        ├── parameters-server-natif.php
        └── parameters-server.php

docs.title: 17.9.2. The GET client – version 1
docs.text:
Client scripts are configured by the following JSON [config-parameters-client.json] file:

{
    "url-get": "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server.php",
    "url-post": "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server.php"
}
  • Line 2: the URL of the target web script for clients GET;
  • Line 3: The URL web script targets clients POST.

Clients send three [prenom, nom, age] parameters to the server. The [parameters-get-client.php] client is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// GET client for a web server—the parameters are encoded by the script

// dependencies
require_once __DIR__ . '/../../../vendor/autoload.php';

use Symfony\Component\HttpClient\HttpClient;
use Symfony\Contracts\HttpClient\Exception\ExceptionInterface;

// the configuration file: first command-line argument if it exists
$configFileName = $argv[1] ?? "config-parameters-client.json";

// retrieve the configuration
if (!file_exists($configFileName)) {
    print "Le fichier de configuration [$configFileName] n'existe pas\n";
    exit(1);
}
try {
    $config = json_decode(file_get_contents($configFileName), true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
} catch (JsonException $ex) {
    print "Erreur lors de l'exploitation du fichier de configuration JSON [$configFileName] : {$ex->getMessage()}\n";
    exit(1);
}

// creates a client HTTP
$httpClient = HttpClient::create();

try {
     // parameters to send
    [$prenom, $nom, $age] = ["jean-paul", "de la hûche", 45];
     // encodes the parameters
    $parameters = "prenom=" . urlencode($prenom)
        . "&nom=" . urlencode($nom)
        . "&age=$age";
     // Send the request
    $response = $httpClient->request("GET", $config["url-get"] . "?$parameters");
     // Response status
    $statusCode = $response->getStatusCode();
    print "---Réponse avec statut : $statusCode\n";
     // retrieves the headers
    print "---Entêtes de la réponse\n";
    foreach ($response->getHeaders() as $name => $values) {
        print "$name: $values[0]\n";
    }
     // display the server response
    print "---Réponse du serveur [{$response->getContent()}]\n";
} catch (ExceptionInterface $ex) {
     // display the error
    print "Erreur de communication avec le serveur : {$ex->getMessage()}\n";
    exit(2);
}

Comments

  • line 14: As with the date/time client, the name of the configuration file can be passed as an argument;
  • line 33: the three parameters are assigned by unpacking an array;
  • Lines 35–37: Encoding of the parameters sent to the server. The parameters [$prenom] and [$nom], which may contain any characters, are encoded using the function [urlencode]: all characters other than the letters and digits ASCII and the characters [-_.] are replaced by [%xx], where [xx] is the hexadecimal value of the byte; a character such as UTF-8 ([û]), encoded over two bytes, thus becomes [%C3%BB]. Spaces are replaced by the character [+];
  • line 39: the requested URL is [URL?paramètres], where [paramètres] is in the form [prenom=val1&nom=val2&age=val3];
  • line 49: the client will simply display the server’s response.

Note: The [http_build_query] function of PHP constructs the same string from an associative array: [http_build_query(["prenom" => $prenom, "nom" => $nom, "age" => $age])].

You might be curious to see what the server receives when a configured GET request is sent. To do this, we launch our [spy-server.php] sniffer server on port 100, in a terminal window open to the [clients-web/02] directory:

php spy-server.php 100

The file [config-espion.json] designates this server for the clients GET and POST:

{
    "url-get": "http://localhost:100/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server.php",
    "url-post": "http://localhost:100/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server.php"
}

We run the client using the command [php parameters-get-client.php config-espion.json]. The spy server displays the following information:

> php spy-server.php 100
Serveur espion en attente d'un client sur le port 100
Client connecté : 127.0.0.1:34944
--- lignes reçues
GET /php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server.php?prenom=jean-paul&nom=de+la+h%C3%BBche&age=45 HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:100
Accept: */*
User-Agent: Symfony HttpClient (Curl)
Accept-Encoding: gzip

--- fin de la communication
  • Line 5: The configured command GET sent by the client. The encoding of certain characters is clearly visible.

docs.title: 17.9.3. The GET / POST server
docs.text:
The server script [parameters-server.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// dependencies
require_once __DIR__ . '/../../vendor/autoload.php';

use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;

// retrieve the request
$request = Request::createFromGlobals();
// retrieve the request parameters
$getParameters = $request->query->all();
$bodyParameters = $request->request->all();

// the response: an array encoded in JSON
$response = new Response(
    content: json_encode([
        "method" => $request->getMethod(),
        "uri" => $request->getRequestUri(),
        "getParameters" => $getParameters,
        "bodyParameters" => $bodyParameters,
    ], JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR | JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE | JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES),
    headers: ['Content-Type' => 'application/json'],
);
$response->setCharset('UTF-8');
// sending the response
$response->send();

Comments

  • line 12: creation of the [Request] object from the web script. This object encapsulates all the information that the web script received from the client;
  • Line 14: The [$request->query] object is of type [InputBag] and contains the parameters of URL. The expression [$request->query->get('X')] retrieves the parameter named X from the [prenom=val1&nom=val2&age=val3] parameters. The expression [$request->query->all()] retrieves the array of all these parameters;
  • Line 15: The object [$request->request], which is also of type [InputBag], collects the parameters sent in the client’s document. These parameters are also said to be "posted." The expression [$request->request->get('X')] returns the posted parameter named X, and the expression [$request->request->all()] returns an array of all posted parameters;
  • lines 20–23: The server returns to the client all the parameters it received, the [GET / POST / …] method used by the client, obtained via [$request->getMethod()], and the requested URI, obtained via [$request->getRequestUri()]. The document sent to the client is the string JSON from an associative array, some of whose values are themselves associative arrays. The option [JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE] specifies that Unicode characters (such as accented characters) be sent as-is and not encoded;
  • line 25: the client is notified that JSON will be sent;
  • Line 29: The response is sent to the client.

Running the client script [parameters-get-client.php] with its default configuration yields the following results:

> php parameters-get-client.php
---Réponse avec statut : 200
---Entêtes de la réponse
date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:55:27 GMT
server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
x-powered-by: PHP/8.5.11
cache-control: no-cache, private
connection: close
content-type: application/json
---Réponse du serveur [{"method":"GET","uri":"/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server.php?prenom=jean-paul&nom=de+la+h%C3%BBche&age=45","getParameters":{"prenom":"jean-paul","nom":"de la hûche","age":"45"},"bodyParameters":[]}]
  • last line:
    • [method]: the method is GET;
    • [uri]: the URL-encoded parameters of the GET request are visible in the requested URI;
    • [getParameters]: the array of parameters from URL, decoded by PHP;
    • [bodyParameters]: the array of posted parameters; it is empty.

The server can also be tested with [curl]. The quotation marks around URL are necessary because the character [&] has a special meaning for the command interpreter:

> curl -i "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server.php?prenom=jean-paul&nom=de+la+h%C3%BBche&age=45"
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:31:46 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.5.11
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
Connection: close
Content-Type: application/json

{"method":"GET","uri":"/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server.php?prenom=jean-paul&nom=de+la+h%C3%BBche&age=45","getParameters":{"prenom":"jean-paul","nom":"de la hûche","age":"45"},"bodyParameters":[]}

docs.title: 17.9.3.1. A version without HttpFoundation
docs.text:
The script [parameters-server-natif.php] performs the same task using only the functions from PHP:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// the same as [parameters-server.php], but using only the functions of PHP

// a specific, filtered parameter: the [age] parameter of GET must be an integer
// filter_input returns null if the parameter is missing, and false if it is invalid
$age = filter_input(INPUT_GET, 'age', FILTER_VALIDATE_INT);

// the response is JSON
header('Content-Type: application/json');
print json_encode([
    "method" => $_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD'],
    "uri" => $_SERVER['REQUEST_URI'],
    "getParameters" => $_GET,
    "bodyParameters" => $_POST,
    "age" => $age,
], JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR | JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE | JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES);
  • Line 8: The arrays [$_GET] and [$_POST] contain character strings, regardless of the expected value type. The [filter_input] function reads a parameter and validates it: here, the [age] parameter of URL ([INPUT_GET]) must be an integer ([FILTER_VALIDATE_INT]). It returns the integer if the parameter is valid, [false] if it is not, and [null] if it is missing;
  • Line 12: the [Content-Type] header in the response;
  • line 14: the HTTP method in the request;
  • line 15: the requested URI;
  • lines 16 and 17: the parameters for URL and those for the document.

Two requests made using [curl]:

> curl "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server-natif.php?prenom=jean-paul&age=45"
{"method":"GET","uri":"/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server-natif.php?prenom=jean-paul&age=45","getParameters":{"prenom":"jean-paul","age":"45"},"bodyParameters":[],"age":45}

> curl -d prenom=jean-paul "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server-natif.php?age=4x"
{"method":"POST","uri":"/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server-natif.php?age=4x","getParameters":{"age":"4x"},"bodyParameters":{"prenom":"jean-paul"},"age":false}
  • In the first query, the parameter [age] is [45]: it is rendered as the integer 45 rather than the string ["45"];
  • In the second query, the option [-d] results in the query being rendered as POST: the parameter [prenom] is in [$_POST], while the parameter [age] from URL is in [$_GET]. Its value, [4x], is not an integer: [filter_input] results in [false].

In the rest of this course, we’ll use [HttpFoundation], which has a more consistent code. But it’s good to understand what’s behind it.

docs.title: 17.9.4. The GET client – version 2
docs.text:
In the previous version of the client script, we URL-encoded the parameters sent to the server ourselves, for educational purposes. The [HttpClient] object can handle this task on its own. This is the [parameters-get-client-2.php] script, identical to the previous one except for the following lines:

try {
     // parameters to send
    [$prenom, $nom, $age] = ["jean-paul", "de la hûche", 45];
     // the request is sent to the server
    $response = $httpClient->request("GET", $config["url-get"], [
         // parameters from URL (query)
        "query" => [
            "prenom" => $prenom,
            "nom" => $nom,
            "age" => $age,
        ],
    ]);
  • lines 37–41: The third parameter of the [request] method is an array of options. The [query] option is the array of parameters to be added to URL. The [HttpClient] object handles their encoding itself.

Results:

> php parameters-get-client-2.php
---Réponse avec statut : 200
---Entêtes de la réponse
date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:55:27 GMT
server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
x-powered-by: PHP/8.5.11
cache-control: no-cache, private
connection: close
content-type: application/json
---Réponse du serveur [{"method":"GET","uri":"/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server.php?prenom=jean-paul&nom=de%20la%20h%C3%BBche&age=45","getParameters":{"prenom":"jean-paul","nom":"de la hûche","age":"45"},"bodyParameters":[]}]
  • Last line: Note that [HttpClient] encoded the spaces using [%20] rather than [+]. Both encodings are accepted by PHP.

docs.title: 17.9.5. The POST client
docs.text:
A client named HTTP sends the following text sequence to the web server: HTTP headers, blank line, document. In the previous client, this sequence was as follows:

GET /url?paramètres HTTP/1.1
… autres entêtes HTTP
ligne vide

There was no document. There is another way to transmit parameters, known as the POST method. In this case, the text sequence sent to the web server is as follows:

POST /url HTTP/1.1
… autres entêtes HTTP
ligne vide
paramètres

This time, the parameters—which, for the GET client, were included in the first line of the request—are part of the document sent after the headers in the POST client.

The script for client POST [parameters-post-client.php] differs from client GET—version 2—only in the following lines:

try {
     // parameters to be sent
    [$prenom, $nom, $age] = ["jean-paul", "de la hûche", 45];
     // Sending the request to the server
    $response = $httpClient->request("POST", $config["url-post"], [
         // document parameters (body)
        "body" => [
            "prenom" => $prenom,
            "nom" => $nom,
            "age" => $age,
        ],
    ]);
  • line 35: we now have a HTTP request of type POST;
  • lines 37–41: the option [body] is the body of the request POST: this is the document sent by the client to the server. When this option is an array, [HttpClient] URL-encodes it and adds the header [Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded]. Here, three parameters are sent: [prenom, nom, age].

The results of executing the client-side script are as follows:

> php parameters-post-client.php
---Réponse avec statut : 200
---Entêtes de la réponse
date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:55:27 GMT
server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
x-powered-by: PHP/8.5.11
cache-control: no-cache, private
connection: close
content-type: application/json
---Réponse du serveur [{"method":"POST","uri":"/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server.php","getParameters":[],"bodyParameters":{"prenom":"jean-paul","nom":"de la hûche","age":"45"}}]
  • Last line: the method is [POST] and the parameters are of type [bodyParameters]. There are no [getParameters] parameters, as shown by [uri].

With [curl], the [-d] option sends a parameter via a POST request, and the [--data-urlencode] option does the same by URL-encoding its value:

> curl -i -d prenom=jean-paul --data-urlencode "nom=de la hûche" -d age=45 http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server.php
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:31:46 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.5.11
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
Connection: close
Content-Type: application/json

{"method":"POST","uri":"/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server.php","getParameters":[],"bodyParameters":{"prenom":"jean-paul","nom":"de la hûche","age":"45"}}

Let’s see what the server receives during a POST request. We restart the spy server on port 100 and run the client with the [php parameters-post-client.php config-espion.json] command. The spy server displays the following information:

> php spy-server.php 100
Serveur espion en attente d'un client sur le port 100
Client connecté : 127.0.0.1:34950
--- lignes reçues
POST /php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server.php HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:100
Accept: */*
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
User-Agent: Symfony HttpClient (Curl)
Accept-Encoding: gzip
Content-Length: 44

prenom=jean-paul&nom=de+la+h%C3%BBche&age=45
--- fin de la communication
  • Line 5: the command POST;
  • line 8: the header HTTP [Content-Type] specifies the type of document sent by the client. The type [application/x-www-form-urlencoded] denotes URL-encoded text;
  • line 11: the header HTTP [Content-Length] specifies the number of bytes in the document that the client will send to the server;
  • line 12: the empty line that marks the end of the headers HTTP and the beginning of the 44-byte document;
  • line 13: the document: the URL-encoded string of parameters. The reader can verify that it indeed has 44 characters.

docs.title: 17.9.6. A mixed POST client
docs.text:
In a POST, you can mix parameters encoded in the URL with parameters encoded in the document sent by the client after the HTTP headers. Here is an example of a [parameters-mixte-post-client.php]:

try {
     // parameters to send
    [$prenom, $nom, $age] = ["jean-paul", "de la hûche", 45];
     // Send the request to the server
    $response = $httpClient->request("POST", $config["url-post"], [
         // document parameters (body)
        "body" => [
            "prenom" => $prenom,
            "nom" => $nom,
            "age" => $age,
        ],
         // URL (query) parameters
        "query" => [
            "prenom2" => $prenom,
            "nom2" => $nom,
            "age2" => $age,
        ],
    ]);

Comments

  • line 35: a POST request;
  • lines 37–41: the URL-encoded parameters in the body (document) of the request;
  • lines 43–47: the URL-encoded parameters in the URL.

Upon execution, the following console output is generated:

> php parameters-mixte-post-client.php
---Réponse avec statut : 200
---Entêtes de la réponse
date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:55:27 GMT
server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
x-powered-by: PHP/8.5.11
cache-control: no-cache, private
connection: close
content-type: application/json
---Réponse du serveur [{"method":"POST","uri":"/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server.php?prenom2=jean-paul&nom2=de%20la%20h%C3%BBche&age2=45","getParameters":{"prenom2":"jean-paul","nom2":"de la hûche","age2":"45"},"bodyParameters":{"prenom":"jean-paul","nom":"de la hûche","age":"45"}}]
  • Last line: We can see that the server was able to retrieve both types of parameters.

docs.title: 17.9.7. A mixed GET client
docs.text:
We’ll try doing the same thing with a GET request. The [parameters-mixte-get-client.php] script differs from the previous one only in its method:

     // the request is sent to the server
    $response = $httpClient->request("GET", $config["url-get"], [

Upon execution, we get the following console output:

> php parameters-mixte-get-client.php
---Réponse avec statut : 200
---Entêtes de la réponse
date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:55:27 GMT
server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
x-powered-by: PHP/8.5.11
cache-control: no-cache, private
connection: close
content-type: application/json
---Réponse du serveur [{"method":"GET","uri":"/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server.php?prenom2=jean-paul&nom2=de%20la%20h%C3%BBche&age2=45","getParameters":{"prenom2":"jean-paul","nom2":"de la hûche","age2":"45"},"bodyParameters":[]}]
  • Last line: We can see that the server did not process the URL-encoded parameters in the document sent by the client.

However, the server sniffer shows that the client did indeed send a 44-byte document:

> php spy-server.php 100
Serveur espion en attente d'un client sur le port 100
Client connecté : 127.0.0.1:34952
--- lignes reçues
GET /php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/05/parameters-server.php?prenom2=jean-paul&nom2=de%20la%20h%C3%BBche&age2=45 HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:100
Accept: */*
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
User-Agent: Symfony HttpClient (Curl)
Accept-Encoding: gzip
Content-Length: 44

prenom=jean-paul&nom=de+la+h%C3%BBche&age=45
--- fin de la communication

PHP only populates the array [$_POST] (and therefore [HttpFoundation] and the object [$request->request]) only starting with the request document POST. The request document GET is ignored.

Finally, which method should be used to send information to the server?

  • The [GET URL?param1=val1&param2=val2&…] method uses a configured URL that can serve as a link. This is its main advantage: the user can add such links to their bookmarks. It is designed for requests that read data without making any changes to the server;
  • in other applications, you may not want to display the parameters sent to the server in a URL. For security reasons, for example: URLs are stored in the browser history and in server log files. In such cases, use a [POST] method and include the URL-encoded parameters in the document sent to the server. This is also the method to use for requests that modify data on the server.

docs.title: 17.10. Web Session Management
docs.text:
In the previous client/server examples, the process worked as follows:

  • the client opens a connection to port 80 on the web server;
  • it sends the following text sequence: HTTP headers, an empty line, [document];
  • in response, the server sends a sequence of the same type;
  • the server closes the connection to the client;
  • the client closes the connection to the server.

If the same client makes a new request to the web server shortly thereafter, a new connection is established between the client and the server. The server cannot tell whether the connecting client has visited before or if this is the first request. Between connections, the server “forgets” its client. For this reason, the HTTP protocol is said to be a stateless protocol. However, it is useful for the server to remember its clients. For example, if an application is secure, the client will send the server a username and password to authenticate itself. If the server “forgets” its client between connections, the client would have to authenticate itself with every new connection, which is not feasible.

To track a client, the server proceeds as follows: when a client makes its first request, the server includes an identifier in its response, which the client must then send back with every subsequent request. Using this identifier—which is unique to each client—the server can recognize the client. It can then maintain a record for that client in the form of a memory entry uniquely associated with the client’s identifier.

Technically, this works as follows:

  • In the response to a new client, the server includes the header HTTP [Set-Cookie: MotClé=Identifiant]. It does this only on the first request;
  • in subsequent requests, the client will send its identifier via the header HTTP [Cookie: MotClé=Identifiant] so that the server can recognize it.

One might wonder how the server knows it is dealing with a new client rather than a returning one. It is the presence of the header HTTP [Cookie] in the client’s HTTP headers that indicates this. For a new client, this header is missing.

All connections made by a given client are referred to as a session.

php8-oct-2026
├── scripts-console
│   └── clients-web
│       └── 06
│           ├── config-session-client-07.json
│           ├── config-session-client-natif.json
│           ├── config-session-client.json
│           └── session-client.php
└── scripts-web
    ├── 06
    │   ├── phpinfo.php
    │   ├── session-config.php
    │   ├── session-server-natif.php
    │   └── session-server.php
    └── 07
        ├── Personne.php
        └── session-server.php

docs.title: 17.10.1. The configuration file [php.ini]
docs.text:
For session management to work correctly with PHP, you must verify that it is configured correctly. Its configuration file is [php.ini]. Depending on the execution context (console, web), the [php.ini] configuration file used may differ. To determine which one is used, run the following [phpinfo.php] script:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// Information about the PHP interpreter executing the script
phpinfo();

The [phpinfo] function provides information about the PHP interpreter that executes the script. In particular, on line [Loaded Configuration File], it provides the path to the [php.ini] configuration file being used. We have already used this function in a console environment when installing PHP. In a web environment, simply request URL and [http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/06/phpinfo.php] using a browser. With [Laragon], the [php.ini] used by the [Apache] server is the one from the folder of the selected PHP version ([<laragon>/bin/php/<version>/php.ini]). It can be opened via the [Laragon] menu: [PHP / php.ini].

This file contains a section named [Session]. Rather than copying it, the following script, [session-config.php], displays the actual values of the directives we are interested in:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// session configuration for the PHP interpreter on the web server
$config = ini_get_all('session', details: false);
// Only the directives covered in the course are displayed
$keys = [
    'session.save_handler', 'session.save_path', 'session.use_strict_mode',
    'session.use_cookies', 'session.use_only_cookies', 'session.name',
    'session.auto_start', 'session.cookie_lifetime', 'session.cookie_path',
    'session.cookie_domain', 'session.cookie_httponly', 'session.cookie_samesite',
    'session.serialize_handler', 'session.gc_probability', 'session.gc_divisor',
    'session.gc_maxlifetime', 'session.cache_limiter', 'session.cache_expire',
    'session.use_trans_sid',
];
header('Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8');
foreach ($keys as $key) {
    print "$key = " . var_export($config[$key], true) . "\n";
}
  • Line 6: The [ini_get_all] function returns the values of the configuration directives for an extension of PHP—in this case, the [session] extension. With [details: false], we obtain an array [directive => valeur];
  • line 19: the function [var_export] displays a value in the form of an expression PHP. An empty string thus appears as [''].

Result:

> curl http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/06/session-config.php
session.save_handler = 'files'
session.save_path = ''
session.use_strict_mode = '0'
session.use_cookies = '1'
session.use_only_cookies = '1'
session.name = 'PHPSESSID'
session.auto_start = '0'
session.cookie_lifetime = '0'
session.cookie_path = '/'
session.cookie_domain = ''
session.cookie_httponly = '0'
session.cookie_samesite = ''
session.serialize_handler = 'php'
session.gc_probability = '1'
session.gc_divisor = '100'
session.gc_maxlifetime = '1440'
session.cache_limiter = 'nocache'
session.cache_expire = '180'
session.use_trans_sid = '0'
  • Line 2: Data from a client session is saved to a file;
  • Line 3: The folder where session data is saved. If empty, it refers to the system’s temporary folder. In the configuration of [Laragon], it refers to a folder named [Laragon] (in the form [<laragon>/tmp]). If this folder does not exist, session management will not function;
  • line 4: In strict mode, the server rejects any session ID that it did not create itself. This is a safeguard against a so-called session fixation attack. It is recommended to enable this;
  • Lines 5–6: indicate that the session ID is managed solely by the headers HTTP, [Set-Cookie], and [Cookie];
  • line 7: the [Set-Cookie] header will be in the form [Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=identifiant_de_session];
  • Line 8: A client session is not started automatically. The server script must explicitly request it using the [session_start()] command;
  • line 9: The session cookie remains valid until the client browser is closed;
  • line 10: the path for which the session cookie must be sent back. If [session.cookie_path = /xxx], then every time the browser requests a URL of type [/xxx/yyy/zzz], it must send back the cookie. Here, the path [/] indicates that the cookie must be sent back for any URL on the site;
  • Lines 12–13: The [HttpOnly] attribute of the cookie makes it inaccessible to the JavaScript code on the page; the [SameSite] attribute prevents it from being sent in response to requests from other sites. These two attributes protect the session ID;
  • line 14: Objects in the session must be serialized in order to be stored in a file. PHP handles this serialization and deserialization;
  • Lines 15–17: Each time a session starts, PHP initiates, with probability [gc_probability / gc_divisor], a cleanup of session files older than [gc_maxlifetime] seconds: sessions that have been inactive for longer than this are lost.

Note: Section [Session] of the 2019 [php.ini] contained the directive [session.sid_bits_per_character = 5]. The directives [session.sid_length] and [session.sid_bits_per_character], which specified the length and character set of the session ID, have been deprecated since PHP 8.4: PHP now uses 32-character hexadecimal identifiers, which are sufficiently secure. These directives should no longer be used.

All of these settings can also be configured by the script itself when the session starts, as we will see later.

docs.title: 17.10.2.1. The server
docs.text:
Session ID management is transparent to a web service. This ID is managed by PHP. A web service accesses the client's session using the [session_start()] statement. From that point on, the web service can read from and write to the client’s session via the array [$_SESSION]. If the [HttpFoundation] library is used, the session is represented by an object of type [Session].

The following code, [session-server.php], demonstrates session-based management of three counters. With each new request, the web script increments these counters and stores them in the session so they can be retrieved during the next request.

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// dependencies
require_once __DIR__ . '/../../vendor/autoload.php';

use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// the client's session
$session = new Session();
$session->start();
// Three counters are managed in the session
if ($session->has("N1")) {
     // incrementing the counter N1
    $session->set("N1", $session->get("N1") + 1);
} else {
     // The counter N1 is not in the session—it is created
    $session->set("N1", 0);
}
if ($session->has("N2")) {
     // Incrementing counter N2
    $session->set("N2", $session->get("N2") + 1);
} else {
     // The counter N2 is not in a session—it is being created
    $session->set("N2", 10);
}
if ($session->has("N3")) {
     // Increment counter N3
    $session->set("N3", $session->get("N3") + 1);
} else {
     // The counter N3 is not in a session—it is created
    $session->set("N3", 100);
}
// The response is JSON, an array containing the three counters
$response = new Response(
    content: json_encode([
        "N1" => $session->get("N1"),
        "N2" => $session->get("N2"),
        "N3" => $session->get("N3"),
    ], JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR),
    headers: ['Content-Type' => 'application/json'],
);
$response->setCharset('UTF-8');

// Sending the response
$response->send();
  • Lines 12–13: A session is created and activated. The object [Session] encapsulates the session data corresponding to the session cookie sent by the client. If the client did not send such a cookie, then no data is stored in [Session]. The web script will include the header HTTP [Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=xxx] in its first response. In subsequent requests, the client will send the headers HTTP and [Cookie: PHPSESSID=xxx] to indicate the session whose content it wants to use. A session is a client’s memory;
  • Lines 15–20: We check whether the session has a key named [N1]. This will be the name of our first counter. If it does not exist, we assign it the value 0 and store it in the session. If it does exist, we:
    • retrieve it from the session;
    • increment its value by 1;
    • put it back into the session;
  • lines 22–34: We do the same for the other two counters, N2 and N3;
  • lines 37–44: The response will be the string JSON, which is an array containing the three counters;
  • line 48: the response is sent to the client. At the end of the script, the session data is saved by PHP to the session file.

In the client-server relationship, the management of the client session on the server depends on both parties, the client and the server:

  • the server is responsible for sending an identifier to the client upon its first request;
  • the client is responsible for sending this identifier back with each new request. If it fails to do so, the server will assume it is a new client and generate a new identifier for a new session.

Results

We use a web browser as the client. By default, the browser does indeed send back to the server the session identifiers that the server sends to it. As requests are made, the browser will receive the three counters sent by the server and see their values increment. The first request yields:

After reloading the page three times (F5), we get:

The fourth request shows that the counters have indeed been incremented. The counter values are indeed being stored across requests.

The browser’s developer tools (F12, [Réseau] tab) display the HTTP headers exchanged. Let’s examine them using [curl]. With the [-c cookies.txt] option, [curl] saves the cookies received from the server to the [cookies.txt] file; with the [-b cookies.txt] option, it sends the cookies from this file back to the server. It then behaves like a browser. First request:

> curl -i -c cookies.txt -b cookies.txt http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/06/session-server.php
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:31:46 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.5.11
Cache-Control: max-age=0, private, must-revalidate
Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=403de000aa6b2ee9ad770f2a00ffb773; path=/
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
Connection: close
Content-Type: application/json

{"N1":0,"N2":10,"N3":100}
  • The header [Set-Cookie] contains the session ID sent by the server in its response to the client’s first request;
  • the first header, [Cache-Control], is set by [HttpFoundation] at the start of the session: the response, specific to this client, must not be cached by an intermediary ([private]) and must be requested again from the server ([max-age=0]);
  • the last line contains the three initialized counters.

The file [cookies.txt] now contains the session cookie:

> type cookies.txt
# Netscape HTTP Cookie File
# https://curl.se/docs/http-cookies.html
# This file was generated by libcurl! Edit at your own risk.

localhost    FALSE    /    FALSE    0    PHPSESSID    403de000aa6b2ee9ad770f2a00ffb773

2nd request:

> curl -i -c cookies.txt -b cookies.txt http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/06/session-server.php
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:31:46 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.5.11
Cache-Control: max-age=0, private, must-revalidate
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
Connection: close
Content-Type: application/json

{"N1":1,"N2":11,"N3":101}
  • [curl] returned the session ID with the header HTTP [Cookie: PHPSESSID=…];
  • In its response, the web service no longer includes the [Set-Cookie] header. It is now the client’s responsibility to send the identifier with each of its requests;
  • Last line: the counters have been incremented.

docs.title: 17.10.2.2. The client
docs.text:
We are now writing a client-side script based on the previous server-side script. In managing the session, it must behave like a web browser:

  • In the server’s response to its first request, it must find the session ID that the server sends it. It knows it will find it in the header HTTP [Set-Cookie];
  • with each subsequent request, it must send the session ID it received back to the server. It will do so using the header HTTP [Cookie].

Client [session-client.php] is configured by the following file: JSON [config-session-client.json]:

{
    "url": "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/06/session-server.php"
}

The code for client [session-client.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// Web service client with session

// dependencies
require_once __DIR__ . '/../../../vendor/autoload.php';

use Symfony\Component\HttpClient\HttpClient;
use Symfony\Contracts\HttpClient\Exception\ExceptionInterface;

// the configuration file: first command-line argument if it exists
$configFileName = $argv[1] ?? "config-session-client.json";

// retrieve the configuration
if (!file_exists($configFileName)) {
    print "Le fichier de configuration [$configFileName] n'existe pas\n";
    exit(1);
}
try {
    $config = json_decode(file_get_contents($configFileName), true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
} catch (JsonException $ex) {
    print "Erreur lors de l'exploitation du fichier de configuration JSON [$configFileName] : {$ex->getMessage()}\n";
    exit(1);
}

// creating a client HTTP
$httpClient = HttpClient::create();
// the session cookie (not yet known)
$sessionCookie = null;
try {
     // we will make 10 requests
    for ($i = 0; $i < 10; $i++) {
         // Send the request to the server
        if ($sessionCookie === null) {
             // without a session cookie
            $response = $httpClient->request('GET', $config['url']);
        } else {
             // with the session cookie
            $response = $httpClient->request('GET', $config['url'], [
                'headers' => ['Cookie' => $sessionCookie],
            ]);
        }
         // response status
        $statusCode = $response->getStatusCode();
        print "---Réponse avec statut : $statusCode\n";
         // retrieve the headers
        print "---Entêtes de la réponse\n";
        $headers = $response->getHeaders();
        foreach ($headers as $name => $values) {
            print "$name: $values[0]\n";
        }
         // We search for the session cookie among the headers [Set-Cookie]
        foreach ($headers['set-cookie'] ?? [] as $cookie) {
            if (preg_match('/^PHPSESSID=(.+?);/', $cookie, $fields)) {
                $sessionCookie = "PHPSESSID=$fields[1]";
            }
        }
    }
     // display the latest response JSON from the server
    print "---Réponse du serveur : {$response->getContent()}\n";
} catch (ExceptionInterface $ex) {
     // display the error
    print "Erreur de communication avec le serveur : {$ex->getMessage()}\n";
    exit(2);
}

Comments

  • line 29: creation of the client HTTP;
  • line 31: the variable [$sessionCookie] will contain the session cookie, in the form [PHPSESSID=xxx]. Its value is [null] until the server sends it;
  • line 34: we will send the same request to the server 10 times: [session-server.php];
  • lines 36–38: If the session cookie is not yet known, we send the command [GET] without the header [Cookie];
  • lines 39–43: otherwise, we send the command [GET] with the header [Cookie]. The [headers] option of the [request] method is the array of HTTP headers to be added to the request;
  • Line 55: The web server may send multiple [Set-Cookie] headers. The session cookie is just one of them. It is uniquely formatted as [PHPSESSID=xxx; …]. If the response does not have a [Set-Cookie] header, the expression [$headers['set-cookie'] ?? []] returns an empty array, and the loop does nothing;
  • line 56: a regular expression is used to find the session cookie;
  • line 62: once the 10 requests have been made, the last response from the server, JSON, is displayed.

Note: The Symfony client [HttpClient] does not manage cookies from one request to the next on its own, which is why this code is included. Session cookie management will be handled in versions of the tax calculation application that use a session.

Results

Running the client script produces the following output (we are showing only the beginning and the end):

> php session-client.php
---Réponse avec statut : 200
---Entêtes de la réponse
date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:55:27 GMT
server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
x-powered-by: PHP/8.5.11
cache-control: max-age=0, private, must-revalidate
set-cookie: PHPSESSID=2dd2d2c53266ff4fb3eff4b943564f74; path=/
connection: close
content-type: application/json
---Réponse avec statut : 200
---Entêtes de la réponse
date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:55:27 GMT
server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
x-powered-by: PHP/8.5.11
cache-control: max-age=0, private, must-revalidate
connection: close
content-type: application/json

---Réponse avec statut : 200
---Entêtes de la réponse
date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:55:27 GMT
server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
x-powered-by: PHP/8.5.11
cache-control: max-age=0, private, must-revalidate
connection: close
content-type: application/json
---Réponse du serveur : {"N1":9,"N2":19,"N3":109}
  • In its first response, the server sends the session ID (header [set-cookie]). In subsequent responses, it no longer sends it;
  • Last line: the three counters [N1, N2, N3] were indeed incremented 9 times. They were initialized during request #1.

docs.title: 17.10.2.3. A version without HttpFoundation
docs.text:
The script [session-server-natif.php] performs the same task using only the functions from PHP:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// same as [session-server.php], but with only the functions from PHP

// session start—the options override the directives [session.*] from php.ini
session_start([
     // Rejects a session ID that the server did not create itself
    'use_strict_mode' => true,
     // The session cookie is inaccessible to the browser's JavaScript
    'cookie_httponly' => true,
     // The cookie is not sent in requests from other sites
    'cookie_samesite' => 'Lax',
]);
// The three counters and their initial values
foreach (["N1" => 0, "N2" => 10, "N3" => 100] as $compteur => $valeurInitiale) {
     // The counter is incremented if it is in the session; otherwise, it is created
    $_SESSION[$compteur] = isset($_SESSION[$compteur]) ? $_SESSION[$compteur] + 1 : $valeurInitiale;
}
// The response is the JSON of an array containing the three counters
header('Content-Type: application/json');
print json_encode([
    "N1" => $_SESSION["N1"],
    "N2" => $_SESSION["N2"],
    "N3" => $_SESSION["N3"],
], JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
  • Lines 8–15: session startup. Starting with PHP 7.0, the [session_start] function accepts an array of options: These are the [session.*] directives from the [php.ini] file, without their [session.] prefix. They apply only to the current request. Here, we enable strict mode and the [HttpOnly] and [SameSite] attributes of the session cookie, as described in the section on the [php.ini] file;
  • lines 17–19: We iterate through the array [compteur => valeur initiale]. For each counter, we increment it if it is in the session [$_SESSION]; otherwise, we add it to the session with its initial value;
  • line 22: the [Content-Type] header of the response;
  • line 23: the JSON document sent to the client.

We run the same client with the configuration [config-session-client-natif.json], which refers to this script: [php session-client.php config-session-client-natif.json]. Start of the display:

> php session-client.php config-session-client-natif.json
---Réponse avec statut : 200
---Entêtes de la réponse
date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:55:27 GMT
server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
x-powered-by: PHP/8.5.11
set-cookie: PHPSESSID=f2bf0d3a4e234d04ccc9e8900a2f83be; path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
expires: Thu, 19 Nov 1981 08:52:00 GMT
cache-control: no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate
pragma: no-cache
content-length: 25
content-type: application/json
  • The session cookie now has the attributes [HttpOnly] and [SameSite=Lax];
  • The headers [Expires], [Cache-Control], and [Pragma], set by PHP at the start of the session, prevent the response from being cached (directive [session.cache_limiter = nocache]).

The last line displayed is the same as before:

---Réponse du serveur : {"N1":9,"N2":19,"N3":109}

docs.title: 17.10.3.1. The server
docs.text:
The following example shows that you can also save the values of an array or an object to the session. We will place an object [Personne] in the session. The [Personne] class in the [scripts-web/07] folder is the same as the one in the JSON example in the [scripts-web/03] folder.

The server script [session-server.php] in the folder [scripts-web/07] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// dependencies
require_once __DIR__ . '/../../vendor/autoload.php';
// The class [Personne] must be known AVANT: the start of the session
require_once __DIR__ . '/Personne.php';

use Modèles\Personne;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Session\Session;

// the client session
$session = new Session();
$session->start();

// various data is managed in the session
// an array
if ($session->has("tableau")) {
     // the array is in the session—all its values are incremented
    $tableau = array_map(fn(int $valeur): int => $valeur + 1, $session->get("tableau"));
} else {
     // the array is not in the session—it is created
    $tableau = [0, 10, 100];
}
// the array is placed in the session
$session->set("tableau", $tableau);

// a dictionary
if ($session->has("assoc")) {
     // [assoc] is in the session—increment all its elements
    $assoc = $session->get("assoc");
    foreach ($assoc as $key => $value) {
        $assoc[$key] = $value + 1;
    }
} else {
     // [assoc] is not in the session—create it
    $assoc = ["un" => 0, "deux" => 10, "trois" => 100];
}
// [assoc] is added to the session
$session->set("assoc", $assoc);

// a Person object
if ($session->has("personne")) {
     // [personne] is in the session—increment its age
    $personne = $session->get("personne");
    $personne->setÂge($personne->âge + 1);
} else {
     // [personne] is not in the session—we create it
    $personne = new Personne(prénom: "Léonard", nom: "Hûche", âge: 0);
     // [personne] is added to the session
    $session->set("personne", $personne);
}

// The response is JSON
$response = new Response(
    content: json_encode([
        "tableau" => $tableau,
        "assoc" => $assoc,
        "personne" => $personne,
    ], JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR | JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE),
    headers: ['Content-Type' => 'application/json'],
);
$response->setCharset('UTF-8');

// sending the response
$response->send();

Comments

  • line 8: the [Personne] class must be loaded before the session starts: upon startup, PHP deserializes the objects placed in the session during previous requests, and it must therefore know their class;
  • Lines 15–16: The current session is retrieved and activated;
  • Lines 20–28: We manage an array [tableau] that has been placed in the session. With each new request, its elements are incremented by 1. The function [array_map] applies a function to each element of an array and returns the array of results. The function here is an arrow function, introduced with PHP 7.4: [fn(int $valeur): int => $valeur + 1];
  • lines 31–42: We manage an associative array [assoc] that is session-scoped. With each new request, its elements are incremented by 1;
  • lines 45–53: We manage a session-scoped object [Personne]. With each new request, this person’s age is incremented by 1. Note that it is not necessary to put the object back into the session after modifying it: the session contains a reference to this object, and it is the modified object that will be saved at the end of the script;
  • Lines 57–64: We send a response JSON to the client: the string JSON from an associative array.

Let’s request this script using a browser. The first two requests return the following results (F5 in the browser for the second one):

We can see that on the second request, all the counters have been incremented.

docs.title: 17.10.3.2. The client
docs.text:
The client is the same as in Example 1. We provide it only with the configuration file [config-session-client-07.json]:

Executing the command [php session-client.php config-session-client-07.json] produces the following results (start and end):

docs.title: 17.11. Authentication
docs.text:
We will now focus on web services intended for specific users only. The client must authenticate with the web service before receiving a response.

php8-oct-2026
├── scripts-console
│   └── clients-web
│       └── 08
│           ├── auth-client.php
│           ├── config-auth-client-https.json
│           ├── config-auth-client-https-verify.json
│           ├── config-auth-client-ko.json
│           ├── config-auth-client.json
│           └── config-espion.json
└── scripts-web
    └── 08
        └── auth-server.php

docs.title: 17.11.1. The client
docs.text:
The client [auth-client.php] is configured by the following file: JSON [config-auth-client.json]:

{
    "url": "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/08/auth-server.php",
    "user": "admin",
    "password": "admin"
}
  • Line 2: the URL of the web service;
  • Lines 3–4: the user credentials.

The client code [auth-client.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// Web service client with authentication

// dependencies
require_once __DIR__ . '/../../../vendor/autoload.php';

use Symfony\Component\HttpClient\HttpClient;
use Symfony\Contracts\HttpClient\Exception\ExceptionInterface;

// the configuration file: first command-line argument if it exists
$configFileName = $argv[1] ?? "config-auth-client.json";

// retrieve the configuration
if (!file_exists($configFileName)) {
    print "Le fichier de configuration [$configFileName] n'existe pas\n";
    exit(1);
}
try {
    $config = json_decode(file_get_contents($configFileName), true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
} catch (JsonException $ex) {
    print "Erreur lors de l'exploitation du fichier de configuration JSON [$configFileName] : {$ex->getMessage()}\n";
    exit(1);
}

// creating a client HTTP
$httpClient = HttpClient::create([
     // user credentials
    'auth_basic' => [$config['user'], $config['password']],
     // Should the server certificate (HTTPS) be verified? Yes by default
    'verify_peer' => $config['verify_peer'] ?? true,
    'verify_host' => $config['verify_host'] ?? true,
]);

try {
     // Send the request to the server
    $response = $httpClient->request('GET', $config['url']);
     // Response status
    $statusCode = $response->getStatusCode();
    print "---Réponse avec statut : $statusCode\n";
     // Retrieve the headers
    print "---Entêtes de la réponse\n";
    foreach ($response->getHeaders() as $name => $values) {
        print "$name: $values[0]\n";
    }
     // Displaying the server's response
    print "---Réponse du serveur : [{$response->getContent()}]\n";
} catch (ExceptionInterface $ex) {
     // display the error
    print "Erreur de communication avec le serveur : {$ex->getMessage()}\n";
    exit(2);
}

Comments

  • Lines 29–35: A parameter was passed to the static method [HttpClient::create]—an associative array of options that will apply to all requests from this client;
  • Line 31: The option [auth_basic] has a value of a two-element array, [user, password]. The client will use these elements to authenticate with the web service. The option [auth_basic] specifies an authentication type called [Basic], named after the value of the header HTTP [Authorization] that the client will send. There are other authentication types;
  • lines 33–34: two useful options for the HTTPS protocol, which we’ll cover a little later. They default to [true] if the configuration file does not specify otherwise;
  • Apart from this code, the client is identical to the previous ones.

To view the HTTP headers sent by the client, we connect it to our monitoring server, running on port 100, with the following [config-espion.json] configuration:

{
    "url": "http://localhost:100/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/08/auth-server.php",
    "user": "admin",
    "password": "admin"
}

The command [php auth-client.php config-espion.json] produces the following output in the spy server’s terminal:

> php spy-server.php 100
Serveur espion en attente d'un client sur le port 100
Client connecté : 127.0.0.1:50388
--- lignes reçues
GET /php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/08/auth-server.php HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:100
Accept: */*
Authorization: Basic YWRtaW46YWRtaW4=
User-Agent: Symfony HttpClient (Curl)
Accept-Encoding: gzip

--- fin de la communication
  • Line 8: We see the header [Authorization: Basic XXX] sent by the client. The string XXX is the Base64-encoded version of the string [user:password].

To verify this, you can decode the received string using the [base64_decode] function from PHP. The [-r] option of the [php] command executes the PHP code that follows it:

> php -r "echo base64_decode('YWRtaW46YWRtaW4='), PHP_EOL;"
admin:admin

Base64 encoding is not encryption: anyone can decode the string.

docs.title: 17.11.2. The server
docs.text:
The server [auth-server.php] is as follows:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// Dependencies
require_once __DIR__ . '/../../vendor/autoload.php';

use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;

// authorized users: login => password
$users = ["admin" => "admin"];
//
// retrieves the current request
$request = Request::createFromGlobals();
// the credentials sent by the client (null if none were sent)
$requestUser = $request->getUser();
$requestPassword = $request->getPassword();
// Does the user exist?
$trouvé = $requestUser !== null && $requestPassword !== null
    && array_key_exists($requestUser, $users)
    && hash_equals($users[$requestUser], $requestPassword);
// Prepare the response
$response = new Response();
// Set the response status code
if (!$trouvé) {
     // not found - code 401
    $response->setStatusCode(Response::HTTP_UNAUTHORIZED);
    $response->headers->set("WWW-Authenticate", 'Basic realm="PHP 8 par l\'exemple"');
} else {
     // Found - code 200
    $response->setStatusCode(Response::HTTP_OK);
}
// response has no content, only headers HTTP
$response->send();

Comments

  • line 12: authorized users—in this case, just one—with the login [admin] and password [admin];
  • line 17: the method [getUser] of the object [Request] returns the user ID, extracted by PHP from the [Authorization: Basic …] header sent by the client, or [null] if the client did not send that header. Without [HttpFoundation], it would be found in [$_SERVER['PHP_AUTH_USER']];
  • line 18: the same applies to the password ([$_SERVER['PHP_AUTH_PW']]);
  • lines 20–22: We search for the user attempting to log in in the list of authorized users. Passwords are compared using the function [hash_equals] rather than the operator [===]: its execution time does not depend on where the two strings differ, which prevents an attacker from guessing a password character by character by measuring response times;
  • lines 26–29: if the user has not been authenticated, the following is sent to the client:
    • the code [401 Unauthorized];
    • a [WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="quelque chose"] header. Browsers recognize this header and display an authentication window prompting the user to log in. HTTP headers must be written using only the characters ASCII. The PHP 7 script used the [utf8_decode] function to convert a string UTF-8 to ISO-8859-1; this function has been deprecated since PHP 8.2. If it were needed, we would use [mb_convert_encoding($texte, 'ISO-8859-1', 'UTF-8')]. Our text [PHP 8 par l'exemple] uses only the characters ASCII;
  • lines 30–32: if the user has been recognized, the code [200 OK] is sent to the client;
  • line 35: the response contains no document, only a status line and headers.

Let’s request URL [http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/08/auth-server.php] using a browser: the browser displays a login window. If incorrect credentials are entered, the browser displays this window indefinitely until the correct credentials are entered: each time, a round trip to the server occurs, always returning the same response, which triggers the browser’s authentication window. Here is the server’s response without credentials:

> curl -i http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/08/auth-server.php
HTTP/1.0 401 Unauthorized
Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:31:46 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.5.11
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="PHP 8 par l'exemple"
Connection: close
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
  • line 2: the code [401 Unauthorized] from the response;
  • the header HTTP [WWW-Authenticate] prompts the client to authenticate;
  • the body of the response is empty.

With the [-u admin:admin] option, [curl] sends the credentials [admin, admin]:

> curl -i -u admin:admin http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/08/auth-server.php
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:31:46 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.5.11
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
Vary: Accept-Encoding
Connection: close
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
  • line 2: the response code [200 OK];
  • the response body is empty.

Let’s run the client [auth-client.php] with the authorized user [admin, admin]. The server’s response is as follows:

> php auth-client.php
---Réponse avec statut : 200
---Entêtes de la réponse
date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:55:27 GMT
server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
x-powered-by: PHP/8.5.11
cache-control: no-cache, private
vary: Accept-Encoding
content-encoding: gzip
connection: close
content-type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
---Réponse du serveur : []
  • Line 2: The server responded with [200 OK];
  • Last line: The response has no content.

Now let's run the client with an incorrect password, using the configuration file [config-auth-client-ko.json]:

{
    "url": "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/08/auth-server.php",
    "user": "admin",
    "password": "x"
}

The response is as follows:

> php auth-client.php config-auth-client-ko.json
---Réponse avec statut : 401
---Entêtes de la réponse
Erreur de communication avec le serveur : HTTP/1.0 401 Unauthorized returned for "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/08/auth-server.php".
  • Line 2: The client successfully received a 401 code;
  • line 4: an exception was thrown in the client. It was thrown by the Symfony client [HttpClient]: it throws an exception of type [ClientExceptionInterface] (4xx codes) or [ServerExceptionInterface] (5xx codes) when the status code of the HTTP response indicates an error and the client attempts to read the response headers or content. The exception message shows that the server responded with [401 Unauthorized] to indicate that the user was not recognized. To read the headers or the body of a response that contains an error anyway, use [$response->getHeaders(false)] or [$response->getContent(false)]. We’ll use this in the tax calculation application, where the server returns a JSON error message along with its error codes.

docs.title: 17.11.2.1. When the server always responds with 401
docs.text:
With certain installations of [Apache], the server responds with [401 Unauthorized] to every request, even with the correct credentials. The cause is not the PHP script: it is the way [Apache] executes PHP. When PHP is a module of [Apache] (mod_php), it receives all the HTTP headers from the request. However, when [Apache] executes PHP in a separate process, according to the FastCGI protocol (modules [mod_fcgid] or [mod_proxy_fcgi]), and by default does not pass on to it the [Authorization] header containing the identifiers: for PHP, the client has never authenticated. For this reason, the [scripts-web] folder contains the following [.htaccess] file, which applies to all its subfolders:

# Pass the header HTTP [Authorization] to PHP (HTTP Basic authentication).
# When PHP is running as an Apache module (mod_php), PHP always receives it. But when
# PHP is executed by FastCGI (mod_fcgid, PHP-FPM...), Apache does not forward it via
# by default: the credentials sent by the client are then lost, and the server
# responds with a 401 to every request. The following two lines fix this.
CGIPassAuth On
SetEnvIf Authorization "(.*)" HTTP_AUTHORIZATION=$1
  • Line 6: instructs [Apache] (version 2.4.13 and later) to pass the [Authorization] header to the FastCGI programs;
  • line 7: a second, older method that copies the [Authorization] header into the [HTTP_AUTHORIZATION] environment variable. The Symfony [Request] class can read the identifiers from there.

With mod_php, these two lines have no effect. We verify that the server is receiving the credentials correctly with [curl], which does not store anything from one request to the next, unlike the browser: [curl -i -u admin:admin "http://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/08/auth-server.php"] should return a 200 status code. If the browser continues to display its authentication window, you must either close it completely (it retains rejected credentials for the entire session) or use an incognito window.

docs.title: 17.11.3. Securing the Client/Server Connection
docs.text:
We’ve seen that to authenticate with the server, the client sends the header:

Authorization: Basic YWRtaW46YWRtaW4=

If this line is intercepted by spyware, it can easily retrieve the [login, mot de passe] credentials encoded in Base64 within the string [YWRtaW46YWRtaW4=]. For this reason, authentication must take place over a secure connection between the client and the server. Secure URL connections use the [HTTPS] protocol instead of the HTTP protocol. The [HTTPS] protocol is the HTTP protocol within a client/server connection encrypted by the TLS protocol (Transport Layer Security, the successor to SSL). Secure URL connections take the form of [https://chemin_document]. The default port for the HTTPS protocol is port 443.

Not all web servers accept URL in this format; they must be configured to do so. The [Apache] server from [Laragon] supports the HTTPS protocol, but it is not enabled by default. You can enable it via the [Laragon] menu: right-click in the [Laragon] window, then select [Apache / SSL / Enabled]. The [Apache] server is then restarted, and the [Laragon] window shows that it is now listening on two ports: port 80 (HTTP) and port 443 (HTTPS). During this activation, [Laragon] generated a so-called self-signed certificate for the server.

Web browsers, on the other hand, reject self-signed certificates by default. With a certificate that is simply unknown, [Chrome] and [Edge] display a warning page (“Your connection is not private”) with a button [Paramètres avancés] followed by a link [Continuer vers localhost (dangereux)]. However, this link is not always provided: it is notably missing when the certificate is deemed non-compliant, or when the browser has cached that the site [localhost] should always be served as HTTPS with a valid certificate (mechanism HSTS). The correct solution is then to trust the certificate for [Laragon]:

  • in the [Laragon] menu, select [Apache / SSL / Add laragon.crt to Trust Store]. [Windows] prompts you to confirm adding the certificate to the user’s trusted root certificate authorities; accept;
  • close the browser completely (all its windows) and restart it: [Chrome] and [Edge] use the certificate store of [Windows], and the certificate for [Laragon] is now accepted without a warning for [https://localhost];
  • if the browser still rejects the page, delete the HSTS rule that it may have cached for [localhost]: open the page [chrome://net-internals/#hsts] (or [edge://net-internals/#hsts] for [Edge]), type [localhost] into the [Delete domain security policies] field and click on [Delete].

As a last resort, and only on your own computer, [Chrome] and [Edge] will allow you to bypass the warning if you type, on the error page itself (without clicking in an input field), the words [thisisunsafe]. This is a browser workaround intended for developers: never use it on a site you do not control. If none of these methods work, use the URL [http://localhost/...] in the browser: we’ll see in the chapter on Version 8 of the tax calculation why this isn’t reckless on your own machine.

Adding the certificate to the [Windows] store does not affect our PHP clients: the [curl] library, which PHP uses, has its own list of certificate authorities. This is illustrated in the following example.

Now that we have a secure server, let’s provide the [auth-client.php] client with the following configuration file, [config-auth-client-https-verify.json]:

{
    "url": "https://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/08/auth-server.php",
    "user": "admin",
    "password": "admin"
}
  • Line 2: The protocol has become [https]. The port is not specified; the default is port 443.

Let’s run the client with this configuration. The console output is as follows:

> php auth-client.php config-auth-client-https-verify.json
Erreur de communication avec le serveur : SSL certificate problem: self-signed certificate for "https://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/08/auth-server.php".

The Symfony client [HttpClient] threw an exception because it did not accept the certificate sent by the server. The TLS connection relies on certificates issued by recognized certificate authorities. The certificate generated by [Laragon] is a self-signed certificate: it is not validated by any certificate authority. The client therefore rejected it, and rightly so: there is no proof that it is communicating with the real server and not an imposter.

It is possible to instruct [HttpClient] not to verify the certificate sent by the server. This is done using the [verify_peer] and [verify_host] options of the [HttpClient::create] method, which our client reads from its configuration file. The [config-auth-client-https.json] file sets them to [false]:

{
    "url": "https://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/08/auth-server.php",
    "user": "admin",
    "password": "admin",
    "verify_peer": false,
    "verify_host": false
}
  • Line 5: Do not verify that the certificate was issued by a recognized certificate authority;
  • line 6: do not verify that the certificate was issued for the machine being contacted ([localhost] in this case).

We had already encountered this problem in the previous chapter, with the [libcurl] library and its [CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER] option. The Symfony client [HttpClient] is actually a [curl] client when the [curl] extension is enabled in the PHP configuration, as is the case here: the class instantiated by [HttpClient::create] is then [CurlHttpClient], which translates its options into [curl] options: [verify_peer] becomes [CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER], and [verify_host] becomes [CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST].

If we now run the client with the command [php auth-client.php config-auth-client-https.json], we get the following result:

> php auth-client.php config-auth-client-https.json
---Réponse avec statut : 200
---Entêtes de la réponse
date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:55:27 GMT
server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
x-powered-by: PHP/8.5.11
cache-control: no-cache, private
vary: Accept-Encoding
content-encoding: gzip
connection: close
content-type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
---Réponse du serveur : []

The user was successfully recognized. With [curl], the option [-k] (or [--insecure]) serves the same purpose as our two options:

> curl -i -k -u admin:admin https://localhost/php8-oct-2026/scripts-web/08/auth-server.php
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:31:46 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.58 (Ubuntu)
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.5.11
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
Vary: Accept-Encoding
Connection: close
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8

Note: Disabling certificate verification is only acceptable during development, on your own machine. A cleaner solution is to specify the server’s certificate to the client using the [cafile] option of [HttpClient] (or the [--cacert] option of [curl]): verification remains enabled, and the client accepts that specific certificate. In production, the server has a certificate issued by a recognized certificate authority (for example, free of charge from Let’s Encrypt), and no option is required.

Now we know how to authenticate with a secure server.
